articles.title: Hollywood Needs a New Pixar
articles.author: Alvy Ray Smith and co-authors
articles.description: Pixar's co-founder argues Hollywood is repeating its old mistake with AI and creator platforms — and lays out what the studios must do instead, with the Disney-Pixar partnership as the model.
articles.body:
Hollywood earned its cultural monopoly by absorbing radical technologies that it first resisted — sound, colour, computer graphics — and the piece argues that AI and creator platforms are the next such technology, and that the industry is mishandling them. Most of the conversation about AI in film revolves around cost savings and artists being displaced, the authors say; those issues matter, but they miss a bigger shift. Ask a teenager where their favourite characters come from, and the answer is as likely to be a creator platform — YouTube, Roblox, TikTok — as a Hollywood studio. Unless moviemakers evolve, they risk losing their place at the centre of culture.

The argument runs through the Pixar precedent. Silicon Valley and Hollywood went through a version of this before, during the early partnership between Pixar and Disney that was crucial to Pixar's success: Disney storytellers gave Pixar pointed feedback on early characters, leading John Lasseter, Pete Docter and the rest of the brain trust to take screenwriting classes, and Pixar did not believe technical people were any less creative than artists. Disney did not produce Toy Story by hiring more CGI artists into its 2-D pipeline; it partnered with Pixar, whose mission was to make movies with the new technology, and eventually acquired it. The Disney-Pixar relationship worked, the authors stress, because Bob Iger gave Pixar co-founder Ed Catmull real power over Disney Animation — other Hollywood acquisitions of gaming studios or creator talent have struggled when the acquired company lacked similar authority.

Something similar needs to happen now, the piece argues, but the rise of creator culture will make the transition harder: during the shift to computer animation the distribution formats stayed the same, while today format, distribution and production technology are changing all at once. YouTube made more than $60 billion last year, about $15 billion more than Netflix brought in, and studios are already adapting creator-platform properties — Backrooms cost about $10 million and collected more than $400 million, Obsession cost under $1 million and made over $520 million, and the Minecraft movie made almost $1 billion, a fraction of the game's $10-12 billion. The prescription is a fundamental shift: studios should stop treating YouTube, Roblox and TikTok as farm systems and start developing stories and characters with audience input, the way creators do — putting out drafts, iterating, using data to find audiences for ambitious work. AI did not cause the shift to creator platforms, but it will accelerate it, and the first 'Toy Story moment' for AI — a work whose artistic appeal makes the technology almost beside the point — may not be far away.

articles.title: Jesse Eisenberg Can't Help Overthinking It
articles.author: Rachel Syme
articles.description: A warm, funny profile of the actor-director at his most neurotic — including the fact that he gave a kidney to a stranger — and a portrait of a fame he insists he doesn't have.
articles.body:
Jesse Eisenberg is what the profile calls 'a real character' — hyperverbal, relentlessly self-deprecating, visibly anxious, often to the point where his whole body shakes, 'like a dachshund in a thunderstorm.' He writes and directs comedic films, three so far, that are character studies of quirky, neurotic people whose drama is almost entirely self-created. His third, 'The Debut,' out next month, stars Julianne Moore as a meek, middle-aged housewife in 1990s New Jersey who gets a part in a dumb musical and treats it like Raging Bull — the pitch, as Eisenberg first framed it to studios, was 'what would take place if a lady gets a part in a dumb musical and treats it like Raging Bull?'

The piece is built from the small, telling details of a life lived at war with itself. Eisenberg, 43, owns four pairs of trousers, wears the same scuffed tennis shoes, rumpled T-shirt and fraying red Indiana University baseball cap every day, and lives with his wife Anna Strout — a non-profit organiser and New York City public-school teacher — and their ten-year-old son Banner in a modest two-bedroom near Washington Square Park. He has been in and out of therapy since childhood for obsessive-compulsive disorder and generalised anxiety, and he finds relief in talking about his struggles and listening to others'. He has written twenty-five Shouts & Murmurs pieces for The New Yorker ('But I sent double that,' he notes), and his wife's verdict, quoted in the piece, is that 'he is sincerely interested in the health update on his makeup artist's third cousin's cat.'

The most startling fact in the profile is the kidney. Last December, Eisenberg gave one of his kidneys to a stranger. He got the idea a decade earlier from a podcast about altruistic organ donation — 'it felt so clean to me,' he says — sent off a saliva sample, heard nothing, and then a doctor told him he could simply walk over to NYU hospital and offer an organ. He scheduled the operation for the first available weekend after closing an Off Broadway one-man show he had written. Kieran Culkin, quoted in the piece, says he plans to hold on to both his kidneys, 'but, when you hear Jesse's reasoning, you gotta admit, Oh, shit, he's right.' The profile's argument is that the donation is the apotheosis of Eisenberg's urge to carbon-offset the advantages of fame — the same impulse that made him agree to appear on Millionaire with Paul Giamatti, win half a million dollars and give his share to Middle Way House, a shelter where he and Strout have volunteered. He is, the piece concludes, a very famous person who frantically insists he is not a typical individual, and the tension between those two facts is the engine of his work.

articles.title: AI Told These Ex-Google Guys How to Build a Billion-Dollar Weapons Business
articles.author: Isabella Ward
articles.description: Two Silicon Valley veterans used an AI model to design their way into the arms trade — and built a $1B+ company making artillery shells for Ukraine. A dispatch from the new military-industrial complex.
articles.body:
When Silicon Valley entrepreneur Chad Steelberg decided he wanted to get involved in the war in Ukraine, he had no idea where to start. So the former CEO of enterprise AI company Veritone did what he knew best: he built an artificial intelligence model to help him figure it out. Today he has proprietary munition and missile designs, several government partnerships, and a defence-as-a-service business valued at more than $1 billion. His firm, Tiberius Aerospace, announced this week it had secured $85 million in Series A financing, led by Lakestar and Rochefort Asset Management, with Ukrainian venture capital firm UA1 also investing.

Steelberg, alongside fellow Google alumnus and former Apple executive Andy Baynes, says they are trying to break the Russia-Ukraine war's 'stalemate,' Silicon Valley-style — applying the rapid iteration they learned building software companies and designing iPhones to a business that has historically moved at the speed of government procurement. Steelberg started itching to 'make a difference' after taking in a couple hundred Ukrainian refugees at his French chateau in early 2022, and he is candid about the profit motive: 'I believe I could really change the outcome of this and every war,' he tells WIRED. 'I'm not saying this is purely altruistic. Of course we're going to be making money doing it.'

The AI model they built quickly ruled out building better defensive technology, because that would only harden the stalemate, and told them to build longer-range artillery munitions instead — 'Don't build another drone,' it suggested. The resulting system, called Sceptre, can be fired from a standard 155-millimeter howitzer, the most common artillery weapon donated to Ukraine, and the company claims it travels farther, reaches supersonic speeds and flies beyond jamming range. In April, Tiberius successfully fired a Sceptre projectile from a NATO-standard howitzer for the first time, and it has announced a $500 million technology collaboration contract with UK partners to manufacture, license and distribute the munition; it is also developing a missile. The AI system itself has become a product called GRAIL, which Steelberg hopes will let Tiberius continuously upgrade the weapon designs it licenses by decentralising manufacturing — copying, as Baynes puts it, 'the Apple model' of outsourcing production to third-party subcontractors. The piece's quiet question is whether Silicon Valley's greatest skill — moving fast — is a virtue or a danger when the product is a weapon.

articles.title: A Star on Planet Earth
articles.author: Mark Guiducci
articles.description: Vanity Fair's Holiday cover story has become a story in itself: 90 minutes with a famously guarded Timothée Chalamet, in the editor's own apartment, with more decor than disclosure.
articles.body:
The cover story began with an unusual arrangement. Timothée Chalamet, Vanity Fair's Holiday 2026 cover star, asked that the magazine's global editorial director, Mark Guiducci — not normally a writer — pen the profile himself, and agreed to just 90 minutes of conversation, held in Guiducci's own one-bedroom apartment in the East 60s, because, as Guiducci explains, Chalamet 'can't go many places in public.' The actor arrived carrying a white paper deli bag, 'starving,' unfurled a Lenwich Italiano at the dining table and devoured it in under two minutes; he wanted New York City tap water, no ice, and Channel Orange playing in the background.

What followed was, by the magazine's own admission, a portrait of a star determined to say very little. Chalamet prefaced no fewer than seven answers by saying he did not want to sound 'pretentious,' declined to discuss his relationship with Kylie Jenner, and answered some questions with 'Okay, pass' or 'I'm going to pull a Frank Ocean and be mysterious.' Guiducci, comparing him in his editor's letter to Marlon Brando and Leonardo DiCaprio, observed that with such stars 'the bigger they get, the less they open their mouth.' The profile became, to the amusement and scorn of online readers, as much a tour of Guiducci's apartment — white walls, black floors, bodega flowers, a French poster for The Graduate, a picture of Edie Sedgwick in the bathroom — as a portrait of its subject.

Still, the piece contains real material. Chalamet is reading The AGI Chronicles, Kevin Roose's book on the sprint to artificial general intelligence, and notes that its first four chapters track the plot of Artificial, Luca Guadagnino's Sam Altman biopic; he recommended it to Marty Supreme director Josh Safdie, who says it 'helped with anxiety.' He discusses Dune: Part Three at length — a film whose scale he says is 'even bigger than The Odyssey's,' with production design drawing on the samurai, SEAL Team 6, the Roman Empire by way of the Third Reich, Islamic extremism, the Russian Orthodox Church, the Bedouins and the Asaro mud men of Papua New Guinea, and ancient Egypt above all. He shaved his famous curls for the role, reasoning that world leaders — 'everyone good and bad' — do not waste time on their hair. And he names the four films and one play that shaped the Iceland cover shoot: Terrence Malick's The Tree of Life, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, Cloud Atlas, Withnail and I, and Koyaanisqatsi. The profile's accidental achievement is to capture the central fact of modern stardom: at 30, famous his entire adult life, Chalamet knows that a single comment in Vanity Fair could 'ricochet around the pinball machine of the internet,' and he has decided the safest performance is silence.

articles.title: The Making of My Chemical Romance's 'The Black Parade'
articles.author: Brian Hiatt
articles.description: Twenty years on, producer Rob Cavallo tells the wild story behind one of rock's last great concept albums — a haunted mansion, night terrors, 159 tracks and Liza Minnelli.
articles.body:
My Chemical Romance did not waste a minute of their abbreviated recording career, and on their third try in the studio they made one of rock's last great concept albums: 2006's The Black Parade, described by Rolling Stone as 'Tommy in a white belt and eyeliner.' The album has just surged from No. 139 to No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — the band's first career chart-topper, twenty years after release — and producer Rob Cavallo, who also worked on much of Green Day's discography, sat down with Rolling Stone's Brian Hiatt to tell the story of how it was made.

It began, Cavallo says, with a song. The band played him a few things at SIR in freezing-cold New York, but the one that blew his mind was 'Mama': 'I remember just jumping off the couch just going, Oh, my God, you guys. That is so great and original.' He could tell the band was operating on a higher conceptual level, and they chose him as producer a couple of hours after that first meeting — helped, he admits, by the fact that he had just made American Idiot, a record of similar ambition. The band then decamped to the Paramour Mansion in Silver Lake, a sprawling estate previously used by Fiona Apple and Gwen Stefani, to live and write together. The mansion lacked reliable heating and cell-phone reception, and the local rumours that it was haunted began to manifest psychologically: Gerard Way suffered debilitating night terrors that he recorded on a portable device and later embedded into the bridge of 'Sleep,' while bassist Mikey Way confronted extreme anxiety and sleep deprivation and briefly stepped away to preserve his mental health. Cavallo remembers the house as 'absolutely haunted and freezing,' a living room with no heat where the team set up a PA and hung microphones to capture the room live in stereo.

The record was about 90 to 95 percent written by the time they left the Paramour, with one famous exception: 'Welcome to the Black Parade' itself, which had existed since the band's inception under the demo title 'The Five of Us Are Dying' and failed to make their first two albums. It was only when they recalibrated the tempo with an urgent punk beat and altered a single crucial note in the chorus melody that Gerard unlocked the anthem. The scale of the production was staggering: mixer Chris Lord-Alge received an initial session of 159 tracks, including 26 separate stems of marching snares, orchestral arrangements and stacked guitars, which had to be consolidated to 44 for the final mix. And then there was 'Mama': wanting a theatrical, vaudevillian presence for the character of Mother War, the band sought Liza Minnelli, and Cavallo arranged the connection directly — she agreed to contribute her guest vocal entirely free of charge. The band promises new music soon, but the piece's real subject is how a group of New Jersey punks, a haunted house and a veteran producer made a monument that refused to compromise on emotional stakes.

articles.title: Venezuela's Collaborator-in-Chief
articles.author: Jon Lee Anderson
articles.description: Jon Lee Anderson, The New Yorker's veteran Latin America correspondent, on Delcy Rodríguez — the woman at the centre of Venezuela's government as US pressure mounts — and what he calls the new American imperialism.
articles.body:
The New Yorker's Letter from Caracas turns to Delcy Rodríguez, the figure at the centre of Venezuela's government, and to the pressure the country now faces from the United States. Anderson, who has covered Latin America for the magazine for decades, frames the piece around Rodríguez's rise and the role she has come to play — not merely as a minister or functionary, but as the collaborator-in-chief of a government under siege, managing its relationship with Washington and its survival at home.

The argument of the piece, as its framing suggests, is that the current American approach to Venezuela amounts to a new imperialism — not the gunboat diplomacy of the last century, but a modern form of pressure built from sanctions, seizures, threats and the assertion of American power over a sovereign neighbour. Rodríguez sits at the hinge of that story: the person who must negotiate with, defy and accommodate the United States at the same time, while holding together a government whose legitimacy Washington contests. Anderson's reporting from Caracas examines how she exercises that power, who she answers to, and what her prominence reveals about the way Venezuela is actually governed — through a small circle around the presidency rather than through institutions.

The piece lands at a moment when Venezuela is back at the centre of American foreign-policy debate, and its value is in the reporting rather than the polemic: Anderson's long acquaintance with the country lets him show, rather than assert, how power works there now. For readers who have followed the headlines — the sanctions, the oil, the migration, the threats — it is the reported account of the woman managing the crisis from the inside, and of what the new American pressure campaign looks like from the receiving end.

articles.title: New estimate of Russian military deaths in Ukraine to be published tonight
articles.description: Meduza, Mediazona and more than a dozen other independent newsrooms have analysed leaked Russian mortality data obtained from the hacker groups "Cyber Partisans of Belarus" and others, and will publish a new estimate of Russian military deaths in Ukraine tonight, after 5 p.m. CET. The project aims to give an independent death toll up to autumn 2026, based on Rosstat mortality records rather than official statements. It is one of the most closely watched independent casualty counts of the war.
articles.body: Meduza, Mediazona and more than a dozen other journalistic teams have spent months analysing leaked Russian mortality data, and will present the results of their independent analysis tonight, after 5 p.m. CET on November 23. The data comes from a leak of Rosstat (Russia's state statistics service) mortality records obtained from the hacker groups "Cyber Partisans of Belarus" and others. The new estimate will cover Russian military deaths in Ukraine up to autumn 2026, offering an independent check on a toll Moscow does not publish. Previous joint investigations by Meduza and Mediazona, based on obituaries, probate records and excess-mortality modelling, have put confirmed Russian deaths far above official figures and estimated total deaths in the hundreds of thousands. The timing matters: the estimate lands as diplomacy around the war intensifies, with a Trump-Putin-Xi declaration in Shenzhen and talk of four-party negotiations before Christmas. For Ukraine and its partners, a credible casualty figure is both a measure of the war's cost to Russia and a data point in assessing how long Moscow can sustain its offensive. The findings will be published jointly by the participating newsrooms this evening.

articles.title: Russia attacked Ukraine's energy sector 100 times in a week; Odesa may be without power for up to three weeks
articles.description: Russia carried out 100 targeted attacks on Ukraine's energy and oil-and-gas infrastructure over the past week, causing 224 recorded incidents of damage, the Energy Ministry said on November 23. Parts of seven regions were without power in the morning, and Odesa — in blackout for a third day — may remain without electricity for up to three weeks after strikes damaged the power line from the South Ukraine nuclear plant. The ministry says Russia is deliberately re-attacking facilities that have already been repaired.
articles.body: Russia launched 100 attacks against Ukraine's energy, oil and gas infrastructure over the past week, leaving consumers without electricity in seven regions, Ukraine's Energy Ministry reported on Monday, November 23. First Deputy Energy Minister Artem Nekrasov told a briefing that the ministry recorded 224 incidents of damage to energy, oil and gas facilities over the same period. As of the morning of November 23, parts of Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Zhytomyr, Odesa, Poltava, Sumy and Kharkiv regions were without power. The situation remains worst in Odesa and Dnipropetrovsk regions, where Russian strikes caused extensive damage to energy facilities. Odesa has been in blackout since the weekend, with severe problems not only with electricity but also water and heating; Forbes reported the city could remain without power for up to three weeks after strikes damaged the transmission line from the South Ukraine nuclear power plant, knocking out three pylons. In Dnipro, a fresh blackout on November 23 stopped the metro and electric transport, with four energy facilities attacked and more than 350,000 households left without power. Across most of Ukraine, hourly outage schedules are in effect, with industrial power restrictions in place. Nekrasov said the attacks were "deliberate" and noted that Russian forces are repeatedly striking facilities that have already been repaired, while constant air raids slow repair crews. A separate strike on gas infrastructure in Dnipropetrovsk region injured three workers, two with concussions and one seriously. President Zelenskyy said Russia has changed tactics to target power grids and transmission lines specifically, aiming to cut Odesa and Dnipro off from energy sources entirely.

articles.title: Pirates begin porting GTA VI to PC after key executable file leaks
articles.description: Hackers from the Cyberleek group published a working Xbox Series X|S build of GTA VI on November 19, deliberately omitting the main executable file — but on November 23 that file was also posted online. At least three pirate teams are now studying the build to make the console version run on PC, with the hackers claiming a working port could be achieved within a week. The prospect of an unofficial PC port arriving before Rockstar's own is a serious challenge for Rockstar and Take-Two, which has not said how it will respond.
articles.body: On November 19 the hacker group Cyberleek published a working build of Grand Theft Auto VI for Xbox Series X|S, with the main executable file intentionally removed; on November 23 that missing file appeared online too. That executable is exactly what the pirate community was waiting for, and according to Notebookcheck at least three teams immediately began studying the build to work out how far and how fast they can get the console version running on PC — the hackers claim a playable result is possible within a week. Before launch, pirates had focused on the PlayStation 5, hoping to extract files from a jailbroken console, but Sony released several mandatory system updates just before the premiere and prevented a quick leak; instead the hackers obtained the Xbox build, dated November 2026, by unknown means, raising questions about Rockstar's security. Experts believe the Xbox version may actually be quicker to adapt than a PS5 one, because Xbox Series X|S processors and modern gaming PCs share the same architecture, so much of the code uses an instruction set both platforms understand — though the pirates still face serious work, since Xbox graphics output relies on specialised console software. The risk for Rockstar and Take-Two is that an unofficial PC port could appear before the publisher's own PC release. Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick was asked about piracy days before launch and acknowledged the publisher would have to strengthen its games' technical protection and legal measures; after the first Cyberleek gameplay leaks, Take-Two's lawyers went to court to identify the group via Discord records, but the results were never disclosed, and it is unknown how the company will react to the port effort. Take-Two previously demanded pirates stop porting GTA V to the original Switch.

articles.title: Nvidia's $1.5 trillion boardroom blunder helped bring Jensen Huang back
articles.description: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday, less than two weeks after accepting his resignation — but the drama cost the company $1.5 trillion in market value since the scandal erupted on November 8. CNN's analysis says the crisis was made possible by the board's own failures: no chair, no succession plan and almost no oversight of a CEO who said he built the company so only he could run it. Governance experts call it a complete failure of corporate governance, with one Yale professor saying "the board should resign, every one of them" — even as Wall Street cheers Huang's return.
articles.body: Nvidia's intense boardroom drama, in which Jensen Huang was ousted and brought back in the span of less than two weeks, would not have been possible without questionable decisions by the company's directors, CNN reports — and now the board faces intense scrutiny over its role in a corporate saga with enormous consequences. While Wall Street loves the return of Huang at the helm, corporate governance experts are horrified by what they view as malpractice: with no chair prior to Huang's ouster, no succession plan and the loosest of leashes on its CEO, the board had set itself up to fail. Huang said he built the company so that he alone could run it — and the stock acted that way, losing $1.5 trillion in market value since the scandal erupted on November 8. An outpouring of support from investors and partners followed, and a shareholder revolt seemed imminent. The board, consisting of many long-tenured Huang supporters, announced its decision to reinstate Huang on Monday, after the same board unanimously accepted his resignation — and directors are bringing him back before the completion of a board-ordered investigation into allegations over whether Huang has been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort." President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he called the board and helped orchestrate Huang's return, putting directors in a no-win scenario: stand pat and risk being ousted, or give in and appear weak. Huang stands accused of serious violations of corporate policy, having acknowledged an affair after reports of a relationship with a major customer, and reportedly being in a relationship with an employee; the board said Monday that US government officials assured them rehiring Huang posed no national security risk, though the investigation continues. "The board should resign. Every one of them," said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. "This is a complete failure of corporate governance." Other experts agreed the board could have avoided the debacle by putting Huang on leave pending the investigation, and noted that most well-run companies have an emergency succession plan — there is no evidence Nvidia had one. The scandal also fed a market meltdown so severe that some suggested the AI bubble was popping before our eyes.

articles.title: UPDATE: Trump pauses Army's planned detonation of hazardous material in Iowa
articles.description: President Donald Trump has weighed in for the first time on the Army's plan to blow up nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, ordering the military not to proceed until the Eighth Circuit court agrees it can go forward — and making the decision subject to incoming Governor-elect Rob Sand agreeing to the operation. The intervention came Monday afternoon, two days before the detonation was scheduled, after a federal judge had already temporarily paused the EPA permit. Trump also warned he would hold Sand responsible if the material explodes spontaneously after being blocked.
articles.body: President Donald Trump intervened on Monday for the first time in the controversy over blowing up five tons of hazardous material at a military outpost in Iowa, saying he is temporarily overruling the Army's decision to carry out the detonation on Wednesday. "I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation," Trump wrote on Truth Social. The post came two days before the Army had said it would use explosives to destroy storage containers filled with unstable lead azide, whether or not a pending appeal to reinstate its EPA permit was granted. Trump added that if Sand or the courts do not agree, "we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation." Sand had written on X on Sunday that because of "decisions that have already been made over the course of months, if not years, no good options exist and the situation is more dangerous and unpredictable than it ever should have been." The lead azide, a volatile compound used to detonate munitions, has been stored for years at the World War II-era Iowa Army Ammunition Plant near Middletown, a town of about 400 people, on a site spanning roughly 19,000 acres. Long-term storage allowed the material to recrystallise inside its containers, making it vulnerable to spontaneous detonation — especially in freezing temperatures, according to the Army. The Army notified the EPA around March 12, explored alternatives including a chemical neutralisation contract with MuniRem Environmental that it cancelled two months later, and concluded controlled detonation was the only safe treatment. The EPA issued a permit effective November 13 authorising the detonation, but the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club won an emergency stay from a judge on Thursday, less than 20 hours before the planned blast, arguing it could expose residents to toxic lead. The Army had postponed the operation from November 20 to November 23, then to November 24, and on Sunday said it would detonate on Wednesday for optimal weather — while the Justice Department asked the appeals court to lift the pause. The government argues the choice is between a planned detonation and an unplanned explosion at any moment, and says EPA rules let the Army proceed without a permit in an emergency; environmental groups counter that no evidence of an emergency has been published.

articles.title: UPDATE: San Francisco braces for near-record tides as storm collides with Thanksgiving travel
articles.description: San Francisco Bay could rise to near-record levels this week as a strong storm meets some of the year's highest tides, with the National Weather Service issuing a rare coastal flood warning from Monday through Thanksgiving Day and the highest water expected Wednesday morning — 8.5 feet, inches shy of the 1983 record of 8.82 feet. Mayor Daniel Lurie called the situation "extremely serious," urged residents to avoid non-essential travel from Monday afternoon through Wednesday, and opened the city's emergency operations centre. Both SFO and Oakland airports sit on low-lying land by the bay, and Waymo has paused Bay Area service.
articles.body: San Francisco Bay could rise to near-record levels this week, as a strong storm coupled with some of the year's highest tides moves ashore, threatening to flood city streets and a major West Coast airport on some of the busiest travel days of the year. The National Weather Service issued a rare coastal flood warning for Monday through Thanksgiving Day, with peak flooding around each morning's high tide, and the highest water expected Wednesday. Water levels may reach as much as 2.8 feet above a normal high tide, approaching the record set in 1983, Dylan Flynn, a lead meteorologist with the National Weather Service's San Francisco Bay Area office, told CNN. As of Monday, forecasters expect water levels to reach 8.5 feet during Wednesday morning's high tide, inches shy of the 1983 record of 8.82 feet, though city officials are preparing for tides exceeding 9 feet. "We could see water at Ocean Beach reach all the way to the seawall," Mayor Daniel Lurie said. The threat is a stack of factors: a cold front stronger than the storms of the past few days, king tides, and El Niño, which alone accounts for about a foot of extra water — ocean water off the coast is in the mid-60s, about 10 degrees above normal. Since early October, tides have run at least a foot above predictions and more than 2 feet higher during some storms. As holiday flyers fill airports, travel disruption is a key concern: SFO handled more than 1.8 million passengers in the 12 days around Thanksgiving last year, and Oakland-San Francisco Bay Airport expects about 250,000 this year, and both sit on low-lying land right along the bay. SFO says drainage areas are clear, pump stations are in top condition, sandbags and portable flood barriers are staged, and backup pumps are ready; Oakland recently finished raising and seismically reinforcing its perimeter dike and has tested its pump systems. The city's mayor warned residents to rethink holiday plans: "I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential starting Monday afternoon and going into Wednesday afternoon." The city opened its emergency operations centre, the Port is deploying flood barriers and pumps, transit agency SFMTA is preparing for disruptions along the Embarcadero, and city workers handed out 10,000 sandbags in a single day. Waymo proactively paused service across the Bay Area and will gradually resume once conditions improve. A high surf warning is in effect for Wednesday along the Pacific coast, with 20- to 30-foot breaking waves at Ocean Beach. The US Coast Guard warned tides could run 1 to 2 feet above normal, the highest predicted in 18 years, and noted another round of high tides is expected December 22–25, expected to be the highest of the season. Sea level is rising about 2 millimetres a year near San Francisco, Flynn said — not much year to year, but over the 40-plus years since the 1983 record it adds up to several inches, so it no longer takes as strong a storm to reach the same water level. Flynn expects the 1983 record to hold, but only just: "We probably won't break that record. We'll be close."

articles.title: EVEN launches Day & Date Vinyl service, cutting vinyl timelines "from months to weeks"
articles.description: Direct-to-fan platform EVEN has launched Day & Date Vinyl, a service announced Monday (Nov 23) that lets artists release vinyl alongside new and catalog albums with as little as two weeks' notice. Artists face no upfront costs, no minimum orders and no inventory risk, and qualifying sales can count toward first-week chart performance in the US and UK. The first release is Windmill, the new album from former NCT member Mark Lee, out December 4.
articles.body: Direct-to-fan platform EVEN has launched Day & Date Vinyl, a product it says lets artists release vinyl alongside new and catalog albums with as little as two weeks' notice, the company announced on Monday, November 23. The offering is available exclusively for releases on EVEN STUDIO, the white-label artist storefront product EVEN launched in September. The first release to use it is Windmill, the new album from singer and former NCT member Mark Lee, out December 4 via Upper Room, the label Lee co-founded in June after leaving SM Entertainment in April. According to EVEN, artists and their teams face no upfront costs, no minimum order quantities and no inventory risk, and records ship by street date, meaning qualifying sales can count toward first-week chart performance in the US and UK under applicable chart rules. EVEN says it produces only as many records as fans order and ships them to more than 90 countries and territories, with partners setting their own prices and receiving fan data from every sale. At launch the product is limited to 12-inch black lathe-cut vinyl in multiple variants, each with its own artwork, tracklist or bonus tracks. EVEN contrasts the model with traditional vinyl manufacturing, which it says can take 10 to 12 weeks or longer and requires teams to predict demand and pay for stock before taking a single order. The company points to demand evidence including J. Cole's The Fall-Off campaign, where vinyl was 71% of first-week sales, and notes US vinyl sales rose 8.6% to 47.9 million units last year, the format's 19th consecutive year of growth.

articles.title: Summer Walker files $20 million cross-complaint against Interscope
articles.description: Summer Walker filed a $20 million cross-complaint against Interscope Records on November 18, alleging breach of contract and claiming the label collected revenue from independently created videos and digital content she says belong to her. Rolling Stone obtained the 10-page filing and first reported it on November 19. The countersuit escalates a dispute that began when Walker gave notice in August that she was terminating her 2017 recording agreement.
articles.body: Summer Walker has filed a $20 million cross-complaint against Interscope Records, alleging breach of contract and escalating her legal battle with the label. Walker filed the cross-complaint on Wednesday evening, November 18, in response to Interscope's $50 million lawsuit over her attempt to terminate a recording agreement she signed in 2017, when she was 19. Rolling Stone obtained the 10-page filing and first reported it on November 19. Walker alleges that under the contract, Interscope's rights to her name, image and likeness were limited to promotional use, but the company collected revenue from audiovisual recordings, digital content and assets tied to her personal YouTube channel, which she claims breaches the agreement. She is seeking at least $20 million in damages for breach of contract, plus an accounting and recovery of profits allegedly earned from those assets, and asks the court to declare the deal became unenforceable in summer 2026, when she gave notice, and to confirm she owns the disputed material. Walker invoked California's seven-year rule to terminate the deal, notifying Interscope she would stop working under the agreement effective August 27, 2026. Interscope maintains the agreement called for five studio albums and credits her with three — Over It, Still Over It and Finally Over It — and sued in October seeking more than $50 million. A separate dispute with her longtime label and management company LVRN has also expanded: LVRN accused Walker of withholding payments from touring income, songwriting royalties and business agreements, including a Savage x Fenty brand partnership and a support slot on Chris Brown's 2025 tour, while Walker alleges LVRN locked her into an oppressive deal and misappropriated money from her budgets. Neither side's claims have been resolved in court.

articles.title: "GTA VI: The Album" aims for a first-ever No. 1 video game soundtrack debut on the Billboard 200; deluxe edition out today
articles.description: Rockstar Games released Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album on Friday, November 20, through Atlantic Records, and Billboard reports it is poised to make history with a No. 1 debut on the Billboard 200 — no video game soundtrack has ever topped the chart. A deluxe edition with 23 brand-new tracks was released today, November 23. The 34-track album features Dua Lipa, Travis Scott, Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, SZA, BLACKPINK's Jennie and more.
articles.body: Rockstar Games released Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album on Friday, November 20, through Atlantic Records as the accompanying soundtrack to the long-awaited video game, which arrived 24 hours earlier, and Billboard reports the album is poised to break new video game ground with a potential No. 1 debut on the Billboard 200. No video game soundtrack has ever topped the Billboard 200 before, and the album's chart fate will be decided by the tracking week ending November 26, with the chart dated December 5. A deluxe edition of the album was released today, November 23, featuring 23 brand-new tracks on top of the original 34. The album, which emulates the music of Florida within the game's fictional setting of Leonida, features 34 original tracks from a diverse ensemble including Playboi Carti, Dua Lipa, Cardi B, Lana Del Rey, SZA, BLACKPINK's Jennie, Don Toliver, Travis Scott, Gunna, Kodak Black, Yung Lean, Future, Metro Boomin, Fred again.., PinkPantheress, Morgan Wallen, Tame Impala and Fuerza Regida. The game itself is a record-breaking launch, grossing over $4.0 billion in four days and selling 44.9 million copies, and the album set a new opening-day record for a soundtrack on Spotify with 29.85 million streams. Eleven singles were released to promote the album, six of them on the September 17 announcement. A live music festival featuring some of the album's artists was held on November 21 at Mana Wynwood in Miami, with Travis Scott, Cardi B, CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso, Metro Boomin, Rauw Alejandro, Justice, Kodak Black and Fcukers. Billboard has ranked all 34 tracks in order, and the album's chart debut next week will show whether gaming's biggest launch can also conquer the albums chart.

articles.title: UPDATE: Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" leads Hot 100 for 29th week as holiday hits return to the top 10
articles.description: Genuine update to the already-covered 28-week story: Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" now leads the Hot 100 for a 29th week on the chart dated November 28, 2026, Billboard's Gary Trust reported November 23. The holiday season has arrived on the chart, with Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" up to No. 4 and Wham!'s "Last Christmas" in the top five, plus Bobby Helms' "Jingle Bell Rock" at No. 9.
articles.body: Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" leads the Billboard Hot 100 for a 29th week on the chart dated November 28, 2026, Billboard's Gary Trust reported on Monday, November 23, extending the longest reign in the chart's history. The song first reached No. 1 on February 14, 2026, and has now spent 29 weeks on top, seven more than the previous record holder, Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You," which led for 22 weeks across holiday seasons. The holiday season has now blasted back onto the chart: Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You" rises to No. 4, Wham!'s "Last Christmas" hits the top five, and Bobby Helms' "Jingle Bell Rock" rings in at No. 9. Stella Lefty's "Boston" holds at No. 2, Tame Impala and JENNIE's "Dracula" stays at No. 3, Tate McRae's "Housewife" is at No. 6, Olivia Rodrigo's "Stupid Song" slips to No. 7, Karol G's "BbY WOW" is down to No. 8, and ADÉLA's "Nicole Kidman" slips to No. 10. The question now is whether any of the holiday classics can topple Langley from No. 1 as December approaches, with Carey's song the obvious challenger given its history of returning to the summit each Christmas. Langley's run has already survived Halloween, when Michael Jackson's "Thriller" surged to No. 2, and the song also holds records on the component charts, including a record-extending 21st week atop Digital Song Sales and a 49th week leading Hot Country Songs. The full Hot 100 dated November 28 will be posted on Billboard's website on November 24.

articles.title: Murmansk governor Andrei Chibis detained on suspicion of embezzling over 1 billion rubles
articles.description: Russia's Interior Ministry has confirmed the detention of Murmansk region governor Andrei Chibis as part of a criminal case alleging fraud and embezzlement on a particularly large scale. Investigators allege the theft of more than 39 million rubles from the regional construction ministry and the misappropriation of over 1 billion rubles allocated to reconstruct the Apatity–Kirovsk road. Chibis, who has governed the Arctic region since 2019, was detained in Moscow after arriving on a work trip.
articles.body: Russia's Interior Ministry said on Monday, November 23, that its officers had detained Andrei Chibis, governor of the northern Murmansk region, as part of a criminal investigation into fraud and embezzlement on a particularly large scale. Interior Ministry spokeswoman Irina Volk said Chibis was detained on suspicion of involvement in a group crime case that includes allegations of embezzling more than 39 million rubles (about $478,000) in budget funds from the regional construction ministry, and misappropriating over 1 billion rubles allocated by the regional transport ministry for the reconstruction of the Apatity–Kirovsk road. Other suspects face charges of fraud, embezzlement and illegal currency operations involving forged documents. The case is under the supervision of the Interior Ministry's investigative department. The detention followed a confused day of reporting: the Mash Telegram channel first reported Chibis had been stopped at the plane's steps on arrival in Moscow, while the region's information minister initially denied the detention, saying he was in Moscow on a planned work trip to give testimony. Chibis has headed the Murmansk region since 2019. His detention is the latest in a series of corruption cases against Russian regional governors, and comes as the Kremlin continues to use anti-corruption prosecutions to discipline regional elites during the war.

articles.title: Medvedev threatens pre-emptive nuclear strike and warns Kyiv and NATO have pushed Russia "to the nuclear line"
articles.description: Former Russian president Dmitry Medvedev published a series of statements on November 23 arguing that Russia has not yet used nuclear weapons, that Kyiv and NATO have already pushed Russia toward the nuclear threshold, and that a pre-emptive nuclear strike cannot be ruled out. He also dismissed the Shenzhen declaration signed by Trump, Putin and Xi and warned the US and China about the inevitability of nuclear proliferation. The rhetoric coincided with Western intelligence warnings that Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite before the end of 2026.
articles.body: Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, published a series of nuclear-themed statements on November 23, explaining why Russia has not used nuclear weapons in the war so far while warning that Kyiv and NATO have already pushed Russia "to the nuclear line". In one of the posts he allowed for the possibility of a pre-emptive nuclear strike, and in another he dismissed the declaration signed in Shenzhen by Trump, Putin and Xi as irrelevant to Russia's nuclear posture. He also addressed the US and China on what he called the inevitability of nuclear proliferation. The outburst comes the same day Western intelligence officials warned that Russia may put a satellite carrying a nuclear weapon into orbit before the end of 2026 — a claim already covered in the morning digest, now amplified by German intelligence assessments reported in the German press. Medvedev's statements are a regular feature of Russian nuclear signalling, but their timing — days after Ukrainian strikes on the Crimean Bridge and amid talk of a possible ceasefire framework — suggests they are aimed at raising the perceived cost of further Western support for Kyiv. Western officials generally treat Medvedev's rhetoric as bluster, but it is read in Moscow as an authorised channel for signalling red lines. The statements were widely reported across Russian state and independent media on November 23.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones halt Novoshakhtinsk oil refinery and hit Lukoil plant in Perm region, killing one
articles.description: Ukraine struck two Russian oil refineries overnight: the Novoshakhtinsk refinery in Rostov region suspended operations after a mass drone and missile attack lasting more than six hours, and drones hit Lukoil's Permnefteorgsintez refinery in Perm region, starting a fire and killing one person. A third target, the Kaleikino oil pumping station in Tatarstan, was also reported hit. The strikes are part of Ukraine's sustained campaign against Russian fuel infrastructure.
articles.body: Ukrainian drones struck two Russian oil refineries overnight into November 23, Russian regional authorities and media reported. The Novoshakhtinsk oil products plant (NZNP) in Rostov region suspended operations after a mass attack by drones and missiles that lasted more than six hours, according to the regional authorities. In Perm region, drones hit the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez refinery, starting a fire at the site; one person was killed in the attack, eyewitnesses and local media reported. A third target, the Kaleikino oil pumping station in Tatarstan, was also reported hit. The strikes continue Ukraine's months-long campaign against Russian refineries and fuel logistics, which has repeatedly forced plants to halt operations and contributed to fuel shortages and price rises inside Russia. Earlier the same weekend, Ukraine confirmed its drones sank the Russian corvette Mercury off Libya and damaged the Crimean Bridge — a run of long-range strikes that Kyiv presents as both military pressure and a message to Moscow and its partners. For Russia, the refinery attacks are a growing economic and domestic-political problem: each shutdown tightens fuel supplies and undercuts the Kremlin's claim that the war is not affecting daily life at home.

articles.title: Armenia publishes draft of new constitution for public comment
articles.description: Armenia has published a draft of a new constitution on a dedicated website where every citizen can read the text and submit suggestions. The draft was posted on November 23, according to Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. Constitutional reform has been a contentious issue in Armenia since its 2020 defeat in the Nagorno-Karabakh war, and the new text is expected to be debated fiercely ahead of any referendum.
articles.body: Armenia has published a new draft constitution, posting it on a dedicated website where every citizen can read the full text and submit their own proposals, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported on November 23. The publication opens a public consultation phase on a document that has been in preparation amid intense political debate. Constitutional reform has been one of the most contested issues in Armenian politics since the country's defeat in the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war, with Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan arguing the current constitution, adopted in the 1990s and amended in 2015, needs to be replaced to reflect Armenia's post-war realities — including removing references to Nagorno-Karabakh that Azerbaijan has demanded be dropped as a condition for a peace treaty. Critics accuse Pashinyan of using reform to entrench his own power and of conceding to Baku's demands. The draft's publication is therefore not a technical step but a political event: its contents will be scrutinised both in Yerevan, where the opposition is already mobilising against it, and in Baku, where officials will read it as a signal of Yerevan's intentions. Any new constitution would ultimately need approval in a referendum, and the debate over the draft is likely to dominate Armenian politics into 2027.

articles.title: "Fair Russia" leader Sergei Mironov reappears in public for the first time in three months
articles.description: Sergei Mironov, leader of the "A Just Russia" party, appeared in public on November 23 for the first time in three months, attending the State Duma, according to a source in the party's faction cited by Interfax. His long absence from public view had fuelled speculation in Moscow about his health and political standing. No explanation for the absence has been given.
articles.body: Sergei Mironov, leader of the "A Just Russia — For Truth" party, appeared in public on November 23 for the first time in three months, arriving at the State Duma, a source in the party's parliamentary faction told Interfax. Mironov, 73, has led the party since its founding in 2006 and has been a fixture of Russia's managed parliamentary opposition, loyal to the Kremlin while presenting a nominally left-wing alternative to United Russia. His three-month absence from public view had gone largely unremarked in state media but fuelled speculation in Moscow political circles about his health and his future at the head of the party. No official explanation for the absence has been offered, and Mironov made no public statement on his return. The reappearance comes as Russia's political system gears up for the 2027 parliamentary cycle and as the Kremlin manages an increasingly brittle elite consensus around the war. For a party that depends heavily on its leader's personal brand, even a brief unexplained absence matters — and the silence around it says something about how little transparency surrounds the health and whereabouts of senior Russian politicians.

articles.title: Kyiv hit by daytime drone strikes: restaurant near Maidan and residential building in Podil damaged
articles.description: Kyiv came under drone attack during the day on November 23, with a strike hitting a restaurant near Maidan Nezalezhnosti and a drone hitting the roof of a six-storey residential building in Podil. The attacks followed a night in which Russia launched 153 attack drones across Ukraine, including 60 jet-powered Shaheds. The daytime strikes on the capital mark an escalation in Russia's targeting of central Kyiv.
articles.body: Kyiv was under drone attack during the day on Monday, November 23, with strikes hitting central districts of the capital. A drone hit a restaurant near Maidan Nezalezhnosti, and another struck the roof of a six-storey residential building in Podil, according to Ukrainian media summaries of the day's events. The daytime attacks came after a night in which Russia launched 153 attack drones against Ukraine, including 60 jet-powered Shahed drones as well as Gerbera decoys and Parodiya drones, according to Ukrainian Air Force data. The strikes on central Kyiv follow a weekend of heavy attacks on the capital region, including the drone strike on a five-storey building in Dymer that killed 11 people — a story already covered in the morning digest. The fact that drones are now reaching central Kyiv in daylight hours underscores the strain on Ukrainian air defences, which are contending with a sharp increase in the volume and speed of Russian drone attacks, including the new jet-powered Shaheds that are harder to intercept. Zelenskyy has appealed to NATO to urgently supply air-defence missiles capable of shooting down Russian ballistic missiles, and has pointed to delays in US Patriot deliveries as a critical gap. For Kyiv residents, the daytime strikes are a reminder that no part of the city is safe, even as the energy crisis deepens with scheduled power outages across most of the country.

articles.title: Trump reportedly questioned further military aid to Ukraine — European leaders deny it
articles.description: Politico reported that Donald Trump questioned the wisdom of further US military support for Ukraine, prompting swift denials from European leaders. Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the report may stem from a translation error, and the French government said Trump did not ask Europe to end military aid. The episode comes as partners push for four-party talks before Christmas and debate a €45 billion EU loan for Ukraine.
articles.body: Politico reported that US President Donald Trump questioned the advisability of further spending on military support for Ukraine, according to a report that circulated on November 23 and was prominently noted in Ukraїnska Pravda's most-read stories. European leaders moved quickly to deny the claim: Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the report may have arisen from a translation error, and the French government stated that Trump did not ask Europe to end military assistance to Ukraine. The confusion comes at a sensitive moment. Partners are pushing for four-party talks on the war before Christmas, and the EU is debating a €45 billion loan for Ukraine that Slovakia has refused to support and the Czech prime minister wants kept outside the EU budget. Trump, Putin and Xi have just signed a joint declaration in Shenzhen from which the Ukraine clause was dropped, and Putin has refused ceasefire talks after the Crimean Bridge strikes. Against that backdrop, any suggestion that Washington is wavering on military aid carries outsized weight in Kyiv and European capitals — which is precisely why the denials came so fast. Whether the Politico report reflected a real shift in Trump's position or a garbled account of a private conversation remains unclear, and the episode illustrates how fragile the information environment around US Ukraine policy has become. For Ukraine, the practical question is unchanged: air-defence missiles, above all Patriots, are in short supply while Russian missile and drone attacks intensify.

articles.title: Slovak foreign minister hints Ukrainians were behind the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia
articles.description: Slovakia's foreign minister has hinted that Ukrainians were behind the 1968 Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia, a remark that drew attention in Ukrainian media on November 23. The comment comes from a government that has already refused to back a €45 billion EU loan for Ukraine. It is the latest in a series of provocative statements from Bratislava straining relations with Kyiv.
articles.body: Slovakia's foreign minister hinted that Ukrainians were behind the 1968 invasion of Czechoslovakia, according to a report highlighted among Ukraїnska Pravda's most-read stories on November 23. The remark revisits one of the most sensitive episodes in Central European history: the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968, in which Soviet troops — including units from the Ukrainian SSR — took part in crushing the Prague Spring. The minister's framing, implying Ukrainian responsibility for an invasion ordered from Moscow, was read in Kyiv as a deliberate provocation. It comes from a Slovak government that has positioned itself as the most Russia-friendly in the EU: Bratislava has already refused to support a €45 billion EU loan for Ukraine, and Prime Minister Robert Fico's government has repeatedly clashed with Kyiv over aid and sanctions. The comment also lands as the Czech prime minister argues Ukraine aid should be financed outside the EU budget, leaving Ukraine's supporters in the bloc increasingly isolated. For Ukraine, the Slovak remark is less about history than about the present: it signals that Bratislava is willing to use historical grievance as a political weapon in the fight over EU support, and it complicates Kyiv's efforts to keep the EU united behind its war effort and its accession path.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones attacked Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland
articles.description: Two Ukrainian drones attacked the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on November 21 as it sailed toward Kaliningrad, according to media reports summarised on November 23. The ship was reported to be carrying military cargo. The attack extends Ukraine's campaign against Russian shipping beyond the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, where the corvette Mercury was sunk off Libya.
articles.body: Two drones attacked the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on November 21 as it headed for Kaliningrad, media reported, with the incident summarised in Ukrainian coverage on November 23. The vessel was reported to be carrying military cargo to the Russian exclave, which has become increasingly dependent on sea supply as overland routes through Lithuania are restricted. The attack follows Ukraine's confirmation that its drones sank the Russian corvette Mercury in the Libyan port of Benghazi, destroying a Ka-27 combat helicopter on board — a strike already covered in the morning digest. Together, the two incidents show Ukraine extending its maritime campaign far beyond the Black Sea: Russian shipping is now being targeted in the Baltic and the Mediterranean as well. For Moscow, the Sparta II attack raises questions about the security of the Kaliningrad supply line, which runs through waters monitored by NATO states. Air-raid sirens were also reported in the Kaliningrad region, and Russia has accused Ukraine of escalating attacks on its logistics. The incidents underline a shift in the war at sea: Ukraine, which has no conventional navy of its own, is using drones to contest Russian shipping across three seas at once.

articles.title: Frontline: 143 combat engagements on November 22, heaviest fighting at Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka
articles.description: Ukraine's General Staff reported 143 combat engagements on the front as of 22:00 on November 22, with the heaviest fighting on the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes. Russia carried out 49 air strikes, dropped 173 guided bombs and used 4,398 kamikaze drones in a single day. Russian forces advanced southwest of Chasiv Yar and on the Kramatorsk axis, according to the Deep State monitoring project.
articles.body: Ukraine's General Staff reported 143 combat engagements along the front as of 22:00 on November 22, with the heaviest fighting concentrated on the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes, according to summaries published on November 23. In a single day Russia carried out 49 air strikes, dropped 173 guided aerial bombs and deployed 4,398 kamikaze drones — a tempo that illustrates the scale of the Russian offensive and the pressure on Ukrainian defences. The Deep State monitoring project reported Russian advances southwest of Chasiv Yar and on the Kramatorsk axis, two sectors where Moscow has been grinding forward for months. The figures come as Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces reported record Russian losses in November — tens of thousands of targets hit in 22 days, according to commander Robert "Madyar" Brovdi. The frontline picture is one of attrition: Russia continues to advance slowly at enormous cost, while Ukraine relies on drones to offset its disadvantage in manpower and artillery. The fighting around Pokrovsk remains the war's central battle, with the city's fate tied to the broader question of whether Russia can achieve a breakthrough in Donetsk region before winter fully sets in. For Kyiv, holding the line there while the energy war rages at home is the defining challenge of the coming weeks.

articles.title: Ukraїnska Pravda investigation: who failed to build protection for energy substations in Kyiv region
articles.description: Ukraїnska Pravda published a major investigation on November 23, "Defenceless energy, or who failed to build protection at energy substations in Kyiv region", examining why substations around Kyiv were left exposed to Russian strikes. The piece, by Roman Romaniuk, is the outlet's lead analytical story of the day and speaks directly to the capital's power and water crisis after the November 20 overnight attack.
articles.body: Ukraїnska Pravda published a major investigation on November 23 titled "Defenceless energy, or who failed to build protection at energy substations in Kyiv region", by Roman Romaniuk, examining why electricity substations around Kyiv were left without adequate physical protection against Russian strikes. The investigation is the outlet's lead analytical piece of the day and lands as Kyiv struggles with serious water supply interruptions, especially on the right bank, after a critical infrastructure facility was heavily damaged in the Russian attack on the night of November 20. The Darnytsia power plant's lack of a backup boiler and the exposure of Kyiv region substations have become central questions in Ukraine's public debate about the energy war: billions were allocated for the protection of energy infrastructure, yet key facilities remain vulnerable to drones and missiles. The investigation seeks to establish who was responsible for the failure to build that protection — a question with direct political consequences, as the government faces criticism over its handling of energy security. The piece also connects to the broader pattern reported across Ukraine: repair crews restoring facilities only for them to be struck again, and a grid that is being degraded faster than it can be rebuilt. For readers, the investigation offers accountability journalism at a moment when the practical consequences — outages, no water, no heating as temperatures fall toward minus 7 degrees — are being felt in every Kyiv household.

articles.title: Xbox bug unlocks 60 FPS in GTA VI — with a catch
articles.description: Digital Foundry has analysed a bug on Xbox Series X|S that removes GTA VI's 30 FPS cap, using the console's Quick Resume feature. The trick works by switching the display refresh rate from 60 Hz to 120 Hz mid-session, but performance is uneven — averaging 30–40 FPS, hitting 60 FPS only when flying straight up — and it can make gameplay and cutscenes run in fast-forward. It also explains why Rockstar shipped no performance mode: the CPU load is so high that frame rates dip below 30 FPS in big shootouts and panicking crowds.
articles.body: Digital Foundry examined a quirk in how Xbox's Quick Resume handles suspended games, which can be exploited to unlock GTA VI's frame rate. The method is fiddly: set the Xbox display to 60 Hz, launch GTA VI until the six-star loading video appears, return to the dashboard, switch to 120 Hz, launch a second game until its intro plays, then switch back to GTA VI — and the 30 FPS limit is gone. Reversing the steps caps the game at 15 FPS instead, a slideshow. In practice the unlocked mode is far from a smooth 60 FPS experience: high-speed driving through downtown Vice City runs at around 30 FPS, rural highways reach about 40 FPS, and only flying a plane straight up into the sky hits 60 FPS, for an average of roughly 30–40 FPS. A bug also speeds up gameplay and cutscenes when performance rises, and high input lag and character inertia remain. The findings clarify Rockstar's design choice: with the CPU under heavy strain in large-scale firefights with explosions or crowds, even a 40 FPS cap would be hard to hold stable — including on PS5 Pro, which shares the base PS5's processor — so a locked 30 FPS was the only consistent option. On Xbox Series X|S, performance can peak at about 35 FPS even in normal play.

articles.title: Russian government plans film-style licences for video games
articles.description: Russia's government plans to introduce distribution certificates for video games, modelled on the licences already required for films, according to sources cited by Kommersant. The idea, first proposed in 2024, may now be backed as part of a draft law on developing and distributing games in Russia, which would also require developers and publishers to register with regulator Roskomnadzor, store data in Russia and install SORM surveillance equipment. Industry figures warn the rules would burden domestic developers most, since every update could need fresh approval.
articles.body: The Russian cabinet is preparing to require "rental certificates" for video games, following the model used for films, Kommersant's sources report. The initiative was first floated in 2024, but the government may now support it within the draft law "On activities for the development and distribution of video games on the territory of the Russian Federation." Under the proposal, game developers and publishers would be recognised as organisers of information distribution online and obliged to register in Roskomnadzor's registry, store data on Russian territory and install SORM interception equipment. The draft has a basic problem, GameMAG notes: it aims to limit foreign companies' access to the Russian market, yet that access is already restricted, and other countries could respond with mirror measures — while the extra burden would fall mainly on domestic developers, who would have to comply with rules international companies ignore. Vasily Ovchinnikov, head of the Video Game Industry Development Organisation (RVI), criticised the bill, pointing to its main blind spot: updates. After release, many games keep evolving and can change almost beyond recognition after a series of patches, which would make controlling every version pointless and create queues, delays and costs for regulators and developers alike. "Expert review of every version of every game is a queue, timelines and costs that will hit our own developers, not those they want to restrict," he said.

articles.title: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after just 11 days out
articles.description: Nvidia's board has voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as president and chairman of the board, ending a boardroom crisis after only 11 days — a turnaround widely compared to Sam Altman's 2023 return to OpenAI. Huang was backed by investors, partners, employees and politicians, with a petition for his return gathering over 150,000 signatures, and Nvidia shares jumped 31% on the news. The board had earlier insisted through chairman Harvey Jones that Huang would not be brought back.
articles.body: Nvidia's leadership has decided to restore Jensen Huang as the company's president and chairman of the board, meaning the top executive spent just 11 days unemployed. The conflict ended following the OpenAI scenario many had predicted: in 2023, AI startup chief Sam Altman was fired, only to be reinstated after demands from investors and ordinary employees. Prominent politicians, entrepreneurs, business partners and rank-and-file Nvidia staff spoke up for Huang, and a petition demanding his return collected more than 150,000 votes. The decision to bring him back was taken by a board vote, even though board chairman Harvey Jones had previously stated publicly that Huang would not be reinstated. Huang himself said he cannot wait to get back to work, and Nvidia's share price jumped 31% on the news. Meanwhile, The New York Times published a new article about Huang's mistress, former Megaspeed head Alice Huang, repeating claims that during the affair she was in close contact with an official from China's Ministry of State Security — though US authorities publicly say they cannot draw firm conclusions about her cooperation with Chinese intelligence, and President Donald Trump has defended Jensen Huang. Update: President Trump has officially stated that US authorities have no evidence of wrongdoing by Nvidia chief Jensen Huang.

articles.title: Final trailer for Marvel's "Avengers: Doomsday" released
articles.description: Marvel Studios has released the final trailer for "Avengers: Doomsday," with the film's US premiere set for December 18. The Russo brothers' film centres on several groups of superheroes uniting against the threat of Doctor Doom, and the trailer's rallying cry is "To me, my X-Men!" The trailer arrives exactly a month before release, as Marvel builds to its biggest ensemble film since "Endgame."
articles.body: Marvel Studios has published the final trailer for "Avengers: Doomsday," the next Avengers film, with its US premiere scheduled for December 18 — one month from the trailer's release. The film, directed by the Russo brothers, is devoted to the confrontation between several groups of superheroes in the face of the threat posed by Doctor Doom. The trailer leans on the X-Men's presence, with the call "To me, my X-Men!" as its centrepiece, signalling the long-awaited full integration of the mutants into the Marvel Cinematic Universe's flagship team-up. Doomsday is positioned as Marvel's biggest ensemble event since "Avengers: Endgame," bringing together the Avengers, the Fantastic Four and the X-Men against a single villain. The final trailer is the last major piece of marketing before the film opens in US cinemas on December 18, capping a year in which Marvel has leaned heavily on nostalgia and cross-franchise team-ups to rebuild momentum.

articles.title: "American Psycho" remake appears cancelled as Luca Guadagnino exits
articles.description: Director Luca Guadagnino is no longer working on the new adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis's "American Psycho," he revealed on a Deadline podcast, effectively killing the remake. A finished script by Scott Z. Burns ("Contagion," "The Bourne Ultimatum") already existed, but Guadagnino left the project without explaining why. The remake was to offer a fresh take on Patrick Bateman, the yuppie banker and serial killer played by Christian Bale in Mary Harron's cult 2000 film.
articles.body: Director Luca Guadagnino ("Queer," "Challengers") is no longer working on the new screen version of Bret Easton Ellis's scandalous novel "American Psycho," the filmmaker said on a Deadline podcast when asked about his upcoming projects — a sign the remake has effectively been cancelled. According to Guadagnino, a script by Scott Z. Burns ("Contagion," "The Informant!," "The Bourne Ultimatum") was already complete, but the director walked away from the project without revealing the reason for his decision. "American Psycho had a fantastic script by Scott Z. Burns. Unfortunately, things aren't coming together with this film," Guadagnino said. He was to offer his own vision of the story of successful New York banker Patrick Bateman, who leads a double life as a serial killer — a role Christian Bale made iconic in Mary Harron's cult 2000 adaptation. Why work on the remake stalled, the director did not specify, and it is unclear whether the studio will try to revive it with another director or abandon it; the project had previously been linked to several possible Bateman actors, including Austin Butler and Patrick Schwarzenegger.

articles.title: DOOM: The Dark Ages was originally planned as an Xbox console exclusive
articles.description: DOOM: The Dark Ages was originally conceived as an Xbox Series X|S console exclusive, former id Software senior technical designer Jordan Turner revealed on the Kiwi Talkz podcast. The shooter was ultimately ported to PlayStation 5 as well, reflecting Microsoft's loosening exclusivity strategy. The disclosure adds to the picture of how Xbox's first-party planning has shifted since the Activision Blizzard era.
articles.body: DOOM: The Dark Ages was originally designed as a console exclusive for Xbox Series X|S, former id Software senior technical designer Jordan Turner said on the Kiwi Talkz podcast. The team later ported the shooter to PlayStation 5, so it launched on Xbox, PlayStation and PC rather than as an Xbox-only title. The revelation is notable because the game was announced as a multiplatform release from the start, and it shows how far Microsoft's exclusivity plans for its Bethesda studios have moved since the Xbox maker began releasing its own games on rival consoles. DOOM: The Dark Ages, the medieval-styled prequel to the modern DOOM reboots, was one of Xbox's flagship 2025 releases, and the decision to bring it to PS5 fits the broader pattern of former Xbox exclusives — from Hi-Fi Rush to Indiana Jones and the Great Circle — appearing on PlayStation. Turner's account suggests the shift happened during development rather than being planned from the outset, underlining how quickly Microsoft's platform strategy changed after its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard closed.

articles.title: Sony to remove at least six games from PS Plus Extra in December
articles.description: At least six games will leave the PlayStation Plus Extra catalogue on December 15, Sony has announced, so subscribers have under a month to play them. Among the departures are the role-playing game Granblue Fantasy: Relink and the adventure Jake Hunter Detective Story: Prism of Eyes, plus a co-op action title. The removals are the regular monthly rotation of the Extra tier's library.
articles.body: Next month, at least six games will be removed from the extended PlayStation Plus subscription library, Sony has confirmed, with the departures scheduled for December 15. Among the titles leaving the catalogue are the role-playing game Granblue Fantasy: Relink, the adventure game Jake Hunter Detective Story: Prism of Eyes, and a cooperative action game — the full list runs to six or more titles across the Extra tier. The removals are part of the regular monthly rotation of the PlayStation Plus Extra catalogue, in which Sony adds new games and retires older ones, and subscribers who want to finish the departing titles have until mid-December. Granblue Fantasy: Relink, Cygames' action RPG, is the highest-profile loss, having been a well-received addition to the service. The December removals sit alongside the month's new additions, and players who own the games outright are unaffected — only the subscription access ends.

articles.title: UPDATE: Thousands evacuated as "unknown substance" fills UK arena during Don Toliver show
articles.description: Thousands of people were evacuated from Manchester's Co-op Live arena on Sunday night after an "unknown substance" — initially believed to be tear gas — was released during a concert by US rapper Don Toliver, filling the venue with plumes of smoke. More than 50 people sought help for eye and respiratory symptoms and one person needed hospital treatment, among more than 12,000 in the audience. Toliver's London show has been rescheduled to December 15.
articles.body: Thousands of people were evacuated after an "unknown substance" was released during a concert starring American rapper Don Toliver in Manchester on Sunday night. Plumes of smoke filled the Co-op Live arena at around 10 p.m. local time, sparking panic among the more than 12,000 revellers in the venue, footage verified by CNN shows. Police initially said a substance believed to be tear gas was let off in the crowd towards the end of the concert, but a later statement referred only to an "unknown substance," and enquiries are underway into what it was and what caused the incident. More than 50 people sought help for eye and respiratory symptoms and one person required hospital treatment, according to Manchester's North West Ambulance Service. Concertgoer Yewande Famutimi said she suddenly felt a "burning sensation" in her throat while dancing: "It was very scary… We were struggling to breathe and coughing really badly. We could see people running out of the arena's floor." The incident triggered a major incident response and rattled nerves in a city that was the scene of a terror attack in 2017, when a suicide bomber killed at least 22 people, including children, during an Ariana Grande concert — a memory several concertgoers said instantly resurfaced. Attendees also complained about lax security and poor communication: Usman Asghar said the 23,500-capacity venue was "a complete mess," that security did not use metal detectors, frisk guests or check bags, and that staff told the crowd Toliver was taking a "break" without explaining what was happening. Toliver said on Monday that his show at London's O2 arena had been rescheduled to December 15 due to the "unfortunate incident," adding that his "heart and prayers are with everyone that was injured last night." Co-op Live said it is working closely with police to identify the cause; the venue did not respond to CNN's questions about security measures.

articles.title: The Ukraine-Russia war is seeping out across Europe — and two reasons it will get worse
