articles.description: Rather than peace, the past week brought stark escalation: Russia launched what President Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year on Friday — a six-hour barrage of drones and missiles — while Ukraine hit Putin's Crimea bridge three times and struck Russian-linked ships off Kaliningrad and near Benghazi, Libya. CNN's analysis argues the war is spreading across the continent, and the months ahead look perilous for two reasons: Moscow has a small window before a pro-Ukrainian Democratic Congress takes power, and the two sides' demands are moving further apart, with Putin now saying Russia has no interest in a ceasefire.
articles.body: Rather than peace, there is stark escalation — the product of over six weeks of shuttling diplomacy, posturing, betrayal of Ukraine's ability to defend itself, Russian intransigence and the US' failed reframing of the process as about European security. Put aside the near-zero public results from the Shenzhen trilateral meeting between Russia, China and the US, and consider the violence of the past week alone. Russia launched Friday what President Volodymyr Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year — a six-hour crescendo of drones and missiles, after weeks of striking Kyiv's bridges and power infrastructure across the country. Dozens have died, and swaths of the country and capital are often in blackout. Ukraine struck Vladimir Putin's prized bridge to occupied Crimea three times in the days around the trilateral, and Kyiv's drones apparently struck both a Russian-military linked ship this weekend off the coast of Kaliningrad and Russian naval assets near the port of Benghazi, on the Libyan coast. The geography matters: Kaliningrad is a Russian enclave between Lithuania and Poland, hitherto considered safe, and the apparent strike on the Sparta 2, a military-cargo vessel, either involved a drone launched from another ship or one flying through Russian territory to the Baltic Sea; Russia chose to blame Lithuania for letting the drone cross its airspace — NATO territory — feeding the fiction that Russia is at war with all of NATO and raising the risk of further Russian sabotage around the Baltics. The Libya strikes further showcase Kyiv's ability to embarrass the Kremlin, whose ships now risk damage in whichever Mediterranean ports they dock. The uptick in violence was unthinkable five years ago: from being contained inside Ukraine, the war spread to Russia in 2024, then to NATO's eastern borders. CNN identifies two reasons the months ahead look perilous. First, the Kremlin has a small window before Capitol Hill is taken over by pro-Ukrainian Democrats, when everything from funding to Elon Musk's role falls under scrutiny, and Trump's peculiar sympathies towards Russia will likely be reined in. Second, the two sides' realities are drifting apart: Putin said in Shenzhen that Russia had no interest in negotiating a ceasefire, claimed to control Kostyantynivka when he palpably does not, and said Ukraine started the war, when it did not. Moscow has tried to reframe the talks as being about wider "European security infrastructure" — a chance to rewrite the conflict as a symptom of NATO's eastward enlargement — while some reports suggest Ukrainian NATO membership has even been floated by the US. On the battlefield, Putin's stated goal is capturing the remainder of the Donbas; Ukraine has kept Russia from occupying Kostyantynivka for two years, but neighbouring Kramatorsk and Slavyansk are close to uninhabitable, and the grind costs at least 40,000 dead and injured a month. The bleak conclusion: the peace process seems merely a process to please Trump, devoid of actual peace, and the only end in sight is the unsettling collapse of either side.

articles.title: Spanish court removes last hurdle to Catalan leader's return from exile
articles.description: Spain's Supreme Court shelved a criminal case against Catalan separatist and former regional leader Carles Puigdemont on Monday, removing the last legal hurdle for him to return to Spain after nearly a decade in self-imposed exile. Puigdemont fled to Belgium in October 2017 after an independence referendum the judiciary deemed illegal. He says he is in no hurry to return and has no plans to do so during the campaign ahead of the November 29 general election, but is considering coming back in December.
articles.body: Spain's Supreme Court shelved a criminal case against Catalan separatist and former regional leader Carles Puigdemont on Monday, thus removing the last legal hurdle for him to return to Spain following nearly a decade of self-imposed exile. Puigdemont fled to Belgium in October 2017 after holding an independence referendum that the judiciary deemed illegal. The failed vote triggered a deep crisis between Madrid and the northeastern region, which has a distinct language and culture as well as a significant secessionist movement that peaked in support that year. After the Constitutional Court ruled last month that the amnesty law for Catalan separatists also applied to embezzlement charges against Puigdemont and the Supreme Court lifted the warrant for his arrest, Monday's ruling was the final step needed for his return. Following the decision, Puigdemont posted on X a poem by Catalan author Jaume Pons Alorda containing foul language and directed at his "dearest enemies." Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's government pushed through the amnesty under a 2023 agreement between his Socialist Party and two Catalan parties, including Puigdemont's Junts, in exchange for their support to be re-elected as premier — a move that unleashed intense social and political opposition from critics at the time. In a recent interview with newspaper El Mundo, Puigdemont said his party had taken advantage of what he described as Sanchez's ambition in order to "defeat" Spain. He added he was in no hurry to return to Catalonia and had no plans to do so during the campaign ahead of the November 29 general election, but was considering coming back in December, on a date yet to be determined. Puigdemont will hold a press conference in Brussels on Wednesday, Junts said.

articles.title: New York judge urges Kalshi to compromise on limiting bets by anyone under 21
articles.description: A New York judge on Monday urged prediction market Kalshi to compromise on limiting sports and culture bets by anyone younger than 21, while denying a temporary restraining order that risked shutting the platform down across all 50 states. The state attorney general claims Kalshi is operating an illegal gambling platform without a state licence, while Kalshi says a shutdown would be a "recipe for chaos" for its 1.5 million customers. The judge gave both sides until November 30 to reach a deal, with a hearing set for early January.
articles.body: A New York judge on Monday urged Kalshi to reach a compromise limiting bets on sports and culture contracts by anyone younger than 21 years old while denying a temporary restraining order that risked shutting down the prediction market across all 50 states. The potential compromise was raised during a hearing in which Judge Melissa Crane heard arguments over the New York attorney general's claims that Kalshi is operating an illegal gambling platform by failing to obtain a state gambling licence, not paying taxes, and allowing users below the legal betting age to participate. The state sought a TRO to shut down Kalshi's bets within or from New York. Judge Crane said she was "very concerned" about the risks to people under 21, who under state law are banned from gambling; Kalshi allows anyone 18 and up to use its platform. "Would your client be willing, at least in New York, to stop these (contracts or bets) for 18- to 21-year-olds just to have a compromise at this point?" she asked. Kalshi's lawyer, Grant Mainland, said the company was "open to engaging" on the 18-to-20-year-old issue and could work out a form of "interim compliance" during the litigation as it relates to sports and culture contracts, noting Kalshi already has consumer protections in place. The judge is giving both sides until Monday, November 30, to reach a deal: "I would like the parties to discuss a way of safeguarding for that age group ultimately." Crane denied the TRO because the state was "really seeking the ultimate relief in the case upfront" without her hearing from the defence, and because she was concerned about broader market disruption if all bets were frozen. Mainland told the judge a TRO is a "recipe for chaos" that would put millions at risk by freezing trades — "a market emergency" and "totally unprecedented." The attorney general's office argued betting on Kalshi has exploded since the New York gaming commission sent a cease-and-desist letter in September 2025: Kalshi's valuation went from $5 billion to $40 billion and contract volume is now $118 billion, up from $5 billion, with 85% of it sports betting. The judge set an expedited schedule with briefs due over the next few weeks and a hearing in early January. The case sits within a broader court debate over whether prediction markets fall exclusively under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission or are subject to state gaming laws; the Supreme Court has been petitioned to resolve the split. CNN notes it has a partnership with Kalshi and uses its data, but CNN editorial employees may not use prediction markets.

articles.title: Belgium's streaming pay right for artists must prevent "double payment," EU Advocate General says in Spotify and majors case
articles.description: An Advocate General at the Court of Justice of the European Union has said Belgium's law giving authors and performers a right to be paid directly by streaming services is not, in principle, incompatible with EU law — but parts of how it operates breach EU law, chiefly because it must not allow the same use of a work to be paid for twice. The case was brought by Streamz and subsidiaries of Spotify, Sony, Universal, Warner, Google and Meta. The opinion is non-binding; the court will rule at a later date.
articles.body: An Advocate General at the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) has said that Belgium's law giving authors and performers a right to be paid directly by streaming services and user-upload platforms is not, in principle, incompatible with EU law. However, Advocate General Maciej Szpunar also said that some of the detailed rules governing how the Belgian right operates breach EU law, chiefly on freedom-to-provide-services grounds. Szpunar's Opinion, delivered on Thursday, November 19, says the Belgian scheme must not allow the same exploitation of a work to be paid for twice, especially where a service has already paid a producer under its licensing deal, and total remuneration must remain appropriate and proportionate. The case, C-663/24, stems from challenges to the law brought by Belgian video streaming service Streamz and by subsidiaries of Spotify, Sony Music Entertainment, Universal Music, Warner Music, Google and Meta. Belgium's law, dated June 19, 2022, transposed the EU's Digital Single Market copyright directive and handed a separate payment entitlement to authors and performers who assigned their exclusive rights to a producer. Szpunar concluded that EU law does not, in principle, rule out splitting the right to authorize a use from the right to be paid for it, but the freedom to provide services precludes the Belgian mechanism to the extent it stops such licenses being granted for online uses in Belgium. Separately, he said EU law does not, in principle, block the Belgian law's remuneration mechanisms for press publishers. Advocate General Opinions are not binding on the CJEU, whose judges have now begun deliberations; the CJEU heard the case on July 6 and 7, following a referral from Belgium's Constitutional Court lodged in October 2024. IFPI welcomed the opinion, saying national remuneration rules must respect the EU single market and should not result in double payments.

articles.title: Nicolás Jaar's Other People — where artists retain all rights — signs worldwide distribution deal with Secretly
articles.description: Secretly Distribution has signed a worldwide distribution deal with Other People, the independent record label, book publisher and artist collective founded by Nicolás Jaar. Other People's contracts let artists keep all rights and set their own share of revenue after recoupment. Secretly will handle physical and digital distribution, marketing and technological support for all of the label's releases.
articles.body: Secretly Distribution has signed a worldwide distribution deal with Other People, the independent record label, book publisher and artist collective founded by Nicolás Jaar. Other People's contracts let artists keep all rights and set their own share of revenue after recoupment, according to the announcement. Secretly Distribution will now handle physical and digital distribution, digital and retail marketing, and technological support for all of the label's releases and initiatives. Established in New York City by Jaar in 2013, and now run by Jaar and Nicolina Claeson, Other People has released more than 90 albums and half a dozen books through its artist-friendly contract structure. Its roster includes Enxin/Onyx (Hiro Kone & Tot Onyx), Eli Wewentxu, Ali Sethi and Jaar himself. "Other People is a uniquely powerful creative force in independent music," said Jacqui Resur, VP Client Relations at Secretly Distribution. Alongside Secretly Distribution, Other People joins a distributed label roster that includes Secretly affiliates Dead Oceans, drink sum wtr, Ghostly International, Jagjaguwar, Merge Records, Sacred Bones Records, Secretly Canadian and Numero Group. The deal follows Secretly Distribution's Distributor of the Year win at the 2026 Libera Awards and the launch of its APAC division. For Secretly, it adds one of independent music's most ideologically distinctive labels, while for Other People it brings global distribution scale without giving up the rights-retention model that defines it.

articles.title: Producer sues Travis Scott, Don Toliver and Sony Music, claiming he owns half the master of JackBoys track "What To Do?"
articles.description: Israeli producer Niv Kalisky, who works as Early Yellow, is suing Travis Scott, Don Toliver and Sony Music over the 2019 JackBoys track "What To Do?", claiming it was built on his recording Moazin99bpm and that he has not been paid any master royalties in nearly seven years. He is asking the court to declare he owns 50% of the master and award him at least half of what it has earned. The complaint was filed in New York federal court on November 17.
articles.body: Israeli producer Niv Kalisky, who works as Early Yellow, is suing Travis Scott, Don Toliver and Sony Music over the 2019 JackBoys track What To Do?, claiming the track was built on a recording of his called Moazin99bpm and that he has not been paid any master royalties for its use in the nearly seven years since the track was released. He is asking the court to declare that he owns 50% of the What To Do? master recording and to award him at least half of what that recording has earned. The complaint was filed in New York federal court on Tuesday, November 17. The lawsuit also names Sheck Wes and producers Mike Dean, London Cyr and Jenius as defendants, plus five corporate defendants: Sony Music Entertainment, Epic Records, Cactus Jack Records, LaFlame Enterprises and London Cyr Productions. According to the complaint, What To Do? has been streamed more than 270 million times on Spotify and played more than 60 million times on YouTube. Kalisky says he emailed Moazin99bpm to a representative for Cyr and Jenius in May and July 2019, and that Cyr sent him a beat incorporating it "for review and approval" on October 30, 2019; the beat was later used in What To Do?, released less than two months later. The complaint claims at least 16 "similarities and identical copies of musical material" between the recordings, and alleges Sony and Epic filed false counter-notices to get the track reinstated on Spotify, Apple Music and YouTube after Kalisky filed takedowns in October. He seeks his actual losses plus the defendants' profits across 44 categories of income, or alternatively statutory damages of $150,000 per infringement, plus at least $250,000 each for unfair competition and the allegedly false counter-notices and $500,000 for unjust enrichment. He also asks for a permanent ban on use of the track, which if granted could take it off streaming services. The complaint notes his copyright registration of Moazin99bpm came only on June 25, 2026, which under US law may limit statutory damages, and cites a March ruling in a separate case against Scott in which Victory Boyd could not claim statutory damages for pre-registration infringement.

articles.title: PlaqueBoyMax wants to find your next favorite artist
articles.description: Streamer PlaqueBoyMax is running a music competition, "Rising Star," giving emerging artists a weekend to show what they can do, as Rolling Stone profiles his move from streaming tastemaker to talent scout. The piece, published within the last day, also notes he has an album of his own in the works.
articles.body: Streamer PlaqueBoyMax is using his platform to find new talent, with a music competition called "Rising Star" that gives emerging artists a weekend to show what they can do. Rolling Stone's profile, published within the last day, frames the streamer as a tastemaker turning talent scout, using his audience and ear for new music to surface artists who might otherwise go unheard. The competition format compresses the discovery process into a single weekend, with artists performing and competing for attention from PlaqueBoyMax's large streaming audience. The profile also notes that PlaqueBoyMax has an album of his own in the works, marking his move from curator and commentator to recording artist in his own right. It reflects a broader shift in how new artists break through, with streamers and online communities increasingly acting as the A&R filter that labels once monopolized. For independent and unsigned artists, a co-sign or a slot in a competition like "Rising Star" can mean instant exposure to hundreds of thousands of listeners. The piece lands as streaming-native discovery continues to reshape the industry, with platforms and personalities, rather than radio or traditional press, deciding which new voices get heard first.

articles.title: Russell Brand's wife will "honor" prison rules barring his messages
articles.description: Laura Brand, the wife of Russell Brand, says she will "honor" the rules at HMP Littlehey barring messages from her husband, after a week of controversy over a message he sent from prison. Brand was sentenced on November 9 to 10 years and six months after being convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
articles.body: Russell Brand's wife Laura Brand says she will "honor" the prison rules barring messages from her husband, after a week of controversy over a message he shared from behind bars. "I understand the parameters set by the brilliant staff at HMP Littlehey [prison]," Laura Brand said, in Rolling Stone's report published within the last day. Brand, 51, was sentenced on November 9 at Southwark Crown Court to 10 years and six months in prison after a jury convicted him of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault against four women between 2004 and 2009; he was acquitted of two further rape charges and one count of indecent assault. He must serve at least two-thirds of the sentence, about seven years, before becoming eligible for parole, and has been placed on the sex offenders register for life. Days after sentencing, Laura Brand appeared alone on the couple's joint podcast, Sunday Service with the Brands, on November 15, reading out a statement from her husband in which he maintained his innocence. That message was later reported to be "urgently investigated" by authorities, per the Prime Minister's office. Brand has been moved to HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a Category C prison. Laura Brand, the daughter of golfer Bernard Gallacher, married Brand in 2017; they have three children together. Page Six has also reported that another woman has come forward in the United States and is consulting high-profile attorneys, suggesting Brand's legal troubles may not be over.

articles.title: 50 years ago today: The Beach Boys play pivotal "Brian's Back" concert in Cincinnati
articles.description: Fifty years ago, on November 22, 1976, the Beach Boys played a pivotal "Brian's Back" concert at the Riverfront Coliseum in Cincinnati, marking Brian Wilson's full return to touring for the first time since 1964. The show previewed two songs from the forthcoming album The Beach Boys Love You and was the last time the band played a significant amount of new material in concert.
articles.body: Fifty years ago, on November 22, 1976, the Beach Boys played a pivotal "Brian's Back" concert at the Riverfront Coliseum in Cincinnati, Ohio, Rolling Stone recalls in an anniversary feature published November 22. The show marked Brian Wilson's full commitment to a winter tour in November and December 1976, after he had been an infrequent presence at the band's summer shows, and his return to the road for the first time since 1964. Band manager Steve Love had decided to rouse Wilson from his bed to generate a groundswell of interest as the Endless Summer nostalgia wave began to fade, promoting the campaign with an NBC television special put together by Lorne Michaels and the original Saturday Night Live team, including the famous "Surf Police" sketch with Dan Aykroyd and John Belushi. Annie Leibovitz shot a classic photo of Wilson standing on the sand in his blue robe that appeared on the November 4, 1976 cover of Rolling Stone. The Cincinnati show opened with "Wouldn't It Be Nice" and "Palisades Park," and previewed two unreleased songs, "Love Is a Woman" and "Airplane," which Mike Love said would be out in January on the group's new album, The Beach Boys Love You. Tickets cost $7.50 in advance and $8.50 on the day, with unreserved seating throughout the venue. The show closed with a long run of surf-era hits ending with "Fun, Fun, Fun." The tour marked the last time the band played a significant amount of new material in concert, and the feature notes the band has since settled into its role as a heritage act.

articles.title: Morgan Wallen's "Last Thing You Need" from the "GTA 6" soundtrack climbs the Hot 100
articles.description: Morgan Wallen's "Last Thing You Need," the fourth single from Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, is climbing the Billboard Hot 100 again, moving up six spots from No. 27 to No. 21 on the chart for the week of November 21. The song, released September 17, debuted on the Hot 100 on October 3 and peaked at No. 9 before dropping off, and the game's release has brought it back into the zeitgeist.
articles.body: Morgan Wallen's "Last Thing You Need," from the Grand Theft Auto VI soundtrack, is climbing the Billboard Hot 100 again, moving up six spots on the chart for the week of November 21. Last week the country hit sat at No. 27; this week it rises to No. 21, according to Billboard chart data reported November 23. The song was released on September 17, 2026, as the fourth single from Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, and made its Hot 100 debut on October 3, peaking at No. 9 before dropping off prior to the game's release. The buzz around the game, which has grossed over $4.0 billion in four days and sold 44.9 million copies according to The Alinea Insight newsletter, has brought the tune back into the zeitgeist. Penned by Wallen, John Byron, Chase McGill, Blake Pendergrass and Ryan Vojtesak, "Last Thing You Need" was initially intended for Wallen's as-yet-untitled fifth album, but when the GTA 6 team approached Wallen about recording music for the soundtrack, the song felt best suited for the game. Pendergrass described the song's central couple as closely resembling Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos' relationship in GTA 6. The track has also peaked at No. 4 on Hot Country Songs and No. 24 on Country Airplay. Wallen released the first single from his as-yet-untitled fifth album, "Been By Now," on July 24, 2026, and that song still sits in the Hot 100 top 10 at No. 9. The climb shows how the game's soundtrack is feeding back into the singles chart, not just the albums chart.

articles.title: P!nk extends Las Vegas Sphere residency into 2028, adding six January dates
articles.description: P!nk is extending her Las Vegas Sphere residency into 2028, adding six January dates after the original nine shows quickly sold out, Billboard reported on November 20. She is the first solo female pop artist to headline the Sphere. The extension underlines the venue's pull as a residency destination for major pop acts.
articles.body: P!nk is extending her Las Vegas Sphere residency into 2028, adding six January dates after the original nine shows quickly sold out, Billboard reported on November 20. She is the first solo female pop artist to headline the Sphere, the Las Vegas venue that has become the most in-demand residency stage in the world since opening. The quick sell-out of the original nine dates prompted the extension, with the new January 2028 shows giving more fans a chance to see the production. Sphere residencies have become a major revenue stream for legacy pop acts, with the venue's immersive visuals and sound offering a spectacle that touring arenas cannot match. P!nk, known for her aerial acrobatics and high-energy live shows, is a natural fit for the format, and her residency follows a run of successful Sphere engagements by rock and pop headliners. The extension also reflects the broader shift toward residencies as a complement to touring, letting artists play multiple dates in one city while reaching a global audience that travels to Las Vegas. Details of the new January dates and on-sale information were announced alongside the extension.

articles.title: Putin agreed to NATO Article 5-style security guarantees for Ukraine — but without allied troops on the ground, Washington Post reports
articles.description: Vladimir Putin has agreed to security guarantees for Ukraine modelled on NATO's Article 5, but without the deployment of allied troops in the country, The Washington Post reports. The proposal would commit partners to respond if Russia attacks again, while stopping short of the troop presence Kyiv has long sought. It is the latest signal in a flurry of diplomacy around a possible settlement — and a test of whether 'NATO-style' guarantees mean the same thing in Kyiv and Washington.
articles.body: According to The Washington Post, cited by Meduza, Putin has accepted the idea of guarantees for Ukraine analogous to Article 5 of the NATO treaty — the alliance's collective-defence clause — but without stationing allied forces on Ukrainian soil. The distinction matters: Kyiv has spent months pressing for guarantees with real teeth, and Zelenskyy said only days ago that he questions whether Kyiv and Washington even mean the same thing by 'NATO-style' guarantees. The report lands in a crowded diplomatic week — Melania Trump said ceasefire talks are under way and a deal could come before Christmas, while the Financial Times reported Trump is pushing for a peace deal by early January, before Democrats take Congress. Putin, for his part, said last week he would not negotiate after Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge. Whether a guarantee without troops on the ground would be enough for Kyiv — or credible enough to deter Moscow — is now the central question, and the details of who would enforce it, and how, remain unclear.

articles.title: US intelligence chief: Putin 'is not America's friend in Ukraine. Not at all'
articles.description: US Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton has pushed back on Donald Trump's repeated description of Vladimir Putin as his 'friend,' telling ABC News: 'Is Vladimir Putin America's friend? He is not America's friend in Ukraine. Not at all. Not at all.' Trump first greeted Putin as his 'friend' at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 19, and has repeated it since. The unusually blunt correction from inside the administration underlines the tension in Trump's Russia rhetoric.
articles.body: Clayton was asked by ABC's anchor whether Putin could be considered a friend of the United States, 'because Trump said he couldn't answer that question' — and answered with unusual directness. Trump greeted Putin as his 'friend' at the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping at the APEC summit in Shenzhen on November 19, then defended the description days later, even while mixing up the Yalta and Tehran conferences in the same remarks. The intelligence chief's reply is striking precisely because it comes from within Trump's own administration, and it lands as the White House pursues a peace deal with Moscow. It also echoes the wider unease in Washington and European capitals about the tone of Trump's outreach to Putin — and about what, if anything, the friendship framing costs Ukraine at the negotiating table.

articles.title: War, day 1,733: Ukraine's defence sector has probably hit its ceiling
articles.description: Meduza's daily war briefing argues that Ukraine's defence industry has probably reached its ceiling, held back by fragmented financing, staff shortages and Russian strikes. The assessment is a sobering one for a sector that has become central to Ukraine's war effort. It suggests the rapid wartime expansion of domestic arms production is running into hard limits.
articles.body: In its day-1,733 war summary, Meduza reports that Ukraine's defence sector has likely hit its ceiling — the point where fragmented funding, a shortage of personnel and relentless Russian strikes on production sites are constraining further growth. The finding matters because domestic production has been one of Kyiv's main answers to the uncertainty of Western aid: drones, missiles and artillery made at home. But the briefing's argument is that the sector cannot simply keep scaling — money arrives in pieces, skilled workers are scarce, and Russia is deliberately targeting the plants. It is a structural problem, not a temporary one, and it frames the debate over Western support: if Ukraine cannot build everything itself, the flow of allied weapons and money remains decisive.

articles.title: Climate summit ends in scandal: 'the worst summit in history'
articles.description: The world's biggest climate conference has ended in scandal, with participants unable to agree the text of its key document, Meduza reports. Delegates called it the worst summit in history. It is the outcome many feared after days of deadlock over just two words in the final text.
articles.body: Meduza sums up the close of the world's biggest climate conference as a scandal: after days of negotiation, the participants could not agree the text of the key document, and the summit ended without the deal it was convened to produce. The collapse follows days of warnings — earlier in the week, reports said two words in the draft text could derail the whole conference. In the end, that is effectively what happened. The failure leaves the central questions of climate finance and emissions commitments unresolved for another year, and hands critics of the COP process its most damaging verdict yet: that the format itself can no longer deliver.

articles.title: Hackers breached the FBI again, gaining access to a national crime database
articles.description: Hackers have again broken into FBI systems, gaining access to a national database of crimes, Meduza reports. It is the latest in a series of breaches of US law-enforcement systems. The scale of what was taken has not been disclosed.
articles.body: Meduza reports that hackers have once again breached the FBI, this time gaining access to a national database of crimes. The report gives few details about how the intrusion happened or what data was exposed, but the fact of a repeat breach is itself the story — US federal law-enforcement systems have been hit more than once, and a database of criminal records is among the most sensitive holdings a government keeps. The incident lands in a week already full of warnings about the fragility of American digital infrastructure, from the Microsoft outage to the FAA ground stop earlier this month, and it will raise fresh questions about how the Bureau protects its own systems.

articles.title: Meet the new owner of Miro, the whiteboard service invented in Perm: Bending Spoons
articles.description: Miro, the online whiteboard service originally created in Perm, has a new owner: the Italian app developer Bending Spoons, Meduza reports. The deal is the latest in Bending Spoons' run of acquisitions. It puts one of the world's best-known collaboration tools in the hands of a company better known for consumer apps.
articles.body: Meduza introduces the new owner of Miro — Bending Spoons, the Milan-based company behind a string of popular consumer apps, which has been buying up software businesses at a rapid pace. Miro began in Perm, Russia, as a whiteboard tool for remote teams, and grew into one of the defining products of the remote-work era, used by millions of teams around the world. The sale is a reminder of how thoroughly the company has left its Russian origins behind, and of Bending Spoons' ambitions: the Italian firm has built a portfolio by acquiring established apps and running them as a group. What changes for Miro's users under the new ownership is not yet clear.

articles.title: Five people injured in Ukrainian drone attack on Krasnodar region; reports of a possible strike on a Rosgvardia building
articles.description: Five people were injured in a Ukrainian drone attack on Russia's Krasnodar region, Meduza reports, citing the Astra Telegram channel. Astra also reported a possible strike on a Rosgvardia building. It is the latest in the steady drumbeat of Ukrainian drone strikes deep inside Russia.
articles.body: According to Meduza, five people were hurt when Ukrainian drones attacked the Krasnodar region, and the Astra Telegram channel reported a possible hit on a building belonging to Rosgvardia, Russia's national guard. The strike is part of the near-daily exchange of long-range drone attacks that has defined this phase of the war — Ukraine hitting refineries, depots and military sites inside Russia, and Russia answering with massed strikes on Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure. Krasnodar, in Russia's south, has been hit repeatedly, and the reported targeting of a Rosgvardia facility suggests the campaign is reaching beyond energy and logistics into the security apparatus itself.

articles.title: Zelenskyy proposed evacuating residents of 15 settlements, following the example of Oleshky
articles.description: President Zelenskyy has proposed evacuating residents of 15 frontline settlements, following the example of Oleshky, Meduza reports. The move reflects the deteriorating conditions for civilians near the front. It comes as Russia presses on multiple axes and winter sets in.
articles.body: Meduza reports that Zelenskyy has proposed evacuating the residents of 15 settlements, citing the precedent of Oleshky — the town in the Kherson region that was evacuated as fighting made it uninhabitable. The proposal is a measure of how hard life has become for civilians near the front: constant shelling, destroyed infrastructure, and now winter, with power, water and heating under repeated attack. Evacuations are a grim routine of this war, but a proposal covering 15 settlements at once signals the scale of the displacement still to come, and the state's effort to move people before the cold and the fighting make it impossible.

articles.title: Zelenskyy confirms Ukrainian drones sank Russian corvette 'Mercury' off Libya and hit a Russian dry-cargo ship
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that Ukrainian sea drones sank the Russian corvette Mercury at a naval base in Benghazi, Libya, and struck a Russian dry-cargo vessel nearby. The operation, on November 22, extends Ukraine's long-range strike campaign far beyond the Black Sea. It shows Kyiv is willing to hit Russian military assets wherever they are deployed.
articles.body: Zelenskyy confirmed the operation himself, according to Ukrainska Pravda's homepage, saying Ukrainian drones sank the Mercury and hit a Russian dry-cargo ship off the Libyan coast. The Mercury was reportedly at a naval base in Benghazi when it was hit, and a separate uncrewed-boat attack struck the cargo vessel ASCALON near the port the same evening. Meduza, citing Naval News, also reported a Russian military ship exploding off Libya. The strike fits a pattern: between November 16 and 21 alone, Ukrainian forces hit Russian refineries, oil depots, the Kerch Bridge and military sites, and the SBU says its 'Ptakh' campaign hit 40 Russian oil depots and military-industrial targets in 50 days. Taking the war to a Russian warship in the Mediterranean is a striking escalation of that campaign — and a signal to Moscow that distance is no longer protection.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: partners want four-party talks by Christmas; Ukraine ready as early as tomorrow
articles.description: President Zelenskyy says Ukraine's partners aim to hold four-party talks by Christmas, and Kyiv is ready to start tomorrow. The comments suggest diplomacy is accelerating after weeks of mixed signals. They follow Melania Trump's remark that ceasefire talks are under way and a deal could come before Christmas.
articles.body: Speaking to reporters, Zelenskyy said Ukraine's partners want four-party talks held by Christmas, and that Ukraine itself is ready to begin as early as tomorrow. The remark, carried on Ukrainska Pravda's homepage, is the most concrete timetable yet for a negotiation that has been discussed for weeks — and it comes after days of contradictory signals, with Putin saying he would not negotiate after the Crimean Bridge strikes, and Melania Trump saying ceasefire talks are under way and a deal could come before Christmas. Who the four parties would be, and what would be on the table, remains unclear, and the gap between Kyiv's readiness and Moscow's stated refusal is the obvious obstacle. But the Christmas deadline gives the diplomacy a shape it did not have before, and a clock.

articles.title: Three killed after strike hits private clinic building in Zaporizhzhia
articles.description: Three people were killed after a strike hit a private clinic building in Zaporizhzhia, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The attack is the latest Russian strike on civilian infrastructure in the frontline city. Zaporizhzhia has been hit repeatedly as Russia presses in the region.
articles.body: A strike on a private clinic in Zaporizhzhia killed three people, according to Ukrainska Pravda's lead story this morning. The clinic is the kind of target that has become grimly familiar in this war — civilian, medical, and far from any front line — and the deaths add to a toll that has been rising across the south and east. Zaporizhzhia region was hit by 489 strikes in a single day last week, with two killed and 22 injured, and the frontline there remains one of the most active, with 131 combat engagements recorded in a day. The clinic strike is a reminder that the war's civilian cost is not measured only in the big overnight barrages, but in single strikes on single buildings.

articles.title: Western intelligence warns Russia is preparing to place nuclear weapons in space
articles.description: Western intelligence agencies have warned several NATO countries that Russia may be preparing to place nuclear weapons in space, according to media reports carried by Ukrainska Pravda. The warning is the latest in a series of alarms about Moscow's space ambitions. It raises the stakes of a domain that has so far stayed out of the war's direct fighting.
articles.body: Western intelligence services have warned a number of NATO states about possible Russian plans to deploy nuclear weapons in space, according to media reports highlighted by Ukrainska Pravda. The warning is short on specifics — what kind of weapon, and on what timetable, has not been made public — but the fact that it was circulated to allies suggests it is being taken seriously. Space has been a growing theatre of the war in quieter ways: Starlink and satellite reconnaissance are central to the fighting, and Russia has repeatedly threatened Western satellites. A nuclear weapon in orbit would be a different order of escalation, and a breach of the Outer Space Treaty. For now, the report is a warning, not a confirmed deployment — but it is the kind of warning NATO does not issue lightly.

articles.title: Russian army attacks Lozova: fires break out, 12 injured
articles.description: A Russian attack on Lozova, in the Kharkiv region, caused fires and injured 12 people, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The town has been hit repeatedly during the war. The attack adds to a weekend of strikes across the east.
articles.body: Russian forces attacked Lozova, a town in the Kharkiv region, starting fires and injuring 12 people, according to Ukrainska Pravda. The report is brief, but Lozova's place on the map explains why it keeps being hit: it is a railway junction in a region that has been under near-constant attack, and Russian forces have struck it with drones and missiles throughout the war. The injuries — 12 people — make it one of the heavier single-town tolls of the weekend, and it comes as emergency power outages remain in effect across several regions after the latest strikes on energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Chernyshov receives notice of suspicion over fictitious employment
articles.description: Chernyshov has been formally notified of suspicion in connection with alleged fictitious employment, Ukrainska Pravda reports. The notice is a formal step in a criminal investigation. It is the latest in the rolling series of corruption cases involving senior Ukrainian officials.
articles.body: Ukrainska Pravda reports that Chernyshov has received a notice of suspicion — the formal Ukrainian procedural step that marks someone as a suspect in a criminal case — over alleged fictitious employment. The details of the allegation have not been spelled out in the headline report, but the case lands in a charged moment: anti-corruption bodies NABU and SAPO have been at the centre of a political storm, with investigators reporting obstruction of their work and the 'Carthage' operation uncovering some 505 fraudulent call centres. Whether this case is connected to that wider sweep is not yet clear. What is clear is that corruption investigations of senior figures remain a live and politically explosive front in Kyiv, alongside the war itself.

articles.title: No backup boiler house launched yet in Darnytsia power plant zone, restoration chief says
articles.description: Not a single backup boiler house has yet been launched in the area served by Kyiv's Darnytsia thermal power plant, the head of the State Agency for Restoration said, according to Ukrainska Pravda. The admission is a worrying one as winter approaches and Russian strikes on energy infrastructure continue. Heating in the capital's left bank depends on the plants holding up.
articles.body: The head of the State Agency for Restoration told Ukrainska Pravda that no reserve boiler house has yet started operating in the zone served by the Darnytsia thermal power plant — one of the facilities that heats Kyiv's left bank. The statement is stark: with winter approaching and Russian strikes on energy infrastructure continuing, the backup heating that was supposed to protect residents if the main plant is hit is not yet in place. Kyiv was left without water after an overnight attack last week, and emergency power outages remain in effect in five regions. The Darnytsia admission will be read as a measure of how much of the winter-preparation work is still unfinished — and how exposed the capital remains.

articles.title: Mykhailiuk rewrites Ukrainian basketball history in the NBA: 39 points and a three-point record
articles.description: Sviatoslav Mykhailiuk has set a new Ukrainian NBA mark, scoring 39 points and setting a three-point record, Ukrainska Pravda reports. It is the best scoring night by a Ukrainian in NBA history. The performance is a rare bright spot in a grim news cycle.
articles.body: Sviatoslav Mykhailiuk scored 39 points and set a record for three-pointers by a Ukrainian in the NBA, rewriting his country's basketball history in a single night. The performance, reported by Ukrainska Pravda, is the highest-scoring game ever by a Ukrainian player in the league — a milestone for a country whose NBA presence has always been small. Mykhailiuk, a veteran of several NBA teams, has built his career on exactly this skill: shooting from deep. A 39-point night with a three-point record is the kind of game that gets a role player noticed, and for Ukrainian fans it is a rare moment of sporting pride in a week dominated by war news.

articles.title: Ex-Rockstar North chief and MindsEye creator apparently fled Britain as his studio faces liquidation
articles.description: Leslie Benzies, the former Rockstar North chief behind MindsEye, has apparently fled Britain, according to new reports surfacing around the GTA VI launch. His studio, Build A Rocket Boy, entered liquidation proceedings in September. The news adds a strange coda to the week the industry's biggest launch has dominated.
articles.body: GameMAG reports that fresh details have emerged about the developers of MindsEye as Grand Theft Auto VI dominates the conversation. Benzies, who once ran Rockstar North, founded Build A Rocket Boy after leaving Rockstar, and the studio's debut game MindsEye was a critical and commercial disappointment. In September it emerged that the studio had begun liquidation proceedings. Now reports suggest Benzies himself has left Britain, though the details of where he has gone remain unclear. It is a remarkable fall for a man who was once at the centre of the biggest franchise in games — and a reminder that the week of GTA VI's record-breaking launch has also been a week of reckoning for the people who used to make it.

articles.title: Rockstar's next game after GTA VI could be L.A. Noire 2 — rumour
articles.description: Rockstar's next game after Grand Theft Auto VI could be a sequel to the detective game L.A. Noire, according to a rumour resurfacing after GTA VI's launch. The claim traces back to a 2023 GTAForums post. It is unconfirmed, but fans have seized on it now that GTA VI is out.
articles.body: GameMAG reports that, with GTA VI finally released, players have revived a 2023 GTAForums post claiming Rockstar's next project is L.A. Noire 2 — a sequel to the 2011 detective game set in 1940s Los Angeles. The rumour is thinly sourced, and Rockstar has said nothing, but the timing is telling: with the studio's biggest game out the door, speculation about what comes next has begun immediately, and Take-Two's chief was already being asked about GTA VII on launch day. L.A. Noire has a devoted following, and a sequel built with modern technology is an appealing idea — but for now it is only a forum post, remembered at the right moment.

articles.title: Castlevania: Belmont's Curse review — the curse of the first hours
articles.description: GameMAG's review of Castlevania: Belmont's Curse says the new entry in the classic series puts players through powerful emotional swings from the very first hours. The reviewer opens with a personal history of the series — then says this game broke the pattern. It is the latest revival of one of gaming's oldest franchises.
articles.body: In its review, GameMAG says Castlevania: Belmont's Curse takes players on such an intense emotional ride in its opening hours that the reviewer abandoned the usual approach of starting with a personal history of the series. The review's framing — 'the curse of the first hours' — suggests a game that is demanding from the start, in the tradition of a franchise that has always been unforgiving. Castlevania is one of the oldest names in gaming, and each revival carries the weight of that history. Whether Belmont's Curse lives up to it is the question the review sets out to answer, and its opening suggests the game does not ease players in gently.

articles.title: Snape, Dumbledore and McGonagall feature in fresh posters for HBO's Harry Potter series
articles.description: HBO has released a new set of posters for its Harry Potter series, this time featuring the teachers — Severus Snape, Albus Dumbledore and Minerva McGonagall. The posters follow an earlier set showing the young trio of Harry, Hermione and Ron. The series is one of the most closely watched adaptations in years.
articles.body: Following posters of the young Hogwarts trio — Harry Potter, Hermione Granger and Ron Weasley, played by Dominic McLaughlin, Arabella Stanton and Alastair Stout — HBO has now published a set featuring the teachers: Severus Snape, Albus Dumbledore and Minerva McGonagall. The slow drip of images is the standard marketing rhythm for a series of this scale, but each one is scrutinised for clues about the show's look and casting. The Harry Potter series is HBO's biggest swing in years, and the posters are the first real sense of how it will present the characters a generation grew up with. Expect every detail to be debated.

articles.title: Sony lays off most Screen Gems staff in restructuring
articles.description: Sony has begun restructuring its Screen Gems film unit and has laid off most of its staff, GameMAG reports. The studio specialised in horror franchises such as Insidious and Evil Dead, and in mid-budget genre films. The cuts reflect the industry's continuing squeeze on the mid-budget studio.
articles.body: Sony has started restructuring Screen Gems, its film subsidiary, and has laid off most of the unit's employees, according to GameMAG. Screen Gems was the home of horror franchises including Insidious and Evil Dead, as well as Until Dawn, and specialised in the mid-budget genre films that have become increasingly hard to sustain as studios concentrate on blockbusters and streaming. The layoffs are part of a broader retrenchment across Hollywood, where even profitable genre labels are being folded into larger operations. What happens to Screen Gems' slate — and to the franchises it housed — is now an open question.

articles.title: Crysis gets a co-op mode thanks to a mod
articles.description: Enthusiasts have added a co-operative mode to Crysis, the 2007 first-person shooter, GameMAG reports. The mod lets up to four players tackle missions together, with a lobby system for finding sessions. It is a reminder of how long a good game can live in the hands of its fans.
articles.body: A group of modders has done what Crytek never did: added full co-operative play to the original Crysis. The modification lets four players take on the 2007 shooter's missions together, and includes a lobby where you can invite friends or find an existing session. Crysis was famous on release for melting PCs — 'can it run Crysis?' became the benchmark joke of a generation — and its open, systems-driven levels turn out to suit co-op well. Nearly two decades after release, the game's community is still building on it, and the mod is a small illustration of why PC gaming's modding culture matters: it keeps old games alive in ways their makers never planned.

articles.title: Disney drops trailer for 'Ice Age: Boiling Point,' out February 5, 2027
articles.description: Disney has released the trailer for 'Ice Age: Boiling Point,' the sixth film in the long-running animated franchise, GameMAG reports. Manny, Sid, Diego, Ellie and Scrat set off on a new adventure. The film reaches cinemas on February 5, 2027.
articles.body: Disney has unveiled the trailer for Ice Age: Boiling Point, the sixth entry in a franchise that began in 2002 and has now spanned nearly a quarter of a century. Manny, Sid, Diego, Ellie and Scrat head off on another journey into uncharted territory, in the familiar formula that has carried the series through five films and more than $3 billion at the box office. The February 5, 2027 release date puts it in the early-year family slot Disney has used before. For a franchise many assumed had ended, the trailer is a statement of intent: Ice Age is still going, and Disney still believes there is an audience for it.

articles.title: Republicans mulling deal that would fund the military but limit operations in Iran
articles.description: Top Senate Democrats and Republicans are in high-stakes talks on a deal that would replenish tens of billions in urgently needed Pentagon funding in exchange for cutting off money for future offensive operations in the Iran war. Senate Armed Services chairman Roger Wicker said there may be a way for Democrats 'to make their point without tying the hands of the commander in chief.' The negotiation comes as the Iran conflict's costs mount and Congress reasserts its say over war powers.
articles.body: According to CNN, lawmakers from both parties are engaged in high-stakes talks about a bargain: Democrats would agree to replenish the tens of billions the Department of Defense says it urgently needs, and in return funding would be cut off for future offensive operations in the Iran war. Wicker, the Republican chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, told CNN on Friday that he sees a path for Democrats to register their opposition 'without tying the hands of the commander in chief and the defense of our country.' The talks reflect the political bind around the war — the administration needs the money, while Democrats, weeks from taking Congress, want limits on a conflict they did not authorise. Any deal would be a rare bipartisan check on presidential war-making, and its shape will set the terms for how the Iran war is funded and fought into next year.

articles.title: Dual storms threaten Thanksgiving plans from coast to coast; Macy's parade balloons at risk
articles.description: Two storm systems threaten to disrupt Thanksgiving travel across the US this week, with a coastal storm set to bring downpours and strong winds to the Northeast on Thanksgiving Day itself — potentially grounding the balloons in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. A separate system brings near-record tides and flooding risk to the San Francisco Bay Area. Travellers have a window of dry weather Tuesday and much of Wednesday to beat the worst of it.
articles.body: From Washington, DC, to Boston, dry weather is expected Tuesday and much of Wednesday before the new coastal system moves in, bringing downpours and strong winds on Thanksgiving Day — and in New York City, the wind could put the giant balloons in the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade in jeopardy even before the rain arrives. This is the same storm that flooded Florida's Space Coast earlier in the week and has been threatening holiday travel up the East Coast for days. Meanwhile, a separate system will pose trouble in the San Francisco Bay Area, where unusually high tides could flood shoreline roads Monday morning even before the storm arrives Tuesday. The National Weather Service has issued a rare coastal flood warning from early Monday through Thanksgiving Day, with the greatest threat around each morning's high tide — and water at the San Francisco tide gauge could come within an inch of its 1983 record close to 11 a.m. PT on Wednesday. It is shaping up to be one of the messiest Thanksgiving travel weeks in years, on both coasts at once.

articles.title: Trump's showdown with Congress is catching fire, weeks before Democrats take power
articles.description: President Trump's confrontation with Congress is escalating weeks before Democrats take power, CNN reports. In a major power play, Trump is seeking to limit who, how and what Democrats can investigate — including an executive order on Friday warning federal contractors to coordinate congressional requests with the White House. Key Democratic investigators are pushing back.
articles.body: In a major power play, Trump is seeking to limit who, how and what Democrats can investigate as they prepare to use their new powers in the next Congress to target his alleged corruption. On Friday he issued an executive order warning businesses that deal with the federal government to coordinate requests for information with the White House, invoking executive privilege. Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin, incoming head of the House Judiciary Committee, said on CNN's 'State of the Union' that the order 'has all the force of an interoffice memo,' and insisted 'we have got the Constitution on our side.' The administration has already threatened Democratic investigators with possible prosecution as it resists probes into White House dealings with corporate CEOs, Trump's architectural projects including his new ballroom, the business activities of his family and Cabinet members, and the origins and conduct of the Iran war. Treacherous days loom for companies caught between the two sides — and the confrontation is only beginning.

articles.title: Trump Organization hosts 'exclusive' dinner to promote president's meme coin
articles.description: President Trump's meme coin club held a private event at his golf club in Virginia on Sunday, CNN reports, where the price of admission was a major stake in the cryptocurrency. The dinner is the latest blending of the Trump family's crypto business with the presidency. It raises the same conflict-of-interest questions that have followed the coin since its launch.
articles.body: The Trump Organization hosted an 'exclusive' dinner at the president's Virginia golf club on Sunday to promote his meme coin, with admission effectively requiring a major holding in the cryptocurrency. The event is the latest in the strange afterlife of the Trump meme coin — a digital asset tied to the sitting president that has drawn scrutiny from ethics watchdogs and Democrats since its launch. The dinner's guest list and the sums involved have not been disclosed, but the format — pay in coin, dine with the brand — captures the way the Trump family's crypto ventures have fused with the presidency. For critics, it is a textbook conflict of interest; for the administration, it is business as usual. Either way, the coin keeps generating headlines — and revenue.

articles.title: San Francisco braces for near-record tides as storm collides with Thanksgiving travel
articles.description: San Francisco Bay could rise to near-record levels this week as a strong storm combines with some of the year's highest tides, CNN reports. The National Weather Service has issued a rare coastal flood warning from Monday through Thanksgiving Day. Water at the San Francisco tide gauge could come within an inch of its 1983 record on Wednesday morning.
articles.body: San Francisco Bay could rise to near-record levels this week, as a strong storm coupled with some of the year's highest tides moves ashore, threatening to flood city streets and a major West Coast airport on some of the busiest travel days of the year. The National Weather Service issued a rare coastal flood warning for Monday through Thanksgiving Day, with peak flooding around each morning's high tide and the highest water expected Wednesday — when the gauge could come within an inch of its 1983 record close to 11 a.m. PT. Several road closures are expected along the low-lying shores of San Francisco and San Pablo bays, and the flooding threat arrives before the storm itself, which reaches the Bay Area on Tuesday. It is the western half of a coast-to-coast Thanksgiving weather mess, with the Northeast facing its own storm on the holiday itself.

articles.title: DNC plans to hold 12 debates for 2028 primary — with a new rule for Democrats who want in
articles.description: The Democratic National Committee has announced it will hold twelve debates for the next presidential primary, starting in June — and is adding a significant new condition for candidates to participate. The 2028 race will be the first in over a decade without Trump on the ballot. The debate plan is the party's first big structural decision for the post-midterm era.
articles.body: The DNC announced on Monday that it will hold twelve debates for the 2028 presidential primary, beginning in June, and is adding a significant new condition for candidates who want to take part — reportedly a pledge on dark money. The announcement is the party's first major structural decision since its sweeping midterm victories, which delivered Democrats their largest House majority this century and scrambled the 2028 field. The 2028 race will be the first in more than a decade without Donald Trump on the ballot, and the debate schedule — twelve encounters, starting in June — suggests the party expects a crowded field and a long fight to define what comes after Trump. The new participation rule is the detail to watch: it will shape who gets on the stage, and who does not.

articles.title: Rumoured for centuries, tunnels found under 1,500-year-old Hagia Sophia
articles.description: A network of newly discovered tunnels and underground spaces, some hundreds of metres long, has been excavated under the Hagia Sophia in Istanbul, CNN reports, with yet more expected to be revealed. The find settles rumours that have circulated for centuries. Türkiye's culture minister inspected the site and announced the discovery on November 20.
articles.body: For centuries there were rumours of tunnels beneath the Hagia Sophia, the 1,500-year-old Istanbul landmark — and now they have been found. A network of newly discovered tunnels and underground spaces, some hundreds of metres long, has been excavated beneath the building, with more expected to be revealed. Minister of Culture and Tourism Mehmet Nuri Ersoy inspected the site and spoke to the media in an announcement on November 20. The Hagia Sophia has been a cathedral, a mosque, a museum and a mosque again across its long life, and its underground has always been part of its mythology. What the tunnels were used for — and how far they run — is now a question for archaeologists, and the discovery is a reminder that even the world's most studied buildings still hold secrets.

articles.title: SoundCloud cracks down on 'AI slop, spam, and excessive uploads' — weeks after striking AI deals
articles.description: SoundCloud has updated its terms of use and community guidelines to target what it calls 'AI slop, spam, and excessive uploads,' CEO Eliah Seton announced in an open letter on November 17. The platform says it may withhold, reverse or recover payouts from users who game its systems with AI. The move comes weeks after SoundCloud struck AI deals with Moises and ElevenLabs — and as Spotify says it removed more than 50 million 'slop and spam' tracks from recommendations in 2026.
articles.body: Seton was blunt: 'AI slop has no place on SoundCloud.' The updated terms let the platform withhold, reverse or recover payouts in response to spam, fraud and deceptive activity, including uploads designed to game the system with AI. The crackdown follows two AI partnerships struck in the past month — an October 21 integration with Moises that lets artists import SoundCloud tracks, finish them and publish them back, and a deal with ElevenLabs. SoundCloud says it hosts more than 400 million tracks from over 40 million artists across 193 countries, so the scale of the problem is enormous. The timing is no coincidence: on the same day as SoundCloud's announcement, Spotify rolled out its Artist Profile Protection tool, and in October Spotify said it had taken more than 50 million 'slop and spam' tracks out of its recommendations so far in 2026. The streaming platforms are all drawing the same line at once — AI tools are welcome, but flooding the catalogue with machine-made filler is not.

articles.title: Eminem co-publisher adds 108 allegedly infringing AI tracks to $47.7m Suno lawsuit, calling Suno's denials 'false'
articles.description: Eminem co-publisher Eight Mile Style has amended its copyright lawsuit against AI music generator Suno, adding 108 more AI-generated tracks it says infringe its songs. The amended complaint, filed November 19 in California federal court, also accuses Suno of stealing Eminem's voice and likeness — though it adds no claim over them — and calls Suno's denials 'false.' Damages sought remain just over $47.7 million.
articles.body: Eight Mile Style first sued Suno on November 6, and the amended complaint filed 13 days later broadens the case substantially, adding 108 allegedly infringing AI-generated tracks to the original claim. The filing responds directly to what Suno told reporters after the first suit, calling the company's denials 'false,' and it now accuses Suno of stealing Eminem's voice and likeness as well — although it adds no separate claim over them, and the damages figure is unchanged at just over $47.7 million across three claims. The case is one front in a much wider legal war: Elvis Presley Enterprises and other rightsholders amended their own Suno suit days ago, adding more than 100 allegedly infringing AI tracks, and UMG and Sony filed their second Suno lawsuit in Boston in September. Suno, meanwhile, has asked a judge to dismiss a proposed class action from Jason Isbell and three other musicians, and is pushing to keep its newer models — including v6 — from being examined until at least 2028. The Eight Mile amendment keeps the pressure on, and keeps Eminem's catalogue at the centre of the fight over what AI music companies owe the artists they trained on.

articles.title: TikTok rolls out Likeness Detection deepfake tool globally, launches public AI-content checker
articles.description: TikTok has started a global rollout of Likeness Detection, a tool designed to help creators and public figures find AI deepfakes of themselves on the platform. The company announced the rollout on November 19 at its Safety and Innovation Forum in London. TikTok says its AI labelling tools have now helped label more than 5 billion AI-generated videos, up from 3 billion in July.
articles.body: TikTok has begun rolling out Likeness Detection globally, a tool that helps creators and public figures find AI deepfakes of themselves on the platform, alongside a public AI-content checker aimed at viewers. The company announced both tools on November 19 at its Safety and Innovation Forum in London. The scale of the problem is visible in TikTok's own numbers: its AI labelling tools have now helped label more than 5 billion AI-generated videos, up from 3 billion in July — a measure of how fast synthetic content is spreading. For musicians, the stakes are direct: unauthorised AI versions of artists are already at the centre of lawsuits against Suno and others, and a tool that lets an artist find and flag a fake of themselves is a practical defence. Whether detection can keep up with generation is the open question.

articles.title: Judge throws out Wixen's claims over 200-plus pre-1978 songs in Meta copyright suit
articles.description: A federal judge has dismissed Wixen Music Publishing's copyright claims over more than 200 songs in its lawsuit against Meta Platforms. Judge John F. Walter issued the order on November 19 in the US District Court for the Central District of California. The ruling removes more than a third of the 569 songs in Wixen's latest complaint — though its remaining infringement claims and a defamation claim survive.
articles.body: Judge John F. Walter has dismissed Wixen Music Publishing's copyright claims over more than 200 pre-1978 songs in its lawsuit against Meta, in an order issued on Thursday, November 19. The ruling strips more than a third of the 569 songs listed in Wixen's latest complaint, leaving the rest of the case — including the remaining infringement claims and a defamation claim — to proceed. Wixen first sued Meta on January 23 over 331 songs, seeking at least $49.65 million. The case is one of several testing how far music publishers can push platforms over unlicensed music in user-generated content, and the pre-1978 cut is a significant narrowing: songs from that era fall under a different copyright regime, and the judge's ruling turns on that distinction. Wixen still has a case — just a smaller one.

articles.title: MBW Explains: 5 things to know about Suno's move into AI video, the DistroKid documents, and the fight over v6
articles.description: Suno has moved into AI video, launching a product called Visuals on November 17 — and MBW's explainer pulls together the five things that matter about the company's busiest week. The launch came days after UMG and Sony withdrew their court motion against DistroKid, and as the majors fight to keep Suno's second lawsuit moving. The piece is a useful map of a legal war that now spans video, distribution and model versions.
articles.body: MBW's explainer starts with the news: Suno launched Visuals, an AI video product, on November 17, built on MiniMax technology — and three Hollywood studios are suing MiniMax. A day before the launch, UMG and Sony told a Manhattan federal court they were withdrawing their motion to force DistroKid to comply with a subpoena, after the distributor handed over documents on its AI-detection tool; the November 16 notice does not say what the documents show. The labels also want their second lawsuit against Suno — filed in Boston on September 18 — to examine the company's newer models, including v6, now rather than in 2028, as Suno's plan would have it. And the fights stretch well beyond the majors: Elvis Presley Enterprises sued Suno in California on November 6, and Suno is also fighting a proposed class action from Jason Isbell and three other musicians. WMG, meanwhile, is a v6 partner and expects AI deals to contribute materially from fiscal 2027. Read together, the five points describe a company expanding into new products while its legal exposure widens on every front.

articles.title: Don Toliver's Manchester show evacuated after 'unknown substance' released in crowd
articles.description: Don Toliver's show in Manchester was evacuated after an unknown substance was released into the crowd, Rolling Stone reports. The incident is the latest in a run of disruptions at large live shows, and details are still emerging. It comes days after Toliver announced his sixth album, 'Nitrous.'
articles.body: Rolling Stone reports that Don Toliver's Manchester show was evacuated after an 'unknown substance' was released among the crowd, forcing the venue to clear. The report, published within the last day, gives few details beyond the evacuation itself — what the substance was, and whether anyone was hurt, had not been confirmed. The incident follows a busy stretch for Toliver, who announced his sixth album, 'Nitrous,' last week and played Rolling Stone's Musicians on Musicians event alongside Malcolm Todd, Alex Warren and Megan Moroney. It is also the latest in a series of safety scares at big arena shows, where a single incident in a dense crowd can force an entire venue to empty. Further details are expected as the venue and local authorities say more.

articles.title: Watch Olivia Rodrigo cover 'Dead Leaves and the Dirty Ground' at Jack White's Blue Room
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo has covered the White Stripes' 'Dead Leaves and the Dirty Ground' at Jack White's Blue Room, Rolling Stone reports. The performance is a meeting of two generations of guitar-driven songwriting. It comes as Rodrigo's album falls to No. 2 on the Billboard 200 after five weeks on top.
articles.body: Olivia Rodrigo stepped into Jack White's Blue Room — the intimate Nashville performance space attached to his Third Man Records — and covered the White Stripes' 'Dead Leaves and the Dirty Ground.' Rolling Stone reports the performance, which pairs one of the defining pop songwriters of her generation with one of the defining rock songs of the early 2000s. The White Stripes' original, from the 2001 album White Blood Cells, is a raw, two-person blast of garage rock; hearing Rodrigo take it on in White's own room is a small event for fans of both. It is also a reminder of Rodrigo's roots: before the pop stardom, she was a songwriter with a guitar, and the cover is a nod to the lineage she comes from.

articles.title: Thom Yorke and Harry Styles come together in epic conversation
articles.description: Thom Yorke and Harry Styles have come together for an epic conversation as Rolling Stone's cover story, the magazine reports. The pairing brings together the Radiohead frontman and the pop star for a meeting of two very different kinds of fame. It is the magazine's big end-of-year conversation piece.
articles.body: Rolling Stone's cover story pairs Thom Yorke and Harry Styles in conversation — two artists who could hardly be more different in how they handle fame, and who have more in common than it first appears. Yorke, the Radiohead frontman who has spent three decades resisting the machinery of stardom, and Styles, who went from the biggest boy band in the world to one of the biggest solo stars on the planet, make for a natural pairing: both are restless, both have remade themselves repeatedly, and both have complicated relationships with the spotlight. The conversation is Rolling Stone's latest in its series of cross-generational pairings, and it is the kind of piece that works precisely because the two men approach music from opposite ends and meet in the middle.

articles.title: The 200 Greatest Rock Songs of the 21st Century So Far
articles.description: Rolling Stone has published its list of the 200 greatest rock songs of the 21st century so far. The ranking is the magazine's latest attempt to define the canon of a century that is only a quarter old. Expect arguments — that is the point.
articles.body: Rolling Stone's new list ranks the 200 greatest rock songs of the 21st century so far, a canon-building exercise for a genre that has spent the century being declared dead and refusing to die. Lists like this are designed to be argued with, and this one will be: the century's rock runs from the garage revival of the early 2000s through the indie boom, the festival era and the streaming age, and any ranking has to weigh commercial impact against influence, and nostalgia against the present. The list sits alongside the magazine's other big recent rankings — the 500 greatest songs of all time, the 100 best Grateful Dead songs — as part of Rolling Stone's ongoing project of writing the history of popular music in list form. The arguments it starts are the feature, not the bug.

articles.title: Daniel Lanois on his life in music
articles.description: Daniel Lanois, the producer behind some of the most celebrated albums of the past four decades, reflects on his life in music in a new Rolling Stone feature. Lanois has shaped records by U2, Bob Dylan, Neil Young and Peter Gabriel. The piece is a rare long conversation with one of music's great behind-the-scenes figures.
articles.body: Daniel Lanois is one of those names that appears in the small print of the greatest albums ever made — producer of U2's The Joshua Tree and Achtung Baby, Bob Dylan's Time Out of Mind, Neil Young's Le Noise, and Peter Gabriel's So, among many others. In a new Rolling Stone feature he reflects on a life spent in studios, shaping the sound of other people's masterpieces while building a solo career of his own. Producers of Lanois' stature rarely give long interviews, and rarer still are the ones that range across a whole career. For anyone who cares about how records actually get made — the rooms, the accidents, the arguments — it is a valuable piece of oral history from a man who was in the room for some of the best of them.

articles.title: Anne Hathaway welcomes third child with husband Adam Shulman
articles.description: Anne Hathaway has welcomed her third child with her husband, Adam Shulman, Rolling Stone reports. The actor has spoken sparingly about her family life in the past. The news is the magazine's most-read story of the day.
articles.body: Anne Hathaway has welcomed a third child with her husband, Adam Shulman, according to Rolling Stone, which lists the story among its most popular of the day. Hathaway, who has been one of Hollywood's most prominent actors for two decades — from The Princess Diaries to The Devil Wears Prada, Les Misérables and her Oscar win — has generally kept her family life out of the spotlight, and the announcement is characteristically low-key. No further details were given. The story's popularity is a reminder of Hathaway's enduring place in the public eye, and of the appetite for even the smallest piece of news about her.

articles.title: ATEEZ earn fourth Billboard 200 No. 1 with 'GOLDEN HOUR: Part.6'; U2's 'Carnaval de Luz' debuts at No. 4
articles.description: ATEEZ have earned their fourth Billboard 200 No. 1 as GOLDEN HOUR: Part.6 debuts atop the chart dated November 28 with 195,000 equivalent album units — 191,000 of them pure sales. U2 collect their 14th top 10 as Carnaval de Luz, their first album of original material in nine years, bows at No. 4 with 49,000 units. Olivia Rodrigo falls to No. 2 after five weeks on top.
articles.body: ATEEZ's five-track EP opened with 195,000 equivalent album units in the week ending November 19, and almost all of it came from people buying it outright: 191,000 traditional album sales, with just 4,000 streaming-equivalent units — a ratio almost no Western act reaches in the streaming age. It is the K-pop group's third No. 1 of 2026 alone, after Part.4 in February and Part.5 in July, and their 10th consecutive top 10 — the most top 10 albums of any group this decade. Billboard notes the EP was sold in 32 CD and vinyl variants packed with photocards and posters. U2's debut is the week's other big story: Carnaval de Luz, the band's first full album of original material in nine years, enters at No. 4 with 49,000 units, 42,500 of them pure sales across 18 physical variants, giving the band top-five albums in five different decades. Elsewhere in the top 10, Olivia Rodrigo drops to No. 2 with 62,000 units, Morgan Wallen holds at No. 3, Noah Kahan places two albums in the top 10, and Lil Baby falls eight spots to No. 10.

articles.title: U2's 'Carnaval de Luz' debuts at No. 4 — the band's 14th Billboard 200 top 10
articles.description: U2 have debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 with Carnaval de Luz, their first album of original material in nine years, earning 49,000 equivalent album units. It is the band's 14th top 10 album in the United States. The debut keeps U2 among the small group of acts with top-five albums in five different decades.
articles.body: U2's Carnaval de Luz enters the Billboard 200 at No. 4 with 49,000 equivalent album units in the week ending November 19, according to figures reported by Billboard on Sunday. Full album sales accounted for 42,500 of those units, spread across 18 different physical variants, with the rest coming from streaming. It is the Irish band's 14th top 10 album in the United States, and their first full album of original material in nine years — a return that lands 50 years after four Dublin school friends formed the band in 1976.
