The top-five finish also keeps U2 among the small group of acts to place albums in the Billboard 200 top five across five different decades, a longevity record that few of their contemporaries can match. The full chart will be published on Tuesday, November 24.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo falls to No. 2 after five weeks at No. 1 on the Billboard 200
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo's 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love' falls to No. 2 on the Billboard 200 after five weeks on top, earning 62,000 equivalent album units — down just 1%. ATEEZ's sales-driven debut ends a run that included holding off Lil Baby by just 3,000 units last week. The album's five-week reign is still one of the longest of the year.
articles.body: After five weeks at No. 1, Olivia Rodrigo's you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love drops to No. 2 on the Billboard 200 dated November 28, with 62,000 equivalent album units earned — down only 1% on the week. The fall is less a collapse than a changing of the guard: ATEEZ's GOLDEN HOUR: Part.6, powered almost entirely by 191,000 pure album sales, simply out-sold her. Rodrigo's run was one of the defining chart stories of the autumn — five weeks on top, including a win over Lil Baby by just 3,000 units last week — and the album's staying power, down just 1% in its sixth week, suggests it is not going far. Morgan Wallen holds at No. 3 with a little more than 49,000 units, and Lil Baby's FRESH drops eight spots to No. 10 in its second week.

articles.title: Tame Impala and Jennie's 'Dracula' matches Hot 100 peak for a second straight week
articles.description: Tame Impala's remix featuring Blackpink's Jennie, 'Dracula,' has matched its Billboard Hot 100 peak for a second straight week, holding at No. 3. The collaboration has now spent 20 consecutive weeks in the Hot 100 top 10 — the longest such run. It also leads Hot Dance/Electronic Songs for a 45th week.
articles.body: The Tame Impala remix featuring Blackpink's Jennie matched its Billboard Hot 100 peak for a second straight week, according to the Korea JoongAng Daily's chart roundup, holding at No. 3 and extending its run in the top 10 to 20 consecutive weeks — the longest consecutive run in the Hot 100's top 10. The collaboration, which climbed six spots when it first reached the top three, also leads Hot Dance/Electronic Songs for a 45th week and Hot Rock & Alternative Songs for a 26th. For Jennie, the run matches the record among female K-pop soloists set by Rosé, and it is a measure of how thoroughly K-pop's biggest stars have crossed into the American mainstream: a psychedelic Australian act and a Blackpink member, holding a top-three spot for months.

articles.title: Drake holds three Hot 100 entries on the November 21 chart
articles.description: Drake holds three entries on the Billboard Hot 100 dated November 21, alongside his feature on Future's 'Ya Hit,' which debuted at No. 38. 'Janice STFU' sits at No. 29, 'Solar Eclipse' at No. 56 and 'Cold Shoulder' at No. 62. The spread of credits shows Drake across solo, lead and featured billing in a single week.
articles.body: On the Hot 100 dated November 21, Drake appears under his own name and alongside other artists across four entries: Future's 'Ya Hit,' featuring Drake, Travis Scott and Loe Shimmy, debuted at No. 38, and Drake's own entries are 'Janice STFU' at No. 29, 'Solar Eclipse' at No. 56 and 'Cold Shoulder' at No. 62. The credits span a solo release, a joint entry with Don Toliver and a collaboration with Don Toliver and Yebba. It is a snapshot of how Drake works in 2026 — everywhere at once, in different configurations, with his name attached to a spread of songs rather than a single flagship single. The 'Ya Hit' debut, already covered earlier in the week, gains context here: it is one of four Drake credits on the same chart.

articles.title: The Christmas climb has started: Mariah Carey jumps 39–18 on the Hot 100
articles.description: Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' has jumped from No. 39 to No. 18 on the Hot 100, and Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' has climbed from No. 37 to No. 14 — making Carey only the week's second-highest-charting holiday hit. The Christmas climb has started, and it is coming for the record held by the singer it is chasing: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' sits at No. 1 for a 28th week.
articles.body: The Hot 100 dated November 21 shows the Christmas climb already under way: 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' jumps from No. 39 to No. 18, while Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' climbs from No. 37 to No. 14 — which makes Carey's song only the week's second-highest-charting holiday hit. The timing matters because of the record in play: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' holds No. 1 for a 28th week, the longest reign in Hot 100 history, and it did so by passing Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You,' which sits second at 22 weeks. The next Hot 100, dated November 28, either prints a 29th week for Langley or closes the longest reign the chart has recorded — and the Christmas songs are climbing fast enough to be part of that story. Langley also broke out of her tie with Carey for the most weeks at No. 1 on Streaming Songs, and leads Hot Country Songs for a 49th week.

articles.title: Grand Theft Auto Used to Satirize American Life. Now We’ve Caught Up With It.
articles.author: Joseph Bernstein
articles.description: The smartest thing written about the biggest game launch in history: Bernstein argues GTA was never really about crime, and asks what happens to satire when reality catches up with the joke.
articles.body:
Grand Theft Auto VI arrived on November 19, 2026, the first new entry in the franchise in thirteen years, and Joseph Bernstein — who played it early — uses the occasion to argue that the series has always been something stranger and more ambitious than a crime simulator. Beneath the car chases and shootouts, he writes, the games were always a cartoonish, obsessive portrait of American life itself: its strip malls, swamps, talk radio, petty hustles and grand delusions, rendered at a scale no other medium has attempted. The new game, set in a fictionalised Florida of Vice City and the surrounding Leonida wetlands, pushes that project further than ever. It took thirteen years and nearly 5,000 Rockstar employees to build, runs to 212 gigabytes, and reportedly took in roughly $1.5 billion in pre-sales — a hand-made, almost medieval-cathedral scale of craft that Bernstein, and the Hard Fork podcast that discussed his piece, suggest artificial intelligence may make impossible to repeat.

The heart of the new game, Bernstein argues, is not mayhem but a love story between its two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, and the game quietly punishes the player who treats it like the old GTAs: going it alone, favouring violence and chaos, damages the relationship at the centre of the story. He reaches for Jorge Luis Borges — an empire that builds a map as large as the empire itself — and for Baudrillard to explain what Rockstar has made: a working miniature of the United States, astonishingly detailed down to 60 species of birds, 30,000 unique non-player characters and a gym where you can deadlift, squat and bench press. The paradox, and the essay's title, is that this miniature was built as satire, and satire needs a gap between the exaggeration and the real thing. Bernstein's claim is that the gap has closed: American disorder has moved from the outside world into people's innermost selves, and reality now routinely outruns the game's most extreme portrayals. What remains, he concludes, is a coherent map of incoherent territory — maybe the last one.

articles.title: The Internet Broke Our Taste. Will A.I. Destroy It for Good?
articles.author: Jonah Weiner
articles.description: A sharp, unsettling essay on the question underneath every feed: if AI can learn taste, what is left of our own judgment — and did the internet already break it first?
articles.body:
Taste has become Silicon Valley's buzzword of the year, and Jonah Weiner's essay asks what that actually means now that machines are learning to have it — or at least to fake it. On one side, taste is being hailed as the last human advantage over artificial intelligence, the thing models cannot replicate; on the other, it is being dismissed as just another pattern a model will learn, given enough examples. The industry is already acting on the second view: AI labs are paying armies of freelancers to grade their systems' output, with one firm reportedly spending millions of dollars a day on human taste as a training input, while tech's own elites — never known for refinement — try to buy taste outright through streetwear drops and designer knits. Weiner interviewed Jony Ive among others for the piece, and the picture that emerges is of an industry simultaneously anxious about taste and intent on industrialising it.

But Weiner's deeper worry is not about the labs; it is about the rest of us. For years, he argues, playlists, influencers and feeds have already been telling us what to like, and we have grown used to outsourcing the work of deciding. Starter-pack memes reduce whole sensibilities to checklists, recommendation engines narrow the field before we ever encounter it, and chatbots now threaten to do the thinking itself. Drawing on René Girard's idea that we want what we see others wanting, Weiner asks what happens to desire when the machine knows our mimetic triggers better than we do. In a world of what he calls slop capitalism, vibe-crafted culture and taste paranoia, why we like what we like feels harder than ever to know — and the essay's closing question lingers: what will we like, and who will we become, when the machines finish learning?

articles.title: This Emerging Artist Is a Hit Restaurateur
articles.author: Nate Freeman
articles.description: A delightful New York double-life story: the owner of the city's best all-around restaurant has been quietly painting in his basement for decades — and the art world just caught on.
articles.body:
Borgo, on a block in the high 20s you swear you have never been down before, opened in 2024 and already feels like it has been there forever — and New York magazine's chief restaurant critic recently named it the city's best all-around restaurant. Its dining room fills with media executives, architects to billionaires and two-time Oscar winners. What almost none of them know is that the man who owns it, Andrew Tarlow, is also a serious painter — a cult favourite whose work hangs on Borgo's own walls, mostly unnoticed, alongside paintings by his daughter. Freeman discovered the double life almost by accident: his server at Borgo one lunch turned out to be Tarlow himself, a painter who used to bartend at The Odeon so he could meet his heroes, and who now paints in a basement studio in the Fort Greene brownstone where he has lived for two decades with his wife and four children.

Tarlow's restaurant career is the stuff of New York legend. He moved to the desolate southern tip of Broadway in Williamsburg in the late 1990s, found a cheap loft across from an abandoned 1920s diner, and in 1999 opened Diner in it — a restaurant that effectively kick-started the Brooklyn aesthetic. Marlow & Sons, a butcher shop, a bakery, a literary magazine and the Wythe Hotel restaurant followed, and then, instead of franchising Diner into a waterfront development, he got weirder, opening a nautical bar called Achilles Heel in a far corner of Greenpoint. All along he kept painting: doodling on notepads during restaurant concept meetings, carrying sketchbooks, and eventually building the basement studio where he now works most nights after dinner, while the kids watch Finding Nemo upstairs. The paintings are bold, colour-blocked, myth-haunted works that remind Freeman of Albert Oehlen and Cy Twombly, with faces multiplying and fading; he has shown recently at Tiwa Select, whose founder describes Tarlow handing over unstretched canvases to be carried home in an Uber.

Freeman's real subject is the strange freedom of the late-blooming, double-life artist. Tarlow, 56, compares himself to William Carlos Williams writing poems between patients, Ruth Asawa making art in her kitchen while raising six children, and Jeff Koons working on Wall Street to fund his sculptures — people for whom a demanding job granted the freedom to make art without needing it to pay. He even shares a hero with his own story: Martin Kippenberger, who also owned a restaurant, hung art in it, and became a part-owner of a Venice spot because, as he put it, you couldn't get a decent Bolognese in Los Angeles. At Borgo, Tarlow now hand-sketches regulars' names onto the paper tablecloths, the way he did for a Tiwa Select dinner — the first time he has put his own work on the premises of his own restaurant, and he barely promotes it. As he tells Freeman, the two jobs are totally separate but complementary in a cosmic way: the focus and passion in one arena lead straight into the other.

articles.title: The Arch and Ballroom Are Just the Beginning
articles.description: Trump's ballroom and arch are only the start: a reported tour of the classical-architecture crusade reshaping federal buildings — and why even its true believers are uneasy.
articles.body:
Donald Trump's ambition to deck out the government in columns and golden hues goes well beyond the White House ballroom and the triumphal arch in Washington. Last month, more than 500 miles from the capital, the General Services Administration broke ground on a new federal courthouse in Chattanooga, Tennessee — the first of seven projects governed by an August 2025 executive order, 'Making Federal Architecture Beautiful Again,' that designates traditional architecture as the federal government's preferred style. The courthouse mixes classical and Art Deco elements into something the piece calls Greco-Deco, a templelike civic building that has actually won praise from admirers of classical architecture. For many of them it marks a welcome return to tradition after decades of modern commissions. But the piece argues it is a Pyrrhic victory: you cannot have the proud courthouse without the bloated arch and ballroom, and both breeds of classicism will coexist as Trump's architectural legacy.

The essay's central observation is that to be a classicist in the second Trump administration is to be caught in a tragicomedy. The president proclaims an affinity for the architecture of Western antiquity, signs orders saying so, and plans monuments in its image — yet as he endorses the style, he butchers it. His projects balloon in size, cost and gilding until they become something more like Neo-Vegas-ism: the ballroom's interior volume will be nearly three times that of the White House's main building, and its first architect, James McCrery II, resigned after clashing with the president over its size. The planned 250-foot arch would loom over Arlington National Cemetery, casting shadows on graves. Even critics who argued for an arch, like Catesby Leigh, now call the plan way too big for the site, and Calder Loth, a historian of classical architecture, is a plaintiff in a lawsuit challenging it. Meanwhile prominent proponents of classicism have gone notably quiet: Justin Shubow of the National Civic Art Society, who helped write the executive order, declined to comment on the ballroom and arch while praising the courthouse.

The piece sets this against the history the order overturned. In 1962, Daniel Patrick Moynihan's 'Guiding Principles for Federal Architecture' put design authority in the hands of the architecture profession, warned against imposing a federal style, and envisioned buildings embodying 'the finest contemporary American architectural thought.' Trump's order reverses that: it requires GSA architects evaluating proposals to have a classical or traditional background and asks that the president be notified if a design goes against the designated preference — effectively making Trump, as the essay puts it, the modernism police. Historians quoted in the piece note the deeper irony: early American architects valued progress and treated mere copying as an insult, and classical architecture at its best negotiates between decoration and restraint, prizing symmetry, economy and harmony. A classical archaeologist at CUNY calls classicism in unsure times 'a security blanket in marble form.' The essay's sting is in its last line: Trump's structures will fool no one — when future Americans come upon a vertigo-inducing arch on the Potomac, they will know precisely which era created it.

articles.title: The Restless Storytelling at the Heart of the Grateful Dead
articles.author: Angie Martoccio
articles.description: A fresh take on the world's greatest jam band: why the Dead's songs are all about people who can't stay put — and why a band that ended in 1995 keeps gaining followers.
articles.body:
The Grateful Dead played their final show together in 1995, yet their following keeps growing — and journalist Alex Pappademas and artist Joan LeMay, the duo behind the Steely Dan book Quantum Criminals, have returned with a new book, Friends of the Devil (Random House, November 3), that tries to explain why. Built from short chapters keyed to individual songs and illustrated with more than a hundred of LeMay's original paintings, the book treats the Dead's songbook as a body of literature: a ramshackle American mythology of West Texas cowboys, brown-eyed women, gamblers, outlaws and sunshine daydreamers. Pappademas's argument, as Martoccio presents it, is that the thread running through it all is restlessness. The people in these songs are always on the move — fleeing, searching, returning, rarely settling at home — and that motion is the key to the band's storytelling and to its hold on listeners decades after the music stopped.

Martoccio walks through the evidence song by song. 'Bertha,' 'Friend of the Devil' and 'Cassidy' all turn on characters who cannot stay put, and guitarist John Mayer — who has spent years playing the music with Dead & Company — is quoted connecting those travelling characters to a shared narrative of escape. The book is unsentimental about its subject: Pappademas admires the band's peaks while conceding that in their rough latter years the members were barely listening to each other, and he places the songs' strange histories alongside the real ones — Joseph Campbell and the Zodiac Killer, college revolutionaries lost in the desert, Bob Dylan wandering in out of the cold. LeMay's gouache paintings, shown in a three-day pop-up at New York's 14BC Gallery from November 19 to 21, give the dreamworld a visual language of its own, and the pair appear at the Strand Book Store on December 3. For longtime Deadheads the book is a fresh annotated tour of familiar ground; for everyone else, Martoccio suggests, it is a way into understanding how a band that stopped playing thirty years ago became, improbably, more culturally present than ever.

articles.title: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
articles.author: Lily Hay Newman, Matt Burgess
articles.description: The week's Microsoft, Apple, bank and NSA outages were not an AI hacking spree — but AI is why they will keep happening, and Wired explains the patching doom loop clearly.
articles.body:
Over one week in mid-November, the outages piled up faster than anyone could explain them away: Microsoft's Outlook and 365 services went down, Apple suffered internal disruptions, half a dozen US banks were hit, United Airlines was affected, and even the NSA's classified internal communications network degraded. Speculation ran wild, including a pervasive feeling that artificial intelligence was somehow to blame. Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess open their Wired piece by clearing that up: the incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree, and taken individually they all have routine explanations. Microsoft traced its massive 365 outage to a flawed infrastructure update compounded by other network failures; officials tied the NSA outage to botched patching after October's critical PHP updates; Apple said its problems related to an internal update. Senator Mark Warner, vice chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, said the same in a statement on November 17: there was no indication of a cyberattack, foreign interference or coordinated campaign.

But the piece's real argument is that the routine explanations are themselves the story — because AI is changing the tempo at which routine breaks things. AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs: more than 100,000 vulnerabilities have been recorded in 2026, compared with around 25,000 in 2022, the last full year before large language models went mainstream, and the 2026 count already doubles the combined totals of 2024 and 2025. Attackers use AI tools to exploit flaws faster, which forces organisations to patch faster, with less time to test — and when patches move that fast, some of them break things. Researchers told Wired again and again that AI's biggest impact is that it speeds everything up. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned this week that more instability could be coming, because a patch now needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, since it is being exploited in the wild.

The numbers, the authors stress, need careful reading. Only about 300 vulnerabilities were added to the US government's catalog of actively exploited flaws this year, and roughly 1,500 known exploited flaws — about 1.5 percent of all bugs found — are in circulation, so discovery and real-world exploitation are very different things. But the strain on the humans in the middle is real: under-resourced IT teams must evaluate a flood of patches and push them onto systems the world relies on, systems that were not built to handle that pace of change. Cloudflare chief executive Matthew Prince expects a turbulent two years before defences may improve. The piece's title is its conclusion: welcome to outage hell, and brace for it to last a while.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un ignores Trump's letters and calls, despite years of outreach
articles.description: Kim Jong Un is ignoring Donald Trump's letters and phone calls, Meduza reports in a retelling of a Wall Street Journal investigation, despite Trump's efforts to restart a dialogue since returning to the White House. Trump tried to reach the North Korean leader by phone in 2025, and a North Korean diplomat left an unopened envelope in front of the US delegation at the UN. Washington and Pyongyang hastily discussed a possible leaders' conversation during Trump's China trip this week, but North Korea set conditions the US found unacceptable.
articles.body: Kim Jong Un is ignoring Donald Trump's letters and phone calls, Meduza reports in a retelling of a Wall Street Journal investigation, despite Trump's efforts to restart a dialogue since returning to the White House in 2024. Trump once boasted that he and Kim had 'fallen in love,' but the relationship has gone cold: in 2025 he tried to reach the North Korean leader by phone, and at the UN a North Korean diplomat left an unopened envelope in front of the American delegation, signalling that Kim is not interested in giving up his nuclear arsenal or in a friendship with the US president. Trump tried again this week, during his visit to China, where Washington and Pyongyang hastily discussed the details of a possible conversation between the leaders — but North Korea put forward conditions the US side found unacceptable. The failed outreach illustrates a wider crisis in the relationship: US intelligence concluded in its 2025 threat assessment that Kim has no intention of giving up his strategic weapons programmes through negotiations. North Korea has also been blamed for the largest crypto exchange robbery in history, with more than $6 billion taken from Binance, and analysts estimate Pyongyang is behind 89% of global losses from such crimes in 2026, up from 15% in 2021. Washington still has no detailed policy plan for Pyongyang, according to the Journal's sources.

articles.title: UPDATE: Denmark expels Russian military attaché and tightens visas after alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
articles.description: Denmark is expelling Russia's military attaché and tightening its visa policy for Russians, in a new escalation after two people were arrested in Denmark over an alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner. The arrests and Denmark's call for EU states to stop issuing tourist visas to Russians were reported this morning; the expulsion is the latest step. The case has turned a suspected assassination plot into a diplomatic row.
articles.body: Denmark is expelling Russia's military attaché and tightening its visa policy for Russians, in a new escalation after two people were arrested in Denmark over an alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasyliev. A Danish court has remanded the two suspects in custody over the alleged murder plot, and Copenhagen's response has now moved from law enforcement to diplomacy: the attaché's expulsion and the visa tightening follow Denmark's call this week for EU states to stop issuing tourist visas to Russian citizens. The case has turned a suspected assassination plot into a diplomatic row, and it fits a wider pattern of European states stepping up scrutiny of Russians — German intelligence officers have been questioning some Russians after passport control at airports since at least September, and Denmark's move adds a formal expulsion to the mix. For Moscow, the expulsion is another diplomatic setback in Europe; for Kyiv, it is a sign that European governments are treating threats against Ukrainians abroad as a security matter, not just a police one. The investigation into the plot itself continues.

articles.title: UPDATE: Child pulled alive from rubble in Dymer as death toll rises; 15 still missing
articles.description: Rescuers have pulled a child out alive from the rubble of the five-storey apartment block in Dymer, near Kyiv, even as the death toll from the overnight Russian drone strike rose, Pravda reports. Two bodies had been recovered by the afternoon and 15 people were still missing — including a 12-year-old girl and a 7-year-old boy — as sniffer dogs kept working the site. The attack was part of a night of strikes that also hit Zaporizhzhia and left five Ukrainian regions without power.
articles.body: Rescuers have pulled a child out alive from the rubble of the five-storey apartment block in Dymer, near Kyiv, even as the death toll from the overnight Russian drone strike rose, Pravda reports. Two bodies had been recovered by the afternoon and 15 people were still missing — including a 12-year-old girl and a 7-year-old boy — as sniffer dogs kept working the site and the search continued for the missing. The strike destroyed an entire entrance of the building, leaving residents trapped under the debris. It was part of a wider night of Russian attacks: Zaporizhzhia was hit in a mass strike with casualties, Dnipro saw a downed drone fall on a residential roof, and Ukraine's Energy Ministry said five regions were left without power after new strikes on energy infrastructure. Odesa, which has been in blackout since the previous day's strikes, reported large-scale damage to power facilities. The rescue of the child alive is the one piece of good news from a grim day in Dymer, and the two missing children remain the focus of the rescue effort as crews work through the rubble.

articles.title: Strike on a Novus supermarket in Vyshneve kills three and injures 15
articles.description: Three people were killed and 15 injured in a strike on a Novus supermarket in Vyshneve, just outside Kyiv, Pravda reports in its lead story today. The attack on a civilian grocery store is the latest Russian strike on a clearly non-military target, and it comes on a day of heavy attacks across Ukraine — from the apartment block destroyed in Dymer to the energy strikes that left five regions without power.
articles.body: Three people were killed and 15 injured in a strike on a Novus supermarket in Vyshneve, just outside Kyiv, Pravda reports in its lead story today. The attack hit a civilian grocery store — a place full of weekend shoppers — and the casualties were among customers and staff. It is the latest Russian strike on a clearly non-military target, and it comes on a day of heavy attacks across Ukraine: the apartment block destroyed in Dymer, where rescuers pulled a child out alive even as the death toll rose; a woman killed and nine injured in Dnipropetrovsk region; a teenager killed by an FPV drone in Sumy region; and energy strikes that left five regions without power. The Vyshneve strike underlines the pattern of the nightly campaign: it is not only energy infrastructure and military targets that are being hit, but the ordinary places of daily life — shops, homes, schools. For Kyiv's suburbs, the attack is a reminder that the war reaches into the supermarket as well as the front line. Emergency services worked at the scene through the day, and the injured were taken to hospital.

articles.title: GTA VI album sets the biggest soundtrack debut in Spotify history
articles.description: The official music album for Grand Theft Auto VI gathered almost 30 million streams on Spotify in its first day, the biggest debut for any soundtrack on the platform. The compilation, prepared with Atlantic Records, features everyone from Travis Scott and Fuerza Regida to Michael McDonald, plus new songs from Lana Del Rey, Dua Lipa and Zara Larsson. Rolling Stone's review calls it 'all over the place (in a good way)' — like a radio dial spinning on hyperspeed.
articles.body: The official music album for Grand Theft Auto VI gathered almost 30 million streams on Spotify in its first day, the biggest debut for any soundtrack on the platform. The compilation was prepared together with Atlantic Records and features everyone from Travis Scott and Fuerza Regida to Michael McDonald, plus new songs from Lana Del Rey, Dua Lipa and Zara Larsson. Rolling Stone's review calls the album 'all over the place (in a good way)' — like a radio dial spinning on hyperspeed, which is exactly the point of a GTA soundtrack. The streaming record is the latest in a run of superlatives for the game: it grossed an estimated $3.79 billion on launch day, the biggest entertainment launch in history, and has now sold 32.5 million copies. The soundtrack's success shows how tightly the game and the music are linked — Rockstar even staged a GTA VI festival in Miami this weekend with Travis Scott, Cardi B and Justice. For the artists on the album, the game is now one of the biggest promotional platforms in music. For Spotify, the numbers confirm that a blockbuster game launch can move as much music as a major album release.

articles.title: Delta flights delayed nationwide, snarling holiday travel after computer problems
articles.description: Delta Air Lines flights are facing delays nationwide after problems with the systems that calculate takeoff weights and ensure safe aircraft settings, according to an FAA advisory. A ground delay at Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport was issued Sunday morning and lifted around 11:30 AM, but more than 400 outbound flights from Atlanta were delayed on Sunday afternoon. The disruption lands at the start of the busiest Thanksgiving travel week, with severe weather also hitting the Northeast.
articles.body: Delta Air Lines flights are facing delays nationwide after problems with the systems that calculate takeoff weights and ensure safe aircraft settings, according to a Federal Aviation Administration advisory. A ground delay at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport was issued on Sunday morning at the airline's request and was cancelled around 11:30 AM ET once Delta's objectives were met, but the knock-on delays continued: more than 400 flights out of Atlanta were delayed on Sunday afternoon, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware, with slightly fewer inbound flights also delayed. Delta said its teams were working to restore automation for departing flight weight and balance calculations. The specifics of the problem remain unclear, but the pattern is familiar: United Airlines had an issue with its weight and balance computer system in 2025 that triggered more than 1,000 delays and dozens of cancellations, and a brief United outage on November 16 affected fewer than 150 flights. Beyond the system failure, severe weather in the Northeast is adding to the strain as millions travel for Thanksgiving, with rain and gusty winds expected to slow flights and roads along the I-95 corridor on Sunday evening.

articles.title: San Francisco braces for record king tides as mayor urges residents to reconsider travel
articles.description: San Francisco is bracing for tides the National Weather Service says it has never seen before in recorded history, as the highest tides of the year — king tides — coincide with storms heading into Thanksgiving week. Mayor Daniel Lurie warned of an 'extremely serious' situation and urged residents to reconsider travel, stock up on supplies and get shopping done early. Forecasters said up to 2 feet of flooding was likely in low-lying areas near shorelines through Monday morning, with the threat continuing along other parts of the Pacific coast through Thursday.
articles.body: San Francisco is bracing for tides the National Weather Service says it has never seen before in recorded history, as the highest tides of the year — king tides — coincide with storms heading into Thanksgiving week. Mayor Daniel Lurie warned of an 'extremely serious' situation and urged residents to reconsider travel for the holiday, telling them to 'take this weekend to get yourself ready, please stock up on supplies, get your shopping done, and know that the city will be out all weekend doing everything possible to protect our residents and our small businesses.' Forecasters said up to 2 feet (0.6 metres) of flooding would be likely in low-lying areas near shorelines and tidal waterways through 6 AM Monday, and through 4 PM Thursday along other areas of the Pacific coast. The deluge is an offshoot of El Niño, the warming of the Pacific near the equator that warps weather patterns worldwide, and the same system has brought historic flooding to central Florida, where heavy rain submerged large parts of the Atlantic coast and trapped people in floodwaters. The expected flooding in California coincides with the busiest travel week of the year, compounding the disruption from the East Coast storm and the Delta computer problems. For San Francisco, the weekend is a test of how a city built on the water handles water it has never seen before.

articles.title: Duetti raises $665M in a round led by a Carlyle-anchored deal
articles.description: Music financing company Duetti has raised $665 million in a round led by a Carlyle-anchored asset-backed security deal, Music Business Worldwide reports in its weekly round-up. It was not the only time Carlyle appeared in the week's music stories: the firm, best known in music for backing Scooter Braun's Ithaca Holdings and founding Litmus Music in 2022, is becoming a major force in music rights financing. The raise underlines how much institutional money is now flowing into music catalogues and artist financing.
articles.body: Music financing company Duetti has raised $665 million in a round led by a Carlyle-anchored asset-backed security deal, Music Business Worldwide reports in its weekly round-up. It was not the only time Carlyle appeared in the week's music stories: the firm, best known in music to date for backing Scooter Braun's Ithaca Holdings, founded Litmus Music in 2022 and has been steadily building its presence in music rights. The $665 million raise underlines how much institutional money is now flowing into music: Duetti buys royalty streams from independent artists and songwriters, giving them upfront cash in exchange for a share of future earnings, and the scale of this round shows investors are comfortable with the model. It comes in the same week Warner Music Group posted the first $2 billion quarter in its history, a result already covered in the digest. Together, the two stories point to a music business awash with capital — from the majors' record revenues to the financing firms betting on independent catalogues. For artists, the question is whether the money reaches them on fair terms; for the industry, the Carlyle connection is a sign that private equity's interest in music is only deepening.

articles.title: Miley Cyrus marries Maxx Morando in Palm Springs wedding
articles.description: Miley Cyrus and drummer Maxx Morando married at a wedding in Palm Springs, Rolling Stone reports. The couple became engaged in December 2025 after four years of dating, and the ceremony was led by the Flaming Lips' Wayne Coyne. It is the latest chapter for a couple who have kept their relationship largely out of the spotlight.
articles.body: Miley Cyrus and drummer Maxx Morando married at a wedding in Palm Springs, Rolling Stone reports. The singer and the drummer became engaged in December 2025 after four years of dating, and the ceremony was led by the Flaming Lips' Wayne Coyne, in keeping with the couple's music-world circle. Cyrus, who has been one of pop's most scrutinised stars since her Disney days, has kept this relationship far quieter than her previous marriage, and the wedding itself was a small, private affair rather than a celebrity spectacle. Morando, the drummer of the band Liily, has been a steady presence in her life since they began dating in 2021, appearing with her at events while staying largely out of the press. The marriage caps a strong year for Cyrus, who has balanced new music with a lower public profile. For fans, the news is a rare personal milestone from an artist who has spent much of her career in the headlines — this time, a happy one.

articles.title: KAROL G's 'BbY WOW' tops Billboard Global Excl. US for a seventh week
articles.description: KAROL G's 'BbY WOW,' with Judeline and rusowsky, has topped the Billboard Global Excl. US chart for a seventh week, after moving up from No. 2. The track has spent 13 weeks on the chart, which ranks songs from more than 200 territories excluding the United States, and it also sits at No. 2 on the Global 200. It is the latest marker of KAROL G's dominance in Latin pop's global moment.
articles.body: KAROL G's 'BbY WOW,' with Judeline and rusowsky, has topped the Billboard Global Excl. US chart for a seventh week, after moving up from No. 2. The track has spent 13 weeks on the chart, which ranks songs from more than 200 territories while excluding the United States, using official streams and download sales in a weighted formula. It also sits at No. 2 on the Global 200, the chart that includes US data. Seven weeks at No. 1 on a chart built from international listening is a measure of how far Latin pop has travelled: a Colombian artist leading a ranking drawn from more than 200 territories. The collaboration pairs KAROL G with Spanish artists Judeline and rusowsky, and the song's staying power — 13 weeks on the chart and counting — suggests it has become a fixture rather than a flash. For KAROL G, it adds another chart record to a year of global dominance. For the chart itself, it is a reminder that the centre of pop gravity is no longer only in the US.

articles.title: Zvyagintsev answers Peskov: 'I have no right to a voice, as hundreds of millions of Russians don't'
articles.description: Director Andrei Zvyagintsev has answered Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, who refused to pass on to Vladimir Putin the speech Zvyagintsev gave at Cannes. Meduza publishes the director's reply, in which he says he has no right to a voice — just as hundreds of millions of Russians do not. The exchange began with Zvyagintsev's Cannes speech, which Peskov declined to relay to the president.
articles.body: Director Andrei Zvyagintsev has answered Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, who refused to pass on to Vladimir Putin the speech Zvyagintsev gave at the Cannes film festival. Meduza publishes the director's reply, in which he says: 'Yes, quite right — I have no right to a voice, as hundreds of millions of Russians do not today.' The exchange began with Zvyagintsev's Cannes speech, which Peskov declined to relay to the president, and the director's answer turns the refusal back on the Kremlin: if the president's spokesman will not carry a citizen's words to the president, then the citizen has no voice at all. Zvyagintsev is one of Russia's most acclaimed directors, and his Cannes appearance put him in the international spotlight at a moment when Russian culture is under intense pressure at home. His reply is short, but it lands as a statement about the state of public speech in Russia: a celebrated artist, speaking at the world's most famous film festival, cannot get his words to his own president. For Meduza's readers, the piece is less about film than about the closing of every channel between Russian citizens and power.

articles.title: Ukrainian OnlyFans models owe the state 385 million hryvnias in unpaid taxes
articles.description: Ukrainian models on OnlyFans have underpaid almost 385 million hryvnias (about $9 million) in taxes to the state budget, according to Ukraine's tax service — and that covers only income from 2020 to 2022. The authorities consider filming porn a crime in Ukraine, but still want to collect tax from those who earn from it. Meduza retells the story of the clash between the law and the taxman.
articles.body: Ukrainian models on the OnlyFans platform have underpaid almost 385 million hryvnias (about $9 million) in taxes to the state budget, according to Ukraine's State Tax Service — and that covers only income from 2020 to 2022. The authorities consider filming pornography a crime in Ukraine, but still want to collect tax from those who earn from it, in a contradiction Meduza's retelling lays out. OnlyFans has become a significant income source for thousands of Ukrainian creators, many of whom began during the war, and the tax service is now going after the unpaid sums. The case raises an awkward question for the state: it prosecutes the activity as a crime while treating the income as taxable, which means creators face both criminal liability and a tax bill. For the models, the demand is a large sum, and the years covered — 2020 to 2022 — suggest the audit is only the beginning. For Ukraine, the episode is a small but telling example of how the war economy has pushed people into new kinds of work faster than the law has caught up.

articles.title: FSB detains Elena Belikova, ex-director of a state youth patriotism centre, in embezzlement case
articles.description: Russia's Federal Security Service has detained Elena Belikova, the former director of a state youth patriotism centre, in Moscow in a case involving the alleged embezzlement of a very large sum, business outlet RBC reported citing two sources. The detention is the latest in a series of corruption cases reaching into state-run patriotic and youth organisations.
articles.body: Russia's Federal Security Service has detained Elena Belikova, the former director of a state youth patriotism centre, in Moscow in a case involving the alleged embezzlement of a very large sum, the business outlet RBC reported citing two sources. The detention is the latest in a series of corruption cases reaching into state-run patriotic and youth organisations, which have received large budgets since the full-scale invasion as the state pours money into patriotic education. Belikova ran a centre tasked with instilling patriotism in young people, a flagship of the official youth policy. The case against her — involving, by the official description, embezzlement 'on an especially large scale' — suggests the money flowing into the patriotism industry is now drawing the attention of the security services. For the Kremlin, such cases are a double-edged sword: they show corruption is being punished, but they also expose how much of the patriotic budget is being stolen. The investigation is at an early stage, and the details of the alleged scheme have not been made public.

articles.title: 'This was no Yalta': how the world's press read the Trump–Putin–Xi summit
articles.description: The leaders of Russia, the United States and China met in person for the first time on November 19 in Shenzhen, and Meduza surveys how the world's press read the summit. The verdict, in the outlet's telling: this was no Yalta, and the idea of a new carve-up of the world between the three powers did not survive contact with reality. The summit produced images, not agreements — and the fighting in Ukraine went on regardless.
articles.body: The leaders of Russia, the United States and China met in person for the first time on November 19 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, and Meduza surveys how the world's press read the summit. The verdict, in the outlet's telling: 'This was no Yalta,' and the idea of a new carve-up of the world between the three powers did not survive contact with reality. Much of the coverage focused on the optics — Trump calling Putin 'my friend' and mixing up the Yalta and Tehran conferences — rather than on any substantive outcome, and the summit produced images rather than agreements. The fighting in Ukraine went on regardless: Russia launched a massive attack on Ukraine the day after the meeting, and Putin has since ruled out even a limited ceasefire. The press roundup captures a summit that was historic as a photograph and thin as a negotiation, with each leader taking home a different story. For Trump, it was a stage for his peace push; for Putin, a return to the top table; for Xi, a demonstration that China hosts the meetings that matter. For Ukraine, the summit changed nothing on the ground.

articles.title: Woman killed and nine injured in Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk region
articles.description: Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk region killed a woman and injured nine people, Pravda reports. The casualties are part of a day of strikes across Ukraine that also hit a supermarket in Vyshneve, an apartment block in Dymer and energy infrastructure in five regions.
articles.body: Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk region killed a woman and injured nine people, Pravda reports. The region, in central-eastern Ukraine, has been hit repeatedly in the nightly campaign, and today's toll adds to a grim day across the country: three killed and 15 injured at a supermarket in Vyshneve, the apartment block destroyed in Dymer, and a teenager killed by an FPV drone in Sumy region. Dnipropetrovsk's casualties came as emergency power cuts were introduced in five regions after strikes on energy facilities, and Odesa remained in blackout. The attacks show the breadth of the Russian campaign — it is not concentrated on one city or one kind of target, but spread across the country and across civilian life. For residents of the region, the day brought the same pattern as elsewhere: sirens, explosions, and the count of the dead and injured. The injured were taken to hospital, and the authorities have not yet given a full account of the damage.

articles.title: Teenager killed in Sumy region by explosion of a Russian FPV drone
articles.description: A teenager was killed in Sumy region by the explosion of a Russian FPV drone, Pravda reports. The death is the latest in the border region's daily toll from drone attacks, and it comes on a day when Russian strikes killed civilians in Vyshneve, Dymer and Dnipropetrovsk region as well.
articles.body: A teenager was killed in Sumy region by the explosion of a Russian FPV drone, Pravda reports. The death is the latest in the border region's daily toll from drone attacks, which have become a constant threat in the communities along the Russian border. Sumy region is hit almost daily by FPV drones, artillery and glide bombs, and the casualties are often civilians — people in villages and small towns far from the front line. The teenager's death comes on a day when Russian strikes killed civilians in Vyshneve, Dymer and Dnipropetrovsk region as well, in a wave of attacks across the country. For the border regions, the FPV drone has become the most feared weapon: cheap, precise, and able to strike a person on a street or in a field. The region's authorities have repeatedly urged residents to take shelter when drones are reported, but the attacks come with little warning. The victim's identity has not been released.

articles.title: Emergency power outages in effect in five regions after new strikes on energy infrastructure
articles.description: Emergency power outages are in effect in five Ukrainian regions after new Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, Pravda reports, in an update to the Odesa blackout reported this morning. The Energy Ministry said the outages follow fresh attacks on substations and power lines, and Odesa reported large-scale damage to its main power networks, with schools switching to remote learning for a week.
articles.body: Emergency power outages are in effect in five Ukrainian regions after new Russian strikes on energy infrastructure, Pravda reports, in an update to the Odesa blackout reported this morning. The Energy Ministry said the outages follow fresh attacks on substations and power lines, and Odesa reported large-scale damage to its main power networks, with the city's schools switching to remote learning for a week. The five-region outage is the latest in Russia's winter campaign against the grid, which has already left Odesa largely without electricity and knocked out water in Kyiv earlier in the week. For residents, the outages mean more than dark homes: heating and water depend on the same grid, and the government is preparing a single digital platform for reporting outages of electricity, heat and water. The strikes are timed for the coldest months, and the pattern is now familiar — a night of attacks, then a morning of emergency cuts. Engineers are working to restore supply, but the ministry has not given a timeline. For Ukraine, the energy war is now a daily fact of winter life.

articles.title: Three Russian missiles violated Polish airspace on November 20, investigators say; Rutte vows to defend 'every centimetre'
articles.description: Three Russian missiles violated Polish airspace on November 20, investigators have said, in the incident behind NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte's promise during a visit to Warsaw to defend 'every centimetre' of Polish territory. The violation is part of a pattern of Russian weapons operating near — and over — NATO territory, and it comes as air-raid sirens sounded in the Kaliningrad region for the first time since the full-scale invasion began.
articles.body: Three Russian missiles violated Polish airspace on November 20, investigators have said, in the incident behind NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte's promise during a visit to Warsaw to defend 'every centimetre' of Polish territory. The pledge is the alliance's standard formula, but it lands with new weight: Poland has become a frontline state in the confrontation with Moscow, and the missile violation is the most serious airspace incident in months. Rutte's visit to Warsaw was a show of solidarity at a moment when the war's spillover risks are rising, with air-raid sirens sounding in the Kaliningrad region for the first time since the full-scale invasion began. For Poland, the promise is reassurance backed by the alliance's collective defence commitment; the finding that three missiles crossed its airspace makes the threat concrete rather than theoretical. For NATO, the incident is a reminder that the war in Ukraine is not contained to Ukraine's borders, and that the alliance's eastern members are living with the consequences daily. The investigation into the violation continues, and the alliance has not said what, if anything, it will do in response.

articles.title: Czech prime minister opposes funding Ukraine under the EU budget
articles.description: The Czech prime minister opposes funding Ukraine under the EU budget, Pravda reports, in the latest friction over long-term support for Kyiv inside the European Union. The objection comes as EU leaders prepare to discuss a budget that preserves up to €100 billion for Ukraine through 2034, and a further €45 billion loan — which Slovakia has already refused to join.
articles.body: The Czech prime minister opposes funding Ukraine under the EU budget, Pravda reports, in the latest friction over long-term support for Kyiv inside the European Union. The objection comes as EU leaders prepare to discuss a budget that preserves up to €100 billion for Ukraine through 2034, alongside a Commission proposal for a further €45 billion loan to Ukraine in 2027 — which Slovakia has already refused to join. The Czech position adds a second sceptical voice to the debate, after Slovakia's refusal, and it complicates the unanimity Brussels wants to project on Ukraine funding. The budget proposal, presented by European Council President António Costa, already faces opposition from the European Parliament's budget rapporteurs, who have rejected the draft. For Ukraine, the Czech objection is a political problem rather than an immediate financial one: the funding can proceed without Prague, but every new package has to be negotiated past governments that would rather not pay. The November 26–27 European Council meeting will show whether the rest of the EU can hold the line on long-term support.

articles.title: Slovakia refuses to take part in the EU's new €45 billion loan for Ukraine
articles.description: Slovakia will not take part in financing the European Union's new €45 billion loan for Ukraine, Prime Minister Robert Fico said. The loan is part of a Commission proposal to be discussed alongside the EU budget at the European Council meeting on November 26–27. Fico's refusal adds to the friction over long-term Ukraine funding inside the EU.
articles.body: Slovakia will not take part in financing the European Union's new €45 billion loan for Ukraine, Prime Minister Robert Fico said. The loan is part of a European Commission proposal to be discussed alongside the EU budget at the European Council meeting on November 26–27, where leaders will also debate a budget that preserves up to €100 billion for Ukraine through 2034. Fico's refusal adds to the friction over long-term Ukraine funding inside the EU: Slovakia under Fico has been one of the most sceptical governments on aid to Kyiv, and the opt-out weakens the sense of unanimity Brussels wants to project. The loan is meant to cover Ukraine's financing needs in 2027, and the Commission has already transferred €7.9 billion to Kyiv, the largest single Ukraine Facility tranche yet. For Ukraine, the Slovak refusal is a political irritation rather than a financial blow — the loan can proceed without Bratislava. But it is a reminder that every new funding package has to be negotiated past governments that would rather not pay. The November 26–27 summit will show whether the rest of the EU can hold the line.

articles.title: UPDATE: GTA VI sold 32.5 million copies on its first day
articles.description: Grand Theft Auto VI sold 32.5 million copies on its first day, Take-Two Interactive said in an official press release — the sales behind the record $3.79 billion launch-day gross reported this morning. The figure makes the launch not only the biggest in entertainment history by revenue, but one of the largest single-day sales totals ever for a video game.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI sold 32.5 million copies on its first day, Take-Two Interactive said in an official press release — the sales behind the record $3.79 billion launch-day gross reported this morning. The figure makes the launch not only the biggest in entertainment history by revenue, but one of the largest single-day sales totals ever for a video game. The game has now tied the original Ocarina of Time's record 99 Metacritic critic score, and its user score has become a battleground after coordinated review-bombing pushed it to around 5.6. Rockstar has also revealed the lead actors — Dylan Rourke as Jason Duval and Manny L. Perez as Lucia Caminos — and the studio's developers are reported to be worried about layoffs once the launch rush passes. For Take-Two, the numbers are a triumph: a 13-year wait since GTA V has produced a launch that dwarfs everything before it. For the industry, the question is what comes next — the company's CEO has already been asked about GTA VII, and the answer was a joke about the wait.

articles.title: Activision wants to teach game bots to joke and gloat using voice-chat recordings
articles.description: Activision is considering using recordings of players' voice chats to train bots in online games, so that virtual teammates could celebrate a win with the squad and rival bots could taunt opponents. The idea, reported by GameMAG, would let bots copy the way real players talk — raising questions about consent and privacy for the recordings.
articles.body: Activision is considering using recordings of players' voice chats to train bots in online games, so that virtual teammates could celebrate a win with the squad and rival bots could taunt opponents. The idea, reported by GameMAG, would let bots copy the way real players talk — their jokes, their celebrations, their trash talk — instead of speaking in canned lines. It is part of a wider push to make AI opponents feel less robotic, and Activision is one of several publishers exploring how to use player data to train game systems. But the proposal raises obvious questions: voice chat is recorded already in many games for moderation, and players may not expect those recordings to become training data for bots. Whether Activision will go ahead, and what consent it would seek, is unclear — the company is said to be 'considering' the idea rather than implementing it. For players, the prospect of a bot that talks like them is both a novelty and a privacy question. For the industry, it is another example of how AI is moving from the lab into the lobby.

articles.title: Fan criticism hasn't changed the Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy's story
articles.description: The story of the Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy was planned from the very beginning and has not changed in ten years, Square Enix has said — not even in response to criticism from some fans. The trilogy's script was set long before the first part released, and the leadership has not made adjustments to it.
articles.body: The story of the Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy was planned from the very beginning and has not changed in ten years, Square Enix has said — not even in response to criticism from some fans. The trilogy's script was set long before the first part released, and the leadership has not made adjustments to it, despite the debate the remake's changes to the original story have provoked. It is a firm answer to a long-running argument in the fan community: the remake trilogy diverges from the 1997 original in significant ways, and some players have hoped the final part would walk those changes back. Square Enix is saying it will not. The statement also shows how long the project has been in the works — a decade of planning for a trilogy that is still not finished. For fans, the message is to judge the story on its own terms when the final part arrives. For Square Enix, it is a defence of creative control: the story was decided, and the criticism, however loud, did not move it.

articles.title: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis will reimagine the 1996 original with much that's new
articles.description: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis takes the original 1996 Tomb Raider as its basis but will differ from it substantially, the developers say. They have reworked many elements, including the structure and look of the locations, the story progression and the gameplay mechanics — while carefully recreating the best moments of the original.
articles.body: Tomb Raider: Legacy of Atlantis takes the original 1996 Tomb Raider as its basis but will differ from it substantially, the developers say. They have reworked many elements, including the structure and look of the locations, the story progression and the gameplay mechanics — while carefully recreating the best moments of the original. It is a remake in the modern sense: not a remaster of the old game, but a reimagining that keeps the spirit and the famous set pieces while rebuilding almost everything else. The 1996 original made Lara Croft one of gaming's defining characters, and the remake arrives as the series approaches its 30th anniversary. For longtime fans, the promise of 'the best moments, carefully recreated' is the key line — the T-Rex, the tombs, the traps, rebuilt for modern hardware. For new players, it is an entry point to a game that defined a genre. No release date has been announced, but the details suggest the project is well into development.

articles.title: Rockstar explains why there are no prostitutes in Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: Every 3D Grand Theft Auto game has let players spend time with a sex worker — but in GTA VI, released days ago, Rockstar has dropped the mechanic. The studio has now explained the decision, after the outlet Shacknews asked about the absence. It is one of several ways the new game breaks with the series' traditions.
articles.body: Every 3D Grand Theft Auto game has let players spend time with a sex worker — but in GTA VI, released days ago, Rockstar has dropped the mechanic. The studio has now explained the decision, after the outlet Shacknews asked about the absence. It is one of several ways the new game breaks with the series' traditions, and the explanation has become a talking point in the days since launch, as players catalogue what has changed. The game has already set records — $3.79 billion on day one, 32.5 million copies — and the discussion around it has ranged from its story and characters to the details of its world. The removal of a mechanic that was present in every 3D entry is a deliberate choice, and Rockstar's willingness to explain it suggests the studio expected the question. For the series, it is a sign of how much the cultural context has shifted since GTA V: what was once a background detail is now a decision that needs a public explanation.

articles.title: 007 First Light named Game of the Year at the TIGA Awards 2026
articles.description: 007 First Light has won the top prize at the British TIGA Awards 2026, taking Game of the Year at the ceremony organised by the association of independent developers. IO Interactive thanked the jury, and the win is a major early honour for the spy action game ahead of the bigger awards season.
articles.body: 007 First Light has won the top prize at the British TIGA Awards 2026, taking Game of the Year at the ceremony organised by the association of independent developers. IO Interactive thanked the jury, and the win is a major early honour for the spy action game ahead of the bigger awards season, which culminates in The Game Awards on December 10. The TIGA Awards celebrate the UK industry in particular, and a win there is a strong signal of how the game is landing with developers themselves. 007 First Light is IO Interactive's take on James Bond — a younger Bond, in a story that reimagines the character's origins — and the award suggests the gamble is paying off. For the studio, best known for Hitman, it is validation of a new direction. For Bond fans, it is a reminder that the character's next big outing is a game, not a film, and that it is already winning prizes.

articles.title: Sinister Japanese horror Ugly Within announced at The Horror Games Awards
articles.description: Serafini Productions, the studio behind the BrokenLore series of first-person psychological horrors, has announced its new game: Ugly Within, a third-person survival horror set in a traditional Japanese estate, revealed at The Horror Games Awards 2026. A Russian text translation is expected, and the game is coming to PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch 2 and PC.
articles.body: Serafini Productions, the studio behind the BrokenLore series of first-person psychological horrors, has announced its new game: Ugly Within, a third-person survival horror set in a traditional Japanese estate, revealed at The Horror Games Awards 2026. Players will face mysterious supernatural entities in the manor, in a shift from the studio's first-person roots to a third-person perspective. A Russian text translation is expected, and the game is coming to PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, Nintendo Switch 2 and PC via Steam. The announcement came at a ceremony that also named Hellraiser: Revival the best horror game of 2026, in a strong year for the genre. For Serafini, Ugly Within is a step up in ambition: a bigger setting, a new perspective, and a Japanese setting that draws on a rich tradition of horror. For horror fans, it is another promising title in a genre that has had a remarkable run. No release date has been announced.

articles.title: Republican chair of the House Rules Committee loses reelection in Democrats' largest majority this century
articles.description: Democrat Chuck Hubbard will unseat longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina, after Foxx conceded the race on Sunday, extending Democrats' largest House majority since the early 1990s. Foxx, the chair of the House Rules Committee, had requested a machine recount after initial results showed her just 331 votes behind; the recount wrapped up on Saturday. Democrats will control at least 259 House seats, with Republicans on 173.
articles.body: Democrat Chuck Hubbard will unseat longtime Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx in North Carolina, after Foxx conceded the race on Sunday, extending Democrats' largest House majority since the early 1990s. Foxx, the chair of the House Rules Committee, had requested a machine recount after initial results showed her just 331 votes behind; the recount wrapped up on Saturday and confirmed the result. Hubbard's win means Democrats will control at least 259 House seats, and they lead in the last uncalled race, in Minnesota, where a recount is scheduled to start on November 30. Republicans will control 173 seats, and runoff elections in Louisiana on December 12 will determine the last two. The result is the latest aftershock of this month's midterm blue wave, in which Democrats swept Congress and statehouses and voters rebuked President Trump. Foxx is one of the most senior Republicans in the House, and losing the Rules Committee chair — the panel that controls what reaches the floor — is a symbolic as well as a practical blow. For the new Democratic majority, the size of the win gives it room to govern; for the GOP, the scale of the defeat is now a matter of record.

articles.title: Iranian attacks in the Strait of Hormuz at the highest levels since the conflict began
articles.description: Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the US–Iran war began in late February, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to reassert control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices. In October, more than 30 attacks were reported to the Royal Navy-affiliated UK Maritime Trade Operations — the first time that figure has been passed — and at least 22 have been reported in November, the second-highest figure since the war began. Three tankers were struck on Friday and Saturday.
articles.body: Reported attacks on shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz are at the highest levels since the US–Iran war began in late February, maritime data shows, as Tehran seeks to reassert control over the critical waterway amid falling oil prices. In October, the number of attacks reported to the Royal Navy-affiliated United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) exceeded 30 for the first time since the war began. As of Sunday, at least 22 attacks were reported in November, the second-highest figure since the war began, according to a CNN analysis of UKMTO data covering the Strait of Hormuz, the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. During the latest attacks, projectiles struck three tankers exiting the strait on Friday and Saturday, according to maritime risk firm Marisks. Fire erupted aboard the Captain Leon, a Marshall Islands-flagged chemical and oil tanker, after it was struck at the bow on Friday. The International Energy Agency attributes the recent decline in oil prices to a recovery in Gulf exports, and analysts say markets increasingly assume a return to full-scale war is unlikely. President Trump said this month the US doesn't 'need a deal' with Tehran and ordered Vice President JD Vance to turn his focus elsewhere. For shipping, the numbers are the story: the waterway that carries a fifth of the world's oil is seeing its worst attacks since the war began.

articles.title: Midterm blue wave scrambles the 2028 race — the first in over a decade without Trump on the ballot
articles.description: The midterm blue wave has scrambled how people talk about the 2028 presidential race, CNN reports in an interview with its Democrats correspondent Edward-Isaac Dovere. It will be the first presidential race in more than a decade that won't feature Donald Trump, and a moment of generational change for both parties. The new primary map, with South Carolina first for Democrats, and a field that includes Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Pete Buttigieg, Gavin Newsom and JB Pritzker, is already taking shape.
articles.body: The midterm blue wave has scrambled how people talk about the 2028 presidential race, CNN reports in an interview with its Democrats correspondent Edward-Isaac Dovere. It will be the first presidential race in more than a decade that won't feature Donald Trump, and a moment of generational change for both parties. The conversation, edited from CNN's What Matters newsletter, ranges over how the blue wave changes things for Democrats, how the radically new primary map will alter the contest, and whether the political environment is too toxic for some of the best-qualified people to bother running. South Carolina will be first for Democrats in 2028, a calendar change that reshapes who can compete. Among the names in play: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who has been shifting her rhetoric; Pete Buttigieg, who campaigned in 38 states; Gavin Newsom, the outgoing term-limited California governor; and JB Pritzker, reelected in Illinois. The interview also notes that Democrats' new generation — James Talarico as senator and Gina Hinojosa as governor in Texas — is already in office. For Republicans, the companion analysis is darker: the party is increasingly dependent on white evangelical voters even as they shrink as a share of society, which could leave it sweating in states like Iowa, Ohio and even Texas in 2028.

articles.title: Margin Call: on Spotify, 'Marketplace', and the price labels pay for promotion
articles.description: Music Business Worldwide founder Tim Ingham's latest 'Tim's Take' examines Spotify's 'Marketplace' — the tools that let labels pay for promotion on the platform — and asks what the price of visibility really is. The analysis lands in a week when Warner posted a record $2 billion quarter and Duetti raised $665 million, and it questions how much of the industry's money now flows through Spotify's promotional machinery.
articles.body: Music Business Worldwide founder Tim Ingham's latest 'Tim's Take' examines Spotify's 'Marketplace' — the tools that let labels pay for promotion on the platform — and asks what the price of visibility really is. The analysis, titled 'Margin Call,' looks at how labels pay Spotify to push their music in front of listeners, and what that costs them in margin. It lands in a week when Warner Music Group posted the first $2 billion quarter in its history and Duetti raised $665 million to finance music royalties, and it asks a pointed question: how much of the industry's money now flows through Spotify's promotional machinery, and who benefits? Marketplace has been controversial since its launch, with critics arguing that it lets the biggest labels buy the visibility smaller artists cannot afford, and defenders saying it is simply advertising. Ingham's piece is the latest in a long-running argument about who controls discovery on streaming. For independent artists, the stakes are practical: if promotion is pay-to-play, then the algorithm is not a level playing field. For the industry, the question is whether the streaming economy's margins can survive the price of being heard.

articles.title: Ex-Hipgnosis exec Alexander Bonavia launches Rendezvous Sound via joint ventures
articles.description: Former Hipgnosis executive Alexander Bonavia has launched Rendezvous Sound, a new music company built through joint ventures with Create Music Group-backed broke and Enhanced. Create owns broke and acquired a 50% stake in Enhanced in December 2024. The launch is the latest move by a veteran of the music-rights boom to build a new venture in the catalogue and services space.
articles.body: Former Hipgnosis executive Alexander Bonavia has launched Rendezvous Sound, a new music company built through joint ventures with Create Music Group-backed broke and Enhanced. Create Music Group owns broke and acquired a 50% stake in Enhanced in December 2024, and the new venture sits at the intersection of the two. Bonavia is a veteran of the music-rights boom — Hipgnosis was the company that turned song catalogues into an asset class — and his new launch is the latest sign that the executives who built that market are now building what comes next. The structure, joint ventures rather than a standalone label, reflects how the modern music business works: partnerships between established operators and new ventures, sharing risk and reach. For artists, Rendezvous Sound is another new home in a crowded market; for the industry, it is a reminder that the catalogue boom's architects are still active, and still betting that music rights are a good place to be. Details of the venture's first signings have not been announced.

articles.title: Boy George on his Israel trip: 'I wasn't able to not say something'
articles.description: Boy George has spoken to Rolling Stone about his trip to Israel, saying he 'wasn't able to not say something' about what he saw there. The Culture Club frontman, one of pop's most outspoken figures, discussed the visit in a new interview that leads Rolling Stone's coverage today.
articles.body: Boy George has spoken to Rolling Stone about his trip to Israel, saying he 'wasn't able to not say something' about what he saw there. The Culture Club frontman, one of pop's most outspoken figures, discussed the visit in a new interview that leads Rolling Stone's coverage today. Boy George has never been shy about his opinions, and the interview is in that tradition: a pop star using a trip to talk about what he witnessed, rather than staying quiet. The piece comes as the Israel question continues to divide the music world, with artists facing pressure from all sides over where they perform and what they say. For Boy George, the calculation was simple — he went, he saw, and he felt he had to speak. The interview does not shy away from the controversy, and it is the kind of celebrity-politics story that has become a staple of Rolling Stone's coverage. For readers, it is a reminder that pop stars of his generation still see the interview as a place to say something real.

articles.title: Don Toliver, Malcolm Todd, Alex Warren and Megan Moroney rock Rolling Stone's Musicians on Musicians event
articles.description: Don Toliver, Malcolm Todd, Alex Warren and Megan Moroney packed the United Theater on Broadway in Los Angeles on Friday for Rolling Stone's Musicians on Musicians 2026 live event, a sold-out night of collaborative performances and candid conversations. The franchise has brought artists together annually since 2019, and this year's edition paired the Nashville-based Warren and Moroney — both of whom released debut albums this year — with Toliver and Todd.
articles.body: Don Toliver, Malcolm Todd, Alex Warren and Megan Moroney packed the United Theater on Broadway in Los Angeles on Friday for Rolling Stone's Musicians on Musicians 2026 live event, a sold-out night of collaborative performances and candid conversations. The franchise has brought artists together annually since 2019, and this year's edition paired the Nashville-based Warren and Moroney — both of whom released debut albums this year — with Toliver and Todd. Moroney dropped 'Cloud 9' in February, which debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, and Warren's 'Wildchild' arrived in August; in a digital cover story ahead of the event, the two told Rolling Stone they have a lot of parallels, from scoring big hits on debut albums to finding even bigger audiences. After an intermission, Toliver and Todd emerged to riotous applause, hiking up the decibel levels — both have seen their careers reach a palpable upswing over the last year, with Todd's follow-up album 'Do That Again' building on his breakout self-titled debut. Rolling Stone recently flagged Toliver's LP as a contender for Best Rap Album at next year's Grammys. For the audience, the night was a chance to see four of the year's rising acts up close; for the artists, it was a conversation about the music shaping their moment.

articles.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' is all over the place (in a good way), Rolling Stone says
articles.description: Rolling Stone's review of 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' calls the soundtrack 'all over the place (in a good way)': featuring everyone from Travis Scott to Fuerza Regida to Michael McDonald, it plays like a radio dial spinning on hyperspeed. The album has already set the biggest soundtrack debut in Spotify history, with almost 30 million streams in its first day.
articles.body: Rolling Stone's review of 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' calls the soundtrack 'all over the place (in a good way)': featuring everyone from Travis Scott to Fuerza Regida to Michael McDonald, it plays like a radio dial spinning on hyperspeed. The review is the critical counterpart to the commercial story — the album gathered almost 30 million Spotify streams in its first day, the biggest soundtrack debut on the platform — and it argues that the sprawl is the point. A GTA soundtrack is meant to sound like a radio dial, and this one does, jumping between genres and eras with the confidence of a game that knows its audience. The review also highlights the new songs on the album, including contributions from Lana Del Rey, Dua Lipa and Zara Larsson, alongside the licensed tracks. For Rockstar, the soundtrack is part of the launch's total dominance: a game, a festival in Miami, and now a record-breaking album. For listeners, the review is an invitation to treat the album as a playlist in its own right — one that works even if you never play the game.

articles.title: Tom Waits' rare 'Orphans: Bonus' EP, previously vinyl-only, now streaming
articles.description: Tom Waits' rare 'Orphans: Bonus' EP, previously available only on vinyl, is now streaming. The release gives a wider audience access to a collection that has been a collectors' item since it first appeared, and it is the latest in a run of catalogue moves that have brought Waits' rarities to streaming.
