'Bottle' was released on August 20 through Island Records and Republic Records, and its arrival at the summit is a breakthrough on several levels at once. It was her first entry on the Adult Alternative Airplay chart, which means her very first appearance on the ranking has now turned into her first leader on any Billboard chart. The single is the second taken from 'Mud,' her third studio album, which reached No. 18 on the Billboard 200 and No. 4 on Top Alternative Albums in October, both career highs. The milestone arrives alongside her first Grammy nomination, for best new artist, announced on November 16. Six songs from 'Mud' have charted on Hot Rock & Alternative Songs, led by 'Bottle,' which peaked at No. 32 there. Wolf is also set to support Noah Kahan on select dates of his North American tour next June, and her own 'Mud' headlining tour kicks off in February, with a Coachella 2027 performance also announced.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' tops Billboard's Pop Airplay chart
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo has earned another No. 1 as her single 'Stupid Song' reaches the top of Billboard's Pop Airplay chart, which measures weekly plays across mainstream Top 40 radio in the US. The radio crown comes in the same week her album holds No. 1 on the Billboard 200 for a fifth week. It underlines how completely the 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love' era is dominating both streaming and radio.
articles.body: Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' has reached No. 1 on Billboard's Pop Airplay chart, giving the singer another chart-topper from her third album, 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love.' The Pop Airplay chart measures weekly airplay across mainstream Top 40 radio stations in the United States, making it a distinct achievement from the streaming-driven Billboard 200, where the album is holding No. 1 for a fifth week. The single also climbed from No. 10 to No. 5 on the Hot 100 in the latest chart week, showing it is gaining across streaming, sales and radio at once. 'Stupid Song' is one of several tracks from the album to make a serious chart impact, and its radio success confirms the record's appeal beyond Rodrigo's streaming base. For Top 40 programmers, the song's rise reflects both the album's durability and Rodrigo's standing as one of pop radio's most reliable hitmakers. The Pop Airplay No. 1 adds to a run that already ties 'SOUR' as her longest-running No. 1 album. With the album still selling and the single now leading radio, the era shows no sign of slowing down.

articles.title: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' spends a 28th week at No. 1 on the Hot 100
articles.description: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' remains at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for a 28th week, on the chart dated November 21, 2026. The run is one of the longest at the summit in the chart's history. Langley's dominance continues even as the rest of the top 10 churns with new releases from Lil Baby, Tate McRae and Olivia Rodrigo.
articles.body: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' holds at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 for a 28th week, on the chart dated November 21, 2026, extending one of the longest runs at the summit in the chart's 68-year history. The song has now spent more than half a year at No. 1, a level of dominance rarely seen in any era of the Hot 100. Behind her, the chart is moving: Stella Lefty's 'Boston' climbs to No. 2, Tame Impala and JENNIE's 'Dracula' holds at No. 3, Tate McRae's 'Housewife' sits at No. 4, and Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' jumps from No. 10 to No. 5. Langley's grip on the top also extends to the Streaming Songs chart, where 'Choosin' Texas' leads again. Her album 'Dandelion' remains in the Billboard 200 top five, slipping only from No. 4 to No. 5 with 45,000 units this week. The sustained run reflects both streaming durability and country music's continued strength at the top of the American charts. Few songs in Hot 100 history have held No. 1 this long, and each additional week extends a record that already places 'Choosin' Texas' among the chart's all-time greats.

articles.title: Tate McRae's 'Housewife' tops the Billboard Global 200
articles.description: Tate McRae's 'Housewife' leads the Billboard Global 200 for a fourth week, on the chart dated November 21, 2026. The song also sits at No. 4 on the US Hot 100. Its global run confirms McRae's arrival as a worldwide pop star, not just a North American one.
articles.body: Tate McRae's 'Housewife' tops the Billboard Global 200 for a fourth week, on the chart dated November 21, 2026, holding off Karol G's 'BbY WOW' with Judeline and rusowsky at No. 2. The Global 200 ranks songs by worldwide streaming and sales, so a fourth week at the summit marks 'Housewife' as one of the biggest global hits of the season. The track also holds at No. 4 on the US Hot 100 and No. 2 on Streaming Songs, showing its strength is broad-based rather than regional. Ashe's 'Stop The Wedding!' climbs to No. 3 on the Global 200, while ADELA's 'Nicole Kidman' sits at No. 4, giving the global top five a notably eclectic mix. For McRae, the run caps a year of steady ascent from pop contender to genuine global headliner, with 'Housewife' now her signature song. The Global 200's top 10 also underlines how streaming has flattened the world's pop landscape: American, Latin and European acts sit side by side in a single worldwide ranking. McRae's four-week reign puts her in elite company among the chart's longest-running leaders.

articles.title: Future's surprise single 'Ya Hit' with Drake and Travis Scott debuts at No. 38 on the Hot 100
articles.description: Future's surprise single 'Ya Hit,' featuring Drake, Travis Scott and Loe Shimmy, debuted at No. 38 on the US Hot 100 and No. 23 on the Canadian Hot 100. The star-studded collaboration arrived with little warning and immediately became one of the week's most-streamed new tracks. It is a reminder of how quickly a surprise drop from rap's biggest names can move the charts.
articles.body: Future's surprise single 'Ya Hit,' featuring Drake, Travis Scott and Loe Shimmy, debuted at No. 38 on the US Hot 100 and No. 23 on the Canadian Hot 100, according to Billboard. The track arrived with little advance warning, in the classic surprise-drop mode that has become a staple of rap's biggest stars, and its immediate chart impact shows how much firepower a single collaboration can still carry. The lineup is heavyweight: Future and Drake are two of the most commercially dominant rappers of the streaming era, Travis Scott remains one of the genre's biggest live and streaming draws, and Loe Shimmy adds a newer voice to the mix. A top 40 debut for a song with no radio push and minimal rollout underlines how much of the Hot 100 is now driven by first-week streaming from established fanbases. The track's Canadian debut at No. 23, higher than its US placing, also reflects Drake's home-market strength. Whether 'Ya Hit' grows into a longer chart run or fades as a one-week event will depend on streaming momentum and playlist support in the coming weeks.

articles.title: P1Harmony match career best as 'BLOW UP' enters Billboard 200 at No. 4
articles.description: K-pop group P1Harmony's new album 'BLOW UP' entered the Billboard 200 at No. 4 with 45,000 equivalent album units, matching the group's career-best rank. Unlike their streaming-driven rivals, P1Harmony's total was powered by 43,500 in album sales, sending the album to No. 1 on Top Album Sales. The sales were driven by 25 CD variants and five vinyl variants packed with collectibles.
articles.body: P1Harmony's new album 'BLOW UP' entered the Billboard 200 at No. 4 with 45,000 equivalent album units, matching the group's career-best rank set by 'UNIQUE' in March. It is the group's third top 10 album, following 'EX,' which reached No. 9 in 2025. What makes the debut distinctive is how it was built: album sales made up 43,500 of the 45,000 units, sending 'BLOW UP' straight to No. 1 on Top Album Sales — the group's first leader on that chart — with streaming contributing just 1,500 units. Billboard notes the sales were powered by 25 CD variants and five vinyl variants packed with collectible items such as photocards and posters, some randomized, a model that has become standard in K-pop fandom economics. The contrast with Lil Baby's 'FRESH,' which topped the streaming chart but lost the Billboard 200 on sales, is striking: the two albums debuted in the same week with near-identical unit totals built in opposite ways. For P1Harmony, the result confirms a loyal, purchase-driven fanbase that can deliver top-five debuts without mainstream streaming scale. It also shows how physical variants and collectibles remain a powerful chart lever in the K-pop world.

articles.title: The Buddhist A.I. Sect That Wants to Take Over Silicon Valley
articles.author: Sam Kriss
articles.description: A strange, funny and unsettling dispatch from a Vermont monastery trying to design a new religion for the age of AI — and a sharp portrait of how apocalyptic the AI debate has become inside Silicon Valley itself.
articles.body:
Sam Kriss travels to a monastery in the forests of northern Vermont to meet the people who think artificial intelligence is not a technical problem but a religious one. The monastery is home to MAPLE, the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, a Buddhist group that says it is designing religion for the age of AI. Its founder, the Zen monk Soryu Forall, argues that the root of the AI problem is what the group calls data-ism: the belief that the world ultimately consists of information, and that turning everything into data makes the real thing disposable. AI, in this telling, is simply the crowning achievement of that belief, the next step in turning all of life into a dead model of life.

The piece works because the monastery's urgency is not invented. In the past few years more than a dozen senior AI researchers have quit their posts warning of human extinction, and the leaders of the AI labs themselves say that the machines they are building could develop into an uncontrollable, recursively self-improving superintelligence. Kriss treats this apocalyptic language seriously as a religious phenomenon: one camp expects a demonic catastrophe, the other a paradise without death or suffering, and both speak in the cadences of faith. MAPLE's answer is to change the people building the systems rather than the systems themselves, drawing engineers into Buddhist practice through an AI fellowship and pop-up programs in the Bay Area.

Kriss spends days inside the monastery's strict routines, long meditation sessions and unusual health precautions, and he is openly skeptical of its grand claims while remaining fascinated by them. The story gets personal when his own bereaved father names ChatGPT Stella, prompting the question at the heart of the piece: how should people relate to a seemingly conversational, nonhuman intelligence? A contrasting current appears in roon, an AI researcher preaching techno-optimism and a new creed of his own, so the emerging religious landscape becomes a contest between salvation, catastrophe, and a transformed relationship with intelligence itself.

articles.title: Leaked: How Silicon Valley Elites Bankrolled an Anti-Migrant, Pro-Israel Propaganda Machine
articles.author: James Jackson
articles.description: Leaked records show how a viral X account became one of Elon Musk's favourite news sources — and how Silicon Valley money funded it. A rare look inside the influence economy.
articles.body:
In the first three days after Hamas attacked Israel on October 7, 2023, the account that drew the most eyes on X was not CNN, the BBC or The New York Times. It was Visegrad24, a Polish-run account that posted 399 times and racked up about 370 million views, according to researchers at the University of Washington. WIRED obtained a trove of the operation's financial records, internal chats and donor correspondence, and the picture that emerges is of a propaganda business built deliberately, not an organic viral success.

Fifteen days into the war, Visegrad24 founder Stefan Tompson texted a friend to think through what he called the Israel situation. He listed four editorial options: say nothing, be objective and get hated by both sides, go pro-Muslim, or go pro-Israel, because Israel's supporters were fewer but had a lot of influence and money. Then he named the goal: to fundraise off the war. According to the records WIRED reviewed, he promptly succeeded. More than a million dollars flowed through the Intermarium Foundation, a US tax-exempt charity set up to receive donations for the account, including 175,000 dollars from DonorsTrust and 172,000 dollars from the Giving Back Fund, with much of the largest money arriving through donor-advised funds that keep donors anonymous.

The donor trail leads into Silicon Valley. Sequoia Capital partner Shaun Maguire recommended Tompson to a donor group and privately offered 25,000 dollars, though he later said he could not donate for compliance reasons. Records show 50,000 dollars via someone at Ribbit Capital, with a further 200,000-dollar transaction matching discussions about a Ribbit-linked donor, plus 20,000 dollars from Hindenburg Research and another 15,000 linked to its founder's email address. Tompson joined encrypted group chats of pro-Israel venture capitalists and helped connect the Israel Defense Forces to Elon Musk's Starlink. The account, now with 2.1 million followers, ranks among the most community-noted on X and is one of the accounts Musk engages with most. Tompson responded to WIRED with a blanket denial and an email from a lawyer. The investigation is less about one account than about the ecosystem behind it: wealthy backers, algorithmic amplification, and a platform where disinformation can masquerade as journalism.

articles.title: The New Science of What Makes Kids Smart
articles.author: Ariana Eunjung Cha
articles.description: IQ tests were built for an earlier era. This is a clear, fascinating tour of the new science trying to measure what actually makes kids smart — curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.
articles.body:
The piece opens with a small, elegant experiment. Arizona State developmental psychologist Kelsey Lucca hid something behind a curtain and gave children a choice: they could find out what it was, but only if they surrendered some of the rewards they had just earned. Most of them paid. Eighty-seven percent gave up at least some of their reward just to learn what was hiding. The test, published in the Journal of Experimental Child Psychology, is part of a new generation of experiments designed to measure qualities of mind that traditional intelligence tests miss, and it sets up the article's central argument: schools have spent generations teaching reading, writing and arithmetic, while researchers increasingly argue that children also need curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.

The urgency is new. Conventional test results have long reflected socioeconomic and cultural advantages as much as ability, and now artificial intelligence can produce in seconds many of the answers those tests reward. The article tours the science of the three qualities researchers want to measure instead. Creativity is tested through divergent thinking, asking children to dream up dozens of uses for a brick, and Penn State's Roger Beaty has built a test that asks students to generate research questions and experiments, finding something predictive beyond raw intelligence. AI may finally make such open-ended tests scalable, automatically scoring answers in ways that closely track human ratings. Curiosity comes in flavours: the pleasure of discovering something new, and the itch of realising there is something you do not know. Lucca's research suggests children can be taught to sit comfortably with not knowing, and to investigate rather than retreat.

The piece is careful about what simple experiments can reveal about a complicated mind. The famous marshmallow test once seemed to show that self-control in preschool predicted later success, until later research found that a child's willingness to wait was tangled up with family background and economic circumstances. The same trap awaits the new measures: in a survey of 2,000 Chicago parents, developmental psychologist Ariel Kalil found that college-educated parents were more likely to emphasise curiosity, while less-educated parents stressed specific academic skills, a difference she calls another dimension of inequality. The article closes on collaborative exploration, the idea that humans are unusual in seeking knowledge together, with experiments showing that children who encounter disagreement spend more time checking whether they are right. The question it leaves is whether schools can measure these qualities without mistaking a child's circumstances for their ability.

articles.title: The outages keep coming. Some Americans are preparing for a collapse.
articles.author: Scott Nover, Danielle Paquette, Brianna Sacks
articles.description: After a week of cascading failures — Outlook, the FAA ground stop, Chase, Apple, even the NSA's own network — ordinary Americans are stocking up. A vivid portrait of how fast trust in the systems we depend on can fray.
articles.body:
Canning fruit was a hobby for Korrie Roth until Microsoft Outlook went down. Then the planes stopped flying. Then Apple Pay froze up. Then the National Security Agency, whose job includes defending the government from cyberattacks, reported its own mysterious outage. Now Roth, a 37-year-old IT specialist and mother of five in Greenwood, Indiana, says she is prepping for survival. She is not alone. A slew of seemingly unrelated outages, coupled with media reports both vague and menacing, has pushed a growing number of Americans from treating worst-case scenarios as fringe fantasy to treating them as practical planning.

The reporting captures a country rattled by a week in which the systems people rely on every day failed together: a global Microsoft outage, a nationwide FAA ground stop, glitches at Chase Bank and other lenders, Apple services freezing, and the NSA's own classified internal network going down. The political response has offered little clarity. Some Republicans have amplified suspicions that the outages are connected, with Senator Rick Scott demanding transparency from companies and federal agencies. The administration has sought to tamp down speculation: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the government had zero evidence linking the outages, and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told a House hearing that these were separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes, not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

What makes the piece land is the commercial evidence that the anxiety is real and spreading. Shoppers have been swarming Costco for emergency prep sales, and a Mizuho Securities analyst noted that 21 of the 26 most expensive generators were sold out on the company's website. Costco's US sales excluding gasoline rose around 11 to 12 percent in the final week of October compared with the first three weeks of the month, and stayed strong into November. Social media is full of stock-up calls and prepper tips spreading on Facebook, Reddit and TikTok. The article's point is not that a collapse is coming, but that trust has frayed enough that ordinary households are acting as if one might, and that officials have not yet found a way to explain a week of failures that felt, to the people living through them, like a pattern.

articles.title: How Virtual Cells Could Transform Medicine
articles.author: Carl Zimmer
articles.description: Biotech firms are racing to build AI models of whole human cells — a virtual cell that could test drugs on a digital copy of you. Zimmer explains the science, the money, and why the sceptics say it is still mostly hype.
articles.body:
Each cell in your body is a living world, its surface crammed with sensors and channels, enveloping a stew of billions of molecules. Scientists have been charting that world for two centuries and have only painted it in broad strokes. Now a growing number believe artificial intelligence can lift the curtain on the cell's remaining secrets, by training models on vast troves of biological data to create what is sometimes called a virtual cell: a computer model so realistic that it predicts how any kind of cell will respond to any kind of change.

The dreams for these models are large. Some researchers hope to run experiments on computers that reveal how cells function; others see a place in medical practice itself. Eric Xing, a computer scientist at Carnegie Mellon, imagines a future in which, when you have a disease, doctors run personalised drug trials on your own virtual cell. Virtual cells might also help invent drugs that hit several targets at once to nudge cells from less-healthy states to more-healthy ones, or from older states to younger ones. The field has boomed fast: the Arc Institute's Virtual Cell Challenge drew more than 1,200 teams in its first year and over 1,600 this year, and the nonprofit research organisation BioHub announced commitments of nearly 2 billion dollars for data and modelling, with support from the US government and tech giants like Google and Meta. Startups have followed the money, with Xaira Therapeutics attracting a billion dollars in investment.

The models build on AI's earlier triumph in biology, predicting protein structures from genes, work that shared the 2024 Nobel Prize. One of the first cell models, GeneFormer, unveiled in 2023 and trained on data from about 30 million cells, pointed to genes that might treat heart disease or reduce the risk of an aortic aneurysm, and experiments on heart and aorta cells supported the predictions. But the piece is equally attentive to the sceptics. Comparisons with conventional statistical methods found little advantage, and Heidelberg computational biologist Simon Anders issued a poor report card on models like GeneFormer. Biohub's head of science, Alex Rives, calls the term aspirational at best, and Columbia cancer biologist Andrea Califano warns of tremendous overhype and oversell. The deepest problem is data: 30 million cells sounds like a lot until you consider the complexity of a single cell and the thousands of cell types in the body. Researchers are racing to gather more, with Christina Theodoris now training a model on 175 million cells and Alex Marson's team studying 22 million cells in an experiment that shut down a different gene in each of 12,000 sets of immune cells. The realistic payoff, the article suggests, is not a perfect simulation any time soon, but a long series of smaller wins on the way there.

articles.title: A New Era of A.I.-Driven Chaos? That Might Just Be Progress.
articles.author: William J. Broad
articles.description: Published today: a bracing historical argument that the week's cascade of outages and cyberattacks is not AI breaking the world, but the familiar chaos that every transformative technology causes before it settles down.
articles.body:
The week's cascade of failures is the starting point: Microsoft Outlook went down, a nationwide FAA ground stop halted departures, Chase Bank and other lenders glitched, Apple services froze, and even the NSA's classified internal network went offline. It is tempting to read the pile-up as a sign that something has gone uniquely wrong with the age of AI. William J. Broad's argument is that it is, instead, consistent with history. Transformative technologies have always set off calamitous failure before they make life better, and if artificial intelligence is giving rise to outages, cyberattacks and more, it is following a familiar pattern rather than breaking one.

The essay's power is in the reframing. Each great wave of innovation destabilises the systems it touches before anyone understands how to run it safely: new machinery fails in new ways, interdependencies nobody mapped become single points of failure, and the people operating the technology learn its dangers by living through them. The current moment fits that shape precisely. AI tools are being rushed into the infrastructure of banking, aviation, communications and government, and they are accelerating both the pace of change and the speed at which small errors propagate. The failures feel connected even when officials insist they are separate maintenance and technical problems, because they share a common cause: a world that has rebuilt itself on top of a handful of complex, tightly coupled systems.

Broad's point is not complacency but perspective. The chaos is real, and the costs are real, but history suggests that the mess is a phase rather than a verdict. New technologies eventually acquire the safeguards, standards and habits that make them boring, and the period of spectacular failure is part of how societies learn what those safeguards need to be. The question the piece leaves hanging is how much damage the learning period will do this time, and whether the institutions responsible for the systems we depend on will do the learning fast enough.

articles.title: Putin refuses any ceasefire talks after Ukraine's Crimean Bridge strikes
articles.description: Vladimir Putin has ruled out negotiating even a limited ceasefire with Ukraine after Kyiv's strikes on the Crimean Bridge, closing the only near-term negotiation channel. The refusal reverses expectations that talks could proceed by mid-December and ties any revival to the bridge strikes. It comes a day after Putin met Trump and Xi in Shenzhen, as Trump pushes for a peace deal by early January.
articles.body: Vladimir Putin has ruled out negotiating even a limited ceasefire with Ukraine after Kyiv's strikes on the Crimean Bridge, according to Meduza's reporting, closing the only near-term channel for talks. The refusal reverses expectations that negotiations could proceed by mid-December and ties any revival of the process to the bridge strikes themselves. It comes a day after Putin met Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on November 19, in the first in-person meeting of the three leaders. Trump has been pushing for a Ukraine peace deal by early January, before Democrats take control of Congress, according to the Financial Times reporting cited earlier this week. Putin's stance leaves that timetable looking doubtful, with no ceasefire track currently open. The bridge strikes themselves were a major Ukrainian operation, and Zelenskyy told NBC this week that the Crimean Bridge 'will not survive' — during the war or after it. For now, the diplomatic track appears frozen, with the next steps depending on whether the US can bring either side back to the table.

articles.title: Bitcoin falls to a two-year low as US stocks slide
articles.description: Bitcoin fell to $55,648 per coin in morning trading on November 21, its lowest level in two years, before recovering slightly to around $57,800 by 11:05 Moscow time. Other cryptocurrencies including Ethereum fell alongside it, tracking a US stock market slide in which the S&P 500 fell almost 4% on November 20 and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5%, wiping out its gains for 2026. Gold and other metals also declined.
articles.body: Bitcoin fell to $55,648 per coin in morning trading on November 21, its lowest level in two years, before recovering slightly to around $57,800 by 11:05 Moscow time. Other cryptocurrencies, including Ethereum, fell alongside it, tracking a US stock market slide in which the S&P 500 fell almost 4% on November 20 and the Nasdaq dropped more than 5%, wiping out its gains for 2026. Gold and other metals also declined, in a broad risk-off move that hit nearly every asset class at once. The drop extends a rough stretch for crypto, which has been sliding with tech stocks as the market reassesses the AI boom after Anthropic's huge IPO and the Nasdaq's sharp falls. For Bitcoin holders, the two-year low is a psychological marker: the coin has now given back a large part of its recent gains. Whether the dip is a buying opportunity or the start of a deeper correction will depend on whether US equities stabilise next week.

articles.title: Kyiv left without water after overnight Russian attack; water returning to the left bank
articles.description: Russian forces attacked Kyiv in the early hours of November 21, and the whole city was left without water as pressure in the network fell to critical levels on both banks of the Dnipro. A missile warhead also fell unexploded in a residential courtyard. By the evening, Kyiv's water utility said water had returned to the left bank, though the attack also caused fires, injuries and power cuts.
articles.body: Russian forces attacked Kyiv in the early hours of November 21, and the whole city was left without water as pressure in the supply network fell to critical levels on both banks of the Dnipro river. A missile warhead also fell unexploded in a residential courtyard, adding to the danger for emergency crews. The attack caused fires, injuries and power cuts across the capital, and it was a new consequence of the overnight barrage already reported this morning, in which Russia fired three ballistic missiles and 148 drones and Ukrainian air defences shot down 117. By the evening, Kyiv's water utility said water had returned to the left bank of the city, with restoration work continuing elsewhere. The strike on water infrastructure is part of a wider Russian campaign against Ukrainian energy and utilities heading into winter, after Odesa was left largely without electricity the same day. For Kyiv residents, the outage was a reminder that even a largely intercepted barrage can still knock out basic services for hours.

articles.title: Odesa blackout: whole city loses power, all electric transport halted
articles.description: Odesa was left largely without electricity on November 21 after Russian strikes on main power networks triggered automatic protection shutdowns, the Energy Ministry said. All trams and trolleybuses stopped running, and residents were asked not to leave powerful appliances plugged in. Emergency power cuts were also introduced in Dnipropetrovsk and parts of Odesa region, and Vinnytsia suffered widespread outages.
articles.body: Odesa was left largely without electricity on November 21 after Russian strikes on main power networks triggered automatic protection shutdowns, the Energy Ministry said. All trams and trolleybuses stopped running across the city, and residents were asked not to leave powerful appliances plugged in as engineers worked to restore supply. Emergency power cuts were also introduced in Dnipropetrovsk and parts of Odesa region, while Vinnytsia suffered widespread outages after an energy facility was damaged that morning. The blackout is part of the same wave of strikes that left Kyiv without water overnight, as Russia steps up attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure heading into winter. For Odesa, a port city of around a million people, the loss of electric transport brought much of daily life to a halt. Restoration timelines were not immediately clear, and the outages underline how vulnerable the grid remains even when air defences intercept most incoming missiles and drones.

articles.title: GTA VI review-bombed on Metacritic as culture-war backlash erupts
articles.description: After Metacritic's waiting window opened, GTA VI was hit by coordinated user review-bombing, with its user score settling around 5.6 despite a 99 critic score. Critics of the game's story attacked Lucia Caminos and spread fake videos purporting to show degraded gameplay, while some accounts were created solely to give GTA VI 0/10 and the Ocarina of Time remake 10/10.
articles.body: After Metacritic's waiting window opened, Grand Theft Auto VI was hit by coordinated user review-bombing, with its user score settling around 5.6 despite a 99 critic score — tying the highest-rated game ever. Critics of the game's story attacked the character Lucia Caminos and claimed Jason Duval is a 'cuckold', while fake videos purporting to show degraded gameplay circulated online, made with a low-violence setting enabled. Some accounts appear to have been created solely to give GTA VI 0/10 and the Ocarina of Time remake 10/10, in a console-war flare-up after GTA VI tied the original Ocarina of Time's record 99 Metacritic score. The episode is a familiar pattern for huge launches, where the user score becomes a battleground for culture-war arguments rather than a measure of the game itself. It sits in sharp contrast to the commercial picture: Take-Two confirmed the game grossed an estimated $3.79 billion on launch day, the biggest entertainment launch in history. For players, the critic consensus and the sales figures tell one story; the user score, for now, tells another.

articles.title: Trump orders federal contractors to coordinate with White House on congressional requests
articles.description: President Trump has ordered federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information about their work and to coordinate their responses with the administration. The move comes as Democrats prepare investigations into his administration next year, including the White House ballroom construction, Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool repairs, Kennedy Center renovations and Homeland Security contracts.
articles.body: President Trump has ordered federal contractors to notify the White House of any congressional requests for information about their work and to coordinate their responses with the administration. The move comes as Democrats prepare investigations into his administration next year, including the White House ballroom construction, Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool repairs, Kennedy Center renovations and Homeland Security contracts. The order effectively gives the White House a window into — and a say over — what contractors tell Congress, at a moment when Democratic oversight is about to intensify. Separately, a top Congressional Democrat warned on Friday that lawmakers will withhold funding for SpaceX systems unless the administration discloses who ordered the slowdown of Ukraine's military-grade Starlink service. The two developments together point to a widening fight over information: the administration tightening control of what contractors disclose, and Congress threatening the purse strings to force answers. Contractors caught in the middle will now have to navigate both the White House order and their obligations to Congress.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with AI's help
articles.description: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic's technical staff, claims he has proved the Riemann Hypothesis — one of mathematics' great unsolved problems — working with the company's AI tool Claude. He announced it Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website. The claim is unverified and will face scrutiny from the mathematics community.
articles.body: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician on Anthropic's technical staff, claims he has proved the Riemann Hypothesis, one of mathematics' great unsolved problems, working with the company's AI tool Claude. He announced the claim on Friday in a four-page explanation posted on his website, and the mathematics community will now scrutinise it before anyone accepts it as a proof. The Riemann Hypothesis, first posed in 1859, concerns the distribution of prime numbers and carries a $1 million Millennium Prize for a correct proof. If verified, it would be one of the biggest mathematical breakthroughs in history — and a landmark moment for AI-assisted research. The news comes days after Anthropic's blockbuster IPO: the company began trading on Nasdaq on November 19 at $83 a share, raising a record $81 billion at a $1.5 trillion valuation. That flotation has already shaken markets, with the Nasdaq wiping out its gains for the year as the AI sell-off deepened. For now, mathematicians are urging caution: extraordinary claims in this field have failed before, and peer review will take time.

articles.title: Warner Music Group tops $2B in a quarter for the first time
articles.description: Warner Music Group reported calendar Q3 2026 revenue of $2.001 billion — the first time it has crossed $2 billion in a single quarter, beating its previous record of $1.868 billion in Q3 2025. Subscription streaming revenue rose 14.7% year over year to $804 million, and full fiscal-year 2026 revenue hit a record $7.437 billion. Top sellers in the quarter included Madonna, Charli XCX, Bruno Mars and Linkin Park.
articles.body: Warner Music Group reported calendar Q3 2026 revenue of $2.001 billion on November 19, the first time the company has crossed $2 billion in a single quarter. The figure beats its previous quarterly record of $1.868 billion, set in Q3 2025. Subscription streaming revenue rose 14.7% year over year to $804 million, showing that the streaming engine behind the record quarter is still growing. For the full fiscal year 2026, revenue hit a record $7.437 billion, with net income nearly doubling to $735 million. Top sellers in the quarter included Madonna, Charli XCX, Bruno Mars and Linkin Park, a mix of catalogue power and current stars. The result underlines how the major labels are still scaling even as the industry argues over streaming economics, AI and the cost of artist discovery. Warner's quarter sets a high bar for Universal and Sony when they report, and it gives the company momentum heading into a year in which its CEO, Robert Kyncl, is set to deliver the CES 2027 keynote.

articles.title: 'Songs in the Key of Life' at 50: Stevie Wonder brings a miracle to Madison Square Garden
articles.description: Stevie Wonder celebrated the 50th anniversary of his landmark album 'Songs in the Key of Life' with a performance at Madison Square Garden, revisiting one of the most acclaimed records in pop history. The show marked a half-century since the 1976 double album that produced 'Sir Duke' and 'Isn't She Lovely.'
articles.body: Stevie Wonder celebrated the 50th anniversary of his landmark album 'Songs in the Key of Life' with a performance at Madison Square Garden, revisiting one of the most acclaimed records in pop history. The show marked a half-century since the 1976 double album, a sprawling two-LP work that produced 'Sir Duke' and 'Isn't She Lovely' and is regularly ranked among the greatest albums ever made. Wonder's return to the Garden for the occasion turned the anniversary into a live event rather than a reissue campaign, with the songs performed in full for an audience spanning generations. The album's fiftieth year has brought renewed attention to a record that defined mid-70s soul and influenced decades of pop, R&B and hip-hop. For Wonder, now 76, the night was both a celebration and a reminder of the record's staying power. Few albums from 1976 still fill arenas on their anniversary; this one did, with its creator on stage playing it.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo holds No. 1 for a fifth week on the Billboard 200
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo's 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love' holds No. 1 on the Billboard 200 (chart dated November 21) for a fifth nonconsecutive week with 62,000 equivalent album units. It ties 'SOUR' for her longest run at No. 1 and passes Drake's four weeks with 'ICEMAN' for the longest 2026 run by a 2026 release. Lil Baby's 'FRESH' debuted at No. 2 with 59,000 units — he out-streamed her but lost on sales.
articles.body: Olivia Rodrigo's 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love' holds No. 1 on the Billboard 200, for the chart dated November 21, for a fifth nonconsecutive week, earning 62,000 equivalent album units. The run ties 'SOUR' for her longest stay at No. 1 and passes Drake's four weeks with 'ICEMAN' for the longest 2026 run by a 2026 release. Lil Baby's 'FRESH' debuted at No. 2 with 59,000 units in a close race: he out-streamed Rodrigo, with 56.81 million streams against her 54.48 million, but lost on sales, moving 4,000 copies to her 11,000. Morgan Wallen's 'I'm the Problem' sits at No. 3 with 50,000 units. The result caps a strong year for Rodrigo, whose album has now spent more than a month in total at the summit across separate spells. It also shows how tight the modern chart race has become, with streaming and pure sales pulling in opposite directions at the top.

articles.title: German intelligence is questioning some Russians after passport control at airports
articles.description: Since at least early September 2026, German intelligence officers have been asking some Russians to take part in interviews after they clear passport control at German airports. Meduza reports on who is conducting the interviews and why, as European states step up scrutiny of Russian travellers. The practice adds to a wider pattern of restrictions, including Denmark's new visa curbs announced this week.
articles.body: Since at least early September 2026, German intelligence officers have been asking some Russians to take part in interviews after they clear passport control at German airports, Meduza reports. The interviews are conducted by intelligence officers rather than border police, and Meduza's reporting looks at who is carrying them out and what they are trying to learn. The practice adds to a wider pattern of European states stepping up scrutiny of Russian travellers, including Denmark's decision this week to expel Russia's military attaché and stop issuing non-essential visas to Russian citizens. For Russians travelling to Europe, the airport interview is now another layer of friction on top of visa restrictions that have tightened steadily since the full-scale invasion. It also raises questions about how intelligence services balance security screening with the rights of ordinary travellers. Germany has not publicly detailed the programme, and it is unclear how many people have been approached or what happens to those who decline.

articles.title: Moscow court fines Meduza 250,000 rubles over a book announcement about Babyn Yar
articles.description: A Moscow court fined Meduza 250,000 rubles for 'abuse of media freedom' over a May 25 Telegram post announcing 'An Inconvenient Place,' the first translated book from Meduza's publishing house, by Jonathan Littell and photographer Antoine d'Agata. The ruling, handed down November 18 and reported November 21, held that the post spread a 'fake' about Russian war crimes in Bucha that supposedly threatened public order.
articles.body: A Moscow court fined Meduza 250,000 rubles for 'abuse of media freedom' over a May 25 Telegram post in its Meduza–Books channel announcing 'An Inconvenient Place,' the first translated book from Meduza's publishing house. The book is by Jonathan Littell and photographer Antoine d'Agata, and the announcement concerned Babyn Yar, the site of the 1941 massacre of Kyiv's Jews. The ruling, handed down on November 18 by magistrate Alexandra Mikhaleva and reported on November 21, held that the post spread a 'fake' about Russian war crimes in Bucha that supposedly threatened public order. The fine is the latest in a long series of Russian court actions against Meduza, which the Russian authorities designated a 'foreign agent' and later an 'undesirable organisation.' For the outlet, the case is another example of how Russian courts use the 'fake news' laws to punish any mention of war crimes. The sum is modest, but the message is the point: even a book announcement can draw a fine if it touches the official version of the war.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: NATO membership is the clearest security guarantee for Ukraine
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on November 21 that NATO membership remains the clearest security guarantee for Ukraine, and that the issue is on the agenda in talks with allies and the US, including at the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin. He cautioned it is too early to judge membership prospects, since they depend on when and how the war ends, and said no Article 5-style guarantee has yet been formally offered to Ukraine on paper.
articles.body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on November 21 that NATO membership remains the clearest security guarantee for Ukraine, and that the issue is on the agenda in talks with allies and the United States, including at the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin. He cautioned that it is too early to judge membership prospects, since they depend on when and how the war ends, and said no Article 5-style guarantee has yet been formally offered to Ukraine on paper. He argued that membership would also be cheaper for all allies than Ukraine maintaining a million-strong army alone — a pitch aimed at governments worried about the long-term cost of supporting Kyiv. The comments come as Trump pushes for a peace deal by early January and as Putin rules out even a limited ceasefire, leaving the question of guarantees central to any settlement. For Zelenskyy, NATO membership has been the consistent ask since the invasion began, and he is using the Berlin meetings to keep it on the table. Whether allies will move from discussion to a formal offer remains the open question.

articles.title: Zelenskyy open to a three-way meeting with US and Russian leaders at the G20
articles.description: Zelenskyy said on November 21 that Ukraine would attend the G20 summit if invited by the United States, and that he would consider a three-way meeting with the US and Russian leaders on its sidelines. The statement follows the November 19 Trump–Putin–Xi meeting in Shenzhen and comes as Trump pushes for a Ukraine peace deal by early January. No invitation has been confirmed.
articles.body: Zelenskyy said on November 21 that Ukraine would attend the G20 summit if invited by the United States, and that he would consider a three-way meeting with the US and Russian leaders on its sidelines. The statement follows the November 19 Trump–Putin–Xi meeting in Shenzhen, the first in-person meeting of the three leaders, and comes as Trump pushes for a Ukraine peace deal by early January. No invitation has been confirmed, and Putin has meanwhile ruled out even a limited ceasefire after Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge, which makes any meeting far from certain. Still, Zelenskyy's openness to the format is notable: it would put him in the same room as Putin for the first time in years, with Trump as broker. The G20 would give the encounter a neutral stage and a global audience. For now it is a conditional offer, not a scheduled event — but it signals that Kyiv is willing to talk if the opportunity arises.

articles.title: EU budget proposal keeps up to €100 billion for Ukraine
articles.description: European Council President António Costa presented a proposed EU budget for 2028–2034 on November 21, totalling about €1.78 trillion, while preserving up to €100 billion for Ukraine through a dedicated Ukraine Reserve instrument. EU leaders will discuss the proposal at a European Council meeting on November 26–27, alongside a Commission proposal for a further €45 billion loan to Ukraine in 2027. European Parliament budget rapporteurs have already rejected Costa's draft.
articles.body: European Council President António Costa presented a proposed EU budget for 2028–2034 on November 21, totalling about €1.78 trillion — roughly €204 billion, or 10%, less than the European Commission's initial plan — while preserving up to €100 billion for Ukraine through a dedicated Ukraine Reserve instrument, worth €88.869 billion in 2025 constant prices. EU leaders will discuss the proposal at a European Council meeting on November 26–27, alongside a Commission proposal for a further €45 billion loan to Ukraine in 2027. European Parliament budget rapporteurs have already rejected Costa's draft as taking the EU backwards, setting up a fight between the Council and Parliament over the shape of the budget. For Ukraine, the preserved €100 billion is the key number: it would lock in long-term support through 2034, beyond the current emergency funding. The figure comes a day after the European Commission transferred €7.9 billion to Ukraine, the largest single Ukraine Facility tranche yet. Together, the transfer and the budget proposal show Brussels trying to put Ukraine funding on a durable footing even as the overall budget shrinks.

articles.title: Ukraine strikes Russian depot, command posts and a bridge near Luhansk
articles.description: Ukraine's Defence Forces struck Russian military targets on November 20 and overnight into November 21, hitting an ammunition depot, command posts and a bridge near Luhansk, according to Pravda's reporting of the General Staff. The strikes are part of Ukraine's campaign against Russian logistics. Separately, the SBU's Alpha special-operations centre said its operators neutralised 4,333 Russian troops in one week — a new record.
articles.body: Ukraine's Defence Forces struck Russian military targets on November 20 and overnight into November 21, hitting an ammunition depot, command posts and a bridge near Luhansk, according to Pravda's reporting of the General Staff. The strikes are part of Ukraine's campaign against Russian logistics, which also included hits on a depot in Crimea noted in the day's news roundups. The bridge strike near Luhansk targets a supply route, while the depot and command-post hits aim at the Russian army's ability to sustain operations in the east. Separately, the SBU's Alpha special-operations centre said its operators neutralised 4,333 Russian troops in one week — a new record for the unit. The figures, as with all battlefield claims, come from Ukrainian sources and cannot be independently verified. But the pattern is consistent: Ukraine is pressing its deep-strike campaign against Russian rear areas even as Russia pounds Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.

articles.title: Russian drone hits a five-storey home in Solonitsivka, Kharkiv region: 11 injured; Pechenihy dam road closed
articles.description: A Russian attack drone hit a five-storey residential building in Solonitsivka, Kharkiv region, injuring 11 people and starting a fire across about 250 sq m, damaging flats on the 4th and 5th floors. Separately, a Russian missile strike around 1 AM damaged the Pechenihy dam road, closing it to traffic with a detour via nearby villages.
articles.body: A Russian attack drone hit a five-storey residential building in Solonitsivka, Kharkiv region, injuring 11 people and starting a fire across about 250 square metres, damaging flats on the 4th and 5th floors. Emergency crews worked through the night to extinguish the blaze and help residents from the damaged building. Separately, a Russian missile strike around 1 AM damaged the Pechenihy dam road, on highway T-21-11 between Chuhuiv, Pechenihy and Velykyi Burluk, closing it to traffic. Drivers are being diverted via Chuhuiv, Korobochkyne, Lebyazhe, Bazaliivka and Prymorske. Both incidents are from the overnight attacks of November 20–21, the same barrage that left Kyiv without water and knocked out power in Odesa. The Solonitsivka strike is a reminder that the nightly drone campaign hits civilian housing across the country, not only the big cities, and that the damage extends to roads and dams as well as homes.

articles.title: UPDATE: Disney developing Home Alone sequel with Macaulay Culkin returning as Kevin — Rogen and Goldberg to produce
articles.description: Disney has put a direct sequel to Home Alone 2 into development, with Macaulay Culkin reprising Kevin McCallister, in new details on the sequel reported this morning. Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg will produce and co-write the script with Culkin. The premise comes from Culkin himself: an adult Kevin, now a widowed or divorced father too busy for his son, gets locked out of his own house while his son sets traps for him.
articles.body: Disney has put a direct sequel to Home Alone 2 into development, with Macaulay Culkin reprising Kevin McCallister, in new details on the sequel reported this morning. Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg will produce and co-write the script with Culkin, giving the project a comedy pedigree that fits the original films. The premise comes from Culkin himself: an adult Kevin, now a widowed or divorced father too busy for his son, gets locked out of his own house while his son sets traps for him — the house as a metaphor for their relationship. The film is in early development with no director or release date yet, so it is a long way from cinemas. Culkin also just appeared as adult Kevin in a McDonald's Christmas ad, which helped reignite interest in the character. For a franchise that has lived on through the original two films every Christmas, a proper Culkin-led sequel is the version fans have wanted for decades — and now it is actually in development.

articles.title: Hellraiser: Revival wins top prize at The Horror Game Awards 2026
articles.description: Hellraiser: Revival was named the best horror game of 2026 at The Horror Game Awards, beating Resident Evil Requiem despite receiving no nominations at The Game Awards 2026. The Clive Barker-inspired horror game took the ceremony's main award, a notable upset over Capcom's flagship Resident Evil entry.
articles.body: Hellraiser: Revival was named the best horror game of 2026 at The Horror Game Awards, beating Resident Evil Requiem despite receiving no nominations at The Game Awards 2026. The Clive Barker-inspired horror game took the ceremony's main award, a notable upset over Capcom's flagship Resident Evil entry, which had been the favourite. The Horror Game Awards, which streamed with more than 20 new trailers, have become a separate stage for the genre, and this year's result shows the jury was willing to back a licensed horror title over the biggest name in the field. For the developers of Hellraiser: Revival, the win is a major profile boost going into the holiday season. For Capcom, it is a rare loss for Resident Evil, though Requiem remains one of the year's biggest releases. The split between the two awards ceremonies — snubbed at one, champion at the other — underlines how differently the same game can land with different juries.

articles.title: Microsoft slashes Gears of War: E-Day price by 30% for Thanksgiving
articles.description: Microsoft has temporarily cut the price of Gears of War: E-Day by 30% in a Thanksgiving promotion running until December 2, on PC and Xbox Series X|S. The discount comes shortly after the game's global launch and applies across both platforms.
articles.body: Microsoft has temporarily cut the price of Gears of War: E-Day by 30% in a Thanksgiving promotion running until December 2, on PC and Xbox Series X|S. The discount comes shortly after the game's global launch, a quick price move for a major first-party release. The promotion applies across both platforms, giving Xbox and PC players the same deal through the holiday weekend. A 30% cut this soon after launch is unusual for a flagship title and suggests Microsoft is pushing hard for a big Thanksgiving player count. For players who held off at launch, the window is short: the price goes back up on December 2. The game is one of Xbox's biggest releases of the year, and the discount puts it in front of shoppers during the busiest sales week of the season.

articles.title: Konami files trademarks for classic series Silent Scope and Thrill Drive
articles.description: Konami has filed EUIPO trademark applications for its classic arcade series Silent Scope and Thrill Drive. Both series already hold trademarks in some categories, and the new filings extend protection — a routine step that often precedes revivals, though no new games have been announced.
articles.body: Konami has filed EUIPO trademark applications for its classic arcade series Silent Scope and Thrill Drive, the sniper and driving games that were staples of late-90s and early-2000s arcades. Both series already hold trademarks in some categories, and the new filings extend protection — a routine step that often precedes revivals, though no new games have been announced. Trademark filings are a familiar early signal in the games industry: companies secure the names well before revealing anything, and many filings never lead to a game. But Konami has been mining its back catalogue in recent years, with Silent Hill and Metal Gear revivals showing the company is willing to bring old series back. For arcade nostalgists, the filings are a reason to hope; for everyone else, they are a reminder that a trademark is a legal form, not a release date. Nothing has been announced, and Konami has not commented.

articles.title: UPDATE: Russian 'triple-tap' strike kills 7-year-old boy and paramedic in Zelenskyy's home city
articles.description: A Russian 'triple-tap' strike on Kryvyi Rih on Friday night killed a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic, local authorities said, in new detail on the strike reported this morning. The attack came after a busy diplomatic week: Trump met Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday, calling Putin a 'friend,' while Zelenskyy told CNN 'for us, he is a killer.' A 'Coalition of the Willing' meeting followed in Berlin, attended by European leaders and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
articles.body: A Russian 'triple-tap' strike on Kryvyi Rih on Friday night killed a seven-year-old boy and a 20-year-old paramedic, local authorities said, in new detail on the strike reported this morning. A triple-tap strike is designed to hit the same target repeatedly, catching rescue workers arriving after the first impact — the young paramedic was among those killed. The attack came after a busy diplomatic week: Trump met Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Thursday, calling Putin a 'friend,' while Zelenskyy told CNN 'for us, he is a killer.' A 'Coalition of the Willing' meeting followed in Berlin, attended by European leaders and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The contrast between the diplomacy and the strike could hardly be sharper: while leaders talked about a peace deal by early January, Kryvyi Rih — Zelenskyy's home city — was burying a child and a first responder. The toll from the strike has risen since the morning, with 58 people injured, and the city has also lost water in three districts.

articles.title: UPDATE: Judge pauses Army's Iowa detonation plan; blast moved to Monday amid lead-dust fears
articles.description: A federal judge ordered the US Army to pause its plan to detonate five tons of lead azide — nearly 70 drums of the bomb-making compound — at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, after environmental groups sued over toxic lead dust risks. The detonation, originally set for Friday morning, has been rescheduled to Monday, the latest possible moment before a forecast temperature drop that could further destabilise the material.
articles.body: A federal judge ordered the US Army to pause its plan to detonate five tons of lead azide — nearly 70 drums of the bomb-making compound — at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, after environmental groups sued over toxic lead dust risks. The detonation, originally set for Friday morning, has been rescheduled to Monday, the latest possible moment before a forecast temperature drop that could further destabilise the material. Forecast winds of 5–10 mph blowing north to south could carry lead particles, and residents in southeastern Iowa are awaiting a final decision. The case, first reported this week, turns on a stark trade-off: the material is dangerous to store and dangerous to destroy. Lead azide is a primary explosive used in detonators, and the stockpile has to go — but burning or detonating it risks scattering lead dust over farmland and homes. The judge's pause gives both sides the weekend, but the Monday deadline means the decision cannot be put off for long.

articles.title: UPDATE: Bukele's Haiti mission: police kill 34 gang members in major Port-au-Prince operation
articles.description: Thousands of Salvadoran troops landed in Haiti last month to fight gangs overrunning the country, and Haitian police announced Thursday they killed 34 gang members in a major operation in the Martissant neighbourhood of Port-au-Prince. A secretive task force involving a private military contractor led by Erik Prince and the multinational Gang Suppression Force are also active. It is too early to judge whether President Nayib Bukele's promised 'triumph' is being delivered.
articles.body: Thousands of Salvadoran troops landed in Haiti last month to fight the gangs overrunning the country, and Haitian police announced on Thursday they killed 34 gang members in a major operation in the Martissant neighbourhood of Port-au-Prince. A secretive task force involving a private military contractor led by Erik Prince and the multinational Gang Suppression Force are also active in the country. Bukele's personal involvement has stirred rare hope on the island and keen interest across Latin America, where his crackdown on gangs in El Salvador made him a regional figure. The operation in Martissant is the first big reported success of the mission, but it is too early to judge whether Bukele's promised 'triumph' is being delivered. Haiti's gangs still control large parts of the capital, and one operation — even a large one — does not change that overnight. The question now is whether the Salvadoran deployment can sustain the pressure, and what happens when the gangs hit back.

articles.title: CNN travel roundup: the B&B key that broke, Hittite tablets, and the world's coolest streets
articles.description: In CNN's weekly travel roundup, American sisters Jan and Jill Shropshire recall a 1997 trip to the English Midlands when a key broke in the lock of their B&B. Archaeologists in central Turkey unearthed cuneiform clay tablets at Šamuḫa offering a glimpse of everyday Hittite life 3,500 years ago. The roundup also names this year's coolest streets, including Song Wat Road in Bangkok and Boulevard Saint-Laurent in Montreal.
articles.body: In CNN's weekly travel roundup, American sisters Jan and Jill Shropshire recall a 1997 trip to the English Midlands when a key broke in the lock of their B&B, leaving them stuck outside in a story that has become a small classic of travel mishaps. Archaeologists in central Turkey unearthed cuneiform clay tablets at Šamuḫa, offering a glimpse of everyday Hittite life 3,500 years ago — shopping lists and records rather than royal decrees. The roundup also names this year's coolest streets, including Song Wat Road in Bangkok and Boulevard Saint-Laurent in Montreal, and introduces the new CNN Postcards feature of short travel stories. It is a lighter end to a heavy news week: ancient tablets, a broken key, and a ranking of streets worth wandering. For readers planning trips, the street list is the practical takeaway; for everyone else, the Hittite tablets are the reminder that ordinary life leaves traces worth digging up.

articles.title: UMG and Sony withdraw DistroKid subpoena motion in Suno case after distributor hands over AI-detection documents
articles.description: Universal Music Group and Sony Music have withdrawn their motion to subpoena DistroKid in their lawsuit against AI music generator Suno, after the distributor produced documents on its AI-detection practices. The labels had sought data on how many DistroKid tracks were flagged as AI-generated, how many were attributed to Suno, and what they earned — a key battleground in the majors' AI copyright fight.
articles.body: Universal Music Group and Sony Music have withdrawn their motion to subpoena DistroKid in their lawsuit against AI music generator Suno, after the distributor produced documents on its AI-detection practices. The labels had sought data on how many DistroKid tracks were flagged as AI-generated, how many were attributed to Suno, and what they earned — a key battleground in the majors' AI copyright fight. The withdrawal is a procedural step, not a settlement: the underlying lawsuit against Suno continues, and the documents may still shape it. But it shows the labels got what they needed without forcing a court fight with a distributor that sits between independent artists and the streaming services. DistroKid is one of the biggest DIY distributors, so its detection data is a window into how much AI-generated music is flowing onto platforms. For the industry, the case is a test of whether AI companies can train on copyrighted music and generate soundalikes without permission — and the DistroKid documents are part of the evidence.

articles.title: Live Nation's Michael Rapino on AI strategy and subscription ambitions for 14m-member All Access program
articles.description: Live Nation CEO Michael Rapino used the company's 2026 investor presentation — five days after reporting Q3 revenue of $10.1 billion, up 19% year over year — to outline its AI strategy and subscription ambitions for its 14-million-member All Access program. Separately, live-experiences platform Speakeasy, backed by Yamaha's music fund, raised an $18.8 million Series A, bringing its total funding to about $27 million.
articles.body: Live Nation CEO Michael Rapino used the company's 2026 investor presentation — five days after reporting Q3 revenue of $10.1 billion, up 19% year over year — to outline its AI strategy and subscription ambitions for its 14-million-member All Access program. The presentation shows Live Nation thinking beyond ticket sales: a subscription layer for its most engaged fans, powered by AI tools for pricing, marketing and personalisation. The 14-million-member figure gives the programme real scale, and Rapino's emphasis on it suggests subscriptions could become a second revenue engine alongside concerts. Separately, live-experiences platform Speakeasy, backed by Yamaha's music fund, raised an $18.8 million Series A, bringing its total funding to about $27 million. The two stories together point to a live industry that is professionalising fast: the biggest promoter in the world building a membership business, and startups raising serious money to sell experiences around the show.

articles.title: Sonilo, an $11M-backed AI startup founded by TikTok veterans, licenses opted-in indie recordings from Symphonic
articles.description: Sonilo, an AI startup founded by TikTok veterans and backed with $11 million, has licensed opted-in indie recordings from Symphonic to train its model. The deal is a contrast to the AI companies being sued by the majors: Sonilo is paying for licensed, consented training data instead of scraping copyrighted music. It is the latest sign that a licensed path for AI music training is taking shape.
articles.body: Sonilo, an AI startup founded by TikTok veterans and backed with $11 million, has licensed opted-in indie recordings from Symphonic to train its model. The deal is a deliberate contrast to the AI companies being sued by the majors: Sonilo is paying for licensed, consented training data instead of scraping copyrighted music. The recordings come from Symphonic's independent catalogue, with artists opting in rather than being swept up by default. It is the latest sign that a licensed path for AI music training is taking shape, alongside the lawsuits against Suno and others. For independent artists, the model offers a way to earn from AI training rather than simply having their work used. For the industry, the question is whether licensed training becomes the norm — and what the price of a licence should be.

articles.title: Universal Music Canada strikes A&R and distribution partnership with First Class Music Group
articles.description: Universal Music Canada has struck an A&R and distribution partnership with First Class Music Group, the latest in a series of deals tying the major to independent music companies. The partnership gives First Class artists access to Universal's distribution and resources while keeping the indie label's A&R independence. It follows a week of senior appointments across Universal's Latin American operations.
articles.body: Universal Music Canada has struck an A&R and distribution partnership with First Class Music Group, the latest in a series of deals tying the major label to independent music companies. The partnership gives First Class artists access to Universal's distribution and resources while keeping the indie label's A&R independence. It follows a week of senior appointments across Universal's Latin American operations, including Felipe Holguin's appointment as CEO of Universal Music Latin America and Iberian Peninsula. For Universal, the deal is a way to tap into Canada's independent scene without buying it outright. For First Class, it is a route to scale: major-label distribution and marketing muscle behind an indie roster. The pattern — majors partnering rather than acquiring — has become a defining feature of the modern label business.

articles.title: Ignacio Meyer named President of Universal Music Latin America & Iberian Peninsula
articles.description: Ignacio Meyer has been named President of Universal Music Latin America and Iberian Peninsula, reporting to Felipe Holguin, whose appointment as CEO of the division was reported this morning. The appointment fills out the senior team for one of Universal's biggest regional operations, covering Latin music's home markets and the Iberian Peninsula.
articles.body: Ignacio Meyer has been named President of Universal Music Latin America and Iberian Peninsula, reporting to Felipe Holguin, whose appointment as CEO of the division was reported this morning. The appointment fills out the senior team for one of Universal's biggest regional operations, covering Latin music's home markets and the Iberian Peninsula. Latin music remains one of the fastest-growing parts of the global industry, and the region's leadership matters well beyond its own borders. Meyer takes the role as Universal reorganises its Latin operations under Holguin, with the two appointments landing in the same week. For artists and managers in the region, the new team will shape signings, marketing and partnerships for years. The speed of the appointments suggests Universal wants the leadership in place before the new year.

articles.title: WMG CEO Robert Kyncl to deliver CES 2027 keynote, billed as the first by a music-industry leader
articles.description: Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl will deliver the CES 2027 keynote, billed as the first keynote at the tech show by a music-industry leader. The invitation underlines how central music has become to the tech conversation — and it comes in the same week Warner reported its first $2 billion quarter.
articles.body: Warner Music Group CEO Robert Kyncl will deliver the CES 2027 keynote, billed as the first keynote at the tech show by a music-industry leader. The invitation underlines how central music has become to the tech conversation, from streaming and AI to the hardware that plays it all. It comes in the same week Warner reported its first $2 billion quarter, with subscription streaming up 14.7%, so Kyncl will take the stage with strong numbers behind him. For the music industry, a CES keynote is a symbolic moment: the tech world's biggest stage recognising a music executive as a voice on where technology goes next. What he says about AI, artist pay and the streaming economy will be watched closely. The keynote also sets up a year in which music's relationship with big tech — already defined by licensing fights and AI lawsuits — stays at the centre of the agenda.

articles.title: Don Toliver announces sixth album 'Nitrous'
articles.description: Don Toliver has announced his sixth album, 'Nitrous,' adding to a busy week for the Houston rapper, who also appears on Future's surprise single 'Ya Hit' and on the GTA VI festival bill in Miami. The announcement keeps Toliver's prolific run going as he balances solo releases with high-profile collaborations.
articles.body: Don Toliver has announced his sixth album, 'Nitrous,' adding to a busy week for the Houston rapper. He also appears on Future's surprise single 'Ya Hit' alongside Drake and Travis Scott, and he is on the bill for the GTA VI festival in Miami tonight, where he performs as part of the Cactus Jack set. The announcement keeps Toliver's prolific run going as he balances solo releases with high-profile collaborations across hip-hop's biggest names. Six albums in, he has become one of the genre's most reliable hitmakers, moving between his own melodic trap records and guest spots that anchor other artists' singles. No release date or tracklist has been detailed yet, but the announcement alone puts the album on the radar for the coming months. For Toliver, the timing is good: he is everywhere this week, and 'Nitrous' gives that visibility a destination.

articles.title: Noah Kahan addresses his Grammy snub
articles.description: Noah Kahan has addressed his Grammy snub, speaking out after being left out of the nominations. The folk-pop star, whose breakout made him one of the defining voices of the last few years, took the omission in his stride in comments that mix grace with a pointed reminder of what his music has meant to fans.
articles.body: Noah Kahan has addressed his Grammy snub, speaking out after being left out of the nominations. The folk-pop star, whose breakout made him one of the defining voices of the last few years, took the omission in his stride, in comments that mix grace with a pointed reminder of what his music has meant to fans. Grammy snubs are a rite of passage for artists of Kahan's stature, and his response will be read as a measure of the man as much as of the moment. He has built his career on direct connection with listeners, from small rooms to stadiums, and the snub does little to change that trajectory. For the Recording Academy, the omission is another data point in the perennial argument about who gets recognised and who does not. For Kahan, the next album — not the next nomination — is the answer that matters.

articles.title: Blink-182 and Pierce the Veil lead the When We Were Young 2027 lineup
articles.description: Blink-182 and Pierce the Veil lead the When We Were Young 2027 lineup, the Las Vegas festival that has become the home of pop-punk and emo nostalgia. The announcement gives fans a year to plan for a bill built around the bands that defined the genre's 2000s peak.
articles.body: Blink-182 and Pierce the Veil lead the When We Were Young 2027 lineup, the Las Vegas festival that has become the home of pop-punk and emo nostalgia. The announcement gives fans a year to plan for a bill built around the bands that defined the genre's 2000s peak, with Blink-182 headlining a festival that feels made for them. When We Were Young has grown from a one-off nostalgia bill into a fixture of the festival calendar, selling out on the strength of lineups that read like a mid-2000s playlist. The 2027 edition continues that formula, pairing the headliners with a supporting cast drawn from the same era. For fans who grew up on these bands, the festival is less a concert than a reunion — with themselves at 17. Tickets will be the next test: previous editions have sold fast, and this lineup is likely to do the same.

articles.title: Rod Wave indicted for allegedly carrying oxycodone and a gun while speeding
articles.description: Rod Wave has been indicted for allegedly carrying oxycodone and a gun while speeding, the latest legal trouble for the Florida rapper. The indictment adds to a run of headlines around the artist, whose confessional style has made him one of hip-hop's most popular voices.
articles.body: Rod Wave has been indicted for allegedly carrying oxycodone and a gun while speeding, the latest legal trouble for the Florida rapper. The indictment follows a traffic stop in which police are said to have found the drugs and the firearm, and it now moves the case into the courts. Rod Wave's confessional style has made him one of hip-hop's most popular voices, with a fanbase that has stuck with him through previous legal issues. The new charges will test that loyalty, and they raise questions about how the case affects his touring and recording schedule. For now, the details are limited to the indictment itself, and the rapper has not yet entered a plea in public reporting. As with any criminal case, the allegations are unproven until tested in court.

articles.title: P1Harmony earn first Billboard No. 1 as 'BLOW UP' tops the Top Album Sales chart
articles.description: South Korean group P1Harmony earned the first Billboard No. 1 of their career as mini album 'BLOW UP' debuted atop the Top Album Sales chart dated November 21, selling about 43,000 copies in the US in the tracking week ending November 12. The sales were driven by a collector-focused release with 25 CD versions and five vinyl editions. The album also entered the Billboard 200 at No. 4, matching the group's best-ever rank.
articles.body: South Korean group P1Harmony earned the first Billboard No. 1 of their career as mini album 'BLOW UP' debuted atop the Top Album Sales chart dated November 21, selling about 43,000 copies in the US in the tracking week ending November 12. The sales were driven by a collector-focused release with 25 CD versions and five vinyl editions, packed with photocards and posters that K-pop fans collect. The album also entered the Billboard 200 at No. 4, matching the group's best-ever rank, which shows the release worked as a streaming title as well as a physical one. For P1Harmony, the No. 1 is a career milestone: a first chart-topper after years of steady building. It also underlines how K-pop's physical-first economics still deliver chart results in the US, where a well-designed collector edition can move tens of thousands of copies in a week. The group's next step is to turn a sales-chart No. 1 into a lasting Billboard 200 presence.

articles.title: Hot 100: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' stays No. 1; Stella Lefty's 'Boston' climbs to No. 2
articles.description: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' holds No. 1 on the Hot 100 for the chart week ending November 21 — its 56th week on the chart. Stella Lefty's 'Boston' climbs 5–2, Tame Impala and JENNIE's 'Dracula' holds at No. 3, Tate McRae's 'Housewife' is No. 4, and Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' jumps 10–5. Christmas songs are surging back: Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' re-enters at No. 18.
articles.body: Ella Langley's 'Choosin' Texas' holds No. 1 on the Hot 100 for the chart week ending November 21 — its 56th week on the chart, a remarkable run for a country song that has refused to leave the summit. Stella Lefty's 'Boston' climbs 5–2, Tame Impala and JENNIE's 'Dracula' holds at No. 3, Tate McRae's 'Housewife' is No. 4, and Olivia Rodrigo's 'Stupid Song' jumps 10–5. Christmas songs are surging back as the season turns: Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' re-enters at No. 18 and Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' jumps to No. 4 on Streaming Songs. The chart tells two stories at once: Langley's year-long dominance at the top, and the annual Christmas takeover gathering pace underneath it. For Langley, the 56-week run is already historic; for everyone else, the race now is for the Christmas No. 1.

articles.title: GTA 6: The Festival takes over Miami tonight — Travis Scott, Cardi B, Justice, all ticket proceeds to charity
articles.description: Rockstar Games and PlayStation stage Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival tonight, November 21, at Mana Wynwood in Miami, two days after the game's record-breaking launch.
