articles.description: BTS won Artist of the Year at the 2026 MAMA Awards in Osaka on November 20 — their eighth win in the category, extending a record that already included seven straight wins from 2016 to 2022. The group also took Best Male Group, while ENHYPEN won Fans' Choice of the Year for a second consecutive year. The win comes during BTS's full-group return with the album ARIRANG after military service.
articles.body: BTS won Artist of the Year on the opening night of the 2026 MAMA Awards at the Kyocera Dome Osaka on November 20, their eighth victory in the category and one of the ceremony's four grand prizes, or Daesangs. The group previously won the award for seven consecutive years from 2016 to 2022, and the latest win comes during their full-group return with the album ARIRANG, their first as a complete unit after military service. BTS also won Best Male Group and a place in the Fans' Choice Male Top 10, while ENHYPEN took the other grand prize of the night, Fans' Choice of the Year, for the second year running, plus Favorite M Countdown Stage. IVE won Best Female Group, TXT's Yeonjun won Best Male Artist and Soyeon won Best Female Artist. The ceremony, hosted by actor Park Bo-gum for the eighth time under the theme 'Music Interstellar', continues on November 21 with its second chapter covering song, performance and genre categories. BTS were not in attendance because of their ongoing world tour, and their album ARIRANG later added Album of the Year on night two. Rookie group CORTIS won Song of the Year for 'REDRED'.

articles.title: Lil Baby's FRESH tops the R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart as 'Dead Fresh' completes a 17-week climb to No. 1
articles.description: Lil Baby's FRESH debuts at No. 1 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart dated November 21, with 59,000 equivalent album units, and also tops the Top Streaming Albums and Top Rap Albums charts. Its single 'Dead Fresh' rises to No. 1 on Hot Rap Songs after a 17-week climb — one of the longest waits to the top this decade. The album debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200, just 3,000 units behind Olivia Rodrigo.
articles.body: Lil Baby's FRESH opens at No. 1 on Billboard's Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart dated November 21, earning 59,000 equivalent album units in the United States in the November 6–12 tracking week, according to Luminate. The 17-track album, released November 6 through Quality Control, Motown and Interscope Capitol, also opens at No. 1 on Top Rap Albums — his sixth leader there — and at No. 1 on Top Streaming Albums, while debuting at No. 2 on the all-genre Billboard 200. It is his fifth No. 1 on the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, following My Turn, The Voice of the Heroes with Lil Durk, It's Only Me and WHAM. The album's de facto title track, 'Dead Fresh', produced by Pharrell Williams and released as the lead single in July, rises to No. 1 on Hot Rap Songs, capping a 17-week journey — one of the four longest waits to No. 1 of the 2020s. The song debuted at No. 2 on the chart dated August 1 and held that spot for 14 non-consecutive weeks behind Drake's 'Janice STFU' before breaking through. Lil Baby places 17 tracks on Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs this week, pushing his career total to 40 top 10s on that chart.

articles.title: Drake's 'Take Care' climbs to No. 14 on the Billboard 200 in its 715th week
articles.description: Drake's Take Care climbed from No. 20 to No. 14 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, in its 715th week on the chart. The album, released in November 2011, turned 15 just after the tracking week ended. Drake now holds three albums between No. 13 and No. 16, with ICEMAN at No. 13 and HABIBTI at No. 16.
articles.body: Drake's Take Care jumped from No. 20 to No. 14 on the Billboard 200 for the chart week dated November 21, 2026, in its 715th week on the ranking. The album, released on November 15, 2011, turned 15 just three days after the tracking week ended on November 12. Two other Drake albums sit close by: ICEMAN rose from No. 15 to No. 13, one spot above Take Care, while HABIBTI slid from No. 14 to No. 16, giving Drake three albums between No. 13 and No. 16 at once. ICEMAN started at No. 1 on the May 30, 2026 chart and held the top spot for four weeks, while HABIBTI opened at No. 2 on the same chart, and both are in their 26th week. Billboard's chart listing gives no unit count for Take Care and offers no reason for the climb. The 15-year-old album's return to the top 15 is a reminder of Drake's catalogue power: a record released a decade and a half ago is charting alongside his two 2026 albums.

articles.title: Steve Aoki scores his first Billboard Dance Airplay No. 1 with 'Gravity'
articles.description: Steve Aoki has earned his first Billboard Dance Airplay No. 1 with 'Gravity', his collaboration with Ely Oaks and SACHA, topping the chart dated November 21, 2026. The track rose on a 20% jump in US dance radio airplay. It is also Ely Oaks' first No. 1 on the chart and SACHA's second this year.
articles.body: Grammy-nominated DJ and producer Steve Aoki has secured his first Billboard Dance Airplay No. 1 with 'Gravity', his collaboration with Ely Oaks and SACHA. Released in July through Dim Mak Records, the track climbed to the top of the chart dated November 21, 2026, following a 20% increase in US dance radio airplay during the November 6–12 tracking period. The collaboration also represents Ely Oaks' first No. 1 on the ranking, while SACHA celebrates her second, following 'Set Me Free' with Armin van Buuren earlier this year. The success follows another major chart accomplishment in August 2026, when 'YAPAQUE', his collaboration with Farruko and Greeicy, topped both the Billboard Latin Airplay and Latin Rhythm Airplay charts. For Aoki, one of electronic music's most durable touring acts, the Dance Airplay No. 1 fills a notable gap in a long chart career. It also underlines how dance radio remains a meaningful route for electronic records even as streaming dominates the genre's discovery.

articles.title: Vans Warped Tour sets its 2027 return: four cities, with presales opening November 20
articles.description: Vans Warped Tour will return in 2027 with four two-day festivals: Washington, D.C. on June 19–20, Long Beach on July 24–25, Mexico City on September 11–12 and Orlando on November 13–14. All four cities hosted the festival in 2026; Montreal drops off the schedule. Presales for the US dates opened on Friday, November 20, with lineups still to be announced.
articles.body: Vans Warped Tour has announced its 2027 festival locations and dates, with the revived punk, metal, hard rock and alternative festival returning to four cities next year. The run opens in Washington, D.C. on June 19–20, 2027, followed by Long Beach, California on July 24–25, Mexico City on September 11–12 and Orlando on November 13–14. All four locations hosted Warped Tour in 2026, while Montreal, the fifth city on this year's schedule, will not return in 2027. Presales for the three US dates began on Friday, November 20, at 9 a.m. PT / noon ET, with lineups for each city to be revealed in the coming weeks. The announcement came as the festival's 2026 season wrapped in Orlando, confirming the revived event's third consecutive year in its current format of individual weekend festivals rather than the travelling tour of its earlier decades. The 2027 dates were first reported by Billboard as part of its music-headlines roundup.

articles.title: Fresh Music Friday: Burna Boy, Gracie Abrams, Lisa, CHVRCHES and TXT lead the week's new releases
articles.description: This week's Fresh Music Friday slate, highlighted by Billboard, features Burna Boy's 'Bigger', Gracie Abrams' 'Lost in It', Lisa's 'Leave with Me', CHVRCHES' 'Evil' and Tomorrow X Together's 'Angel Bite'. The releases span Afrobeats, alt-pop, K-pop and synth-pop, and all arrived on Friday, November 20.
articles.body: This week's new-music roundup, flagged in Billboard's Daily Music Headlines for Friday, November 20, is led by Burna Boy's 'Bigger', Gracie Abrams' 'Lost in It', Lisa's 'Leave with Me', CHVRCHES' 'Evil' and Tomorrow X Together's 'Angel Bite'. The releases span Afrobeats, alt-pop, K-pop and synth-pop, and arrive on the same day as the week's new Billboard charts dated November 21. Gracie Abrams' new track lands as her album Daughter from Hell continues to draw attention, while Lisa's solo release keeps the BLACKPINK members' individual runs going alongside Jisoo's new single for The Angry Birds Movie 3. CHVRCHES' 'Evil' is the Scottish synth-pop band's latest new music, and TXT's 'Angel Bite' extends the group's busy release schedule. Burna Boy's 'Bigger' adds to a year of high-profile Afrobeats releases. The Friday drop is the week's main release slate, with the tracks now streaming across all major platforms.

articles.title: Can American Socialism Survive Its Success?
articles.author: Jill Lepore
articles.description: A sweeping, lucid history of American socialism from its 1912 peak to the D.S.A.'s 2026 midterm surge — essential context for the Mamdani moment, and a sharp warning that winning elections is the easy part.
articles.body:
Lepore opens in 1912, which she calls American socialism's best year ever. The Socialist Party of America then counted about 120,000 members and some 300 newspapers and magazines, including the Appeal to Reason, with three-quarters of a million subscribers. Socialists were winning real elections: Victor Berger became the first socialist in Congress in 1910, and by 1912 more than a thousand socialists held office, including fifty-six mayors in cities as different as Berkeley and Flint, plus 160 city councilmen and 145 aldermen. Eugene V. Debs ran for President that year denouncing 'wage slavery,' on a platform calling for collective ownership of railroads, mines, banks and the currency, a shorter workweek, a minimum wage, old-age pensions, unemployment insurance, the abolition of child labor, a graduated income tax, female suffrage, and the abolition of the Senate, the Presidential veto and the Electoral College.

The movement's collapse, Lepore argues, followed a pattern that has repeated ever since: socialist ideas flourished while socialist organizations withered. The party was battered by internal divisions, opposition to war, and government repression, and much of its agenda was eventually absorbed by the Democratic Party — the New Deal and later reforms carried socialist planks into law while the party itself faded. That absorption is the heart of her question about today: the Democratic Socialists of America, with about 130,000 members, has just had its best electoral year since 1912. Six D.S.A.-backed candidates won House seats in the November 3 midterms, D.S.A. candidates won mayoral races in Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., Ann Arbor and Providence, Zohran Mamdani is mayor of New York and Katie Wilson mayor of Seattle, and Gallup finds 43 percent of Americans approve of socialism while about two-thirds back Medicare for All.

But Lepore warns that the D.S.A.'s own 2026 program echoes the 1912 platform almost plank for plank — including abolishing the Senate and replacing the presidency and Supreme Court with bodies subordinate to Congress — and that the same structural trap awaits. All of the newly elected socialists ran as Democrats and will sit in a Democratic caucus, where the party's sheer majority will limit their leverage. She also traces a stranger convergence: the old socialist faith that history moves toward a classless future now meets Silicon Valley's faith that artificial intelligence is destiny, with figures like Musk and Sam Altman promising a post-work world. In Lepore's phrase, Marxism has become Muskism, and universal basic income starts to look less like liberation than a hedge against revolution. The essay's power is in refusing the easy celebration — the red-baiting of 2026 backfired and the label is no longer toxic, but the test is whether a movement can build institutions durable enough to survive its own success.

articles.title: An N.B.A. Player Got Hooked on Sports Betting. Soon, He Became the Bet
articles.author: Nick Berardini
articles.description: A gripping investigation into Jontay Porter, the NBA gambling scandal and the mob-linked hustlers behind it — the dark side of the betting boom now baked into every sports broadcast.
articles.body:
The story centers on Jontay Porter, a Toronto Raptors forward who got deep into FanDuel and ended up in debt to the wrong people. Berardini reconstructs how a young player with a modest contract fell into compulsive betting on his own sport, and how the only way out, as it seemed to him, was to gamble on himself — placing 'under' bets on his own statistics and then leaving games early or underperforming so those bets would cash. Porter eventually pleaded guilty to wire fraud, becoming the face of a federal investigation that saw more than thirty people arrested in October 2025, with Miami Heat guard Terry Rozier also implicated and facing trial in February 2027.

What makes the piece more than a scandal recap is the world Berardini maps around Porter. Legalized sports betting has put a sportsbook in every pocket — half of American men under fifty now hold a betting account — and the leagues that once warned about gambling now take its money and promote its apps. Into that gap stepped organized, mafia-linked hustlers who, Berardini reports, cultivated Porter and other players, turning an addiction into an asset. Working with the podcast host Pablo Torre, Berardini fact-checks Porter's story, interviews people around the case, and presses the question the federal case leaves open: was Porter the mastermind of the scheme, or was he himself played — a vulnerable addict steered by professionals who understood exactly how to exploit him?

The result is a portrait of a new gambling empire and what it is costing. It follows the money from a phone screen to a locker room to a courtroom, and it asks who bears responsibility when a league, a betting industry and a criminal network all profit from the same young man's compulsion. For anyone who has watched betting ads swallow sports broadcasts, it is the human cost made concrete.

articles.title: Just Ridiculous': A Famed Philosopher Takes on AI Consciousness
articles.author: Steven Levy
articles.description: The philosopher behind 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' — fresh off a $1 million prize — dismantles the idea that chatbots could be conscious, and calls building AI that pretends to feel 'criminal.'
articles.body:
Thomas Nagel is 89 years old, a professor emeritus at NYU, and the author of the 1974 essay 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' — the landmark text on consciousness in nonhuman minds. This week he won the million-dollar Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, and in an interview at his Greenwich Village home with WIRED's Steven Levy he used the occasion to say what he thinks of the idea that AI systems might be conscious: it is, in his words, 'just ridiculous.'

Nagel's argument is aimed at functionalism, the view that consciousness is a matter of computation and therefore independent of physical substrate. He calls that assumption the central error of the philosophers and AI researchers who take machine consciousness seriously. Consciousness, he argues, likely depends on physical systems analogous to a nervous system — and a data center, however complicated, has nothing in common with one. Large language models, he says, produce only language emulated from human-authored texts, and language by itself is not a natural manifestation of consciousness; most beings we regard as conscious, from cats to birds, do not use language at all.

He is equally blunt about the industry. Nagel criticizes companies — singling out Anthropic's Claude — for encouraging the public to treat chatbots as intentional minds, arguing that commercial interests promote systems that feign self-reflection and trick users into believing machines are conscious. He goes so far as to call building AI that feigns consciousness a dangerous project, even 'criminal,' because software with no internal mental life holds no actual beliefs and sits outside the moral universe. Whether or not you agree, it is a bracing counterweight to a debate usually conducted by the people selling the machines — philosophy's most famous consciousness skeptic, at the top of his field, refusing to be impressed.

articles.title: Sam Altman Is 'Still Unknowable' to Andrew Garfield, Even After Playing the OpenAI Co-Founder in Artificial
articles.description: Garfield says he never met the man he plays; Altman insists they waved at each other. A delicious, revealing night with the cast of the OpenAI movie — and a pointed challenge to Vanity Fair's own Altman cover.
articles.body:
At Vanity Fair's Screening Room at LACMA on November 14, Luca Guadagnino sat down with the stars of his new film Artificial — Andrew Garfield, who plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever, and Monica Barbaro as Mira Murati — for a post-screening conversation led by Vanity Fair's global editorial director Mark Guiducci. The film, written by Simon Rich and released by NEON on Christmas Day after Amazon MGM dropped it over the summer, dramatizes the 2023 OpenAI boardroom coup that briefly ousted Altman before an employee revolt brought him back five days later. It premiered at the New York Film Festival in October and holds a 95 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes.

The liveliest part of the evening was the dispute over whether Garfield and Altman ever actually met. Altman told Vanity Fair in October that he was walking to get coffee when he saw the crew filming outside his house, spotted Garfield dressed exactly like him — same backpack, same mannerisms — and waved. Garfield, who says he was watching every tinted car window and checking for security guards that day, insists it never happened: 'I never had any interaction with him. I've never seen him in real life.' Barbaro was equally skeptical, calling Altman's account 'textbook' for a man known for telling contradictory stories. Garfield also admitted he finds Altman unknowable — 'I'm fascinated by him continuously and exponentially' — while Altman has said the film isn't accurate, except for the way Garfield walks.

Guadagnino, for his part, insisted the film is not really about AI at all, but about 'the people who imagined it, who created it, who exploited it and who are still in the mix.' The conversation also turned pointedly on Vanity Fair itself, when Barbaro asked Guiducci why the magazine had put Altman on the cover of its revived New Establishment issue — 'pedestalizing' him, in her word — at the very moment the film questions his myth. Guiducci defended the cover as photojournalism, a document of the time, though the magazine's parent company, Condé Nast, has a content deal with OpenAI. It is a revealing snapshot of Hollywood, tech power and magazine-making colliding in one room.

articles.title: The Parents Who Never Stop Tracking Their Kids
articles.author: Sarah Zhang
articles.description: The Atlantic's December cover story: three-quarters of parents now track their teenagers' every move, and even Life360's own founder admits 'safetyism' is a problem. Funny, unsettling and uncomfortably relatable.
articles.body:
Sarah Zhang opens as a new mother, describing the apps that colonized her phone from the day her daughter was born: the baby monitor she could gaze at on a night out, the Snoo smart bassinet logging sleep by the minute, the $299 Owlet sock that would beam a baby's pulse and oxygen to her phone. The panopticon, she writes, does not end with babies. Parents now track grades the instant they are posted, watch Ring doorbell footage, scrutinize sleepaway-camp photos for signs of sunburn or social ostracism — and, above all, track their children's location everywhere they go. Three-quarters of parents with teenagers ages 14 to 17 have access to their kids' location data, and more than half of college students are now tracked, according to the psychologist Michaeline Jensen. Life360, the leading app, has 102 million monthly users and lets parents review 30 days of time-stamped location history, monitor driving speed and get alerts when a child arrives at or leaves a saved place.

The piece's strength is in the stories. A college counselor describes a moms' group chat that tracked daughters through sorority rush — until one mother reported her daughter was still in her dorm ten minutes before a math test and asked someone to send a kid to knock on her door. A recent graduate, Faith, tells how her mother showed up at a friend's house because she did not recognize an address on Life360, and drove out to random locations when the app glitched. A college junior notes the hypocrisy of parents who wax nostalgic about roaming free in the eighties while stalking their kids on their phones. And Russell Shaw, a former head of Georgetown Day School, recalls getting lost at age seven in the 1970s — no phones, no GPS — and how the experience taught him he could get through hard things, a small triumph that constant rescue would have erased.

Zhang, who spoke with dozens of experts, parents and teenagers, is careful not to present tracking as pure villainy. The studies so far find mixed or only very small effects on the parent-teen relationship, and the apps are genuinely useful for logistics — about a third of parents cite coordination as the main reason. The deeper problem she identifies is what the tools do to both sides over time: teenagers get fewer chances to make mistakes and recover from them, while parents lose the practice of letting go. She quotes the researcher Louise Barkhuus, who studies location tracking at NYU and still tracked her own daughter's subway rides: 'We're oversurveilling our children in a way that's not necessary, but I don't know how to take it away.'

The essay widens into a cultural history of 'safetyism' — from Hanna Rosin's 2014 Atlantic piece 'The Overprotected Kid' to the statistic that the share of British parents letting seven- and eight-year-olds walk home alone fell from 80 percent in 1971 to 6 percent in 2010 — even as teenagers have become safer than ever by nearly every measure, with violence, smoking, drinking, drug use and teen pregnancy all down by more than half. Yet teens are also less likely to get a job, go on a date or drive, and anxiety and depression keep climbing. Even Life360's co-founder Chris Hulls, himself a very free-range kid who traveled alone to Kenya at eleven, tells Zhang he agrees that 'safetyism is a thing, and it's not a good thing' — while arguing his app gives parents the peace of mind to grant more freedom, not less. It is a funny, unsettling and deeply relatable cover story about how a tool meant for emergencies became a habit nobody knows how to break.

articles.title: Trump pushing for a Ukraine peace deal by early January, before Democrats take Congress, FT reports
articles.description: U.S. negotiators have told European and Ukrainian officials that the White House wants a Russia-Ukraine peace deal by early January 2027, before Democrats take control of both chambers of Congress, the Financial Times reports. The deadline adds pressure to talks already strained by disagreements over security guarantees. A European official warned Kyiv may be forced into major concessions to meet the timetable.
articles.body: The White House is pushing for Russia and Ukraine to reach a peace deal by early January 2027, the Financial Times reported, citing four people familiar with the matter. The timing matters because Democrats are set to take control of both chambers of Congress, which U.S. negotiators reportedly see as a window that could close. A European official told the FT he fears Ukraine may have to make major concessions to meet the deadline. The report lands the same day President Volodymyr Zelenskyy questioned whether Kyiv and Washington even mean the same thing by the 'NATO-style' security guarantees at the center of the talks, and reiterated that postwar Ukraine would need foreign troops on its soil. Jared Kushner, one of Donald Trump's negotiators, has said the United States persuaded Russia to accept guarantees based on NATO's Article 5. The January target compresses a negotiation that has already seen Trump tell European leaders Putin wants to end the war, while Putin says Moscow will not negotiate with Kyiv after the Crimean Bridge strikes. For Ukraine, the risk is that a deadline driven by U.S. domestic politics, rather than battlefield conditions, produces terms Kyiv cannot accept.

articles.title: Denmark to expel Russia's military attaché after arrests in alleged plot to kill Ukrainian rapper
articles.description: Denmark will expel Russia's military attaché, who must leave the country within seven days, Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen announced. The decision follows the arrest of two Danish citizens accused of plotting to assassinate Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner, real name Albert Vasilyev. The case is the latest alleged Russian-ordered assassination plot on European soil.
articles.body: Denmark will expel Russia's military attaché, who must leave the country within seven days, Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen announced at a press conference. The decision followed the arrest of two Danish citizens accused of plotting to assassinate the Ukrainian rapper Kyivstoner, whose real name is Albert Vasilyev. According to the Russian Embassy's website, Russia's military attaché in Denmark is Vladimir Grekov. The expulsion is a direct diplomatic response to what Danish authorities describe as a Russian-directed murder plot against a Ukrainian public figure living in exile. It fits a wider pattern of alleged Russian operations targeting Ukrainian and dissident figures across Europe, which have prompted a series of expulsions and prosecutions in recent years. The case also highlights the reach of such plots into Scandinavia, a region that has stepped up counterintelligence work since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Kyivstoner, a Ukrainian rapper, has been a visible cultural figure in the Ukrainian diaspora, and the alleged plot underscores how Russian operations have extended beyond military and political targets to cultural ones.

articles.title: Russian missiles and a drone fell on Polish soil during overnight attack on Ukraine, Warsaw says
articles.description: Poland issued air raid alerts in two provinces bordering Ukraine as Russia attacked Ukraine overnight into November 20. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said three Russian objects fell on Polish territory: two missiles and a jet-powered drone. The incident confirms what had only been suspected in the morning — that a Russian missile crossed into Polish airspace during the barrage.
articles.body: Poland issued air raid alerts in two provinces bordering Ukraine as Russia attacked Ukraine overnight into November 20, and Warsaw later confirmed that Russian weapons landed on its territory. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said three Russian objects fell on Polish soil: two missiles and a jet-powered drone. A Kh-101 cruise missile came down in the village of Nowy Lipowiec, another missile in the town of Rudnik nad Sanem, and the drone in Mołodycz. The confirmation is a significant development from the morning, when reports only suggested a missile may have entered Polish airspace. The overnight barrage itself was one of the largest of the war, with roughly 100 missiles and more than 400 drones fired at Ukraine, killing eight people and injuring 28. In Kyiv, ballistic missiles damaged three bridges across the Dnipro River for the first time since the invasion began. The Polish incident raises the stakes for NATO, which has scrambled jets in response to earlier Russian airspace violations, and it comes as the alliance debates how to respond to repeated incursions without escalating into direct confrontation with Moscow.

articles.title: Swedish police say Russian money is being laundered through Revolut
articles.description: Swedish police examined suspicious transactions totaling 259 million euros linked to the laundering of funds from Russia and found Revolut was the most common route for moving the money out of Sweden, the Financial Times reported. The findings put a spotlight on how fintech platforms can be used to evade sanctions. Revolut has not been accused of wrongdoing in the report.
articles.body: Swedish police examined suspicious transactions totaling 259 million euros linked to the laundering of funds from Russia and found that Revolut was the most common way to move the money out of Sweden, the Financial Times reported. The investigation traced a network of suspicious transfers connected to Russian funds, with the fintech app emerging as the preferred channel for moving money abroad. The findings highlight a growing enforcement challenge: digital banking platforms that make cross-border transfers fast and easy can also be exploited to circumvent sanctions imposed on Russia since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Swedish authorities have been stepping up scrutiny of financial flows linked to Russia, and the scale of the transactions — a quarter of a billion euros — suggests the activity was systematic rather than incidental. The report does not accuse Revolut itself of wrongdoing, but it raises questions about how effectively fintech companies monitor suspicious activity. For European regulators, the case adds pressure to tighten anti-money-laundering controls on fast-growing digital banks that operate across borders with lighter traditional banking oversight.

articles.title: At least 17 women from former Soviet countries were drawn into Epstein's sex-trafficking network, Reuters reports
articles.description: At least 17 women from Russia and other former Soviet countries were drawn into financier Jeffrey Epstein's sex-trafficking network, Reuters reported. The finding adds a new dimension to the long-running Epstein files saga, which has newly released documents drawing fresh scrutiny. The women were identified through documents and interviews reviewed by Reuters.
articles.body: At least 17 women from Russia and other former Soviet countries were drawn into financier Jeffrey Epstein's sex-trafficking network, Reuters reported. The finding, based on documents and interviews reviewed by the news agency, adds a new dimension to the Epstein files saga, which has returned to the headlines as newly released documents draw fresh scrutiny in the United States. The women from the former Soviet space were among the many recruited into Epstein's network, which operated across borders and relied on intermediaries to bring victims to him. The report comes as the U.S. political debate over the Epstein files intensifies, with lawmakers and the public pressing for full disclosure of documents held by the Justice Department. For the women involved, the Reuters reporting underscores how Epstein's operation reached deep into Eastern Europe, exploiting economic vulnerability in the post-Soviet states. The story also connects to a broader reckoning with how trafficking networks operated with impunity for years, protected by Epstein's wealth and connections.

articles.title: As Patriarch Kirill turns 80, Meduza retraces his journey from backing Ukrainian self-determination to blessing the invasion
articles.description: Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill turned 80 on November 20. Meduza retraces how the head of the Russian Orthodox Church went from supporting Ukrainian self-determination to defending Moscow's full-scale invasion. His transformation mirrors the church's own shift into a pillar of the Kremlin's war effort.
articles.body: Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill, born Vladimir Gundyaev, turned 80 on November 20, and Meduza used the milestone to retrace his long transformation. In earlier decades, Kirill was known as a relatively cosmopolitan churchman who at times spoke in favor of Ukrainian self-determination and engaged with the West. Today he is one of the most prominent public defenders of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, framing the war in spiritual terms and presenting Russia's cause as sacred. His journey mirrors the transformation of the Russian Orthodox Church itself, which under his leadership since 2009 has become closely aligned with the Kremlin and a central pillar of its ideological justification for the war. Kirill has described the invasion as a defense of Orthodox civilization and has blessed Russian soldiers, while the church has faced a schism in Ukraine, where many parishes have broken away. The anniversary comes as the church's role in wartime Russia continues to grow, with Kirill recently speaking about the creation and purpose of Russia's nuclear weapons. His 80th birthday is being marked with official celebrations in Russia, even as his reputation abroad has collapsed.

articles.title: Was Putin humiliated in China? Meduza sums up the Shenzhen summit with a China expert
articles.description: The Shenzhen meeting of Putin, Trump and Xi was billed by many media as a potential 'new Yalta,' but the summit produced no radical statements. The leaders called on the International Criminal Court not to 'abuse its powers' and proposed reforming the United Nations. Meduza discusses what the summit really means for Ukraine with Carnegie Berlin Center China expert Temur Umarov.
articles.body: The meeting of the leaders of Russia, the United States and China in Shenzhen was billed by many media outlets as a potential 'new Yalta,' but the summit ended with no radical statements. Putin, Trump and Xi Jinping called on the International Criminal Court not to 'abuse its powers' and proposed reforming the United Nations — a modest outcome for a gathering that had been framed as a possible turning point for the war in Ukraine. Meduza discusses the results with Temur Umarov, a China expert at the Carnegie Berlin Center, asking whether the summit was really a failure for Putin and what it says about the prospects for ending the Russia-Ukraine war. The analysis notes that Putin had reportedly wanted to use the meeting to discuss Ukraine, but the final communiqué offered little on that front. For Kyiv, the lack of any deal struck over its head is a relief, even if the summit also produced no progress toward peace. The discussion also examines whether Putin was humiliated in China, as some commentary suggested, or whether the optics of standing alongside Trump and Xi served his purposes regardless of the substance.

articles.title: Air defense neutralized 462 targets in overnight barrage, including ballistic missiles
articles.description: Ukraine's Air Force said air defense neutralized 462 enemy targets during Russia's massive combined attack overnight into November 20. The barrage included around 100 missiles — Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, Kh-101, Kalibr and Iskander-K — plus 404 Shahed-type drones. At least 12 Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers took part, and strikes still hit more than 20 facilities.
articles.body: Ukraine's Air Force said air defense neutralized 462 enemy targets during Russia's massive combined attack on the night of November 20. The barrage was one of the largest of the war: at least 12 Tu-95MS and Tu-160 strategic bombers were in the air, and Russia fired ballistic Iskander-M and S-400 missiles, Zircon hypersonic missiles, 84 Kh-101 cruise missiles, Kalibr missiles, Iskander-K cruise missiles, and 404 Shahed-type attack drones. Despite the scale of the interception, strikes hit more than 20 facilities across the country, including energy infrastructure, bridges in Kyiv and a railway station in Lviv. The Air Force's figures show the sheer volume of Russia's nightly campaign, which has increasingly combined ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and mass drone swarms to overwhelm defenses. The attack also prompted air raid alerts in Poland, where Russian weapons later fell on Polish territory. For Ukraine, the interception rate is a measure of how far its air defenses have come, but the damage shows that even a high interception rate leaves enough through to cause casualties and infrastructure losses.

articles.title: Kyiv death toll rises to eight killed and 28 injured as strikes damage three Dnipro bridges
articles.description: The death toll from Russia's overnight attack on Kyiv rose to six in the capital and eight across Ukraine, with 28 people injured. Ballistic missiles damaged three bridges across the Dnipro — Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi — the first time Russia has struck Kyiv's bridges since the invasion began. A Kyivvodokanal water utility facility was also hit, and emergency power outages followed.
articles.body: The number of people killed in Kyiv in Russia's overnight attack rose to six, with eight killed across Ukraine in total and 28 injured, according to updated figures. Ballistic missiles damaged three bridges across the Dnipro River — the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges — the first time Russia has struck Kyiv's bridges since it launched its full-scale invasion. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the strikes targeted critical infrastructure and the river crossings that link the capital's two banks. A facility belonging to Kyivvodokanal, the city's water utility, was also hit, and emergency power outages were imposed in four regions and in Kyiv after the strikes. Traffic across Dnipro's bridges was temporarily halted in the morning before reopening, and DTEK adjusted outage schedules for November 20. The bridge strikes mark a new escalation in Russia's campaign against Kyiv, which had previously spared the river crossings that are vital to the city's daily life and to military logistics. Repair work and damage assessments were underway during the day, with all 372 boiler houses in Dnipro reported running.

articles.title: Russian strike on Lviv's Sknyliv railway station kills two and injures ten
articles.description: Russian jet-powered drones and missiles struck the ticket terminal at Sknyliv railway station in Lviv overnight, killing two people and injuring at least ten, four of whom were hospitalized. Residential buildings and infrastructure were also damaged in one of the largest attacks on the Lviv region. The strike shows Russia's barrage reached far beyond the front lines into western Ukraine.
articles.body: Russian jet-powered drones and missiles struck the ticket terminal at Sknyliv railway station in Lviv overnight into November 20, killing two people and injuring at least ten, four of whom were hospitalized. The two people killed were reported to be employees of Kyivvodokanal, according to preliminary information. Residential buildings and infrastructure facilities in the region were also damaged in what local authorities described as one of the largest attacks on the Lviv region since the full-scale invasion. Rescue workers clearing the rubble found a kitten alive in the debris, a small detail that captured attention amid the destruction. The strike on Lviv, a city far from the front lines near the Polish border, shows the reach of Russia's overnight barrage, which combined missiles and hundreds of drones across the country. Energy infrastructure in the region was damaged and power outage schedules were updated for November 20. The attack on a civilian railway station also underscores Russia's continued targeting of transport infrastructure, which it has hit repeatedly in an effort to disrupt logistics and civilian life.

articles.title: Ukrainian nuclear plants forced to cut output after massive Russian attack
articles.description: Ukrainian nuclear power plants were forced to reduce their generating capacity as a result of Russia's massive attack on November 20. The cutback is a direct consequence of damage to the power grid and substations that connect the plants to consumers. It adds strain to an energy system already under emergency outages in four regions and Kyiv.
articles.body: Ukrainian nuclear power plants were forced to reduce their generating capacity as a result of Russia's massive attack on November 20, in what officials described as a forced decision. The cutback follows damage to the power grid and to substations that transmit electricity from the plants, rather than any direct hit on the reactors themselves. Nuclear power is the backbone of Ukraine's electricity system, so any reduction in output immediately tightens supply across the country. Emergency power outages were already in effect in four regions and in Kyiv after the overnight strikes, and DTEK adjusted outage schedules during the day. The attack fits Russia's long-running campaign against Ukraine's energy infrastructure, which intensifies each winter as Moscow tries to leave Ukrainians without heat and light. The nuclear cutback is a reminder of how vulnerable the system is: even without a direct strike on a plant, damage to the grid around it can force operators to throttle generation. Repairs and grid stabilization work were underway, but officials warned of possible new large-scale attacks before the end of the week.

articles.title: SBU campaign 'Ptakh' hit 40 Russian oil depots and military-industrial sites in 50 days
articles.description: Ukraine's Security Service says its 'Ptakh' (Bird) campaign has struck 40 Russian oil depots and military-industrial facilities in 50 days. The operation is part of Ukraine's deep-strike campaign against the fuel and weapons infrastructure sustaining Russia's war. The figures were reported as Ukraine's own long-range strikes, including on the Crimean Bridge, made headlines this week.
articles.body: Ukraine's Security Service says its 'Ptakh' campaign has struck 40 Russian oil depots and military-industrial facilities in the past 50 days. The operation, whose name means 'Bird,' is part of Ukraine's deep-strike campaign against the fuel and weapons infrastructure that sustains Russia's war effort. The pace — nearly one facility a day — reflects the scale of Ukraine's long-range drone and missile operations inside Russia, which have repeatedly hit refineries, depots and chemical plants. The latest such strike came overnight into November 20, when Ukrainian drones hit a fertilizer plant in Dorogobuzh in Russia's Smolensk region that also produces components for explosives. The campaign has become a central element of Ukraine's strategy: degrading Russia's ability to fuel its military and its economy while the front lines remain largely static. The SBU's figures were reported as Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge, carried out three times in a week, also dominated the week's news. For Kyiv, the deep-strike campaign is both a military tool and a message — that Russia's rear is not safe, even as Moscow's own barrage against Ukrainian cities continues.

articles.title: Operation Carthage: is there a coordinated campaign against anti-corruption bodies NABU and SAPO?
articles.description: Ukrainska Pravda's UP.Chat panel examined whether Davyd Arakhamia, SBU General Serhiy Duka and former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko share an interest in discrediting anti-corruption agencies NABU and SAPO. The discussion covered the continuation of Operation Carthage, Duka's testimony before a parliamentary commission, and the role of the President's Office. It is the latest chapter in a domestic political fight over Ukraine's independent anti-corruption institutions.
articles.body: Ukrainska Pravda's UP.Chat panel examined whether Servant of the People faction leader Davyd Arakhamia, SBU General Serhiy Duka and former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko share an interest in discrediting the anti-corruption agencies NABU and SAPO. The discussion, featuring journalists Tetiana Danylenko, Mykhailo Tkach, Inna Vedernikova and Daria Kaleniuk, covered the continuation of Operation Carthage, General Duka's testimony before a parliamentary temporary investigative commission, and the possible involvement of the President's Office in pressure on law enforcement. Panelists also discussed why the Arakhamia case has dragged on, why parliament and its committees are stalling key anti-corruption legislation, and how corruption remains a tool of Russian influence. The episode touched on the Khimprom drug syndicate, casinos and gambling as shadow markets, and the question of elections during wartime. The debate reflects a deepening domestic political fight over Ukraine's independent anti-corruption institutions, which have become a flashpoint as the war continues. For Ukraine's Western partners, the independence of NABU and SAPO is a key condition of continued support, which makes the political struggle over them a matter of national importance.

articles.title: Russian Geran drone strike recorded in Moldova as barrage spills across borders
articles.description: A Russian Geran jet-powered drone strike was recorded in Moldova during the overnight barrage on Ukraine, according to reports. The incident adds Moldova to the list of neighboring countries affected by Russia's November 20 attack, alongside Poland, where missiles and a drone fell. It underscores how Russia's mass strikes are spilling beyond Ukraine's borders.
articles.body: A strike by a Russian Geran jet-powered drone was recorded in Moldova during the massive overnight attack on Ukraine, according to reports. The incident adds Moldova to the list of neighboring countries affected by Russia's November 20 barrage, alongside Poland, where two missiles and a drone fell on Polish territory and air raid alerts were issued in two border provinces. Moldova, which borders Ukraine to the southwest, has repeatedly found Russian drone debris on its territory during the war, but a recorded strike is a more serious incident. The spillover comes as Russia's attacks grow larger and more complex, combining ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and hundreds of drones in a single night, which increases the risk of weapons going off course or being deliberately sent across borders. For Moldova, a small country with limited air defenses, the incident is a reminder of its vulnerability to the war next door. It also adds to the pressure on NATO and the European Union to strengthen air defense along Ukraine's western borders.

articles.title: Take-Two confirms GTA VI as the biggest entertainment launch in history: 32.5 million pre-release copies and $3.79 billion on day one
articles.description: Take-Two has released the first official GTA VI sales figures, and they dwarf every previous record. The game sold 32.5 million copies before launch and took in $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales, making it the biggest entertainment launch of any kind in history. The official numbers are far above the third-party estimates of around $2.36 billion that circulated on Thursday.
articles.body: Take-Two Interactive has confirmed the first official sales figures for Grand Theft Auto VI, and they are staggering: 32.5 million units sold pre-release, a record across all platforms, and $3.79 billion in day-one retail sales through the end of November 19. The company calls it the biggest entertainment launch in history, ahead of any film, book or music album. The figures put the earlier Sensor Tower estimate of 24.58 million copies and about $2.36 billion in the shade, and they are roughly three times the launch-day performance of GTA V, which sold 11.2 million copies for $800 million in 2013. Engagement data from Circana underlines the scale: on launch day, 61% of US PlayStation 5 players and 56% of Xbox players globally played GTA VI, averaging more than eight hours each. The game also earned a near-perfect 99 on Metacritic. Take-Two shares nevertheless slipped on Thursday, a reminder that even a record launch does not guarantee a smooth ride for the stock. No PC release date has been announced yet.

articles.title: November PlayStation Plus games are live: Death Stranding 2, Atomfall and Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake headline the lineup
articles.description: Sony has opened the November PlayStation Plus catalogue for Extra, Premium and Deluxe subscribers. The Extra tier gains seven games, led by Death Stranding 2: On the Beach, Atomfall and Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii. Premium and Deluxe add two classics: Soul Reaver 2 and Freedom Wars Remastered.
articles.body: Subscribers to PlayStation Plus Extra, Premium and Deluxe can now download November's new additions on PS4 and PS5. The Extra catalogue grows by seven titles: Hell Let Loose, Death Stranding 2: On the Beach, Atomfall, Dragon Quest III HD-2D Remake, Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii, Cricket 26: The Official Game of the Ashes, and Trepang2. Death Stranding 2 is the standout, arriving on the service only months after its launch, alongside the well-received Atomfall and the latest Like a Dragon spin-off. Premium and Deluxe members also get two classics: Soul Reaver 2 and Freedom Wars Remastered, both playable on PS5 and PS4. The drop lands in the middle of the GTA VI launch week, giving PlayStation owners plenty to play once they step away from Leonida. Sony refreshed the catalogue as part of its regular monthly rotation, and the games are available to download now.

articles.title: Ubisoft cuts 166 jobs in Montreal and Quebec and spins up an AI studio to build NPCs with memory
articles.description: Ubisoft has laid off 166 staff across its Montreal and Quebec City studios, the teams behind Assassin's Creed, citing changing production needs. The cuts came on the same day the company reported half-year results, with Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced beating expectations. Ubisoft also unveiled Motherbrain, a new subsidiary dedicated to AI-driven gameplay.
articles.body: Ubisoft announced on November 19 that it is cutting 166 positions at its Montreal and Quebec City studios, the Canadian teams that work on Assassin's Creed. The company said production needs are changing as its portfolio evolves, and team sizes are being adjusted to match current priorities. Some of those let go had worked on Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, which ironically carried the quarter: revenue for the three months reached 389 million euros, about $450 million, against a forecast of roughly 370 million, up around 50% year on year. The remake reportedly sold 3.5 million copies in its first two weeks, with premium editions selling better than expected. On the same day, Ubisoft presented Motherbrain, a new subsidiary focused on AI for gameplay, including smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters running large systemic worlds, building on its Teammates generative-AI demo from November 2025. The cuts are the latest in a grim week for the industry: a day earlier, Firaxis, the Civilization and XCOM studio, laid off about a third of its staff, around 60 people, as work on a new XCOM reportedly stalled.

articles.title: Nintendo's Black Friday deals start today: Switch 2 Mario Kart bundle for $499.99 and $20 off Metroid Prime 4
articles.description: Nintendo's Black Friday 2026 sale begins today in the US, headlined by a Switch 2 bundle with Mario Kart World for $499.99. Metroid Prime 4 and Donkey Kong Bananza are each $20 off, and the wider sale runs through the holiday weekend. It is Nintendo's biggest discount push of the Switch 2's first year.
articles.body: Nintendo's Black Friday deals for 2026 start today in the United States, and the headline offer is a Nintendo Switch 2 bundle with Mario Kart World for $499.99. The sale also cuts $20 from two of the year's biggest Switch 2 titles, Metroid Prime 4 and Donkey Kong Bananza, which only launched in recent weeks. The timing is no accident: the Switch 2 is in its first holiday season, and Nintendo is using the bundle to pull in buyers who held off at launch. Retailers are expected to match or stack their own offers over the weekend, and the sale comes as rivals run their own events, with Xbox discounting more than 2,000 games by up to 80% through December 2. For players who have been waiting for a price break on Nintendo's new hardware, this is the first meaningful one since launch.

articles.title: Valve's Steam Machine goes on open sale in the 512GB model as the 2TB waitlist closes
articles.description: Valve's Steam Machine is now available to buy outright in its 512GB configuration, ending the waitlist scramble for the entry model. The 2TB version's waitlist has closed, suggesting supply of the higher-end model is spoken for. The living-room PC is Valve's biggest hardware bet since the Steam Deck.
articles.body: Valve has put the 512GB Steam Machine on open sale, meaning buyers can now order the entry-level model of its living-room PC without joining a queue. At the same time, the waitlist for the 2TB version has closed, a sign that the higher-capacity model's initial allocation is full. The Steam Machine is Valve's attempt to bring PC gaming into the living room in a console-sized box, following the success of the Steam Deck handheld. The open sale is a notable step: Valve hardware launches have often been supply-constrained, and the company appears to be prioritising availability for the cheaper model during the holiday season. Pricing and regional availability vary, and Valve has not said when the 2TB waitlist might reopen.

articles.title: The Horror Game Awards 2026 stream live today with more than 20 new trailers, including ILL and Sally Face 2
articles.description: The fifth-anniversary Horror Game Awards stream live from London today at 2:00 PM EST, with 21 awards across more than 100 nominated games. Over 20 new trailers are promised, including looks at ILL, Sally Face 2 and Sker: The Bleeding Veil. It is the genre's biggest showcase of the year.
articles.body: The Horror Game Awards 2026 stream live from London on Friday, November 20, at 2:00 PM EST, marking the fifth anniversary of the genre-focused ceremony. This year's show features 21 awards across more than 100 nominated games, covering the best horror releases of a crowded year. The organisers have promised over 20 new trailers and announcements, including footage of ILL, Sally Face 2 and Sker: The Bleeding Veil. For horror fans, the show has become the genre's equivalent of a summer showcase, a place where small studios can break out alongside bigger names. The stream lands in the middle of a huge week for gaming, a day after the GTA VI launch, but it gives horror a dedicated stage of its own.

articles.title: Nasdaq wipes out its gains for the year as Anthropic's IPO plunge deepens the AI sell-off
articles.description: A sell-off in technology stocks intensified on Friday, wiping out the Nasdaq Composite's gains for the year as investors pulled money out of the AI trade. The Nasdaq fell 5.3% and the S&P 500 dropped 3.6%, on track for a seventh straight day of losses. Even Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO debuted the day before, saw its shares plunge almost 10%.
articles.body: A sell-off in technology stocks intensified on Friday, wiping out the Nasdaq Composite's gains for the year, as investors continued to pull money out of the once high-flying AI trade. The Nasdaq fell 5.3% on Friday and is now down almost 2% for the year, while the S&P 500 dropped 3.6%, on track for a seventh day of losses, its longest losing streak since February 2020, when Wall Street began bracing for the Covid pandemic. Even Anthropic's blockbuster stock market debut quickly lost its shine, with shares in the AI lab plunging almost 10% a day after its IPO. CoreWeave, the Nvidia-backed neocloud provider, slumped 12% on Friday, and Nvidia itself is down 20% on the week, set for its worst week since November 2018. It is a meltdown right now, Arun Sundaram, senior vice president of investment strategy at CFRA Research, told CNN. The rout raises fresh questions about whether the AI boom that has driven markets for two years is finally cooling, or whether this is a sharp correction before the next leg up.

articles.title: Judge halts the Army's plan to detonate five tons of bomb-making material in Iowa over lead exposure fears
articles.description: A federal judge has ordered the US Army to pause its plan to detonate five tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, after environmental activists sued over lead exposure risks. The detonation of 68 drums of the unstable explosive had already been pushed from Friday to Monday after public outcry. Residents near the plant in Middletown say they plan to evacuate when it eventually goes ahead.
articles.body: A federal judge has ordered the US Army to pause its plans to detonate five tons of lead azide on Monday after environmental activists filed a lawsuit expressing concerns about the potential impacts of the explosion. Officials at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, in coordination with the US Environmental Protection Agency, planned to destroy 68 drums of lead azide, a material used to detonate munitions. The detonation in the southeastern town of Middletown was initially scheduled for Friday but was postponed to Monday after pushback from the public and elected officials. The Army has said the material degraded earlier this year, creating a highly unstable and dangerous situation, and that moving it posed an unacceptable risk of accidental detonation, a possibility that increases in cold weather. Monday was described as the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilisation of the material. Residents near the plant told CNN they plan to evacuate, and a public advisory on Sunday was the first time some communities as far as 100 miles away learned of the potential impact.

articles.title: Top Democrat warns no funding for Musk's SpaceX without answers on Ukraine Starshield slowdown
articles.description: Democratic Rep. Jim Himes, who will chair the House Intelligence Committee in January, is warning that lawmakers will withhold government funding for Elon Musk's SpaceX systems unless the administration explains who ordered slowdowns of Ukraine's military-grade Starlink service. In a classified letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Himes demanded clarity on changes made to the Starshield service in October.
articles.body: A top Congressional Democrat is warning that lawmakers will withhold government funding for systems developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX if the Trump administration and the tech billionaire refuse to disclose who is responsible for ordering the slowdown of Ukraine's military-grade Starlink satellite service, CNN has learned. In a classified communication sent to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Democratic Rep. Jim Himes, who will become chairman of the House Intelligence Committee in January, demanded clarity on what led to the slowdown of Ukraine's Starshield connection speed on multiple occasions in recent months. Himes asked for an explanation of the changes made to the Starshield service in October 2026, why those changes were made, and whether they were made unilaterally by SpaceX or directed by a US government official. The warning adds a new front to the standoff between congressional Democrats and the administration ahead of the party taking control of Congress, and it puts SpaceX's lucrative government contracts at the centre of the fight over support for Ukraine.

articles.title: Storm that flooded Florida's Space Coast now threatens Thanksgiving travel up the East Coast
articles.description: A storm that has drenched eastern Florida with more than 16 inches of rain this week is now charging up the East Coast, threatening early Thanksgiving travel for millions. More than 100 people have been rescued from flooded homes along the Space Coast, and a rare Level 4 of 4 flood risk is in place from Cape Canaveral to Daytona Beach through Friday night.
articles.body: A storm flooding Florida's Atlantic coast could hamper early Thanksgiving travel for millions as it charges up the East Coast with soaking rain and gusty winds. The storm has drenched eastern parts of the state with over 16 inches of rain this week, flooding homes and forcing dozens of water rescues along the Space Coast and in Miami's northern suburbs. A rare Level 4 of 4 high risk of flooding rain is in place from Cape Canaveral to Daytona Beach through Friday night. More than 100 people had been rescued by the end of the day Thursday, mostly from flooded homes, and roughly 65 homes in the Palm Bay Estates mobile home park in Brevard County were under a mandatory evacuation order after a bridge washed out and cut off the only access road. Around 20 rescues have been conducted in Volusia County as of Friday morning. Forecasters expect rain and gusty winds to expand into Georgia and the Carolinas on Saturday, then reach the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast on Sunday, with possible airport delays along the East Coast. More weather woes are possible after this system departs: another storm could impact the East Coast on Wednesday into Thanksgiving Day.

articles.title: Fans mourn Fiona, the beloved Cincinnati Zoo hippo who died at 9 after swallowing a knit hat
articles.description: Fiona, the famous hippopotamus at the Cincinnati Zoo, died Thursday at age 9 after ingesting a knit hat that accidentally landed in her habitat. Born premature at a record-low 29 pounds, she became a global favourite as fans watched her grow up. Her death has sparked an outpouring of grief and frustration on social media.
articles.body: Her keepers and adoring fans across the globe are mourning the sudden and tragic death of Fiona, the famous hippopotamus at the Cincinnati Zoo, who died Thursday at age 9 after ingesting a knit hat that accidentally landed in her habitat. Fiona became a star nearly a decade ago when she was born premature at a record-low weight of only 29 pounds, and millions followed her fight to survive and grow into what fans called the queen of Cincinnati. The Cincinnati Reds Hall of Fame and Museum showed a screen memorialising the hippo, and the mood at the zoo was sombre, with keepers and visitors grieving. Fiona fought a lot of obstacles in her life, and that just showed a lot of character, Debby Manning told CNN affiliate WKRC, noting that she truly was the queen of Cincinnati and the nation. Her death has sparked frustration as well as grief, with fans asking how a hat ended up in her enclosure.

articles.title: US security agencies warn aviation industry of Al Qaeda calls for attacks ahead of the busiest travel week
articles.description: US security agencies are warning airlines, air cargo carriers and airports of recent public messages from Al Qaeda affiliates praising September's attempted hijacking of a Tel Aviv-bound Flydubai flight and encouraging similar attacks. The FBI, DHS and TSA sent a joint notice on Thursday, days before the busiest travel week of the year, when about 6 million people are expected to fly domestically.
articles.body: US security agencies are warning commercial airlines, air cargo carriers and airports around the nation of recent public messaging by terrorists calling for attacks similar to September's attempted hijacking by the pilot of a Tel Aviv-bound Flydubai flight. On Thursday, the FBI, Department of Homeland Security and Transportation Security Administration jointly sent an informational report to members of the aviation industry indicating affiliates of Al Qaeda and the terror group's supporters have released multiple messages praising the attempted hijacking and encouraging similar attacks against perceived US, Israeli and Jewish interests, according to a copy of the report obtained by CNN. The notice comes ahead of the busiest travel week of the year: AAA anticipates about 6 million people will travel by air on US domestic flights from November 24 to November 30 for Thanksgiving. Officials have not pointed to a specific credible plot, but the warning puts the aviation industry on heightened alert just as holiday travel begins.

articles.title: Producer sues Travis Scott, Don Toliver and Sony Music over JackBoys hit 'What To Do?'
articles.description: Israeli producer Niv Kalisky, who records as Early Yellow, is suing Travis Scott, Don Toliver and Sony Music in New York federal court, claiming he owns half the master of the 2019 JackBoys track 'What To Do?' He says the song was built on his recording 'Moazin99bpm' and that he has received no master royalties in nearly seven years. The case also accuses Sony and Epic of filing false counter-notices to restore the track to streaming services after his takedowns.
articles.body: Israeli producer Niv Kalisky, who works as Early Yellow, filed suit in New York federal court on November 17 against Travis Scott, Don Toliver, Sheck Wes and Sony Music over the 2019 JackBoys track 'What To Do?', which appeared on the Billboard 200 No. 1 album JackBoys. Kalisky claims the track was built on his recording 'Moazin99bpm', which he emailed to representatives of producers London Cyr and Jenius in May and July 2019, and says he has not been paid any master royalties in the nearly seven years since the song's release. He is asking the court to declare him a 50% owner of the master and to award him at least half of what the recording has earned, with the track streamed more than 270 million times on Spotify and played over 60 million times on YouTube. The complaint says Kalisky first demanded payment in August 2020, and that after he filed copyright takedown notices in October, Sony and Epic filed counter-notices on Apple Music, Spotify and YouTube, getting the track reinstated. Kalisky alleges those counter-notices were false, and is seeking at least $1 million across claims for unfair competition, false counter-notices and unjust enrichment, plus statutory damages of up to $150,000 per infringement. He is also asking for a permanent injunction that could pull 'What To Do?' from streaming services entirely. The case follows a separate producer royalty suit against Sony filed last month by Ishmael Sadiq Montague over Chris Brown's 'Party'.

articles.title: NetEase Cloud Music's Q3 revenues dip 0.9% to $290m as subscription growth slows
articles.description: NetEase Cloud Music's revenues fell 0.9% year-on-year to $290 million in the third quarter, as its subscription revenue growth slowed to roughly a third of its pace a year earlier. The Chinese streaming service has re-signed with all three major labels this year, but growth is cooling in a maturing market. The results underline the pressure on China's second-biggest music streamer to find new revenue beyond subscriptions.
articles.body: NetEase Cloud Music's revenues fell 0.9% year-on-year to $290 million in the third quarter of 2026, the company has reported, after its subscription revenue growth slowed sharply. Subscription revenues grew 5.3% in the first half of the year, but the pace has now slowed to roughly a third of what it was a year earlier, according to MBW's report on the results. NetEase Cloud Music is China's second-largest music streaming service, and it has re-signed licensing deals with all three major labels — Universal, Sony and Warner — this year, securing its catalogue. Even so, the figures point to a maturing Chinese streaming market where subscriber growth is harder to come by and monetisation depends increasingly on value-added services such as live streaming, social features and advertising. The slowdown matters for the majors too, since China is one of the fastest-growing recorded-music markets in the world and a key source of future streaming growth. NetEase's results follow a period in which the company has leaned on cost discipline and diversified revenue, but the latest quarter shows the limits of that strategy when core subscription growth stalls.

articles.title: Switzerland's MusicBird secures up to $200m credit facility to scale its catalogue
articles.description: Swiss music company MusicBird has secured a revolving credit facility of up to $200 million, arranged by Truist and Fifth Third. The financing will help it scale its portfolio of music rights. The deal is the latest sign that debt markets remain open to music-rights buyers even as the catalogue gold rush cools.
articles.body: Switzerland's MusicBird has secured a revolving credit facility of up to $200 million, arranged by Truist and Fifth Third, the company has announced. MusicBird says the new financing will help it scale its portfolio of music rights, giving it firepower to acquire catalogues and invest in its existing assets. Revolving credit facilities have become a standard tool for music-rights companies, letting them draw down funds for acquisitions and repay as royalties come in, rather than raising equity for each deal. The size of the facility puts MusicBird among the better-funded independent players in the rights market, which has seen a wave of consolidation and refinancing as interest rates have stayed high and investors have grown more selective. Truist and Fifth Third arranging the deal also signals that US banks remain willing to lend against music royalties, a bet on the durability of streaming income. The announcement comes in a week when music finance has been in focus, with Duetti raising $665 million in a Carlyle-anchored deal, suggesting capital is still flowing into music rights even as the market matures.

articles.title: TikTok says 94% of songs entering the Billboard Global 200 in 2025 went viral on its platform first
articles.description: TikTok says 94% of the songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 in 2025 went viral on its platform first, up from 84% in 2024. The figure comes from TikTok's 2026 Music Impact Report, prepared by Luminate and published on November 18. It is the platform's strongest claim yet that it, not radio or playlists, is now the main launchpad for global hits.
articles.body: TikTok says 94% of the songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 in 2025 went viral on its platform first, up from 84% in 2024, according to its 2026 Music Impact Report. The report was prepared by data firm Luminate and published on Wednesday, November 18, and it is TikTok's most assertive claim yet that it has become the primary discovery engine for global hits. The 10-percentage-point jump in a single year suggests the platform's grip on music discovery is still tightening, even as short-form video competitors and streaming services have tried to build their own viral mechanics. For labels and artists, the figure underlines how much of a song's global chart prospects now depend on catching fire on TikTok before it reaches the charts, rather than the other way round. It also strengthens TikTok's hand in licensing negotiations with the music industry, since the data positions the app as indispensable to breaking new music rather than merely a promotional channel. The report lands as the industry debates TikTok's value to artists, with some arguing the platform drives discovery without paying fairly, while others say its promotional power is unmatched. Either way, the 94% figure is likely to be quoted in every label boardroom and licensing meeting in the months ahead.

articles.title: Unreleased D'Angelo song 'Kamikazi' surfaces in 'GTA VI'
articles.description: Players digging through GTA VI on launch day found a previously unreleased song by the late D'Angelo, 'Kamikazi', playing on the in-game radio station Worldwide FM. The track was confirmed as D'Angelo's work by his former collaborator DJ Dojah, though neither Rockstar nor the estate has commented officially. D'Angelo, who died in October 2025, had a long relationship with Rockstar, contributing 'Unshaken' to Red Dead Redemption 2.
articles.body: A previously unreleased song by the late D'Angelo, titled 'Kamikazi', has surfaced in Grand Theft Auto VI, where players found it playing on the in-game radio station Worldwide FM. The discovery spread on launch day after a gameplay clip was shared on Reddit and picked up by music journalists, with DJ Dojah, a former D'Angelo collaborator, confirming it as the singer's work and revealing its official title. Rockstar Games has made no official comment, and the track does not appear on the game's official soundtrack album, 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album', which arrives Friday with 34 original songs. Rockstar's own game credits reportedly place 'Kamikazi' on Worldwide FM, hosted by Gilles Peterson, and name Terry Slingbaum and D'Angelo as its writers. D'Angelo died on October 14, 2025, aged 51, after a battle with pancreatic cancer, and his brother has confirmed a posthumous album is on the way, drawn from a vault of unreleased music, with no collaborations. The singer had a long relationship with Rockstar: he contributed the original song 'Unshaken' to 2019's Red Dead Redemption 2 and regularly visited the company's New York office to play its new titles, once staying until 4 a.m. The 'Kamikazi' discovery is the most talked-about music moment of GTA VI's launch week, and fans are now wondering whether it is a preview of the posthumous album to come.

articles.title: CMA Awards 2026: Taylor Swift honours Brooks & Dunn and throws back to 'Our Song'
articles.description: Taylor Swift was one of the headline moments of the 2026 CMA Awards, delivering a speech honouring Brooks & Dunn and performing her early hit 'Our Song'. The night also featured Lainey Wilson debuting a new song with an all-female band, a Stephen Wilson Jr. and Chris Stapleton collaboration, and a Miranda Lambert and Ella Langley duet. Rolling Stone rounded up the 12 best, worst and most WTF moments from the ceremony.
articles.body: The 2026 CMA Awards delivered a night of big performances and surprises, with Taylor Swift at the centre of it. Swift gave a speech honouring country legends Brooks & Dunn, calling their catalogue 'eternal bangers', and threw it back to her own early career with a performance of 'Our Song', the 2007 single that first made her a country star. Lainey Wilson debuted a new song, 'Just a Woman', backed by an all-female band, while Stephen Wilson Jr. teamed up with Chris Stapleton for a collaboration on 'I'm a Song'. Miranda Lambert and Ella Langley gave the live debut of their duet 'Snakeskin Boots', and Kacey Musgraves joined Lambert for a duet on 'Horses and Divorces'. Rolling Stone's roundup of the night picked out the 12 best, worst and most WTF moments, capturing a ceremony that leaned heavily on cross-generational pairings and nostalgia. The show also saw Halestorm, Brothers Osborne and Hardy join forces for a ferocious Brooks & Dunn tribute, and Ella Langley perform 'Loving Life Again'. For Swift, the night was a full-circle moment: nearly two decades after 'Our Song' launched her career, she returned to the CMA stage as one of the biggest stars in the world, honouring the duo who helped define the genre she started in.

articles.title: Beastie Boys' Mike D brings solo album — and his sons — to Tiny Desk
articles.description: Beastie Boys' Mike D has brought his solo album to NPR's Tiny Desk Concert, performing with his sons alongside him. The appearance marks a new chapter for the rapper, decades after the Beastie Boys became one of hip-hop's defining acts. It is one of the most personal Tiny Desk sets of the year.
articles.body: Beastie Boys' Mike D has taken his solo album to NPR's Tiny Desk Concert, performing in the intimate format with his sons joining him for the set. The appearance marks a new chapter for Mike D, who rose to fame as one third of the Beastie Boys, one of hip-hop's most influential and enduring groups, before the death of Adam 'MCA' Yauch in 2012 effectively ended the band. Going solo has meant stepping out from behind one of the most famous group identities in music, and the Tiny Desk performance, with his sons at his side, framed it as a family affair as much as a musical one. The Tiny Desk series has become a rite of passage for artists of every generation, and Mike D's set sits alongside recent appearances by artists across genres who have used the stripped-back format to show a different side of their work. For longtime Beastie Boys fans, seeing Mike D perform with his children adds a poignant, generational note to the performance, connecting the group's legacy to the next generation of his own family.

articles.title: Atlas Sound returns with surprise new album 'Thanatos', first LP in 15 years
articles.description: Atlas Sound, the solo project of Deerhunter's Bradford Cox, has returned with a surprise new album, 'Thanatos', its first LP in 15 years. The release comes with little advance warning, in keeping with Cox's low-key approach to the project. It is one of the most unexpected comeback albums of the year.
articles.body: Atlas Sound, the solo project of Deerhunter frontman Bradford Cox, has returned with a surprise new album, 'Thanatos', the project's first LP in 15 years. The album arrived with little advance warning, a fittingly low-key return for a project that has always operated in the margins of Cox's more visible work with Deerhunter. Atlas Sound's previous albums, released in the late 2000s and early 2010s, were bedroom-recorded, experimental records that built a cult following for their intimacy and strangeness, standing apart from Deerhunter's widescreen indie rock. A 15-year gap makes 'Thanatos' one of the most unexpected comeback albums of the year, and its surprise release means fans are discovering it in real time, without the usual rollout of singles and interviews. The title, drawn from the Greek personification of death, suggests a darker, more reflective record, in keeping with Cox's recent work. The album is now streaming, and early reactions from fans have treated it as a major event for one of indie music's most idiosyncratic voices.

articles.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' is here, featuring Dua Lipa, Lana Del Rey, Cardi B and more
articles.description: The companion album to Grand Theft Auto VI arrives today, Friday November 20, with 34 original songs made for the game. The tracklist includes new music from Travis Scott, Cardi B, Playboi Carti, Dua Lipa, Lana Del Rey and JENNIE, running just over 97 minutes. It is one of the biggest soundtrack releases of the year, arriving a day after the game itself launched.
articles.body: 'Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album' is out today, Friday, November 20, a day after the game itself launched to enormous anticipation. The album features 34 brand-new songs made for the game, running just over 97 minutes, led by Travis Scott, Cardi B, Playboi Carti, Dua Lipa, Lana Del Rey and JENNIE. Rockstar Games and Atlantic Records announced the album in September and released 10 of its songs as singles in the run-up to launch, with the full 34-track running order leaking last weekend after photos of the vinyl edition surfaced online. Sources close to the project have since confirmed the full list to both Billboard and Rolling Stone, and Apple Music's listing matches the leaked order track for track. The album opens with Justice featuring Michael McDonald on 'Starting From Zero', and Justice also composed the game's original score, which arrives separately on December 11. The rollout continues on Saturday, November 21, with Grand Theft Auto VI: The Festival at Mana Wynwood in Miami, bringing the album's artists together live. With the game expected to be one of the biggest entertainment launches ever, its companion album is set to be one of the most-streamed soundtrack releases of the year.

articles.title: Gracie Abrams' 'Daughter from Hell' gets the deluxe treatment
