articles.description: Gracie Abrams has released a deluxe edition of her latest album, 'Daughter from Hell', which she has called her most ambitious and musically varied offering to date. The expanded version arrives as Abrams continues a breakthrough run that has included a Rolling Stone interview residency at New York's Cherry Lane Theatre. The deluxe adds new material to an album that has already defined her year.
articles.body: Gracie Abrams has released a deluxe edition of her latest album, 'Daughter from Hell', expanding the record she has described as her most ambitious and musically varied offering to date. The original album marked a step forward for Abrams, who has grown from a bedroom-pop songwriter into one of the most prominent young artists in pop, with a fanbase that has followed her through sold-out tours and a string of hit singles. The deluxe edition arrives as Abrams continues a high-profile run: last month she joined Rolling Stone's residency at New York's historic Cherry Lane Theatre for a live edition of The Rolling Stone Interview, discussing her dream collaborations, the challenge of marketing herself and the perspective that comes with entering adulthood. Deluxe editions have become a standard way for artists to extend an album's life on streaming, adding new tracks that can drive fresh playlist placements and chart runs. For Abrams, the expanded 'Daughter from Hell' caps a year in which she has consolidated her place as one of pop's defining young voices, and the new material gives fans a reason to return to an album that already shaped 2026.

articles.title: Childish Gambino's 'This Is America' video joins YouTube's billion-views club
articles.description: Childish Gambino's politically charged 2018 video for 'This Is America' has passed one billion views on YouTube, becoming his first video to reach the milestone. The Hiro Murai-directed clip was one of the defining music videos of its era, sparking debate about gun violence and race in America. Eight years on, its message still resonates.
articles.body: Childish Gambino's video for 'This Is America' has passed one billion views on YouTube, becoming the first of the artist's videos to reach the milestone. Released in 2018 and directed by Hiro Murai, the video was one of the defining cultural moments of its era: a densely symbolic, single-take-style depiction of gun violence, entertainment and Black life in America that sparked days of analysis, debate and frame-by-frame breakdowns. The song itself, released under Donald Glover's musical alias, won four Grammy Awards including Record of the Year and Song of the Year, and debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100. Its billion-view milestone comes eight years after release, a testament to the video's staying power as a piece of political art that continues to be watched, shared and taught. The achievement adds to a year in which Glover's work has continued to be revisited, and it underlines how a music video can outlive its chart run to become a lasting cultural document. 'This Is America' remains one of the most discussed videos of the streaming era, and its entry into YouTube's billion-views club cements its place in that history.

articles.title: Yamaha acquires visual technology company Disguise for $280 million
articles.description: Yamaha has acquired Disguise, the visual technology company behind the LED and projection systems used in major concerts and live events, for $280 million. The deal is the biggest in Billboard's latest roundup of music-industry transactions. It signals Yamaha's push beyond instruments and audio into the visual side of live production.
articles.body: Yamaha has acquired Disguise, the visual technology company whose systems power the LED walls, projections and real-time visuals at major concerts and live events, for $280 million, Billboard reports in its latest Deals roundup. Disguise's technology sits behind some of the most ambitious stage productions of recent years, letting artists and designers build immersive visual environments that respond to the music in real time. For Yamaha, a company built on instruments and audio equipment, the acquisition is a significant move into the visual side of live production, reflecting how concerts have become as much a visual spectacle as a musical one. The $280 million price tag makes it one of the larger music-adjacent deals of the year, and it comes as the live industry invests heavily in production technology to justify rising ticket prices and create experiences that cannot be replicated at home. The deal also highlights the growing convergence of audio and visual technology companies, as the firms that supply the tools of live performance consolidate into broader production groups. Yamaha has not yet detailed how Disguise will be integrated into its business, but the acquisition positions it at the centre of the next generation of concert staging.

articles.title: Marlon Jackson reveals stage 4 prostate cancer diagnosis: 'God has me'
articles.description: Marlon Jackson, the Jackson 5 member, has revealed he has been diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer, writing 'God has me' in a message to fans. The announcement has drawn support from across the music world. Jackson, 69, was a core member of one of the most successful family acts in pop history.
articles.body: Marlon Jackson has revealed that he has been diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer, sharing the news with fans in a message in which he wrote 'God has me'. Jackson, 69, was a member of the Jackson 5, one of the most successful family acts in pop history, alongside his brothers Jackie, Tito, Jermaine and Michael. The group, signed to Motown as children, scored a string of No. 1 hits in the early 1970s and became one of the defining acts of their era, with Marlon's harmonies and stage presence a core part of their sound. His announcement has drawn an outpouring of support from fans and fellow artists, many of whom grew up with the Jackson 5's music. Stage 4 prostate cancer means the disease has spread beyond the prostate, and Jackson's message struck a note of faith and resilience rather than detail about his treatment. The news comes in a difficult period for the Jackson family, and follows other health announcements from veteran artists this year. Jackson has not shared further details about his prognosis or treatment plans, and fans have responded with messages of support and prayers.

articles.title: Jordan Brunoli, bassist with Australian indie rockers Bugs, dies at 31
articles.description: Jordan Brunoli, the bassist with Australian indie rock band Bugs, has died at the age of 31. The band and the Australian music community have paid tribute to a musician remembered as a central part of the Brisbane indie scene. No cause of death has been shared publicly.
articles.body: Jordan Brunoli, the bassist with Australian indie rock band Bugs, has died at the age of 31, Billboard reports. Bugs are a Brisbane indie rock band who built a loyal following in Australia's independent scene, with Brunoli's bass playing a central part of their sound and live shows. News of his death has drawn tributes from the band, fellow musicians and fans across the Australian music community, many of whom remembered him as a warm presence and a key figure in the Brisbane scene. No cause of death has been shared publicly, and the band has asked for privacy as they grieve. The loss of a musician at 31 has resonated beyond Australia's indie circles, a reminder of how tightly knit the country's independent music community is, and how much its members rely on each other. Bugs had been active on the Australian touring circuit, and Brunoli's death leaves a gap in a band that was still building its audience. Further details, including any memorial plans, are expected to be shared by the band in due course.

articles.title: Russian missiles hit three Kyiv bridges overnight, killing three and cutting the city in two
articles.description: Russia launched a combined missile and drone attack on Kyiv overnight into November 20, striking three bridges across the Dnipro River — the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi crossings — in the biggest attack on the capital's river links since the full-scale invasion began. Mayor Vitali Klitschko said three people were killed and at least 15 injured, with traffic closed or restricted across the city of some 3 million people. The strikes also damaged critical infrastructure and knocked out power in several districts. It matters because the bridges are Kyiv's lifelines between its left and right banks, and hitting them is a deliberate attempt to paralyse the capital.
articles.body: Russian forces attacked Kyiv with missiles and drones overnight into November 20, targeting critical infrastructure and three bridges across the Dnipro River, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Ballistic missiles damaged the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi Bridge crossing, where traffic from the right bank to the left bank was completely closed, as well as the Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi (Southern) bridges, which sustained damage but remained open to vehicles for now. Three people were killed and at least 15 others injured, the mayor said; some reports later put the death toll at six, with the dead including employees of the Kyivvodokanal water utility. The attack caused power outages in the Pecherskyi, Solomianskyi and Holosiivskyi districts and disrupted public transport across the city. Russia's Defence Ministry confirmed the strikes, claiming it had targeted military-industrial facilities, missile and drone production and storage sites, and energy and transport infrastructure in Kyiv and six other regions. The strikes came immediately after the APEC summit in Shenzhen ended, where Vladimir Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping met, and days after Ukraine's third strike in a week on the Crimean Bridge — a sequence Kyiv's allies read as retaliation. For Kyiv's roughly 3 million residents, who commute daily across just six main bridges, the damage threatens prolonged disruption to movement, emergency services and the power grid as winter approaches.

articles.title: Zelenskyy questions whether Kyiv and Washington mean the same thing by 'NATO-style' guarantees
articles.description: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy questioned whether Kyiv and Washington mean the same thing by 'NATO-style' security guarantees, after US negotiator Jared Kushner said the United States had persuaded Russia to accept guarantees based on NATO's Article 5. Zelenskyy reiterated that postwar Ukraine would need foreign troops on its soil. The exchange matters because security guarantees are the centrepiece of the emerging peace framework, and Kyiv and Washington still appear to define them differently.
articles.body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has publicly questioned whether Kyiv and Washington mean the same thing when they talk about 'NATO-style' security guarantees for Ukraine, in comments reported by Meduza on November 20. The remarks follow statements by Jared Kushner, one of Donald Trump's negotiators, who said the United States had persuaded Russia to accept security guarantees for Ukraine based on Article 5 of NATO's founding treaty — the alliance's collective-defence clause. Zelenskyy reiterated that postwar Ukraine would need foreign troops stationed on its soil, a position that goes beyond a paper commitment. The gap matters because the guarantee question sits at the heart of the diplomacy now unfolding after the first-ever trilateral summit of Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, which ended with a four-point 'peace declaration' but no deal on Ukraine. Kyiv's concern is that a guarantee modelled loosely on Article 5, without troops or a clear trigger, would leave Ukraine exposed once fighting stops. European leaders are also involved: a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin this week, attended by Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff, discussed the same guarantees. Zelenskyy has said Europeans will be included in negotiation formats with the Russians. The public questioning suggests Kyiv is pushing back on a US framing it fears could be sold as a breakthrough while leaving the hardest questions — who deploys, under what mandate, and what happens if Russia attacks again — unanswered.

articles.title: Trump tells European leaders Putin wants to end the war — but Putin says Moscow won't negotiate after bridge strikes
articles.description: Donald Trump told European leaders that Vladimir Putin wants to end the war in Ukraine, but Putin said Moscow will not negotiate with Kyiv after Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge. The contradiction, reported by Meduza, captures the gap at the centre of the Shenzhen diplomacy: the US president presenting the Russian leader as ready for peace while Putin publicly rules out talks with Kyiv. It matters because the trilateral summit ended with a peace declaration but no Ukraine deal, and the two leaders' accounts point in opposite directions.
articles.body: Donald Trump told European leaders that Vladimir Putin wants to end the war in Ukraine, but Putin said Moscow will not negotiate with Kyiv after the Crimean Bridge strikes, Meduza reported on November 20. The two statements, delivered within hours of each other, expose the central tension in the diplomacy that followed the first-ever trilateral summit of Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. Trump has been presenting the Russian leader as a partner for peace, and the summit ended with a four-point 'peace declaration' — but no agreement on Ukraine itself. Putin, meanwhile, has used Ukraine's three strikes on the Crimean Bridge in a single week as a reason to refuse negotiations, and acknowledged serious damage to the bridge's road section while threatening retaliation. The bridge strikes were carried out with Ukrainian Neptune missiles and, according to reports, Ruta missiles, and satellite images published on November 19 showed a collapsed span. Trump also told European leaders that Putin was angered by Zelenskyy over the Kerch Bridge attack. The conflicting accounts leave European allies, who met in Berlin this week in the Coalition of the Willing format, uncertain whether the US-Russia channel is producing real movement or a performance of peacemaking. For Kyiv, the risk is that Washington treats Putin's private assurances as progress while Moscow publicly hardens its position.

articles.title: US charges 25-year-old Russian with spying on Palantir employees
articles.description: US authorities have charged a 25-year-old Russian man with spying on employees of Palantir, the American data-analytics company. Prosecutors say he photographed their laptops in a coffee shop and tracked their movements. The case matters because Palantir's software is used by US defence and intelligence agencies, and the charges point to old-fashioned human surveillance targeting the tech sector rather than a cyber intrusion.
articles.body: The United States has charged a 25-year-old Russian man with spying on employees of Palantir, the American data-analytics and defence-technology company, Meduza reported on November 20. According to prosecutors, the man photographed employees' laptops while they worked in a coffee shop and tracked their movements, gathering information about people working for a company whose software is used by US defence and intelligence agencies. The case is striking for its low-tech methods: rather than hacking networks, the alleged spying relied on physical observation — photographing screens over a shoulder and following targets in person. Palantir, founded by Peter Thiel and Alex Karp, builds data platforms used by the Pentagon, intelligence agencies and allied governments, making its staff a natural target for Russian intelligence. The charges come amid a broader wave of Russian espionage cases in the West and heightened scrutiny of Moscow's intelligence networks since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It also fits a pattern of Russian operations that blend traditional tradecraft with targeting of the private technology sector, which now sits at the centre of Western defence and surveillance capabilities.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones hit Russian fertilizer plant that also makes components for explosives
articles.description: Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant in Dorogobuzh, in Russia's Smolensk region, overnight into November 20. The plant produces ammonium nitrate, a component used in industrial explosives, and the strike is part of Ukraine's sustained campaign against Russian military-industrial targets deep inside Russia. It matters because Kyiv is systematically degrading the supply chains behind Russia's war effort, from oil refineries to explosives precursors.
articles.body: Ukrainian drones struck a chemical plant in the town of Dorogobuzh, in Russia's Smolensk region, overnight into November 20, Meduza reported. The target was a fertilizer plant that also produces ammonium nitrate, a chemical used as a component in industrial explosives, making it a dual-use facility feeding Russia's military supply chain. The strike is the latest in Ukraine's long-range drone campaign against Russian industry, which has already nearly halved Russian oil refining capacity over the past 20 days, according to Ukrainian reports, and cut refining by 45% since late October, according to Reuters. Ukrainian forces also hit an ammunition depot in Luhansk region in the same overnight wave, with large-scale detonations reported. The campaign reflects a deliberate Ukrainian strategy: rather than only striking frontline positions, Kyiv is hitting the factories, refineries and depots that sustain Russia's war machine, forcing Moscow to defend a vast rear area. Russian air defences have struggled to cover the full depth of the country, and each successful strike adds to the cost of the war for Russia's economy. The Dorogobuzh plant's role in explosives production makes it a particularly significant target, linking civilian chemical industry directly to battlefield munitions.

articles.title: Russia wants people in bankruptcy to sign up to fight in Ukraine
articles.description: The Russian government has submitted a bill to the State Duma that would let people in bankruptcy proceedings sign military contracts and go to fight in Ukraine while keeping assets worth up to 10 million rubles, with creditors taking the loss. The proposal is a new recruitment incentive as Moscow seeks more soldiers without a formal mobilisation. It matters because it shows the Kremlin reaching deeper into vulnerable groups to sustain the war effort.
articles.body: The Russian government has submitted a bill to the State Duma that would let people going through bankruptcy sign military contracts and fight against Ukraine while keeping assets worth up to 10 million rubles in total, Meduza reported. Under the proposal, recruits could shield their property during bankruptcy proceedings, and their creditors would take the loss — effectively turning debt relief into a recruitment bonus. The bill is the latest in a series of incentives Moscow has offered to keep volunteer numbers up without declaring a new mobilisation, which the Kremlin has avoided since the unpopular partial mobilisation of 2022. Previous measures have included large signing bonuses, debt write-offs and fast-tracked citizenship, but targeting bankrupt citizens marks a new step: it explicitly recruits from people in financial distress. The proposal also reveals the fiscal strain of the war economy, with the state effectively asking private creditors to subsidise military recruitment. It comes as Russia's State Duma approved the 2027–2029 federal budget in its second reading, with military spending remaining dominant. If passed, the law would let the state convert personal financial ruin into manpower for the front, a trade that critics say exploits the most vulnerable Russians.

articles.title: Tankers carrying Russian diesel sent to the US under Trump-Putin deal arrive in Brazil instead
articles.description: Tankers carrying Russian diesel that were sent to the United States under a diesel deal struck between Trump and Putin have arrived in Brazil instead, The Maritime Executive reported. The diversion raises questions about how the arrangement actually works in practice. It matters because the deal is one of the few concrete economic outcomes of the Trump-Putin channel, and its first shipments are not going where they were supposed to.
articles.body: Tankers carrying Russian diesel that were sent to the United States under a diesel deal agreed between Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have arrived in Brazil instead, The Maritime Executive reported, according to Meduza. The cargoes were part of an arrangement under which Russian fuel would be supplied to the US market, an unusual deal given the sanctions regime and the political sensitivity of Russian energy exports. Instead of reaching American ports, the tankers diverted to Brazil, one of the world's large diesel importers and a frequent buyer of discounted Russian fuel. The diversion raises questions about the terms, transparency and real purpose of the deal: whether it was a commercial arrangement, a political gesture, or a sanctions workaround that never functioned as announced. Brazil has become a major destination for Russian diesel since 2022, buying at a discount while Western buyers pulled back. The episode also illustrates how opaque the Trump-Putin economic channel remains, with headline agreements producing murky outcomes. For energy markets, the practical effect is limited — the diesel still found a buyer — but for the diplomacy, it underlines how little of the US-Russia understanding is visible or verifiable.

articles.title: Russia fires around 100 missiles and 400 drones at Ukraine overnight; one missile may have entered Polish airspace
articles.description: Russia launched one of its largest combined attacks of the war overnight into November 20, firing around 100 missiles — roughly 80 cruise and up to 20 ballistic — and about 400 drones at Ukraine, according to the Ukrainian Air Force. The main missile blow fell on western Ukraine and energy infrastructure, while ballistic missiles targeted Kyiv and its bridges. Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat said one cruise missile may have crossed into Polish airspace, prompting an air alert in the Lublin region. It matters because the scale and the possible Polish incursion raise the stakes for Ukraine's allies as well as for Kyiv.
articles.body: Russia launched a massive combined missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight into November 20, firing around 100 missiles and about 400 drones, Ukrainian Air Force spokesperson Yuriy Ihnat told the national telethon, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda. The barrage included roughly 80 cruise missiles and up to 20 ballistic missiles, plus around 400 drones, of which about 120 were jet-powered. Russia deployed strategic aviation — at least 12 Tu-95MS and Tu-160 bombers were airborne at once — and Black Sea Fleet ships launching Kh-101 and Kalibr cruise missiles. Missiles entered Ukrainian airspace from several directions, from the north and from the south through central regions. The main missile strike fell on western Ukraine, targeting energy facilities, while ballistic missiles were aimed primarily at Kyiv, Kyiv region and the capital's bridges. In Lviv region, drone debris fell near student dormitories of the Polytechnic university, damaging cars and windows, and two people were reported killed in the west. Ihnat also flagged a possible violation of Polish airspace: preliminary information suggests one Russian missile may have crossed the state border, and an air alert sounded in Lublin, in eastern Poland, with an explosion heard near the border. The attack is one of the largest of the war by missile count and comes days after Ukraine's strikes on the Crimean Bridge, in what Kyiv reads as retaliation. For Ukraine's partners, the possible Polish incursion is a reminder that Russia's war does not stay neatly inside Ukraine's borders.

articles.title: Frontline: 278 combat engagements in a day as Russia presses on multiple axes
articles.description: Ukraine's General Staff reported 278 combat engagements over the past day, with Russian forces launching 72 air strikes and dropping 236 guided aerial bombs. The Lyman direction saw 13 attacks and Sloviansk five, while fighting continues around Pokrovsk, Dobropillia and Kostiantynivka. Russian personnel losses for the day were estimated at 2,150, bringing the total since the full-scale invasion to about 1,633,130. The figures matter because they show the front remains intensely active even as diplomacy dominates the headlines.
articles.body: Ukraine's General Staff reported 278 combat engagements over the previous day in its morning update on November 20, a sharp rise from the 165 engagements reported on November 17. Russian forces carried out 72 air strikes and dropped 236 guided aerial bombs across the front, pressing on multiple axes at once. On the Lyman direction there were 13 attacks and on the Sloviansk direction five, while heavy fighting continues around Pokrovsk — long the hottest sector — as well as Dobropillia and Kostiantynivka, where Ukrainian forces are holding defensive lines. Russian claims about capturing settlements require verification against Ukrainian command data and independent observers, the morning review noted. The General Staff estimated Russian personnel losses for the day at 2,150, bringing cumulative Russian losses since February 2022 to about 1,633,130. The intensity of the fighting underlines that the diplomatic activity in Shenzhen and Berlin has not slowed the war on the ground: Russia is continuing offensive operations while simultaneously talking about peace. For Ukraine, the figures also frame the urgency of the air-defence debate — President Zelenskyy has called air defence the country's top priority and asked partners to supply interceptor missiles. The frontline picture is a reminder that any ceasefire discussion happens against a backdrop of daily assaults and heavy casualties on both sides.

articles.title: Coalition of the Willing pledges €90 billion from the EU and €70 billion in NATO military aid for Ukraine
articles.description: Following the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, the EU will provide Ukraine with €90 billion through the end of 2027, and NATO partners will supply €70 billion in military aid in 2026. The pledges were announced after the meeting attended by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The sums matter because they give Ukraine financial and military certainty into 2027 — and because they were agreed even as Washington questions further spending on military support.
articles.body: The Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin has produced major financial commitments for Ukraine: €90 billion from the European Union through the end of 2027, and €70 billion in military aid from NATO partners in 2026, Ukrainian media reported on November 20. The pledges follow the November 19 meeting in Berlin, where US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner sat down with the Ukrainian team and the European negotiating group to discuss security guarantees. President Zelenskyy had described the Berlin meeting as important in his evening address on November 18, saying Ukraine was preparing new support packages for defence and energy. The €90 billion EU figure builds on the European Commission's earlier proposal of a €45 billion loan for Ukraine for 2027, to be repaid from Russian assets — a plan now effectively doubled in scope. The commitments land against a complicated backdrop: Politico reported that Trump has questioned whether further spending on military support for Ukraine is worthwhile, while Kushner said the US had persuaded Russia to accept Article 5-style security guarantees. Zelenskyy has said Europeans will be included in negotiation formats with the Russians, and the Berlin pledges signal that Europe intends to underwrite Ukraine's defence regardless of Washington's wavering. For Kyiv, the money means it can plan its war effort and energy repairs into 2027 rather than living month to month.

articles.title: Emergency power outages in four regions and Kyiv after overnight strikes; Ukrenergo denies fake blackout claims
articles.description: Emergency power outages were introduced in four regions and in Kyiv on November 20 after Russia's overnight strikes on energy infrastructure, with hourly outage schedules also in effect in Lviv, Ivano-Frankivsk and Zakarpattia regions. Grid operator Ukrenergo denied Telegram claims that outages were being drastically tightened or that power 'might not return at all', calling the situation difficult but 'fully under control'. It matters because the energy grid is now a central battlefield as winter approaches, and disinformation about blackouts spreads as fast as the outages themselves.
articles.body: Emergency power outages were introduced in four regions of Ukraine and in Kyiv on November 20 after Russia's massive overnight attack on energy infrastructure, with hourly outage schedules also imposed in Lviv, Ivano-Frankivsk and Zakarpattia regions. In Lviv, hourly blackouts ran in blocks such as 10:30–14:00 and 21:00–00:00 depending on the queue, and emergency cut-offs can differ from the published schedules. Grid operator Ukrenergo issued a statement denying claims circulating on Telegram channels that outages were being sharply tightened and that electricity 'might not return at all' — claims falsely presented as the company's own position. Ukrenergo said the reports 'have nothing to do with reality', while acknowledging that the situation in the energy system is genuinely difficult after massive Russian attacks on generation, transmission and distribution facilities, though 'fully under control'. Hourly outage schedules remain in force in all regions except those under emergency cut-offs. The context is grim: Russia has launched more than 1,000 strikes on Ukraine's energy system since September, mostly against high-voltage substations, according to the Energy Ministry, and repairs are repeatedly undone by follow-up attacks. Kyiv region is accelerating construction of protective structures at priority substations, but as of mid-November they were only 55% ready. With winter approaching, the grid — and the information war around it — is becoming as important as the frontline.

articles.title: Russian intelligence is hunting Kyiv's cogeneration plants to strike them, officials warn
articles.description: Russian intelligence and sabotage services are trying to locate Kyiv's cogeneration plants so they can be struck or sabotaged, Ukrainian officials warned on November 20. The warning comes as Russia's overnight attacks already targeted energy infrastructure and bridges across the capital. It matters because cogeneration plants supply both electricity and heat to Kyiv — knocking them out in winter would leave hundreds of thousands cold as well as dark.
articles.body: Russian intelligence and sabotage services are trying to establish the locations of Kyiv's cogeneration facilities in order to strike them or stage sabotage, Ukrainian officials warned on November 20, as reported by Ukrainska Pravda. Cogeneration plants produce both electricity and heat, making them critical nodes in the capital's energy system — and high-value targets as winter sets in. The warning came on the same morning Russia launched its largest combined missile and drone attack in weeks, hitting Kyiv's bridges and energy infrastructure and killing three people. It also follows a pattern: Russian strikes have repeatedly hit energy facilities, with more than 1,000 attacks on the energy system since September, and repair crews have been targeted by repeat strikes. Ukrainian authorities have stepped up protection of energy sites, but Kyiv region's priority substations were only 55% protected as of mid-November, and officials acknowledge the grid cannot be fully shielded. The hunt for cogeneration plants suggests Russia is refining its targeting, seeking the facilities whose loss would hurt most — those that keep both the lights and the heating on. For Kyiv's residents, the warning is a reminder that the energy war is deliberate and systematic, aimed at making the city unlivable in winter rather than at any single military target.

articles.title: Neptune missiles played the key role in the latest Kerch Bridge strike, Ukrainian officials say
articles.description: Ukrainian Neptune missiles played the key role in the latest attack on the Kerch Bridge, Ukrainian officials said on the national telethon, adding a new detail to a strike already covered this week. The bridge was hit a third time in a week, with satellite images showing a collapsed span, and Putin acknowledged serious damage to the road section. The detail matters because it shows Ukraine's domestically produced missiles — not only Western-supplied weapons — are behind the campaign against Russia's most symbolic infrastructure.
articles.body: Ukrainian Neptune missiles played the key role in the latest attack on the Kerch Bridge, officials said on the national telethon 'Yedyni Novyny', as reported by Ukrainian media on November 20. The new detail adds to a story already covered this week: Ukraine struck the bridge three times in seven days, with satellite images published on November 19 showing a collapsed span, and Putin acknowledging serious damage to the road section. The Neptune is a Ukrainian-developed anti-ship cruise missile adapted for land attack, and its central role in the bridge campaign underlines how far Ukraine's domestic missile programme has come. Earlier reporting said the strikes also involved Ruta missiles, produced by a Swiss firm founded by a Russian-born entrepreneur, and the operation was carried out without Starlink, using Ukraine's own communications technology. The bridge, which links occupied Crimea to Russia, is both a military supply route and a prestige project for Putin, who has now said Moscow will not negotiate with Kyiv after the strikes. Ukraine has been explicit about why it is targeting the bridge: Zelenskyy has said destroying it is necessary to cut Russian logistics to Crimea and the southern front. The Neptune detail matters because it shows the campaign rests on Ukrainian industry, not only on allied supplies — and because it signals Kyiv can keep hitting the bridge as long as it chooses.

articles.title: How a Ukrainian surgeon is saving soldiers' arms with titanium implants
articles.description: Surgeon Yurii Lazarenko is saving Ukrainian soldiers' arms with titanium implants, treating patients at a hospital in Vinnytsia where surgical interventions have risen from up to 20 a week before the full-scale invasion to 25–30 a day. The implants let doctors restore limbs that might otherwise be amputated. The story matters as a rare piece of hopeful, human news from the war — medicine keeping pace with the battlefield's injuries.
articles.body: Surgeon Yurii Lazarenko is saving Ukrainian soldiers' arms with titanium implants, Ukrainska Pravda reported in a feature highlighted this week. Lazarenko treats soldiers at a hospital in Vinnytsia, where the number of surgical interventions has risen from up to 20 a week before the full-scale invasion to 25–30 a day — a measure of the war's human cost and of the medical system's adaptation. Titanium implants allow doctors to rebuild shattered bones and restore function to arms that might otherwise have to be amputated, giving wounded soldiers a chance to regain the use of a limb rather than losing it. The work sits at the intersection of battlefield medicine and advanced materials science: titanium is light, strong and biocompatible, and 3D-printed or custom-shaped implants can be fitted to the specific damage of each patient. The feature is part of a broader story about Ukraine's medical system, which has had to scale up trauma care enormously while under attack itself — hospitals have been struck, staff work through air raids, and rehabilitation demand keeps growing. For readers following the war through casualty figures and frontline maps, Lazarenko's work is a reminder of the individual recoveries behind the numbers: each implant is a soldier who keeps his arm, and each operation is a small act of repair in a war built on destruction.

articles.title: GTA VI revenue tops $2.3 billion, with $515 million spent on launch day alone
articles.description: Grand Theft Auto VI has now earned more than $2.3 billion, according to estimates from analytics firm Sensor Tower, with players spending about $515 million on launch day itself. The figure is a sharp jump from the $1.65 billion banked before release and confirms the game as the biggest entertainment launch in history. Rockstar's open-world blockbuster released worldwide on November 19 for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI keeps rewriting the record books: analytics firm Sensor Tower now estimates the game's revenue has passed $2.3 billion, with roughly $515 million of that spent by players on launch day alone. The new total is a major step up from the $1.65 billion in pre-orders and early sales reported just a day earlier, and it puts the game far ahead of any previous entertainment launch, including the biggest film openings. The surge came as the game finally reached players worldwide on November 19, after years of anticipation and a pre-order campaign that had already made it the most pre-ordered game ever tracked. Sensor Tower's tracker had shown pre-orders climbing steadily through the final week, with PlayStation accounting for about three-quarters of sales and Xbox the rest. Analysts had predicted the game could pass $2 billion in its opening weekend alone, and the launch-day spike suggests it may clear that bar even faster. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar's parent company, has not published its own sales figures, but it previously said pre-orders were running well ahead of expectations. Industry watchers now expect the game's first-week total to land somewhere between $3.3 and $5.2 billion, which would dwarf GTA V's $1 billion in three days back in 2013. The game remains console-only for now, with a PC version rumoured for early 2027.

articles.title: The Game Awards 2026 nominees are out — GTA VI leads the race for Game of the Year
articles.description: Geoff Keighley announced the nominees for The Game Awards 2026 on November 17, with Grand Theft Auto VI leading the field in total nominations. Six games will compete for Game of the Year: 007 First Light, Control Resonant, GTA VI, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil: Requiem and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The winners will be revealed at the ceremony in Los Angeles on December 10.
articles.body: The race for Game of the Year 2026 is officially on: host Geoff Keighley revealed the full list of nominees for The Game Awards during a livestream on November 17. Grand Theft Auto VI leads the pack in overall nominations, but it faces serious competition for the top prize from five other titles: 007 First Light, Control Resonant, Phantom Blade Zero, Resident Evil: Requiem and a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. The six-way field spans a James Bond origin story, a supernatural action sequel, Rockstar's record-breaking open world, a stylish Chinese action game, the next Resident Evil and Nintendo's beloved classic rebuilt for modern hardware. The nominees were chosen by a jury of more than 100 media outlets and influencers, and only games released by November 20, 2026 were eligible — which is why GTA VI, released November 19, just made the cut. Fans can vote for their favourites on The Game Awards website until December 9 at 6 PM Pacific, and the Players' Voice nominees will be announced separately on November 30. The ceremony itself takes place on December 10 at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. Other notable categories include Most Anticipated Game, where Fable, Final Fantasy VII: Revelation, God of War: Laufey, Resident Evil: Veronica and The Witcher 4 are nominated, and Best Independent Game, featuring Big Walk, Cairn, Denshattack, Mewgenics and Mina the Hollower.

articles.title: BioWare co-founder wants to save Mass Effect — and a KOTOR veteran is ready to join him
articles.description: BioWare co-founder Trent Oster says he is looking into ways to bring back the studio's franchises after Electronic Arts closed BioWare and cancelled the next Mass Effect game last month. Former BioWare creative director James Ohlen, who led design on Baldur's Gate and Knights of the Old Republic, has confirmed he would be interested in joining him. Acquiring the rights to the Mass Effect and Dragon Age franchises from EA is the key condition for any revival.
articles.body: The campaign to save Mass Effect has gained its most credible champions yet: BioWare co-founder Trent Oster says he is exploring ways to bring the studio's franchises back, and former BioWare creative director James Ohlen has confirmed he is interested in joining him. Oster, who co-founded BioWare in 1995, has been thinking aloud about what a revival could look like, and he named acquiring the rights to BioWare's intellectual property as the key condition for any such project. Ohlen, who was lead designer on Baldur's Gate and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and later co-founded Archetype Entertainment, is the kind of veteran whose involvement would give a rescue attempt real weight. Their comments come about a month after Electronic Arts announced on October 21 that it was closing BioWare after more than 30 years and cancelling the next Mass Effect game, as part of around 400 job losses across the company. The closure followed EA's $55 billion leveraged buyout backed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, and fans responded with the #SaveMassEffect movement: more than 300,000 people signed a petition, a banner truck circled EA's headquarters, and on November 13 fans sent a dozen N7 cupcakes to the company, echoing the 2012 cupcake protest that helped change Mass Effect 3's ending. Whether Oster can actually secure the rights and assemble a team of former developers remains unknown, and EA has said nothing about the future of the Mass Effect and Dragon Age names. But with a UK Parliament motion tabled on November 16 lamenting the closure, the pressure on EA is now coming from more than just fans.

articles.title: G-STAR 2026 opens in Busan with 1,237 companies — and Crimson Desert sweeps the Korea Game Awards
articles.description: South Korea's biggest gaming expo, G-STAR 2026, opened on November 19 in Busan, running through November 22 at the BEXCO exhibition centre with 1,237 companies from 41 countries taking part. The show opened with a headline win for Pearl Abyss: its open-world action game Crimson Desert took a record eight prizes at the Korea Game Awards 2026. Publishers are using the event to show off major upcoming releases, including Webzen's MMORPG MU Theos and Nexon's Temppal: Overgeared.
articles.body: G-STAR 2026, South Korea's largest gaming exhibition, opened on November 19 in the port city of Busan and runs through November 22 at the BEXCO convention centre. This year's show brings together 1,237 companies from 41 countries, making it one of the biggest editions of the event ever held. The opening day came with a headline result for the host country's industry: Pearl Abyss's open-world action game Crimson Desert won a record eight awards at the Korea Game Awards 2026, the prizes handed out alongside the expo. Exhibitors are using the four days to show playable builds and new trailers, with Webzen presenting a teaser for its MMORPG MU Theos and opening registration for a closed test of its tactical game Gate of Gates, while Nexon began pre-loading for its cross-platform MMORPG Temppal: Overgeared in South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macau. The expo is also a showcase for smaller studios: developers of the narrative adventure Goodbye Seoul showed a new trailer and confirmed an early 2027 release, and the Arctic survival simulator POLYARIS announced a full launch date of January 19, 2027. For the global industry, G-STAR has become one of the key late-year events, a place where Asian publishers set the agenda for the following year — and with GTA VI dominating headlines elsewhere, the Busan show is where the rest of the industry is making its case.

articles.title: The Wachowskis are trying to take back The Matrix
articles.description: Lana and Lilly Wachowski are trying to reclaim the rights to The Matrix, the franchise they created nearly three decades ago. The sisters are seeking to take back control of the series from Warner Bros., though the legal path to doing so is far from straightforward. The move comes as the franchise remains one of Warner Bros.' most valuable properties.
articles.body: Lana and Lilly Wachowski are trying to win back The Matrix. The sisters, who created the franchise nearly three decades ago, are seeking to reclaim the rights to the series they wrote and directed, in a move that would return one of the most influential science-fiction properties of all time to its creators. The Matrix debuted in 1999 and went on to spawn two sequels, a fourth film in 2021, animated anthologies, video games and comics, becoming one of Warner Bros.' most recognisable and valuable franchises. The rights situation is complicated: the Wachowskis created the films under contract with the studio, and reclaiming a franchise of this scale typically involves either a negotiated buyback, a reversion clause, or a legal challenge — none of which is simple or cheap. No details of the sisters' legal strategy have been made public, and Warner Bros. has not commented. The attempt fits a broader pattern of creators trying to regain control of landmark work decades after signing it away, and it lands at a moment when studios are leaning harder than ever on established franchises. For fans, the prospect of the Wachowskis steering The Matrix again — rather than the studio developing it without them — is the real story, even if the legal road ahead is long.

articles.title: Hacker claims to have leaked a near-complete build of GTA VI
articles.description: An anonymous hacker calling themselves Cyberleak claims to have published a nearly complete build of Grand Theft Auto VI, dated November 2026. The leak reportedly includes almost the full game, but is missing one important file. Rockstar Games has not commented on the claim.
articles.body: A hacker going by the name Cyberleak claims to have leaked a nearly complete build of Grand Theft Auto VI, just a day after the game's official release. According to reports, the anonymous hacker announced the publication of a full build of the game dated November 2026, though the package is said to be missing one important file. The claim has not been independently verified, and Rockstar Games has not commented on it. If genuine, the leak would be one of the most significant in gaming history, coming on top of the 2022 hack that exposed early GTA VI footage and led to the conviction of a teenage hacker in the UK. The timing is striking: the game only launched on November 19, and a leaked build would give pirates and dataminers access to the game's code far earlier than the usual cycle. It also raises questions about how a current build could circulate so soon after launch, and whether the missing file is a deliberate omission or a sign the leak is incomplete. Rockstar has historically moved quickly to have leaked material taken down, and a takedown effort is widely expected. For players, the practical advice is unchanged: unofficial builds can carry malware, and downloading them risks both security and legal trouble.

articles.title: The original Fallout is getting a fan-made HD remaster — first trailer shows modern lighting and weather
articles.description: A fan project is rebuilding the original 1997 Fallout in high definition, and the first trailer shows the classic post-apocalyptic RPG with modern lighting and weather effects. The remaster keeps the original game's isometric view and turn-based combat while overhauling the visuals. No release date has been announced.
articles.body: The original Fallout is getting a fan-made high-definition remaster, and the first trailer suggests it could be the definitive way to revisit the 1997 classic. The project rebuilds Interplay's post-apocalyptic RPG with modern lighting, weather effects and higher-resolution visuals, while keeping the isometric perspective, turn-based combat and story that made the original a landmark. The trailer shows the familiar wasteland — Vault 13, the Hub, the Brotherhood of Steel — rendered with a clarity the 1997 game could never manage, but without changing the look that fans remember. Fan remasters of classic games have become a fixture of the scene, filling gaps left by publishers that have not revisited their back catalogues, and Fallout is a natural candidate: the franchise is bigger than ever after the success of the Amazon TV series, yet the first two games remain awkward to play on modern systems. The project is unofficial, so it exists at the mercy of the rights holder — Bethesda has tolerated some fan projects and shut down others. For now, there is no release date, only the trailer and the promise of a faithful visual overhaul of one of the most influential RPGs ever made.

articles.title: Hours after Trump calls Putin 'tired' and ready for a deal, Russia hits Ukraine with massive strikes
articles.description: Russia launched a deadly missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight into Friday, just hours after Vladimir Putin met Donald Trump and Xi Jinping for historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen. Kyiv said Russia fired at least 110 missiles — an unusually large number — plus some 400 drones, killing eight people and injuring at least 28. The assault came after Trump told European leaders that Putin was 'tired' and ready for a peace deal.
articles.body: Moscow launched one of its largest aerial assaults of the war on Ukraine overnight into Friday, just hours after Russian President Vladimir Putin left China following a day of meetings in Shenzhen with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. Kyiv said Russia fired at least 110 missiles overnight — an unusually large number even amid Russia's frequent aerial assaults — along with some 400 drones, including 120 jet-powered drones that are essentially compact cruise missiles. Eight people were killed and at least 28 injured in an attack that lasted more than eight hours, according to Ukrainian authorities. Russia's defence ministry said it launched a 'massive strike using high-precision weapons from land, sea, and air,' targeting military and energy facilities, port infrastructure in the Odesa region and transport infrastructure in Kyiv. But President Volodymyr Zelensky said 'absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure — things that literally sustain people's lives,' including a hospital in Kharkiv and residential buildings in the Dnipropetrovsk, Lviv, Vinnytsia, Sumy and Chernihiv regions. Three of Kyiv's bridges were damaged, according to mayor Vitaly Klitschko, halting transport links between the two sides of the capital, and power was knocked out in several regions as temperatures begin to drop. The timing was pointed: Trump had spoken to European leaders after the Shenzhen talks and, according to a senior European official, described Putin as 'tired' and ready for a deal, urging allies to 'reach out and grasp at the opportunity.' The trilateral summit itself produced no breakthrough on Ukraine and no official declaration. The attack also followed Putin's vow of revenge for Ukraine's recent strikes on the Crimean Bridge, which Kyiv has now hit three times in a week.

articles.title: Drawing a line in the sand': Democrats put Trump administration on notice over alleged document destruction
articles.description: Democrats and the White House are already in a showdown over alleged document destruction — and the party hasn't even taken control of Congress yet. Democratic lawmakers have sent preservation letters across the federal government demanding officials save records and turn off auto-delete settings on encrypted messaging apps, warning that destroying records could mean prosecution for obstruction of Congress.
articles.body: Democrats and the White House are already in a showdown over alleged document destruction, and the party hasn't even taken control of Congress yet. Democratic lawmakers and investigators are increasingly concerned that the Trump administration is destroying documents and not adhering to preservation laws before Democrats take control of Congress after their November 3 election victory, setting off a flurry of letters across the federal government demanding officials properly save documents and turn off auto-delete settings on encrypted messaging applications. Democratic Representative Jamie Raskin, who is in line to chair the House Judiciary Committee, has sent preservation letters to the Department of Justice, the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Bureau of Prisons. Raskin raised particular concerns about the use of Signal by federal employees as a way to circumvent future Democratic oversight, noting that a Signal conversation between the FBI's general counsel and an associate of Donald Trump Jr. appeared to have been set for messages to auto-delete after a week. 'What I think you're seeing in Congress with these document preservation letters is Congress is drawing a line in the sand and maintaining a record so that if people do destroy records they could potentially be prosecuted in a future administration for obstruction of Congress,' Jim Secreto, who worked in the Obama White House Counsel's office on congressional investigations and compliance with the Presidential Records Act, told CNN. The letters are part of a broader Democratic effort to lay the groundwork for sweeping investigations into the Trump administration once the new Congress is seated.

articles.title: DHS pushes through billions for deportations and border projects as Democrats prepare oversight
articles.description: The Department of Homeland Security is rushing to lock in billions of dollars in contracts for deportation flights, border infrastructure and detention facilities before Democrats take control of Congress. In recent months DHS has awarded a nearly $1.3 billion contract for ICE deportation flights and at least $1.5 billion for border infrastructure. A CNN analysis found ICE and Customs and Border Protection signed new contracts worth over $41.7 billion in fiscal year 2026.
articles.body: The Department of Homeland Security is moving fast to lock in billions of dollars in spending on President Donald Trump's mass deportation agenda before Democrats take control of Congress and ramp up oversight. On a recent Tuesday afternoon, Deputy Homeland Security Secretary Troy Edgar stood before dozens of contractors and industry leaders and boasted of his department's multibillion-dollar budget, claiming it was bigger than that of American Airlines — a message, described by two people in attendance, that DHS was eager as ever to spend money to advance the president's deportation campaign promise. In recent months, DHS has awarded a nearly $1.3 billion contract for Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation flights, at least $1.5 billion for border infrastructure, a multimillion-dollar contract to transport ICE detainees, and nearly $13 million for a canine facility. A CNN analysis of government records found that in fiscal year 2026, which ran from October 2025 through September 2026, ICE and CBP signed new contracts valuing at over $41.7 billion — with the potential to increase to $63.7 billion. Democrats hope to build 'guardrails' around the spending once they hold the gavels, and the contract spree is already drawing scrutiny from lawmakers who say the administration is trying to entrench its immigration enforcement apparatus before oversight begins. The scale of the spending reflects how central mass deportation has become to the administration's agenda, and how much of it is now being carried out through private contractors rather than government employees.

articles.title: How two words could derail the world's biggest climate conference
articles.description: Deep divisions remain between countries at the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, as the talks grind into what is supposed to be their final day. The most contentious issue boils down to two words: fossil fuels. The first draft of the COP31 cover decision called for 'the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems' — language some countries are fighting to water down.
articles.body: Deep divisions remain between countries at the COP31 climate negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, as the talks grind into what is supposed to be their final day — and the most contentious issue boils down to two words: fossil fuels. The annual UN-led climate conference, believed to be the highest-attended COP yet, comes at a critical time for the planet, but it has been mired in conflict between countries pushing for ambitious action and those wanting to water down commitments. The first draft of the COP31 'cover decision' — the overarching agreement that sets out the conference's conclusions — was published on Monday and called for 'the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems.' That language has become the central battleground of the negotiations, with fossil-fuel-producing states and their allies resisting wording that would commit the world to moving away from oil, gas and coal. Finance and electrification are also on the table, with developing countries pressing for more funding to adapt to climate impacts and build clean energy systems. Negotiations will continue on Friday and potentially into the weekend if COP31 runs overtime, which these talks often do. The stakes are high: the cover decision is the document the world will read as the outcome of the summit, and whether it keeps the fossil-fuel language intact will signal whether the conference delivered real momentum or a watered-down compromise.

articles.title: My hometown voted Republican for 50 years. Then came an election shaped by economic frustration
articles.description: For the first time in more than 50 years, Colorado Springs — a longtime Republican stronghold — elected a Democrat to Congress. Jessica Killin won 50.5% of the vote, unseating Republican Jeff Crank, who received 45.8%. Cost-of-living concerns and an energy price shock after five-plus years of high inflation were front and centre on the campaign trail.
articles.body: Colorado Springs, a city that had voted Republican for half a century, has elected a Democrat to Congress for the first time in more than 50 years. Democrat Jessica Killin won 50.5% of the vote in Colorado's 5th District, unseating Republican Jeff Crank, who received 45.8%, in one of the most surprising results of the 2026 midterm elections. The outcome stunned even seasoned observers of Colorado politics: the district, home to a large military community and a deeply conservative political culture, had seemed safely Republican. But residents, like those in many other cities across the country, are enduring the financial gut punches that come with an energy price shock and five-plus years of high inflation, and cost-of-living concerns were front and centre on the campaign trail. Killin told CNN in an interview that affordability dominated her conversations with voters, and the result showed that Colorado Springs could become a politically purple city — or at least a maroon one. The race is a vivid illustration of how economic frustration reshaped the 2026 midterms, delivering a slew of unexpected outcomes across the nation, and it raises questions about whether other long-held Republican seats are more vulnerable than the parties assumed.

articles.title: Flooding submerges parts of Florida's Space Coast as storm threatens Thanksgiving travel
articles.description: Flooding has submerged parts of Florida's Space Coast as a developing storm batters the state, in a new chapter of the severe weather that has been slamming Florida this week. The storm is now threatening to snarl early Thanksgiving travel across the region. CNN video shows streets and neighbourhoods under water along the coast.
articles.body: Flooding has submerged parts of Florida's Space Coast, as a developing storm continues to batter the state in the run-up to the Thanksgiving holiday. CNN video from the coast shows streets and neighbourhoods under water, the latest impact from a storm system that has been bringing intense flooding to Florida this week. The storm is now threatening to snarl early Thanksgiving travel, with millions of Americans set to hit the roads and airports in the coming days. The Space Coast flooding follows days of heavy rain and storm surge along Florida's Atlantic coast, and forecasters are watching whether the system strengthens further as it moves. For residents, the flooding adds to a week of disruption, and for travellers it raises the prospect of delays and cancellations at one of the busiest travel periods of the year. Emergency services are monitoring the situation as water levels remain high in low-lying coastal areas.

articles.title: Elvis Presley rightsholders amend Suno lawsuit, adding more than 100 allegedly infringing AI tracks
articles.description: Elvis Presley Enterprises and fellow rightsholders have amended their lawsuit against AI music generator Suno, adding more than 100 allegedly infringing outputs just one week after filing. The amended complaint, filed November 13 in California federal court, now cites at least 58 outputs said to reproduce songs they control and at least 40 that use Presley's voice or likeness. It matters because the case is among the first to test Tennessee's ELVIS Act in federal court, and it keeps the pressure on Suno while the major labels' own Suno cases are also moving.
articles.body: Elvis Presley Enterprises, Authentic Brands Group and Raleigh Music Publishing have filed an amended complaint against AI music generator Suno, one week after first suing the company. The amended filing, made on Friday, November 13 in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, adds more than 100 Suno outputs the plaintiffs say infringe songs or imitate Presley's voice. It now cites at least 58 outputs said to reproduce songs they control, up from 17 in the original complaint, and at least 40 that use Presley's voice or likeness, up from 38. One newly added output, titled 'Recording session', allegedly infringes five songs in a single track: 'Can't Help Falling in Love', 'All Shook Up', 'If I Can Dream', 'Love Me Tender' and 'A Little Less Conversation'. The filing also adds at least 72 outputs tied to other songs Presley recorded that the plaintiffs do not own, and it takes aim at a statement Suno gave the press about the original suit, saying the examples reflect 'the same prompts that Suno publicly and falsely stated to Billboard do not exist'. The damages claim is unchanged at up to $128.85 million in statutory copyright damages across 859 songs, plus $23.62 million over alleged DMCA violations, while Elvis Presley Enterprises is separately seeking damages believed to exceed $50 million under Tennessee's ELVIS Act, which protects voice and likeness. None of the allegations has been tested in court, and Suno has not yet answered the amended complaint in this action. The case is being watched closely because it is among the first to put the ELVIS Act's tool provision before a federal court, and it lands alongside a wave of publisher suits against Suno and Anthropic that are all expanding at once.

articles.title: Quavo's 'Bubble Gum' copyright lawsuit moves toward a settlement
articles.description: A copyright lawsuit claiming Quavo's 'Bubble Gum' copied a demo handed over in 2016 is close to being settled, lawyers told a Los Angeles federal court this week. The notice, filed November 11, describes a 'settlement in principle' between Louisiana rapper Lamount London, who performs as L.Mont, and the defendants, with the parties expecting to wrap things up within 40 days. No terms have been shared, and the deal covers UMG Recordings, Universal Music-MGB NA and Warner-Tamerlane Publishing.
articles.body: A copyright fight over Quavo's 'Bubble Gum' that has dragged on for more than two years may finally be ending. Lawyers for Louisiana rapper Lamount London, who performs as L.Mont, told a Los Angeles federal court this week that the case is close to being resolved, as reported by Music Business Worldwide. London claims Quavo's track copied a demo he handed over in 2016. The notice, filed on November 11, describes a 'settlement in principle' between the parties, though nothing is final yet and no terms have been shared, including whether London gets paid. The parties expect to wrap things up within 40 days. The deal covers UMG Recordings, Universal Music-MGB NA and Warner-Tamerlane Publishing. The case is one of a cluster of demo-theft lawsuits that have been working through the courts, and MBW notes that two other cases in the same lane, one involving BTS and another tied to Drake's 'Janice STFU', were dropped in recent weeks. For artists and labels, the settlement track matters because demo-submission claims have become a recurring legal risk around hit songs, and a negotiated resolution avoids a trial over how a demo became a released record. If the settlement is completed as described, it will close the case without a court ruling on whether any copying took place.

articles.title: RAYE leads the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11 nods; Rosalía shortlisted in nine categories
articles.description: RAYE leads the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11 nods, the most of any artist this year, with Rosalía close behind on nine. The nominations, announced November 17, set up a wide-open race at the 2027 ceremony, where Beyoncé also made history as the first artist ever to reach 100 career nominations. For RAYE, the haul caps a remarkable rise from label disputes to one of pop's biggest stages.
articles.body: RAYE leads the 2027 Grammy nominations with 11 nods, more than any other artist, according to Music Business Worldwide's coverage of the nominations announced on Tuesday, November 17. Rosalía is shortlisted in nine categories, making the two of them the frontrunners heading into the 2027 ceremony. The nominations also produced a historic milestone for Beyoncé, who became the first artist ever to earn 100 Grammy nominations in her career. For RAYE, the leading tally is the latest chapter in a striking turnaround: the British singer-songwriter left her major-label deal after years of frustration, rebuilt her career independently, and has since become one of pop's most decorated live and recording acts. Rosalía's nine nominations underline her continued pull across Latin and global pop categories. The breadth of the nominations list reflects a year in which established superstars and fast-rising acts are competing directly across the general-field categories, and the 11-nod lead gives RAYE a strong platform going into awards season. The nominations arrive as the industry's biggest night continues to draw scrutiny over who gets recognized and who gets overlooked, with several high-profile snubs also reported this week.

articles.title: Reservoir expands its Suno and Anthropic suits, adding hundreds more allegedly infringed songs
articles.description: Publisher Reservoir has filed amended complaints in its cases against Suno and Anthropic, sharply expanding the number of songs at issue. The Suno case now covers 1,368 songs, up from 1,050, and the Anthropic case 1,143, up from 853 — a combined 2,511 works. The filings add new exhibits of alleged infringing AI outputs, including one tied to an Evanescence song, as the publisher cases against AI companies keep growing.
articles.body: Music publisher Reservoir has expanded its lawsuits against AI companies Suno and Anthropic, filing amended complaints on November 11, 2026 in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. Reservoir first sued the two companies on October 21, and the amended filings substantially widen both cases. The number of songs at issue against Suno has risen from 1,050 to 1,368, while the Anthropic case has grown from 853 to 1,143 songs, a combined total of 2,511 works, up from 1,903. The Suno complaint adds two exhibits that Reservoir says show 34 recorded examples of Suno outputs infringing its songs. The amended complaint also points to an Evanescence example that it says contradicts Suno's argument, made in a November 3 motion to dismiss a separate class action brought by Jason Isbell and three other musicians, that its outputs do not infringe. Both Suno's argument and Reservoir's allegation remain positions on paper until a court weighs them. The expansion mirrors moves by other rightsholders this month: Elvis Presley Enterprises has amended its own Suno suit to add more than 100 allegedly infringing outputs, and MBW reports that Round Hill Music has amended its Suno complaint to list 3,271 works. Taken together, the amended filings show the AI music litigation is escalating in scale rather than settling, with publishers using concrete output examples as their core evidence and AI companies arguing their tools do not copy. No court has yet ruled on the substance of any of these claims.

articles.title: Symphonic artists will not receive royalties from Roblox after all, MBW correction confirms
articles.description: Symphonic Distribution's deal putting hundreds of thousands of its songs inside Roblox will not pay artists royalties from the platform, Music Business Worldwide confirmed in a correction. The original announcement wrongly said royalties were included, and the corrected reporting states plainly that no per-play payouts flow to artists through the partnership. For independent artists, the deal is now a discovery play, not a revenue stream.
articles.body: Symphonic Distribution's partnership with Roblox, announced on November 12, 2026, will not pay royalties to the artists whose music is used inside the platform, Music Business Worldwide confirmed in a correction to its reporting. The original announcement said Symphonic artists would receive royalties from Roblox under the newly announced music partnership, but that claim came from an erroneous press release. MBW's corrected report, published November 14, explicitly states that Symphonic artists will not be paid royalties by Roblox through this partnership. Under the deal, hundreds of thousands of curated Symphonic recordings spanning Latin, hip-hop, pop, rock and electronic music are available inside Roblox games and virtual experiences, through the Roblox Creator Store and the Moments discovery tab, where game developers can preview tracks and drop them into games, jukeboxes and sound objects. The official Symphonic announcement published on November 16 focuses on exposure and music discovery, not per-play payouts. The correction matters because early coverage, including analysis that framed gaming platforms as a new streaming-style royalty surface, advised artists to treat the deal as income. Roblox has also partnered with Too Lost in July 2026, following an earlier DistroKid arrangement announced in 2024. For independent artists weighing whether to opt their catalogs into gaming platforms, the episode is a reminder to check the payment terms behind the discovery pitch.

articles.title: How 'GTA VI' got its Vice City sound: Trick Daddy, Trina and more
articles.description: With Grand Theft Auto VI out today, Rolling Stone looks at how Rockstar built the game's Vice City sound, from a 34-track companion album to a score by French duo Justice. Miami rap legends Trick Daddy and Trina host a new station, Dirty South Classics, while the album features Cardi B, Travis Scott, SZA and Tame Impala. Music has always been part of GTA's identity, and this time Rockstar has gone further than ever.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI arrived on November 19, and Rolling Stone's new piece digs into how Rockstar built the sound of its return to Vice City, the game's Miami-inspired setting. The game comes with a 34-track companion album, GTA VI: The Album, whose singles include Cardi B's 'Don't Chart' and Travis Scott's 'RHYNO', and Yung Lean's 'That's It' featuring Future and Metro Boomin. Grammy-winning French duo Justice composed the game's adaptive original score, with their single 'Flower in a Hurricane' featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard. For the in-game radio, Miami rap legends Trick Daddy and Trina host a new channel called Dirty South Classics, playing tracks including JT Money and Solé's 1999 hit 'Who Dat' and DJ Khaled's 2006 song 'Born-N-Raised', with verses from Trick Daddy, Rick Ross and Pitbull. Slip-N-Slide Records founder Ted Lucas helped curate the station. The game also weaves fictional music into its story: longtime friends Bae-Luxe and Roxy rap as Real Dimez after signing with a fictional label, Only Raw Records. 'Me and Trina been representing Miami and the South from day one, so being able to bring that same energy to Grand Theft Auto just makes sense,' Trick Daddy said in a statement. The six stations previewed so far make up only part of the lineup, with 22 radio stations in total reported across the game, including celebrity-hosted channels fronted by Keith Richards, Buddy Guy, Lindsey Buckingham, Michael McDonald and Slayer's Kerry King and Tom Araya. The official score album follows on December 11 with 30 tracks. For a game that has already banked more than $1.5 billion before launch, the music is both a selling point and a cultural event in its own right.

articles.title: Phoebe Bridgers rings in the holidays with an Adrianne Lenker cover
articles.description: Phoebe Bridgers has revived her annual holiday-cover tradition, releasing her take on Adrianne Lenker's 'Anything' on November 19. The lush rendition samples Lenker's own original recording, and all proceeds from both artists will go to the Palestine Children's Relief Fund. It is Bridgers' first holiday cover since boygenius honored Sinéad O'Connor in 2023.
articles.body: Phoebe Bridgers has brought back her annual tradition of releasing a Christmas charity cover, sharing her rendition of Adrianne Lenker's 'Anything' on November 19. The Big Thief singer's 2020 solo track gets a shimmering, faithful treatment from Bridgers, whose delicate vocals carry its Christmas Eve story of family tension: 'Christmas Eve with your mother and sis / Don't wanna fight but your mother insists.' The cover even samples Lenker's own original recording. Bridgers produced the track with Tony Berg, Ethan Gruska and Jack Antonoff, with acoustic guitar by Blake Mills and Will Maclellan, piano by Gruska and horns by CJ Camerieri. All proceeds from the single, from both Bridgers and Lenker, will benefit the Palestine Children's Relief Fund. It has been several years since Bridgers released a holiday cover: the last was in 2023, when boygenius honored Sinéad O'Connor with a rendition of 'The Parting Glass'. Before that she covered Tom Waits' 'Day After Tomorrow' in 2021, Merle Haggard's 'If We Make It Thru December' in 2020, Simon & Garfunkel's '7 O'Clock News/Silent Night' in 2019, McCarthy Trenching's 'Christmas Song' in 2018 and 'Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas' in 2017. The release lands as Bridgers tours her new album Lost Weekend, which was just nominated for Album of the Year at the Grammys, and after her November 14 performance on Saturday Night Live. She is currently on her Lost Tour and has just revealed 2027 dates.

articles.title: Rolling Stone UK Awards 2026: James Blunt takes the Icon Award as Wolf Alice, Blossoms and Holly Humberstone win big
articles.description: The fourth Rolling Stone UK Awards took place at London's Roundhouse on November 19, with James Blunt collecting the Icon Award and joking that he has gone from one-hit wonder to 'internet meme'. Wolf Alice won the Group Award, Blossoms took Live Act, Holly Humberstone won Song of the Year for 'To Love Somebody', and the War Child charity compilation HELP(2) won Album of the Year.
articles.body: The fourth Rolling Stone UK Awards night took place at London's Roundhouse on Thursday, November 19, handing out prizes across album, live, song and group categories. James Blunt collected the Icon Award, joking that he has gone from being labelled a one-hit wonder to becoming 'just an internet meme', and delivered one of the night's most entertaining speeches as he accepted the prize, presented in connection with Visit West Hollywood. Blunt, who recently fulfilled a tongue-in-cheek promise to adopt the name Ryan Bel Air after Airplane Mode reached number one, has enjoyed a career spanning more than two decades behind global hits including 'You're Beautiful'. Wolf Alice collected the Group Award, with vocalist Ellie Rowsell taking the trophy from Fearne Cotton, rounding out a strong year for the north London band. Blossoms won the Live Act Award, collecting the prize days before their first arena tour behind their sixth album, Songs from the Wedding Cake. Holly Humberstone won Song of the Year for 'To Love Somebody', taken from her 2026 album Cruel World. The Album Award went to HELP(2), the multi-artist War Child charity set featuring Fontaines D.C., Arctic Monkeys, Wolf Alice, The Last Dinner Party and others. British rap pioneer Giggs received the Trailblazer Award, Rachel Chinouriri was named Artist of the Year, and Saturday Night Live UK took the Television Award. Emerging talent was recognized too, with Madra Salach collecting the Breakthrough Award, Arjé Rayne receiving the Untapped Award and kwn crowned the Play Next winner. Hosted by Danny Dyer for a second consecutive year, the ceremony featured performances from Shygirl, Madra Salach and Arjé Rayne, while Jacob Lusk delivered a tribute to Freddie Mercury and George Michael.

articles.title: YouTube rejects the UK government's request to take down a Russell Brand video
articles.description: YouTube has rejected a request from the UK government to remove a video by Russell Brand, Rolling Stone reports. The refusal sets up a fresh clash between the platform and British authorities over how much power governments should have to order content removed. Brand remains a polarizing figure whose videos continue to draw large audiences despite the serious allegations against him.
articles.body: YouTube has rejected a request from the UK government to take down a video by Russell Brand, according to Rolling Stone. The decision puts the platform on a collision course with British authorities at a moment when governments in the UK and Europe are pressing tech companies to act faster on harmful and misleading content. Brand, the comedian and commentator, has remained a high-profile and polarizing figure online, and his videos continue to draw large audiences even as he faces serious allegations.
