YouTube's refusal to comply with the takedown request raises familiar questions about where the line sits between government pressure and platform independence, and about how consistently the company applies its own rules when the request comes from a state rather than from its own moderation systems. The UK government has been pushing platforms to take more responsibility for what circulates on their services, and a public refusal from YouTube is likely to feed into the wider debate over online safety law and enforcement. For creators and publishers, the episode is a reminder that takedown requests from governments do not automatically succeed, and that the biggest platforms are willing to push back when they judge a request to go beyond their policies.

articles.title: Mariah Carey's big Christmas hit gets released on tiny vinyl
articles.description: Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' is getting a tiny vinyl release, Rolling Stone reports, as the song begins its annual climb back up the charts. The novelty format is the latest way the 1994 classic keeps finding new audiences and new revenue three decades on. This week the track is already back at No. 18 on the Hot 100, with Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' at No. 14.
articles.body: Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' is getting released on tiny vinyl, Rolling Stone reports, as the 1994 classic begins its annual return to the charts. The miniature format is the latest novelty twist for a song that has become one of the most durable commercial assets in pop music, generating fresh sales and streams every holiday season more than three decades after its release. The timing is no accident: the Christmas chart season is already under way, with Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' at No. 14 on this week's Hot 100 and Carey's own hit back at No. 18, alongside a wave of seasonal re-entries including Bobby Helms' 'Jingle Bell Rock' and Brenda Lee's 'Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree'. Carey's song has now logged 22 weeks at No. 1 on the Hot 100 across its lifetime, a record for a holiday song, and its yearly return has become a fixture of the music calendar. Small-format and collectible vinyl has become a growth niche for labels looking to sell physical product to fans who already stream everything, and a miniature pressing of the most famous Christmas song of the modern era is an obvious fit. For Carey, whose holiday branding now spans the whole season, the tiny vinyl is one more way the song keeps earning long after most hits fade.

articles.title: Snoh Aalegra turned heartbreak into an LP with help from Stevie Wonder, Janet Jackson and more
articles.description: Snoh Aalegra has a new album shaped by heartbreak and built with an extraordinary cast of collaborators, including Stevie Wonder and Janet Jackson. Rolling Stone reports on how the Swedish-Iranian singer turned a painful period into a record, leaning on the guidance of artists she grew up admiring. The album continues her run as one of R&B's most refined voices.
articles.body: Snoh Aalegra has turned heartbreak into a new LP, and Rolling Stone reports that she made it with help from an extraordinary cast of collaborators, including Stevie Wonder and Janet Jackson. The Swedish-Iranian singer has built her reputation on refined, classicist R&B, and the new album draws directly on a painful personal period, reframing it through songs shaped with the guidance of artists she grew up admiring. Wonder's involvement brings one of the great songwriters of the last half-century into the room, while Jackson's presence connects the record to the lineage of pop and R&B royalty that has always informed Aalegra's sound. The piece traces how Aalegra worked through the material, leaning on collaboration rather than isolation to process the heartbreak at the record's center. For an artist whose previous albums earned her a devoted following and critical acclaim without chasing chart trends, the new LP is a statement of intent: a deeply personal record made with the help of legends. It also arrives at a moment when R&B's veteran voices are increasingly visible as mentors and collaborators for a younger generation, and Aalegra's album is one of the clearest examples of that exchange working on record.

articles.title: Pierce Brosnan welcomes Robert Pattinson into the James Bond role: 'Enjoy the ride'
articles.description: Former James Bond Pierce Brosnan has welcomed Robert Pattinson into the 007 role, telling him to 'enjoy the ride'. The passing of the torch between two Bonds comes as Amazon's Jeff Bezos confirmed he was personally involved in choosing Pattinson to play the spy. Brosnan played Bond in four films from 1995 to 2002.
articles.body: Pierce Brosnan has welcomed Robert Pattinson into the role of James Bond, telling the new 007 to 'enjoy the ride'. The message from one former Bond to the next is a classic piece of franchise ritual, and it lands as the casting of Pattinson continues to dominate film news. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos said this week that he personally helped choose Pattinson for the role, telling reporters there was 'something special about Rob' after the Amazon chief was closely involved in the casting process. Brosnan played Bond in four films, from GoldenEye in 1995 through Die Another Day in 2002, and his blessing carries weight with fans who still regard his era fondly. Pattinson, best known for Twilight, The Batman and a run of acclaimed arthouse roles, is a less conventional choice than some of the names floated for the part, and the casting has split opinion among Bond watchers. Brosnan's warm welcome is the kind of public endorsement that helps settle a new Bond in with the audience, following a tradition in which outgoing 007s publicly embrace their successors. With Amazon now steering the franchise, the Pattinson era is shaping up as the biggest test yet of Bond's future.

articles.title: Meet the 'GTA' fans spending thousands on the setups they wanted as kids
articles.description: For the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI, some fans are spending thousands of dollars on the gaming setups they dreamed about as kids, Rolling Stone reports. After 13 years waiting for a new GTA, players are marking the moment with high-end consoles, monitors and full battlestations. It is a sign of how much the game means to a generation that grew up with the series.
articles.body: Grand Theft Auto VI finally launched on November 19 after 13 years of waiting, and Rolling Stone reports that some fans are marking the occasion by spending thousands of dollars on the gaming setups they wanted as kids. For players who grew up with the series, the new game is not just a release but a milestone, and the launch has become an excuse to build the dream battlestation: high-end consoles, big monitors, new chairs, lighting and audio, all assembled for the return to Vice City. The piece captures a generation of players who first encountered GTA as teenagers, sometimes on a shared family television, and who now have the money to buy the setup they imagined back then. It is also a snapshot of the game's scale as a commercial event: GTA VI has already banked more than $1.5 billion before launch and drew a record 20 million pre-orders, and the hardware spending around it shows how the launch ripples beyond software sales. Retailers and console makers have been leaning into the moment, and the fans profiled treat the setup as part of the experience rather than an accessory to it. For Rockstar, the enthusiasm is the payoff for more than a decade of anticipation, and for players it is a chance to finally play the game the way they always pictured it.

articles.title: P1Harmony scores first Billboard No. 1 as 'BLOW UP' tops the Top Album Sales chart
articles.description: P1Harmony has earned the first No. 1 of its career on a Billboard chart, with mini album BLOW UP debuting atop the Top Album Sales ranking dated November 21. The six-member group sold about 43,000 copies in the US in the week ending November 12, after previous releases peaked at No. 2 on the sales chart. The album also debuts at No. 4 on the Billboard 200, matching the group's best-ever position.
articles.body: South Korean group P1Harmony has secured the first No. 1 position of its career on a Billboard chart, with its latest mini album BLOW UP debuting at the top of the Top Album Sales ranking dated November 21, Billboard reported on November 20. According to Luminate, BLOW UP sold approximately 43,000 copies in the United States during the tracking week ending November 12, making it the best-selling album of the week in pure sales. The achievement marks a new milestone for the six-member act, whose previous releases had reached as high as No. 2 on the sales chart. It is also the group's seventh top-10 entry on Top Album Sales. BLOW UP, the group's tenth mini album, arrived on November 6 and set a new first-week sales record for P1Harmony in South Korea. The album also debuts at No. 4 on the Billboard 200, matching the group's previous best position on the all-genre chart, set by UNIQUE in March. Its 45,000 equivalent album units were built almost entirely on sales, with 43,500 of them from album purchases and only about 1,500 from streaming, a sales-first profile powered by 25 CD variants and five vinyl variants full of photocards and posters. Elsewhere on the Top Album Sales top 10, Kings of Leon and Steven Wilson debut, while Vince Guaraldi Trio's A Charlie Brown Christmas soundtrack returns and Ariana Grande's Christmas & Chill reaches the top 10 for the first time after a new vinyl variant. The result underlines how K-pop acts continue to convert physical fandom into US chart success.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo holds off Lil Baby for a fifth week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 — by just 3,000 units
articles.description: Olivia Rodrigo's 'you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love' spends a fifth nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, edging Lil Baby's FRESH by only 3,000 equivalent album units. Rodrigo earned 62,000 units to Lil Baby's 59,000 in one of the closest chart races of the season. The five weeks tie her debut album Sour for her longest run at No. 1.
articles.body: Olivia Rodrigo's you seem pretty sad for a girl so in love notches a fifth nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 chart dated November 21, 2026, holding off major new releases from Lil Baby and P1Harmony in one of the closest chart races of the season. In the tracking week ending November 12, Rodrigo's album earned 62,000 equivalent album units in the United States, up 9% according to Luminate data reported by Billboard. Lil Baby's FRESH debuted at No. 2 with 59,000 units, just 3,000 behind, in a contest decided by the balance between streaming and sales. Lil Baby actually out-streamed Rodrigo, pulling 56.81 million on-demand streams to debut at No. 1 on Top Streaming Albums, but he sold only 4,000 albums to her 11,000, and sales put her over the top. Rodrigo's album sales jumped 53% on the week, lifting it from No. 11 to No. 5 on Top Album Sales. The five weeks at No. 1 tie 2021's Sour for Rodrigo's longest command of the chart, and among albums released in 2026 no one has spent longer at the top, passing Drake's four weeks with ICEMAN. FRESH, announced October 20 and released November 6, is Lil Baby's eighth top 10 album, and remarkably all eight have debuted inside the top five. Morgan Wallen's I'm the Problem holds at No. 3 with 50,000 units, while P1Harmony's BLOW UP enters at No. 4 with 45,000 units and Ella Langley's Dandelion slips to No. 5 on the same total. FRESH also gives Lil Baby his fifth No. 1 on the Top R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart, and its single 'Dead Fresh' reaches No. 1 on Hot Rap Songs. A sixth week at No. 1 would make Rodrigo's third album her biggest by that measure.

articles.title: Kings of Leon debut at No. 4 on Billboard's Top Rock chart with self-produced 'O My Beloved'
articles.description: Kings of Leon's tenth studio album, O My Beloved, debuts at No. 4 on Billboard's Top Rock & Alternative Albums chart dated November 21, the highest debut on the ranking this week. The album also becomes the band's sixth top-20 title on the Billboard 200. It is the first Kings of Leon record produced entirely by the four Followill brothers themselves.
articles.body: Kings of Leon will debut at No. 4 on Billboard's Top Rock & Alternative Albums chart dated November 21, 2026, with O My Beloved, the highest debut on the genre ranking this week. The placement also brings the band its sixth top-20 title on the Billboard 200. O My Beloved is the band's tenth studio album, released through Love Tap Records, and it marks the first time the four Followills, Caleb, Nathan, Jared and Matthew, have produced an entire studio album themselves. The album sold 11,000 copies in its first week, enough for a No. 6 debut on the Top Album Sales chart, and its arrival continues a chart career that has already produced No. 1 albums with Because of the Times, Only By The Night, Come Around Sundown, Walls and When You See Yourself. The record's writing centers on family, reflection and gratitude, according to the band, and the self-produced approach is a deliberate statement from a group more than two decades into its career. The debut shows the band's US audience is still there even as rock's chart presence has thinned, and it gives the Followills a new commercial marker to go with a record they made entirely on their own terms.

articles.title: Dominic Fike's 2018 song 'Babydoll' becomes his second Alternative Airplay No. 1 after a TikTok revival
articles.description: Dominic Fike's 'Babydoll', released in 2018 on a largely anonymous mixtape, has climbed to No. 1 on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart after a resurgence driven in part by TikTok. It is Fike's second No. 1 on the chart and his first since '3 Nights' in 2019. The eight-year-old song's second life is the latest example of TikTok rewriting chart history.
articles.body: Dominic Fike's 'Babydoll', released in 2018, has become the singer's second No. 1 on Billboard's Alternative Airplay chart, according to Billboard's chart highlights for the week dated November 21. The song's rise is a revival story: it first appeared on a largely anonymous mixtape eight years ago and has found a second life this year thanks in part to TikTok, where the track has been picked up by a new wave of listeners. It is Fike's first chart-topper on the Alternative Airplay ranking since '3 Nights' in 2019. The result is the latest in a long line of TikTok-driven resurrections, in which songs years removed from their release return to the charts on the strength of short-form video. Billboard's own chart data underlines the platform's power: TikTok says 94% of songs that entered the Billboard Global 200 in 2025 went viral on its platform first. For Fike, the No. 1 gives an old song a new commercial life and a new audience, and it shows that a track's chart story no longer ends in its release year. The song's climb also reflects how alternative radio has become receptive to catalog tracks that arrive with proven streaming momentum.

articles.title: ENHYPEN to close out 'The Sin' series with spinoff album 'The Sin: Parallel World' on Friday
articles.description: ENHYPEN will release a three-track spinoff album, 'The Sin: Parallel World', on Friday, closing out their 'Sin' series. It is the group's third new release this year, following the EPs 'The Sin: Vanish' and 'The Sin: Bliss', which each sold more than 2 million copies in their first week. ENHYPEN also just dropped the new single 'I Want You' to close the series.
articles.body: ENHYPEN will roll out a three-track spinoff album, 'The Sin: Parallel World', on Friday, according to Belift Lab, bringing the group's 'Sin' series to a close. The forthcoming single album is the third new work the group is putting out this year, following seventh EP 'The Sin: Vanish' and eighth EP 'The Sin: Bliss'. Both mini albums sold over 2 million copies in their first week, and each entered the Billboard 200, at No. 2 and No. 1 respectively. The new release will be the final installment of the 'Sin' series, which has anchored ENHYPEN's 2026. The group also just dropped the new single 'I Want You' to close out the series, as reported by Billboard. ENHYPEN remains one of K-pop's most reliable chart acts, and the rapid cadence of three releases in a single year shows how the group's label is keeping the momentum going between full album cycles. For fans, the spinoff is a short, focused coda to a year-long storyline, and for the charts it is another release likely to make an immediate impact on the Billboard 200 and World Albums rankings.

articles.title: Michael Bublé's 'Christmas' vaults 119–35 on the Billboard 200 as the holiday season takes over the charts
articles.description: Michael Bublé's 2011 album Christmas vaults from No. 119 to No. 35 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, the highest-charting seasonal album of the week. The jump leads a holiday takeover that also puts eight Christmas songs on the Hot 100, led by Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' at No. 14. The seasonal surge arrives earlier and stronger each year.
articles.body: Michael Bublé's Christmas, from 2011, vaults 119–35 on the Billboard 200 dated November 21, making it the highest-charting seasonal album of the week, according to Billboard's chart highlights. The leap of 84 places is the clearest sign yet that the holiday season has taken over the charts, with the album's annual return now a reliable fixture of the November rankings. The surge mirrors the Hot 100, where eight Christmas songs now chart, led by Wham!'s 'Last Christmas' at No. 14, up from No. 37, and Mariah Carey's 'All I Want for Christmas Is You' at No. 18, up from No. 39. Bobby Helms' 'Jingle Bell Rock' re-enters at No. 28, Brenda Lee's 'Rockin' Around the Christmas Tree' is back at No. 30, and Olivia Rodrigo's first holiday song, 'Take Me Home (4 Christmas)', debuts at No. 32. Ariana Grande's 'Santa Tell Me', Kelly Clarkson's 'Underneath the Tree' and Andy Williams' 'It's the Most Wonderful Time of the Year' are also back on the chart. Bublé's Christmas has become the definitive modern holiday album, returning to the top 40 every year without any new promotion, and its jump this week shows the seasonal catalog business at full strength. For labels, the holiday surge is now one of the most predictable revenue events of the year, and it arrives earlier each season.

articles.title: Would You Dissect a Human Body?
articles.author: Dhruv Khullar
articles.description: A physician visits a lab where yoga teachers and massage therapists — not medical students — cut into cadavers, and asks what the rest of us can learn from holding a human body in our hands.
articles.body:
Dhruv Khullar, a practising physician and New Yorker writer, visits the Institute for Anatomical Research, a lab where the people cutting into donated cadavers are not medical students but yoga teachers and massage therapists — practitioners whose work depends on understanding the body from the outside, and who have decided they need to see it from the inside. The teacher behind the lab is Gil Hedley, who wants to 'democratize knowledge of the body'. The piece opens with one of his students, Sundip Aujla, a London-based alternative-medicine practitioner with a long grey beard who has trained in osteopathy, psychotherapy, Pilates and clinical hypnotherapy over a thirteen-year career — and whose life was changed by Hedley's 'Integral Anatomy' dissection videos. As a teenager, Aujla was better acquainted with delinquency, once taking refuge from a gang of young men with knives.

Khullar's question is what draws people like Aujla to the dissection table, and what they take away from it. For doctors, cadaver dissection is a rite of passage, a first encounter with mortality that is also a lesson in detachment. For the lay practitioners in this lab, it is something else: a chance to ground years of hands-on work in the actual architecture of muscle, fascia and bone — to feel the structures they have only imagined through skin. The piece explores the strange intimacy of the work, the ethics of who gets access to the dead, and the way a body on a table changes how you think about the living bodies you treat. It is a quiet, curious piece about expertise: how much of what we call knowing is really touching, and what happens when people who were never supposed to hold a scalpel pick one up.

articles.title: Big Oil, Climate Change, and a 'Smoking Gun'
articles.author: Rebecca John
articles.description: A major investigation, in collaboration with DeSmog, into the documents showing Shell funded climate science for decades while funding denial — and the typhoon survivors now suing the company in London.
articles.body:
Rebecca John's investigation, published in collaboration with DeSmog, opens with Arnold Obguia, who did not leave his island when Typhoon Rai — known locally as Odette — approached the Philippines in December 2021. The forecast said it was no big deal, just another tropical storm. A few hours later the winds escalated to 121 miles per hour sustained, with gusts of up to 167, and waves so large they almost pulled him out to sea. Clinging to a piece of broken sea wall, he survived; his house was completely destroyed. Now Arnold and more than 100 other survivors of the typhoon are suing Shell in the English courts, alleging the company helped make the typhoon more destructive through its contribution to historic greenhouse gas emissions and its funding of climate denial — despite knowing since at least 1965 that burning fossil fuels was the primary cause of man-made climate change.

The investigation's centre is a set of documents preserved at the University of East Anglia, rescued from a dumpster where they had been thrown after the retirement of the Climatic Research Unit's first director, the pioneering climatologist Hubert Lamb. They show Shell playing a pivotal role in establishing the unit — the UK's first specialist climate research centre, opened in 1972 — with an initial contribution of £10,000, later increased to £20,000, and then paying the unit to carry out an in-depth 'North Sea Storms Study' from the mid-1970s. The study warned that storm frequency was likely increasing because of CO2 — evidence one expert calls a 'smoking gun', since it shows the company funding research into the very risks it would later spend decades denying. Shell executive R. O. Chalkley first contacted Lamb in September 1966 after reading his work on climatic variability. In other words, the company was funding serious climate science — including research into worsening storms — at the same time as it would later fund campaigns denying the science. The case, taken up by the British law firm Hausfeld, was filed in full in July, and a date for the first hearing at London's High Court is expected early next year. Shell has dismissed the lawsuit as 'baseless', saying the company had no 'unique knowledge about climate change' and that it does not believe litigation is the right response, and it did not respond to a request for comment about its historical climate research. If the survivors win, the case could open the door for other hard-hit communities around the world to sue fossil-fuel companies on their home turf.

articles.title: Is Air Travel Getting Less Safe?
articles.author: James Fallows
articles.description: A veteran pilot investigates whether America's aviation system — long the safest in the world — is quietly fracturing, just as a week of outages and a nationwide ground stop put the question on everyone's mind.
articles.body:
James Fallows, a veteran pilot and longtime aviation writer, argues that the US aviation safety system — which went nearly sixteen years without a major-airline fatal crash until the January 29, 2025 collision over the Potomac that killed 67 people — is now under enormous strain from understaffing, overcrowding and deregulation. His question is whether the safest system in the world is quietly fracturing.

Fallows traces the 'lessons written in blood' behind that safety record: the 1956 Grand Canyon collision and the 2009 Buffalo crash each produced reforms — new rules, new technology, new institutions — that made the next disaster less likely. He contrasts that history with the present, in which the Trump administration has dismantled advisory committees, fired FAA staff, and failed to implement a third of the NTSB's 33 recommendations issued after the Potomac collision. The numbers point the same way: serious runway incursions rose from 7 in 2024 to 14 in 2025, with 2026 on a similar path.

Fallows writes from inside the cockpit culture — the checklists, the discipline, the habit of treating every small failure as a warning — and his argument is that safety in aviation is not a single thing but a system, and systems fail the way they did this week: not all at once, but in a cascade of small breakdowns that suddenly add up. He is careful to say that flying remains statistically very safe. The piece is a warning, not an alarm: the record was built deliberately, and it can be dismantled just as deliberately.

articles.title: Beto O'Rourke Says He'd 'Do Anything' for James Talarico and Gina Hinojosa — Including Work for Them
articles.author: Joe Hagan
articles.description: After the Democrats' shock victories in Texas, a portrait of Beto O'Rourke's second act: the twice-defeated candidate quietly building the party's future from behind the scenes.
articles.body:
After the Democrats' 2026 midterm victories in Texas — James Talarico flipping a Senate seat against Ken Paxton and Gina Hinojosa winning the governor's race — it was hard not to look over the shoulders of the two winners and see the shadow of Beto O'Rourke, Joe Hagan writes. O'Rourke, who lost statewide races for Senate in 2018 and governor in 2022, stepped aside a year ago, concluding the moment needed 'something and someone new', and threw himself into organising through his voter-registration group Powered by People.

Hagan's piece is a portrait of a politician in his second act. O'Rourke convened Talarico, Colin Allred and Joaquin Castro about a statewide slate, endured Paxton's attempt to prosecute his PAC, and criticised Chuck Schumer as Senate leader. He says he would do anything for Talarico and Hinojosa, including working in their administrations, and he is focused on winning Texas's 40 electoral votes in 2028. The piece asks what that shift means for the Democratic Party in Texas, a state Democrats have dreamed of flipping for a generation and where last week's results finally gave them something real to build on — and what it means for O'Rourke himself, whether a man who was once the future of the party can be content being its scaffolding.

articles.title: The EPA's Chemical-Detecting Plane Isn't Doing Its Job Anymore
articles.author: Ames Alexander
articles.description: A short, sharp investigation into a federal plane built to sniff out toxic disasters — now flying fewer missions and unable to give responders real-time data, just as chemical emergencies multiply.
articles.body:
The Environmental Protection Agency owns a plane with a very specific job: fly to the scene of a toxic disaster, sniff the air, and tell emergency responders in real time what chemicals they are dealing with. Ames Alexander reports that the EPA's ASPECT chemical-sensing Cessna isn't doing its job anymore. Designed to respond around the clock to toxic emergencies, it has answered only seven emergencies since early 2021 — and it stayed on the ground during an ammonia leak in Weatherford, Oklahoma, a Valero refinery fire in Texas, and a fatal recycling-plant explosion in Toledo.

In June the EPA's inspector general found the plane could no longer identify airborne chemicals in real time, with manual analysis taking about a week — too slow to guide evacuations. Former staff trace the decline to lost personnel and institutional knowledge since 2019. The EPA blames ageing sensors and expects replacements by 2027, but five former programme staff say the new sensors are the wrong fix — a concern underscored by disputed ASPECT data after the Smitty's Supply explosion and the East Palestine derailment.

The piece is a case study in how quiet, technical capabilities erode. The plane was built for the moments when minutes matter — a train derailment, a factory fire, a chemical spill — when first responders need to know what is in the air before they send people in. Now the aircraft sits idle more often, its missions cut back, its data delayed. For anyone who has watched a chemical fire on the news and wondered how the people on the ground know what they are breathing, the answer is increasingly that they don't — or not fast enough.

articles.title: "AI DJs Completely Kill My Groove"
articles.author: Lauren Goode
articles.description: A first-person field test of the AI DJ features Spotify and YouTube Music are pushing into everyone's playlists — directly relevant to how music fans actually experience streaming now, and a cautionary tale about AI features that interrupt rather than enhance listening.
articles.body:
WIRED software reporter Lauren Goode, a self-described beta-feature enthusiast who uses YouTube Music as her main streaming service, tried living with the synthetic DJ hosts both YouTube Music and Spotify now build into their apps — and ended up turning both of them off. YouTube's version, called "Beyond the Beat" and available through YouTube Labs, randomly interrupts a queue for about 30 seconds between songs to explain the track, set up a vibe shift, and offer context. Spotify introduced its own AI DJ back in 2023 and expanded it in November 2026 with more host personalities and extra controls over the commentary.

The breaking point came during a pop-divas workout playlist. After a Slayyyter track, YouTube's AI DJ launched into a long, platitude-filled monologue about the next Charli XCX song — mispronouncing the artist's name as "Charli XXC" and offering generic commentary with no real substance. Goode's verdict is that the effect is closer to interruption than curation: stilted banter, confidently wrong song trivia, and filler words like "um" and "like" meant to sound human, all breaking the flow of the music the features are supposed to celebrate. Spotify's version fared no better in her testing, despite its head start and its November expansion to eight English-language voices.

The piece's larger point is about where generative AI is being bolted on. Both features remain optional betas that listeners can disable, and Goode argues that is exactly what most listeners will do: the synthetic hosts strip away the human nuance, serendipity, and cultural context that made radio DJs and human curators valuable in the first place, reducing songs to data points wrapped in awkward small talk. For anyone building or marketing music, it is a useful reality check on the gap between the demo promise of "AI curation" and what listeners actually tolerate.

articles.title: "They left the Kennedy Center to survive. It was an artistic rebirth."
articles.author: Philip Kennicott
articles.description: A vivid account of how the Washington National Opera rebuilt itself from zero after walking away from the Kennedy Center — and why the enforced exile produced better, bolder art. A strong arts-institution story with direct lessons for any independent arts organisation.
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's takeover of the Kennedy Center nearly destroyed the Washington National Opera. After Trump stacked the centre's board with loyalists, had himself appointed chairman in 2025, and then put his own name on the venue — a living memorial to John F. Kennedy — ticket sales fell, and the opera's board concluded there was no viable way to continue an association dating back to the centre's opening in 1971. In January 2026 the board voted to leave, and the company scrambled to finish the last two operas of the 2025–26 season at George Washington University's Lisner Auditorium in March.

The break was total. The opera had been affiliated with the Kennedy Center since 2011, and under that arrangement the centre provided all of its infrastructure — so when it declared independence in January it had no employees, no insurance, no bank accounts, and no infrastructure at all. It also lost the centre's $2.75 million annual subsidy. General director Timothy O'Leary describes it as a do-or-die situation: the company had to rebuild the entire institution while keeping the show going, and just eight weeks after declaring independence it staged a sold-out performance of Scott Joplin's Treemonisha, which the New York Times called a miracle. More than 3,000 donors from 47 states have since chipped in, including one anonymous $500,000 gift.

Now, Kennicott argues, the hardship has ignited a genuine artistic rebirth. The company has turned DAR Constitution Hall — Washington's largest concert hall, an acoustically problematic space never designed for theatre — into a dynamic contemporary opera house, decking over the main seating area and building a three-quarter thrust "Revolutionary Stage" ringed with café-style seating. Its fall residency there pairs a traditional but explosively powerful new Madama Butterfly (Nov 7–20) with a new staging of John Adams's Nixon in China (Nov 14–21), which Kennicott calls not only one of the greatest operas of the past century but an oracular vision of a world we are only beginning to inhabit. The 2026–27 season, its first as a fully independent company in its 70th anniversary year, runs five full-length productions across five venues — Constitution Hall, Arena Stage, Shakespeare Theatre Company's Harman Hall, Strathmore, and its own Takoma Park studio theatre — with 27 performances, down from 38 in 2024–25, but with more different works and star singers including Renée Fleming, Thomas Hampson, and Isabel Leonard. Kennicott's conclusion: the company is making art that outclasses and transcends the politics that displaced it.

articles.title: "The Radical Intimacies of Ryûsuke Hamaguchi"
articles.author: Justin Chang
articles.description: A rich, intimate profile of the Drive My Car director and his ambitious new three-hour film about caregiving, mortality, and radical empathy — part biography, part masterclass in how he makes actors and audiences truly pay attention to each other.
articles.body:
Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, 47, the Japanese director whose Drive My Car (2021) won the Oscar for Best International Feature and made him only the third Japanese filmmaker ever nominated for Best Director, has made a new film, All of a Sudden, that tackles caregiving, illness, and mortality head-on. The profile follows Chang's conversations with Hamaguchi in Tokyo and Cannes as the film — Japan's official Oscars submission for Best International Feature — heads for its US release. Its unusual source is a book of letters between philosopher Makiko Miyano, who had metastatic breast cancer, and medical anthropologist Maho Isono; the two women met in 2018, corresponded as Miyano's health declined, and the book was published in September 2019, a couple of months after Miyano's death.

Hamaguchi told Chang he was moved viscerally by the book but doubted it could be filmed, since so much of the correspondence was abstract — until the French company Cinéfrance Studios proposed a co-production. Working with French screenwriter Léa Le Dimna, he set the story at a nursing home in suburban Paris run by Marie-Lou Fontaine (Virginie Efira), and built the film around Humanitude, a real care methodology for vulnerable patients, especially those with dementia, that stresses relationship-centred, hands-on treatment: direct eye contact, calm encouraging speech, gentle touch, and standing upright. Marie-Lou wants her overworked staff to adopt it; they resist its time-consuming, touchy-feely demands. Her life changes when she meets Mari Morisaki (Tao Okamoto), a Japanese experimental theatre director with terminal cancer, and the two women's friendship — intellectual, emotional, and possibly romantic — becomes the film's centre, including a long overnight conversation along the Seine that Hamaguchi modelled on Éric Rohmer's My Night at Maud's.

The piece also traces Hamaguchi's formation: a chubby manga-and-movies kid who saw The NeverEnding Story as his first film in a theatre, tore through Spielberg and Cameron on VHS, then discovered Cassavetes (whose Husbands thrilled him with its rawness) and Rohmer at university; a failed attempt to enter Tokyo University's film programme, a thesis on Cassavetes, and film school at Tokyo University of the Arts, where a Kiyoshi Kurosawa class taught him that the camera is an acutely observant recording machine — "there is almost a documentary power to the camera in itself" — and his films have tried to "create the conditions" that fool it into documenting fiction. His rehearsal method, born from an actor's suggestion to read lines flatly and repeatedly until theatricality falls away, descends from Bresson. And the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, which struck while he was finishing his four-hour student film Intimacies, sent him to the devastated region to film survivors for a documentary trilogy — an experience that taught him documentaries have a fiction element too, and that being in front of the camera himself was the only fair way to film other people's hurt. The film's Cannes premiere in May ended with Efira and Okamoto sharing the Best Actress prize, and a Variety critic said it "achieves a kind of levitating grace." Hamaguchi's own coda is about burnout: the Drive My Car awards tour left him feeling he was "becoming a rather unpleasant person," shutting people out — and All of a Sudden, a story about caregivers whose will and resources are sapped by the system, is his way of reclaiming unhurried time and attention, for himself and for his characters.

articles.title: "A Star on Planet Earth" (Timothée Chalamet, Vanity Fair Holiday 2026 cover story)
articles.author: Mark Guiducci
articles.description: The Holiday 2026 cover story on the defining young movie star of the moment, built around a striking Iceland shoot and a candid conversation about Dune: Part Three, creative ambition, and the Knicks — a good culture read on fame, craft, and choosing the work over the persona.
articles.body:
Timothée Chalamet is Vanity Fair's Holiday 2026 cover star, photographed by Aidan Zamiri over three days in Iceland and interviewed by the magazine's global editorial director Mark Guiducci, following an October conversation between the two. Rather than a conventional celebrity portrait session, Chalamet helped shape the shoot as something closer to a film or music video, citing Terrence Malick's The Tree of Life as the biggest visual inspiration and saying the process of creating the images mattered almost as much as the photographs themselves.

The biggest professional subject is Dune: Part Three, which arrives in North American theatres and IMAX on December 18, 2026 (December 16 internationally) and concludes Denis Villeneuve's trilogy. The film picks up nearly two decades after Paul Atreides takes control of the Imperium; Paul is now an emperor confronting the consequences of his rule as political threats, betrayal, and personal conflict close in. Chalamet describes making it as more isolated and psychologically demanding than the earlier films: he studied historical leaders whose ambition curdled into destructiveness, researched megalomaniacs to understand Paul's rise, and even shaved his familiar curls for the role's increasingly austere turn. The through-line is Frank Herbert's Dune Messiah warning about charismatic leadership and cults of personality.

The conversation ranges well beyond the franchise. Chalamet talks about his devotion to the New York Knicks — he describes himself as living two lives, one as an actor and one as a Knicks fan, and says the team embodies New York's identity in a way that goes beyond sport — and about the films that shaped him: The Tree of Life, One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, Cloud Atlas, and the experimental documentary Koyaanisqatsi, choices that reveal a taste for work that experiments with structure, emotion, and scale. Directors who have worked with him weigh in too: Villeneuve speaks about his growing ambition, Greta Gerwig about an actor who needs creative freedom and room to keep a scene alive. Guiducci's portrait is of a star whose fame keeps growing while he stays guarded about his private life, letting the performances do the talking — from Call Me by Your Name and Lady Bird through Wonka, A Complete Unknown, and Marty Supreme (for which he was the Best Actor frontrunner at the March 2026 Oscars, losing to Michael B. Jordan for Sinners) — and who hints at a future collaboration with a prominent filmmaker he won't yet name.

articles.title: "Gracie Abrams: 'I Was Thrown Into the Deepest End Possible'" (The Rolling Stone Interview)
articles.author: Alex Morris
articles.description: A live, intimate Rolling Stone Interview with one of pop's defining young songwriters, recorded at New York's Cherry Lane Theatre — on her acting debut, getting offline, and the album that just gave her her first No. 1.
articles.body:
Last month Gracie Abrams joined Rolling Stone's residency at New York's historic Cherry Lane Theatre for a live edition of its deep-dive conversation series, The Rolling Stone Interview, speaking with Alex Morris. The conversation, published November 17, ranges across her acting debut, her relationship with being online, and why she can't wait to get back on the road. Her latest album, Daughter From Hell, is her most ambitious and musically varied offering to date — and a reflection of the perspective that comes from entering adulthood.

The album arrived in July 2026 and debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200, Abrams's first-ever chart-topping album, with 15 tracks produced with Aaron Dessner of The National, her longtime collaborator. Abrams describes the record as an exploration of what she calls the "in-between quality" of your twenties — "one foot in a past life and one foot in the future" — written after a quiet period following the end of her tour, when being in your twenties "can feel lonely in a new way and it can feel thrilling in a new way." Collaborators on the album include Justin Vernon (Bon Iver), her best friend and songwriting partner Audrey Hobert, and her partner Paul Mescal, who co-wrote the track "Imaginary Friend."

The interview's most quoted moment concerns the three months Abrams spent filming her first feature, Please, the latest film from Babygirl director Halina Reijn — she released the album the day before flying to Berlin to shoot it. "I was thrown into the deepest end possible," she says of the experience, "and then it felt weirdly more relaxing than a lot of other parts of my life have felt over the past few years. I think it was a relief to spend three months not thinking about myself and about presentation." Morris draws out Abrams's signature humour and her candour about the challenge of marketing herself, the pressure of constant self-presentation, and how she is trying to give herself some grace — the portrait of a 27-year-old who came up posting bedroom recordings online, opened Taylor Swift's Eras Tour, and is now deliberately stepping out of the pop-star frame to try something harder.

articles.title: "How a Bunch of YouTube Auteurs Are Reinventing Hollywood"
articles.description: The summer's two biggest box-office surprises were micro-budget horror films by twenty-something YouTubers — and Hollywood is now scouting YouTube for its next directors. A sharp, fun piece on how the creator economy is becoming the film industry's talent pipeline.
articles.body:
The mad scramble for Imax tickets to The Odyssey and the Marvel Cinematic Universe's resurgence with Spider-Man: Brand New Day were supposed to be the stories of the 2026 summer movie season. Instead, the biggest buzz belonged to two small-scale horror films from a couple of young YouTube auteurs. First came Obsession, from 27-year-old Curry Barker, which earned well over $150 million worldwide on a budget of less than $1 million. The film follows Bear, a meek young man who yearns for a romantic relationship with his friend Nikki and uses a magical object to make his wish come true; by turns moody, funny, and shocking, it proved audiences are hungry for something other than reheated IP. Barker got his start with the YouTube sketch-comedy channel That's a Bad Idea.

Then came Backrooms, from 21-year-old Kane Parsons, which earned over $120 million worldwide on a $10 million budget, surpassing Marty Supreme as A24's highest-grossing movie ever. Parsons gained a cult following as a teenager experimenting with visual effects and creepy atmospherics; a series of shorts he made in his teens culminated in the feature, which picks up the story of his earlier YouTube videos — themselves inspired by an old 4chan meme and internet folklore about haunted liminal spaces. It stars Chiwetel Ejiofor as Clark, a depressed divorcé running a failing furniture warehouse who stumbles through a wall into an apparently infinite maze of fluorescent-lit hallways. Critics have read it as a commentary on generative AI, which mindlessly reproduces and regurgitates its training data in permutations that don't make sense; Parsons has spoken out against AI several times since release, calling it "a symptom of a broader cultural and economic rot."

The article's argument is that this is a structural shift, not a fluke. Parsons told WIRED earlier in the year that YouTube is "the only viable avenue" for long-form filmmakers seeking mainstream respect — "I don't think there's a lot of Instagram filmmakers or a lot of TikTok filmmakers that go for long-form content in a way that would actually be looked at or respected as film" — and that among twentysomething directors entering the industry today, "it's very unlikely that you would have a filmmaker who is sort of reaching that place right now… who has not at some point in the last 20 years put stuff on YouTube." Studios have noticed: after a screening of Barker's Obsession at the 2025 Toronto International Film Festival, A24 and Neon entered a bidding war before Focus Features picked it up for roughly $15 million, and Netflix reportedly lost a bid to take it straight to streaming. The piece also name-checks Zach Cregger — sketch-comedy beginnings with The Whitest Kids U' Know, following 2025's Weapons with a 2026 Resident Evil adaptation — as part of the same wave. The conclusion: while Hollywood consolidation threatens to stifle creativity, a new wave of artists are betting on themselves, and some are winning. (Note: Wired's piece cites higher grosses — $500M+ and $400M — but other trackers, including Box Office Mojo, put the totals nearer $156M and $126M, so the lower figures are used here.)

articles.title: The Geo-Located Generation: What Nonstop Surveillance Is Doing to Children
articles.author: Sarah Zhang
articles.description: The Atlantic’s December cover story asks what happens to children — and their parents — when every step can be tracked, and it ends with a plea to let kids do things on their own again.
articles.body:
Sarah Zhang’s cover story for The Atlantic’s December issue starts from a simple observation: parents today can functionally track their children around the clock, from birth through adulthood, and most of them do. The tools start with products like the Snoo smart bassinet and Apple AirTags sewn into toddler backpacks, and they run through school portals, WhatsApp parent groups and location-sharing apps like Find My Friends and Life360. Zhang examines what this constant surveillance is doing to children — above all to their resilience and independence — and what it is doing to their parents, who are becoming more anxious even as they gain more information.

The piece is built around reporting and research rather than polemic. Zhang quotes a UK study that found the share of children aged seven and eight walking to school alone fell from 80 percent in 1971 to 6 percent in 2010, and she tells the story of a mother in a Facebook group for college parents who, seeing her daughter’s phone still in her room ten minutes before a maths test, typed: “Could someone ask their kid to go knock on her door?” Developmental psychology, Zhang writes, suggests that constant monitoring eventually becomes unhealthy for children, partly because they absorb the sense that danger lurks around every corner, and partly because they never get to solve problems on their own. Parents, too, are supposed to undergo their own transformation as children grow, relinquishing knowledge and control — and the apps make that relinquishing almost impossible.

The story’s centre of gravity is the work of psychologist Camilo Ortiz, who with a colleague invented “independence therapy”: for several weeks, anxious children do one new thing on their own every day, and their parents have to let them. One of the first participants was a nine-year-old girl who was afraid to sleep in her own bed; she chose to ride the city bus by herself, missed her stop, found a grown-up who helped her backtrack, and slept in her own bed that night for the first time. Zhang also gives generous space to Lenore Skenazy and the Let Grow movement, which she credits with a decade of arguing for childhood independence, and notes that thirteen US states have now passed reasonable-childhood-independence laws and more than a thousand schools have assigned the Let Grow Experience. The cover story ends with a plea: let kids start doing things on their own, and everyone is better off — the kids, the parents, the community.

articles.title: Venezuela’s Collaborator-in-Chief
articles.author: Jon Lee Anderson
articles.description: Jon Lee Anderson reports on Delcy Rodríguez and the new American imperialism in Venezuela — the most consequential piece in this week’s New Yorker on a story that is still unfolding.
articles.body:
Jon Lee Anderson’s piece in the November 23 issue of The New Yorker examines Venezuela through the figure of Delcy Rodríguez, the country’s leader in the aftermath of the American intervention, and asks what her rule reveals about a new American imperialism. Anderson is one of the magazine’s most experienced foreign correspondents, and the piece draws on his long reporting history in Latin America to place the current moment in a longer story of US involvement in the region.

The article sits alongside Anne Applebaum’s piece in The Atlantic’s December issue, “After the Apocalypse,” which covers how Venezuela struggles to recover and how the US is exploiting the country for oil and money — a sign of how central Venezuela has become to the foreign-policy debate. Anderson’s focus is on Rodríguez herself: how she governs, whom she relies on, and what her collaboration with Washington means for Venezuelans who lived through years of crisis under Maduro. The question at the heart of the piece is whether the new order is a genuine break with the past or a different kind of domination wearing a friendlier face.

For readers following the story, the piece is valuable because it goes beyond the headlines about oil and sanctions to the politics of collaboration itself: who benefits, who is sidelined, and what happens to a country when its future is negotiated between its own leaders and a foreign power. It is the kind of reported essay that The New Yorker does best — patient, sourced, and sceptical of easy narratives from any side.

articles.title: Why We Can’t Look Away from Medea
articles.author: Anahid Nersessian
articles.description: A sharp essay on Edith Hall’s new history of Medea — and on why, when a mother kills her children, we reach for diagnosis instead of tragedy.
articles.body:
Anahid Nersessian’s essay in the November 23 issue of The New Yorker takes Edith Hall’s new history of Medea as its starting point and asks a question that is really about us: when a mother kills her children, why do we reach for diagnosis, and what do we lose by doing so? Hall’s book gives Medea, the original murderous mother, what Nersessian calls the “girlboss treatment” — a reframing that makes the ancient figure newly legible to a contemporary audience. Nersessian’s interest is in what that reframing reveals and what it obscures.

The essay’s argument is that our therapeutic categories — trauma, pathology, disorder — obscure what the Greeks knew about tragedy and what we forget at our peril. Medea’s story is not a case study; it is a tragedy, and tragedy works by a different logic than diagnosis. It asks us to sit with actions that cannot be explained away, and with a figure whose motives remain partly opaque even to herself. To reduce her to a syndrome is to make her manageable, and to miss the point.

Nersessian writes as a critic who knows the classical material deeply and is impatient with both easy moralising and easy psychologising. The essay is a pleasure to read for its sentences alone, but its real value is the way it uses an ancient story to diagnose a modern habit: our preference for explanations that let us look away from the thing itself. It is the most literary piece in this week’s selection, and the one most likely to change how you think about a story you thought you knew.

articles.title: I Am a 2026 National Book Award Finalist. The U.S. Denied My Visa
articles.author: Abdelrahman ElGendy
articles.description: A National Book Award finalist writes about being denied a US visa days before the ceremony — a first-person account of what the new immigration politics feels like from the inside.
articles.body:
Abdelrahman ElGendy, an Egyptian writer and translator whose memoir Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming is a finalist for the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction, writes in The New Yorker about being denied a US visa days before the ceremony. ElGendy had hoped to travel to New York for the November 18 awards ceremony, where the winners are announced. Instead, after his application was placed in administrative processing, he learned that his visa had been denied, with no specific explanation given.

The essay’s power comes from the story behind it. ElGendy was seventeen when he was arrested at a demonstration in Cairo in 2013, two years after the January 25 revolution, and he spent six years as a political prisoner, writing his memoir steadily and smuggling the pages out one visit at a time. He fled Egypt, moved constantly between countries in search of a visa and a semblance of home, and in 2022 received a full ride to pursue an MFA in nonfiction at the University of Pittsburgh. He left the United States in 2025 amid concerns about immigration enforcement and the possibility of being returned to Egypt, where he feared further persecution.

At the visa interview, the consular officer nodded at the Penguin Random House letterhead and the printout of the National Book Foundation page, seemed reassured that his flights and accommodation were fully covered, and squinted and nodded at his European residence permit. Then came the line: “Unfortunately, I can’t decide on this application now. We have to consult Washington first, then get back to you.” The next morning he woke to a formal denial in his inbox. They would not put in writing what the system had flagged or the reason Washington provided overnight, only that he was found ineligible for a visitor visa under the Immigration and Nationality Act. It is a short essay, but it says more about the state of American openness than a shelf of policy papers — a writer who survived an Egyptian prison cannot get into the country to accept a literary prize.

opportunities.description: Six-week live-in, community-engaged residency Mar 14–Apr 24, 2027 on the theme of SERVICE, working with local partners (For All Seasons, Kent County Food Pantry, Sumner Hall). Three artists selected; $7,500 stipend plus up to $1,000 travel and $1,500 studio/gallery reimbursement, on-site housing.
opportunities.eligibility: Career artists based in the USA (international only with a US work visa); current degree candidates ineligible

opportunities.title: Jan van Eyck Academie Residency 2028

opportunities.price: ~€79 application fee; €2,750 enrolment fee after selection (both figures from secondary listings — not confirmed on official page)

opportunities.title: Turmhaus Residency, Balzers, Liechtenstein — for a Ukrainian artist
opportunities.organizer: Office for Cultural Affairs of the Principality of Liechtenstein, with Artist-Solidarity Program Europe (ASoP) and Office Ukraine

opportunities.eligibility: Individual Ukrainian artists in any discipline (visual arts, performance, literature, music, film, interdisciplinary); may be based in Ukraine or internationally; professional experience required

opportunities.title: Emmanuel College Artist-in-Residence 2027

opportunities.eligibility: Individual artists not currently enrolled in any academic program; one place each in Ceramics, Photography, Printmaking and Social Practice

opportunities.title: HMVC Gallery '2026' December Online Group Art Show
opportunities.description: Online group show Dec 1–31, 2026; all participating artists featured on website/virtual gallery, certificate of participation, and a video of all works screened on a Times Square jumbotron in December; Best of Show $150, Second Place $100, Third Place gets a one-month online solo show.
opportunities.eligibility: All artists internationally; works must have been made in 2026; all visual media except AI-created art and video/film
opportunities.price: $40 for the 1st image + $10 per additional image

opportunities.title: NODE Foundation WHATIF Residency
opportunities.description: Five-month digital-art residency at NODE Studio NYC (SoHo) to pursue one burning question through digital art and technology. $5,000/month stipend ($25,000 total), dedicated workspace, technical support, plus a paid visit to NODE's Palo Alto HQ (flights + lodging). Apply with a 5-minute video, written introduction/plan and portfolio link.
opportunities.eligibility: 18+; any discipline (artists, technologists, scientists, writers, researchers welcome — need not come from the art world). Must be based in New York and work in person at NODE Studio NYC, SoHo. No housing, relocation, transport, living expenses, health insurance or visa sponsorship. Individuals or collectives of up to 2 (one shared stipend).

opportunities.title: New Music Creator Fund 2027
opportunities.description: Project grants up to $5,000 (plus one $10,000 Musgrave grant) for individual music creators to develop new or existing projects. 2026 cycle distributed $216,500 across 64 grantees. Strong direct fit for Andrew as a NYC composer.
opportunities.eligibility: Individual US-based music creators (composers, improvisers, songwriter-performers) creating new original work. 2027 geographic focus includes New York State (plus Southern/Western states, US territories, Native nations). Full 2027 eligibility and amounts published Dec 7, 2026.

opportunities.eligibility: Composers of all ages and nationalities. New works for solo six-string classical guitar only.
